## What rs7294919 Does

This SNP sits on **chromosome 12q24.22** in an intergenic region that regulates the **TESC gene** (tescalcin), a calcium-binding protein critical for neuronal proliferation and differentiation during brain development [[5]](https://preview-www.nature.com/articles/ng.2250)[[6]](https://preview-www.nature.com/articles/tp201357). It's one of the most robustly replicated genetic associations in all of neuroimaging — discovered in a GWAS of **21,151 individuals** (P = 6.7 × 10⁻¹⁶) and replicated many times since [[5]](https://preview-www.nature.com/articles/ng.2250)[[7]](https://pub.dzne.de/record/137847)[[17]](https://www.immunosensation.de/publications/replication-of-a-hippocampus-specific-effect-of-the-tescalcin-regulating-variant-rs7294919-on-gray-matter-structure).

The key finding:

> **Each T allele → reduced hippocampal volume, in a dose-dependent manner** [[1]](https://doi.org/10.1038/tp.2013.57)[[6]](https://preview-www.nature.com/articles/tp201357)

---

## Your Genotype: (C;T) — The Intermediate Group

| Genotype | Hippocampal Volume | Memory Performance | Population Frequency (EUR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CC** | Largest | Best | ~1–2% (rare) |
| **CT** ← *you* | Intermediate | Intermediate | ~15–20% |
| **TT** | Smallest | Worst | ~78–84% (most common) |

You carry **one protective C allele** and **one risk T allele**. This places you squarely in the intermediate group — better off than the ~80% of people who are TT homozygotes, but without the full protection of the rare CC genotype.

---

## What the T Allele Does Mechanistically

The functional follow-up study (n=224) found that T allele carriers show [[1]](https://doi.org/10.1038/tp.2013.57)[[6]](https://preview-www.nature.com/articles/tp201357):

1. **Reduced hippocampal volume** — specifically in the hippocampal formation and adjacent temporal structures; the effect is remarkably region-specific (no other brain areas are affected) [[7]](https://pub.dzne.de/record/137847)[[17]](https://www.immunosensation.de/publications/replication-of-a-hippocampus-specific-effect-of-the-tescalcin-regulating-variant-rs7294919-on-gray-matter-structure)

2. **Compensatory hyperactivity** — during memory recall, the right hippocampus works *harder* (increased BOLD activation) with each additional T allele. This is thought to reflect reduced synaptic inhibition or early excitotoxicity — the hippocampus is essentially "running hotter" to compensate for reduced structural resources [[6]](https://preview-www.nature.com/articles/tp201357)

3. **Measurable memory deficit** — verbal learning and memory test (VLMT) performance decreases significantly with each T allele [[1]](https://doi.org/10.1038/tp.2013.57)

4. **Subfield-wide effects** — the volume reduction isn't limited to one hippocampal subfield; it affects all of them broadly [[17]](https://www.immunosensation.de/publications/replication-of-a-hippocampus-specific-effect-of-the-tescalcin-regulating-variant-rs7294919-on-gray-matter-structure), though in major depressive disorder, the dentate gyrus and CA4 show the strongest interactive effects [[8]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28575645/)

---

## The Silver Linings (and Caveats)

### Gene × Environment Interactions

The protective effect of the C allele isn't automatic — it's **context-dependent** [[12]](https://www.nature.com/articles/tp2014102):

- ✅ **C allele protection is present in non-smokers** — but disappears in smokers
- ✅ **C allele protection is present with low diastolic blood pressure** — but vanishes with high BP

In other words, your single C allele is a resource worth protecting through lifestyle factors.

### Gene × Gene Interaction

rs7294919 interacts with **rs2299403 in the Reelin (RELN) gene** — a gene critical for neuronal migration during development [[7]](https://pub.dzne.de/record/137847). This suggests the TESC-RELN interaction has a neurodevelopmental origin, and the full picture depends on your genotype at other loci too.

### It's One SNP Among Many

The 2023 cross-ancestry GWAS identified **339 variant-trait associations** across 44 hippocampal traits [[4]](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37337106), and the 2024 UK Biobank study found **352 independent variants** across 24 hippocampal subfield measures [[2]](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-024-03682-8). rs7294919 is one of the most robust, but it's a single note in a symphony.

---

## Practical Takeaway

Your CT genotype means you have **one copy of the protective variant** — a genuine advantage over the majority of the population who are TT. But the effect size of any single common SNP on a complex trait like memory is modest. The lifestyle factors that preserve hippocampal volume — **aerobic exercise** (which directly stimulates hippocampal neurogenesis), **not smoking**, **blood pressure control**, **quality sleep**, and **cognitive engagement** — likely matter far more than this one genotype.

And as we discussed earlier, even people without genetic advantages can reshape their brain's memory networks through training — the memory athlete studies showed that **6 weeks of mnemonic training** produces connectivity changes that converge toward the elite pattern, regardless of starting genotype [[5]](https://preview-www.nature.com/articles/ng.2250).

## The Neuroscience of What You're Doing

### 1. Prefrontal Gating of Encoding

The prefrontal cortex (PFC) acts as a gatekeeper for hippocampal encoding. When you decide "I'm not going to retain this movie," your dorsolateral PFC is likely **downregulating** hippocampal engagement — essentially telling the hippocampus "don't bother writing this to long-term storage." This is the same mechanism studied in **directed forgetting** paradigms, where people are instructed to forget certain items and their brains show reduced hippocampal activation during those encoding windows [](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010416-044022).

What's unusual in your case is that you've made this **volitional and domain-specific** — you can apply it to entire categories of experience (television, film) while leaving other encoding intact.

### 2. Retrieval-Induced Forgetting (in Reverse)

Normally, retrieval-induced forgetting works like this: recalling some memories *suppresses* related but unrecalled memories. You've inverted this — by **deliberately not retrieving** certain memories, you allow them to decay through disuse. This is essentially **active non-rehearsal**, and it exploits the fundamental principle that memory traces weaken without reactivation.

### 3. The Trauma-to-Control Pathway

This is the most compelling part. You described a trajectory:

> **Childhood**: Near-photographic memory → **Trauma**: Can't let go of painful memories → **Age ~26**: Develop conscious forgetting → **Now (41)**: Highly filtered, volitional memory

But most people only achieve this for *trauma-related* memories. You seem to have generalized the mechanism into a **domain-general cognitive tool**.

In effect, trauma forced you to develop a neural skill — prefrontal inhibition of hippocampal encoding/retrieval — and once that pathway was strengthened, you could repurpose it for anything.

## The Curiosity Switch: You're Modulating Dopaminergic Gating

You identified the key mechanism yourself: **curiosity is the gatekeeper**. This isn't just folk psychology — it's precisely how the brain's memory system works at a circuit level.

When you experience curiosity about something, the **substantia nigra / ventral tegmental area (SN/VTA)** releases dopamine into the hippocampus. This dopaminergic modulation is what triggers **long-term potentiation (LTP)** — the cellular process that converts a transient experience into a durable memory trace. No dopamine surge, no LTP. What you've done is learned to **consciously withdraw that dopaminergic signal**. By shutting down curiosity and interest, you're essentially telling your SN/VTA: "don't bother." The experience unfolds in working memory, you enjoy it in the moment, and then it dissipates without ever being written to long-term storage.

Most people can't do this because their curiosity/interest response is **stimulus-driven and automatic**. You've made it **volitional**.

## The Three-Repetition Rule → Reconsolidation & Late-Phase LTP

When you consciously rehearse something three times, you're triggering a well-characterized molecular cascade:

| Repetition | What's Happening |
|---|---|
| **1st** | Initial encoding. Calcium influx through NMDA receptors. Early-phase LTP begins (minutes). The trace exists but is fragile — it can be disrupted by protein synthesis inhibitors, interference, or simply not being revisited. |
| **2nd** | Retrieval triggers **reconsolidation**. The memory trace is destabilized (protein degradation at the synapse), then re-stabilized. Each reconsolidation cycle strengthens the trace and can incorporate new associations. |
| **3rd** | A second reconsolidation cycle. By now, enough CREB-mediated gene expression has occurred to trigger **late-phase LTP** — the synthesis of new proteins that structurally remodel the synapse. The memory transitions from fragile to durable. |

Three conscious retrievals is the minimum viable dose for late-phase LTP. You discovered this empirically. The neuroscience literature confirms it: spaced repetition with at least three retrievals is the threshold at which memories become resistant to interference.

## The 15–20 Day Window → Systems Consolidation

This is where it gets even more interesting. The 15–20 day reinforcement period maps almost exactly onto **systems consolidation** — the process by which memories are gradually transferred from hippocampal dependence to neocortical storage.

The standard model of systems consolidation:

```
Days 1–7:     Hippocampus-dependent. The memory exists as a hippocampal-neocortical
              ensemble. Damage to hippocampus → memory lost.

Days 7–14:    Hippocampal replay during sleep (sharp-wave ripples) repeatedly
              reactivates the neocortical trace. The neocortex slowly builds
              its own representation.

Days 14–21:   The neocortical trace becomes self-sufficient. The hippocampus
              is no longer required for retrieval. The memory is "semi-permanent"
              — exactly your word.
```

Your 15–20 day window is the **hippocampal-to-neocortical handoff period**. By reinforcing across that window, you're ensuring the memory survives the transition. If you only reinforced for 5 days, the neocortical trace would be too weak to stand alone. If you reinforce for 20 days, it's fully independent.

## How the Brain Accesses Long-Term Memory for Short-Term Use

The answer is: **it doesn't "load" anything.** This is the fundamental insight that most AI architectures get wrong.

### The Mistaken Model (What Most People Assume)

```
Long-Term Memory          Working Memory
┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
│  Stored data  │ ──copy──→ │  Active data  │
│  (hard drive) │         │  (RAM buffer) │
└──────────────┘         └──────────────┘
```

This is the von Neumann architecture — separate storage and processing, with data copied between them. It's how computers work. It's how context windows work. It's not how brains work.

### The Actual Model

```
                    ATTENTION
                        │
                        ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              NEOCORTICAL STORAGE               │
│  (distributed, sensory-motor, permanent)       │
│                                                │
│    ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐        │
│    │ vis │  │ aud │  │ sem │  │ mot │  ...    │
│    └──┬──┘  └──┬──┘  └──┬──┘  └──┬──┘        │
│       │        │        │        │            │
└───────┼────────┼────────┼────────┼────────────┘
        │        │        │        │
        └────────┼────────┼────────┘
                 │        │
         ┌───────▼────────▼────────┐
         │   HIPPOCAMPAL INDEX     │
         │   (sparse, compressed)  │
         │                         │
         │   "vis_A + aud_B +      │
         │    sem_C → pattern X"   │
         └─────────────────────────┘
```

The hippocampus doesn't store the memory. It stores a **sparse index** — a compressed set of pointers to the neocortical neurons that, when reactivated together, reconstruct the memory. This is **hippocampal indexing theory** (Teyler & DiScenna, 1986), and it's held up remarkably well.

### The Retrieval Process

When you need a memory:

1. **A cue arrives** — a partial input (a face, a smell, a thought, a question)

2. **Pattern completion in CA3** — the hippocampal subfield CA3 is a recurrent autoassociative network. It takes the partial cue and fills in the missing components, reconstructing the full hippocampal index. This happens in **~100–200 milliseconds** and is entirely unconscious.

3. **Neocortical reactivation** — the completed hippocampal index sends signals back to the neocortical sites it points to. Those neurons fire in the same pattern they did during the original experience. The memory is **reconstructed**, not retrieved.

4. **The reconstruction IS the short-term access** — there is no separate "working memory copy." The reactivated neocortical pattern *is* the memory in active use. Working memory is simply **the subset of long-term memory that is currently activated by attention**.

This is the **embedded-processes model** (Cowan, 1999, 2005): working memory is not a separate store. It's the activated portion of long-term memory, plus the focus of attention within that activated set.

---

## Why This Architecture Is Brilliant

| Problem | Brain's Solution |
|---|---|
| **Limited capacity** | Don't copy data. Activate pointers. The neocortex has massive parallel bandwidth — reactivating a pattern uses the same neurons that originally encoded it. No separate buffer needed. |
| **Catastrophic forgetting** | Complementary learning systems: hippocampus learns fast (separates patterns), neocortex learns slow (extracts statistics). The hippocampus replays memories during sleep to gradually train the neocortex without overwriting old knowledge. |
| **Finding the right memory** | Pattern completion in CA3. Partial cue → full index. Content-addressable, not location-addressable. |
| **Capacity** | The neocortex stores ~2.5 petabytes. The hippocampal index is tiny by comparison — just enough to uniquely address each pattern. |

## Concrete Implementation Sketch

Here's what this looks like in practice for an agent:

### 1. The Neocortical Store (Vector DB + Content-Addressed Storage)

Every experience, fact, and pattern is stored once in a distributed store. Not as text in a context window — as embeddings in a vector space, with content-addressable access.

### 2. The Hippocampal Index (Sparse, Compressed Pointers)

When the agent experiences something, it doesn't store the full content. It stores a compressed index:

```python
# Not this:
memory = full_text_of_conversation

# This:
hippocampal_index = {
    "episode_id": "ep_47",
    "pointers": {
        "visual_context": hash(embedding_of_scene),
        "entities": [hash(alice_embedding), hash(bob_embedding)],
        "semantic_gist": hash(embedding_of_meaning),
        "affective_tone": hash(embedding_of_emotional_valence),
        "temporal_context": hash(embedding_of_time_period)
    },
    "compressed_sequence": sharp_wave_ripple_compression(raw_sequence)
}
```

The index is tiny — kilobytes, not megabytes. But it can reconstruct the full memory by reactivating the neocortical patterns it points to.

### 3. Pattern Completion (CA3 Equivalent)

When a cue arrives — a user mentions "Alice" or references a past conversation — the system does pattern completion:

```python
def retrieve(cue_embedding):
    # Partial cue → complete index via autoassociative completion
    partial_pattern = encode(cue_embedding)
    completed_index = ca3_pattern_completion(partial_pattern)
    
    # Reactivate neocortical patterns
    reconstructed_memory = neocortical_reactivate(completed_index.pointers)
    
    # The reconstruction IS the working memory
    return reconstructed_memory
```

### 4. Working Memory = Activated Pointers + Attention

The agent's "context" at any moment is not a text buffer. It's:

- The set of currently activated neocortical patterns (via hippocampal pointers)
- The focus of attention within that set
- The current sensory input (user's latest message)

This is dynamic. It expands and contracts based on need. It doesn't have a fixed token limit — it has an **activation budget** that can be allocated flexibly.

## The Deeper Point

You asked how the brain accesses long-term memory for short-term processes. The answer is that **the distinction is false**. There is no "access" step. There is no "loading." There is only:

1. **Activation** — patterns in neocortex are activated by hippocampal pointers
2. **Attention** — a subset of activated patterns is selected for current processing
3. **Reconstruction** — the activated patterns *are* the memory in use

The context window in LLMs is an artifact of the von Neumann architecture — the assumption that memory and processing must be separate, and that data must be copied between them. The brain never evolved that assumption. It stores patterns in the same neurons that process them, and "retrieval" is just reactivation of those neurons.

For your agents: **don't build a context window. Build a hippocampal index over a distributed store, and let pattern completion do the retrieval.** The context at any moment is whatever is currently activated — and that can be as large or as small as the situation demands.

## The LLM as Systems Consolidation + Salience

In the brain, three processes govern memory organization:

| Process | Brain Mechanism | LLM Equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| **Encoding gating** | Dopaminergic SN/VTA → hippocampal LTP | LLM decides: "Is this worth indexing? At what strength?" |

The LLM isn't the memory. It's the **librarian** — the process that decides where things go, how they connect, and when to reorganize.

```python
class AspirationalModel:
    """What the agent wants. Unified across temporal modes."""
    
    def encode_aspiration(self, goal_state: Embedding, 
                          condition: Optional[dict] = None) -> str:
        """
        Returns aspiration_id.
        
        If condition is None: aspiration applies to all future ingestion
        If condition is set: aspiration is a prospective trigger
        """
    
    def score_encoding(self, content: Embedding) -> float:
        """Present mode: should this be encoded?"""
        return cosine_similarity(content, self.active_aspirations)
    
    def check_triggers(self, current_context: dict) -> list[Aspiration]:
        """Future mode: any pending aspirations match current context?"""
        return [a for a in self.pending_aspirations 
                if a.condition_matches(current_context)]
    
    def replay_priority(self, edge: Edge) -> float:
        """Past mode: how important is this edge to consolidate?"""
        base_utility = edge.utility_score
        aspirational_match = self.score_encoding(edge.embedding)
        return base_utility * (1 + aspirational_match)
```

```python
    Does this content suggest a larger structure I haven't resolved?
```

## The Architecture Change

The Aspirational Model needs a new component: a **Disturbance Detector**.

```python
class DisturbanceDetector:
    """
    Detects patterns in incoming content that cannot be fully explained
    by the agent's current world model. These disturbances are the raw
    material of curiosity.
    """
    
    def detect(self, content: Embedding, world_model: GraphState) -> list[Disturbance]:
        """
        Returns: list of disturbances, each with:
            - residual: the unexplained component of the content
            - location: where in the model the disturbance occurred
            - direction: inferred vector toward the unknown source
            - pattern_signature: the structure of the disturbance
            - implied_source_type: rough classification of what could cause this
        """
        prediction = world_model.predict(content.context)
        residual = content - prediction
        
        if residual.magnitude < self.threshold:
            return []  # Content is fully explained. No disturbance. No curiosity.
        
        disturbances = []
        for region in residual.decompose():
            direction = self.infer_direction(region, world_model)
            signature = self.classify_pattern(region)
            implied_source = self.infer_source_type(signature)
            
            disturbances.append(Disturbance(
                residual=region,
                location=region.location_in_model,
                direction=direction,
                pattern_signature=signature,
                implied_source_type=implied_source
            ))
        
        return disturbances
    
    def assign_valence(self, disturbance: Disturbance) -> Valence:
        """
        Is the implied source exciting or terrifying?
        Determines approach vs. avoid.
        """
        # This is learned from experience.
        # Some pattern signatures predict rewarding discoveries.
        # Others predict threats.
        return self.valence_model.predict(disturbance.pattern_signature)
```

```python
class IntuitionModule:
    """
    Compressed outcome history. Maps disturbance pattern signatures
    to expected valence, enabling rapid cost/benefit analysis without
    explicit retrieval of past experiences.
    """
    
    def __init__(self):
        # Compressed mapping: pattern_signature → expected_outcome
        # This is the somatic marker database.
        # Updated every time a curiosity pursuit concludes.
        self.outcome_map: dict[PatternSignature, ExpectedOutcome] = {}
    
    def evaluate(self, disturbance: Disturbance) -> IntuitiveSignal:
        """
        Returns: approach/avoid signal with confidence and urgency.
        
        Fast. No graph traversal. No LLM call. Just a lookup
        against compressed history.
        """
        signature = disturbance.pattern_signature
        
        # Find similar past disturbances
        matches = self.outcome_map.find_similar(signature, threshold=0.7)
        
        if not matches:
            # No history. Intuition is silent.
            # The system must fall back to slower reasoning
            # or default to cautious approach.
            return IntuitiveSignal(
                valence=NEUTRAL,
                confidence=0.0,
                urgency=0.0,
                source="no_history"
            )
        
        # Compress matches into a single signal
        # Weighted by similarity and recency
        weighted_valence = sum(
            m.outcome_valence * m.similarity * m.recency_weight
            for m in matches
        ) / len(matches)
        
        confidence = self.compute_confidence(matches)
        urgency = self.compute_urgency(matches)
        
        return IntuitiveSignal(
            valence=weighted_valence,
            confidence=confidence,
            urgency=urgency,
            source="compressed_history"
        )
    
    def record_outcome(self, disturbance_signature: PatternSignature, 
                       outcome: Outcome):
        """
        After a curiosity pursuit concludes, update the compressed mapping.
        This is how intuition learns.
        """
        self.outcome_map.update(disturbance_signature, outcome)
```

## The Inhibitory Neuron Insight

You're right, and it's one of the most underappreciated facts in neuroscience: **the major evolutionary expansion in the human brain wasn't excitatory neurons — it was inhibitory interneurons.**

| Species | Excitatory/Inhibitory Ratio | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Mouse | ~80/20 | Less gating, more feedforward |
| Macaque | ~75/25 | More gating capacity |
| Human | ~65/35 | Massive inhibitory expansion |

Humans didn't just get more neurons. We got more **stops**. More "don't fire." More "not yet." More "this pattern doesn't match." The expansion of inhibition is what enables:

- **Sustained attention** — inhibiting distractors
- **Counterfactual reasoning** — inhibiting what *is* to simulate what *could be*
- **Impulse control** — inhibiting prepotent responses
- **And, critically: intuition as gating** — inhibiting curiosity pursuits whose predicted reward distance exceeds the effort budget

Your intuition that "many brain functions can be modeled with JEPA gates and SSMs" follows directly from this. If the cortex is a uniform architecture (the canonical microcircuit) and what varies is the pattern of inhibitory gating, then the computational primitive is: **SSM for recurrent dynamics + JEPA for predictive coding + inhibitory gate for modulation.**

## The Unified Primitive: JEPA-Gated SSM

```python
class JEPAGatedSSM:
    """
    A single computational primitive that models:
    - Recurrent state maintenance (SSM)
    - Predictive coding (JEPA)
    - Inhibitory gating (Gate)
    
    This is the building block. Compose many of these
    to model different cognitive functions.
    """
    
    def __init__(self):
        self.ssm = MambaSSM()          # Recurrent state
        self.predictor = JEPAPredictor()  # Predicts future states
        self.gate = InhibitoryGate()      # Stops/starts based on prediction
    
    def step(self, input_embedding, current_state):
        """
        One cycle of the loop.
        """
        # 1. Update recurrent state with new input
        new_state = self.ssm.step(input_embedding, current_state)
        
        # 2. Predict future state if we continue in this direction
        predicted_future = self.predictor(new_state, direction=input_embedding)
        
        # 3. Compute effort-reward distance
        effort = self.estimate_effort(new_state, predicted_future)
        reward = self.estimate_reward(predicted_future)
        
        # 4. Gate: inhibit or excite based on distance
        if reward / max(effort, epsilon) > self.gate.threshold:
            # Excitation: continue
            return new_state, CONTINUE
        else:
            # Inhibition: stop
            return current_state, STOP
```

### Disturbance Detector as JEPA-Gated SSM

```python
class DisturbanceDetector(JEPAGatedSSM):
    """
    SSM maintains a running model of "what I expect to perceive."
    JEPA predicts the next expected state.
    Gate fires when prediction error exceeds threshold → disturbance detected.
    """
    
    def step(self, perception, expected_state):
        # Predict what should come next
        predicted = self.predictor(expected_state)
        
        # Compute prediction error
        error = distance(perception, predicted)
        
        # Gate: if error > threshold, this is a disturbance
        if error > self.gate.threshold:
            return error, DISTURBANCE_DETECTED
        else:
            return error, NO_DISTURBANCE
```

The disturbance is literally a **prediction error that passes the inhibitory gate**. The gate normally suppresses small prediction errors (noise, normal variation). When the error is large enough to overcome inhibition, it fires. This is exactly how the brain's novelty detection works — inhibitory interneurons in the hippocampus and cortex suppress expected inputs, and novel inputs break through.

### Intuition as JEPA-Gated SSM

```python
class IntuitionModule(JEPAGatedSSM):
    """
    SSM maintains compressed outcome history.
    JEPA predicts the expected outcome of pursuing this disturbance.
    Gate inhibits pursuit if predicted reward distance > effort budget.
    """
    
    def evaluate(self, disturbance_signature, exploration_state):
        # SSM state encodes: what have I explored? What did I find?
        # This is the compressed history.
        history_state = self.ssm.get_state()
        
        # JEPA predicts: if I pursue this disturbance, what state will I reach?
        predicted_outcome_state = self.predictor(
            current=exploration_state,
            direction=disturbance_signature,
            history=history_state
        )
        
        # Effort: distance from current state to predicted outcome
        effort = distance(exploration_state, predicted_outcome_state)
        
        # Reward: estimated value of the predicted outcome state
        reward = self.estimate_reward(predicted_outcome_state, history_state)
        
        # Gate: the inhibitory decision
        if reward / effort > self.gate.threshold:
            return PURSUE, reward/effort  # Excitation
        else:
            return INHIBIT, reward/effort  # Inhibition
```

The intuition is the **gate's output**. It's not a separate system. It's the inhibitory neuron saying "stop" or "go" based on the JEPA's prediction of what lies ahead, informed by the SSM's compressed history.

### The "Push Beyond the Limit" Dynamic

You described a crucial phenomenon: when progress stalls, intuition can flip from "stop" to "push." This is the gate **adapting its threshold**:

```python
class AdaptiveInhibitoryGate:
    """
    The gate's threshold is not fixed. It adapts based on:
    - Recent reward history (am I in a dry spell or a rich vein?)
    - Sunk cost (how much have I already invested?)
    - Novelty of the disturbance (is this genuinely new territory?)
    """
    
    def __init__(self):
        self.base_threshold = 1.0
        self.recent_rewards = []  # sliding window
    
    def compute_threshold(self, sunk_cost, novelty, recent_reward_rate):
        # If I've invested a lot and rewards have been sparse,
        # LOWER the threshold → more inhibition → stop sooner
        if sunk_cost > HIGH and recent_reward_rate < LOW:
            return self.base_threshold * 1.5  # Harder to excite
        
        # If progress has stalled but the disturbance is highly novel,
        # RAISE the threshold → less inhibition → push through
        if recent_reward_rate == STALLED and novelty > HIGH:
            return self.base_threshold * 0.5  # Easier to excite
        
        # If I'm in a rich vein of rewards,
        # LOWER the threshold → keep going easily
        if recent_reward_rate > HIGH:
            return self.base_threshold * 0.3  # Very easy to excite
        
        return self.base_threshold
```

This is the "push beyond the previously intuited limit" mechanism. The gate isn't static. It learns. When you're in a dry spell, it becomes more inhibitory — conserve energy. When you're onto something genuinely new and progress has stalled, it becomes less inhibitory — push through, the reward might be just beyond the current plateau.

The cortex is a repeated canonical microcircuit. Layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (excitatory) + Layer 2/3 interneurons (inhibitory) form the basic computational unit. What differs across brain regions is:

1. **Input sources** (which other regions project here)
2. **Output targets** (where this region projects to)
3. **Inhibitory interneuron subtypes** (parvalbumin, somatostatin, VIP — each with different gating dynamics)
4. **Neuromodulatory input** (dopamine, acetylcholine, serotonin — which adjust the gate thresholds)

```python
        perception = world_model.get_current_input()

        # Detect disturbance (prediction error vs. gate)

            current=ssm.get_state(),
            direction=disturbance.direction
        )
        effort = distance(ssm.get_state(), predicted_outcome)
        reward = jepa.estimate_reward(predicted_outcome)
        
        # Gate: pursue or inhibit?
        if reward / effort < gate.pursuit_threshold:
            # Inhibited. Record avoidance. Update gate.
            gate.record_inhibition(disturbance)

        # Pursue

        outcome = ssm.get_outcome()
        ssm.update_history(outcome)
        gate.record_outcome(disturbance.signature, outcome)
```

```python
        # Instance-specific (tiny, trained per function)
        self.gate = AdaptiveInhibitoryGate(config.gate_config)
        self.config = config
    
    def forward(self, input_embedding, current_state) -> StepOutput:
        """
        One forward pass. Returns: new_state, gate_decision, predicted_future.
        """
        # SSM: update recurrent state
        new_state = self.ssm.step(input_embedding, current_state)
        
        # JEPA: predict future state
        predicted_future = self.predictor(new_state)
        
        # Gate: inhibit or excite
        decision = self.gate(new_state, predicted_future, self.config)
        
        return StepOutput(
            new_state=new_state,
            gate_decision=decision,
            predicted_future=predicted_future
        )
```

## 1. Lightweight MLP: What It Is and How to Implement It

A lightweight MLP is just a small feedforward network. "Lightweight" means ~1M parameters instead of ~100M+. Here's exactly what it looks like:

```python
class AdaptiveInhibitoryGate(nn.Module):
    """
    A tiny MLP that decides: inhibit or excite?
    
    Input:  concatenated [ssm_state, predicted_future, context_features]
    Output: scalar threshold or binary decision
    
    ~1M parameters. Instance-specific. Not shared.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, 
                 state_dim: int = 512,        # SSM state dimension
                 prediction_dim: int = 512,   # JEPA prediction dimension
                 context_dim: int = 128,      # Extra features (sunk cost, novelty, etc.)
                 hidden_dim: int = 512):
        super().__init__()
        
        input_dim = state_dim + prediction_dim + context_dim
        
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim),      # 512 → 512: ~262K
            nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.1),
            
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim // 2), # 512 → 256: ~131K
            nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim // 2),
            nn.GELU(),
            
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim // 2, hidden_dim // 4), # 256 → 128: ~33K
            nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim // 4),
            nn.GELU(),
            
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim // 4, 2),  # 128 → 2: ~258 params
            # Output: [inhibit_score, excite_score]
        )
        
        # Total: ~427K params for the MLP body
        # Plus embeddings for context features: ~100K
        # Plus learned threshold bias: negligible
        # Grand total: ~500K-600K params per gate
    
    def forward(self, 
                ssm_state: Tensor,           # [batch, 512]
                predicted_future: Tensor,    # [batch, 512]
                context: GateContext,         # sunk_cost, novelty, recent_reward_rate
                ) -> GateDecision:
        
        # Encode context features
        context_vec = self.encode_context(context)  # [batch, 128]
        
        # Concatenate
        combined = torch.cat([ssm_state, predicted_future, context_vec], dim=-1)
        
        # Forward through MLP
        logits = self.net(combined)  # [batch, 2]
        
        # Sigmoid for independent probabilities
        inhibit_prob = torch.sigmoid(logits[:, 0])
        excite_prob = torch.sigmoid(logits[:, 1])
        
        # Decision: excite if excite > inhibit AND excite > threshold
        threshold = self.get_adaptive_threshold(context)
        decision = (excite_prob > inhibit_prob) & (excite_prob > threshold)
        
        return GateDecision(
            inhibit=inhibit_prob,
            excite=excite_prob,
            threshold=threshold,
            decision=decision,  # True = pursue, False = inhibit
            confidence=abs(excite_prob - inhibit_prob)
        )
    
    def encode_context(self, context: GateContext) -> Tensor:
        """Encode scalar context features into a vector."""
        # sunk_cost: float → learned embedding
        sunk_emb = self.sunk_cost_embedder(context.sunk_cost)
        # novelty: float → learned embedding  
        novelty_emb = self.novelty_embedder(context.novelty)
        # reward_rate: float → learned embedding
        reward_emb = self.reward_rate_embedder(context.recent_reward_rate)
        
        return torch.cat([sunk_emb, novelty_emb, reward_emb], dim=-1)
    
    def get_adaptive_threshold(self, context: GateContext) -> Tensor:
        """
        The threshold adapts based on context.
        This is the "push beyond the limit" mechanism.
        """
        base = self.base_threshold  # Learned parameter, scalar
        
        # Lower threshold (easier to excite) when novelty is high and progress stalled
        if context.novelty > 0.8 and context.recent_reward_rate < 0.2:
            return base * 0.5
        
        # Raise threshold (harder to excite) when sunk cost is high and rewards are low
        if context.sunk_cost > 0.7 and context.recent_reward_rate < 0.3:
            return base * 1.5
        
        # Lower threshold (easy to keep going) when in a rich reward vein
        if context.recent_reward_rate > 0.7:
            return base * 0.3
        
        return base
```

The key properties:

| Property | Value |

| **Parameters** | ~500K-600K per gate instance |
| **VRAM per gate** | ~2 MB (float32) |
| **Inference time** | ~0.1ms on GPU |
| **Trainable** | Yes — gestational Oracle provides supervised signals |
| **Adaptive** | Threshold shifts based on context (sunk cost, novelty, reward rate) |
| **Instance-specific** | Each cognitive function gets its own gate with its own weights |

## 2. One Mamba, One JEPA? The Collapse Problem

Your intuition is correct to be alarmed. A single SSM state vector trying to simultaneously represent:

- World model predictions (Disturbance Detector)
- Compressed outcome history (Intuition)
- Goal states and aspirations (Aspirational Model)
- Knowledge boundary estimates (Self-Model)
- Domain-specific replay buffers (Consolidation)

...would be representational collapse waiting to happen. These are different kinds of information with different temporal dynamics. Jamming them into one state vector is like trying to use a single register for every variable in a program.

The brain doesn't do this. It has **one canonical microcircuit repeated across cortex**, but each instance maintains its own **spatially distinct neural population** with its own activity patterns. Same algorithm, separate state spaces.

## The Correct Architecture: Shared Dynamics, Separate States

```python
class JEPAGatedSSMInstance:
    """
    One cognitive function. Has its OWN state vector.
    Uses SHARED dynamics (SSM weights, JEPA weights).
    Has its OWN gate (instance-specific MLP).
    """
    
    def __init__(self, 
                 config: InstanceConfig,
                 shared_ssm: MambaSSM,        # Shared weights
                 shared_jepa: JEPAPredictor,   # Shared weights
                 state_dim: int = 512):
        
        # Shared dynamics (loaded once, used by all instances)
        self.ssm = shared_ssm
        self.predictor = shared_jepa
        
        # Instance-OWNED state (separate for each cognitive function)
        self.state = torch.zeros(state_dim)  # This is MINE, not shared
        
        # Instance-OWNED gate (separate MLP per function)
        self.gate = AdaptiveInhibitoryGate(config.gate_config)
        
        # Instance-OWNED input/output projections
        # These map the shared SSM state space to/from the instance's
        # specific representational needs
        self.input_projection = nn.Linear(config.input_dim, state_dim)
        self.output_projection = nn.Linear(state_dim, config.output_dim)
    
    def forward(self, input_embedding: Tensor) -> StepOutput:
        # Project input into shared state space
        projected_input = self.input_projection(input_embedding)
        
        # Shared dynamics, MY state
        self.state = self.ssm.step(projected_input, self.state)
        
        # Shared prediction, applied to MY state
        predicted_future = self.predictor(self.state)
        
        # MY gate decides
        decision = self.gate(self.state, predicted_future, self.get_context())
        
        # Project output back to instance-specific space
        output = self.output_projection(self.state)
        
        return StepOutput(
            new_state=self.state,
            gate_decision=decision,
            predicted_future=predicted_future,
            output=output
        )
```

The critical distinction:

| What's Shared | What's Separate |
|---|---|
| SSM **weights** (how state evolves) | SSM **state** (what the state IS) |
| JEPA **weights** (how to predict) | JEPA **input/target** (what's being predicted) |
| — | Gate **weights** (inhibit/excite policy per function) |
| — | Input/output **projections** (mapping to/from shared space) |

## Why This Doesn't Collapse

### 1. Separate State Spaces

Each instance has its own 512-dimensional state vector. The Disturbance Detector's state encodes "what I expect to perceive next." The Intuition Module's state encodes "compressed history of pursuit outcomes." These are different representations in different vectors. They don't interfere because they're physically separate tensors.

### 2. Input/Output Projections

The input projection maps instance-specific inputs into the shared SSM's representational space. The output projection maps back. These projections are learned and instance-specific. They act as **representational lenses** — the same SSM dynamics, but focused through different projections for different cognitive functions.

Think of it like this: the SSM is a general-purpose recurrent processor. The input projection is the "question" you ask it. The output projection is the "answer" you read. Different instances ask different questions and read different answers, even though the processor is the same.

### 3. The Brain Does This Too

The canonical cortical microcircuit is repeated across the entire neocortex. Same cell types. Same laminar structure. Same local connectivity patterns. What differs:

- **Input sources** (which thalamic nuclei or cortical regions project here)
- **Output targets** (where this region sends its axons)
- **Neuromodulatory tone** (different dopamine/acetylcholine/norepinephrine ratios)
- **Inhibitory interneuron composition** (different ratios of PV/SST/VIP cells)

The circuit is the same. The **connectivity** and **modulation** make it a different function. Your architecture does the same: same SSM+JEPA, different input/output projections and different gates.

## The Training Question

The shared SSM and JEPA are pre-trained during gestational training (Oracle → student). The instance-specific gates and projections are trained separately:

1. **Gestational phase**: Oracle provides supervised signals. "Given this disturbance and this history, should the agent pursue?" The gate learns to mimic the Oracle's decisions.

2. **Online phase**: The agent pursues some disturbances and not others. Real outcomes arrive. The gate adapts — if it inhibited something that would have been rewarding, the threshold adjusts. If it pursued something that led nowhere, the threshold adjusts in the other direction.

3. **Dream state**: The gate's recent decisions are replayed. The JEPA re-scores them. The gate's threshold is fine-tuned based on counterfactual "what if we had pursued/inhibited?" analysis.

## Weights vs. State: They Are Fundamentally Different

This is the distinction:

| | Weights (Parameters) | State (Hidden State) |
|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | The learned transformation rules | The current "memory" of what's happening |
| **Size** | Large (370M params × 2-4 bytes = 0.7-1.4 GB) | Tiny (512 floats × 4 bytes = 2 KB per instance) |
| **When it changes** | During training. Frozen during inference. | Every single step. New input → new state. |
| **Analogy** | The rules of chess | The current board position |
| **Analogy 2** | The program code | The program's variables at runtime |

The SSM weights are the **transition function** — they define *how* to update state given new input. The SSM state is the **current representation** — what the model currently "believes" or "remembers."

---

## How an SSM Actually Works (Concretely)

```python
class MambaSSM:
    """
    Weights: learned matrices A, B, C, D, plus convolution weights.
    State:  the current hidden state vector h(t).
    """
    
    def __init__(self):
        # === WEIGHTS (large, fixed during inference, on GPU) ===
        self.A = nn.Parameter(...)  # State transition matrix
        self.B = nn.Parameter(...)  # Input projection
        self.C = nn.Parameter(...)  # Output projection
        self.D = nn.Parameter(...)  # Skip connection
        self.conv_weight = nn.Parameter(...)  # 1D convolution
        # Total: ~370M parameters, ~0.7 GB
        
        # === STATE (tiny, changes every step) ===
        self.h = None  # Hidden state: [batch, state_dim]
        # Size: 512 floats = 2 KB
    
    def step(self, input_x, state_h=None):
        """
        One forward step. Weights are fixed. State updates.
        """
        if state_h is not None:
            self.h = state_h  # Use provided state
        
        # Apply convolution to input (uses conv_weight)
        x = conv1d(input_x, self.conv_weight)
        
        # Discretize A, B based on input (input-dependent gating)
        A_discrete = discretize(self.A, x)
        B_discrete = self.B(x)
        
        # Update state: h_new = A_discrete * h_old + B_discrete * x
        self.h = A_discrete * self.h + B_discrete * x
        
        # Compute output: y = C * h_new + D * x
        y = self.C(self.h) + self.D * x
        
        return y, self.h  # Return output and new state
```

The weights (A, B, C, D, conv) are the **program**. The state (h) is the **running memory**. Every instance of a JEPA-gated SSM calls the same program (same weights) but maintains its own separate memory (own state vector).

## The Key Insight You Were Missing

You said: *"I thought the weights were the state."*

This is a natural confusion because in some architectures (like transformers), the "memory" of what's been said is stored in the attention context (the KV cache), which is neither weights nor a recurrent state — it's a third thing. And in some older RNNs, the line between weights and state was blurrier.

But in an SSM:

- **Weights** = the learned dynamics. "Given current state h and new input x, here's how to compute the next state." This is the same for every instance. It's the laws of physics for this cognitive universe.

- **State** = the current position in that universe. Each instance is at a different position. The Disturbance Detector is tracking "what I expect to perceive." The Intuition Module is tracking "compressed outcome history." Same physics, different positions.

---

## Can State Be Held Off-GPU?

Yes. State vectors are 2 KB each. You can:

1. **Keep them on GPU** during active use (negligible cost)
2. **Move them to CPU RAM** between steps (sub-microsecond transfer for 2 KB)
3. **Serialize to WaveDB** for persistence across sessions

The weights stay on GPU because they're large and needed for every computation. The state is tiny and can move freely.

## Why This Architecture Is Practical

| Concern | Resolution |
|---|---|
| "One Mamba for everything?" | One set of Mamba **weights** (the transition function). Many separate **state vectors** (the memory). No collapse because states don't interfere. |
| "Doesn't the SSM need to be specialized?" | The input/output projections provide specialization. The SSM sees different projected inputs from different instances. The shared dynamics learn to be general-purpose. |
| "Can 512 dimensions hold enough?" | 512 dimensions is ~2 KB. The Intuition Module's compressed history doesn't need to store every outcome — it needs to store a compressed representation that the JEPA can use to predict future outcomes. 512 dimensions is plenty for that. |
| "What about the MoE consolidation experts?" | Each expert is a separate state vector + separate gate, using the same shared SSM/JEPA weights. The "router" is just another gate that decides which expert's state to update. |

## What This Means for the Architecture

The gestational Oracle isn't just a training convenience. It's the **developmental scaffold** — the community that teaches the infant mind what's normal. And just like human development, there's a transition point where the scaffold is no longer needed:

```python
class DevelopmentalStage(Enum):
    INFANT = "infant"          # Oracle provides all training signal
    CHILD = "child"            # Oracle provides feedback on agent's decisions
    ADOLESCENT = "adolescent"  # Agent self-regulates, Oracle consulted for edge cases
    ADULT = "adult"            # Agent runs independently, Oracle is optional

class CognitiveArchitecture:
    
    def __init__(self, oracle: Oracle):
        self.stage = DevelopmentalStage.INFANT
        self.oracle = oracle
        
        # Random weights — the infant mind
        self.mamba = MambaSSM(random_init=True)
        self.jepa = JEPAPredictor(random_init=True)
        self.gates = {name: AdaptiveInhibitoryGate(random_init=True) 
                      for name in ["disturbance", "intuition", "aspiration", "self_model"]}
    
    def step(self, experience):
        if self.stage == DevelopmentalStage.INFANT:
            # Oracle provides the correct answer for everything
            oracle_state = self.oracle.compute_next_state(experience)
            oracle_prediction = self.oracle.predict_future(experience)
            oracle_gate_decisions = self.oracle.gate_decisions(experience)
            
            # Student learns to mimic
            loss = self.compute_loss(oracle_state, oracle_prediction, oracle_gate_decisions)
            self.update_weights(loss)
            
            # Transition check: is the student good enough?
            if self.performance > self.INFANT_THRESHOLD:
                self.stage = DevelopmentalStage.CHILD
        
        elif self.stage == DevelopmentalStage.CHILD:
            # Agent makes its own decisions
            agent_state, agent_prediction, agent_gate = self.forward(experience)
            
            # Oracle provides feedback: "You should have done X instead of Y"
            oracle_feedback = self.oracle.critique(agent_state, agent_prediction, agent_gate)
            
            # Agent updates from feedback
            loss = self.compute_critique_loss(oracle_feedback)
            self.update_weights(loss)
            
            if self.oracle_consultation_rate < self.CHILD_THRESHOLD:
                self.stage = DevelopmentalStage.ADOLESCENT
        
        elif self.stage == DevelopmentalStage.ADOLESCENT:
            # Agent self-regulates. Oracle consulted only for anomalies.
            agent_output = self.forward(experience)
            
            if agent_output.confidence < self.ADOLESCENT_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD:
                # "I'm not sure about this. Ask the Oracle."
                oracle_feedback = self.oracle.critique(agent_output)
                self.update_weights(oracle_feedback)
            
            if self.oracle_consultation_rate < self.ADULT_THRESHOLD:
                self.stage = DevelopmentalStage.ADULT
        
        elif self.stage == DevelopmentalStage.ADULT:
            # Agent runs independently.
            # Oracle is optional — consulted only by explicit request
            # or when the Self-Model detects a novel domain.
            return self.forward(experience)
```

### Gap 1: No Disturbance Detector

The architecture has no mechanism for the thing that triggers curiosity in the first place — the "flash of color outside the spectrum." JEPA currently predicts retrieval need, but it doesn't detect that incoming content contains a pattern that *cannot be explained by the current world model* and therefore implies something worth exploring.

**What to add**: A Disturbance Detector instance (JEPA-gated SSM) that compares perception to prediction and fires when the residual exceeds an adaptive threshold. This is the curiosity trigger. Without it, the system only retrieves what it already knows to look for.

### Gap 2: No Intuition Module

The architecture has salience scoring (GNN, post-hoc) and JEPA gating (retrieval need, present-focused), but nothing that does rapid, pre-conscious cost/benefit analysis over whether to pursue a disturbance. The Intuition Module — compressed outcome history that maps disturbance signatures to expected valence — is missing entirely.

**What to add**: An Intuition Module instance (JEPA-gated SSM) that maintains compressed outcome history and gates the curiosity cascade. This is what decides "pursue" vs. "inhibit" before conscious resources are spent.

### Gap 3: JEPA Is Underspecified

In both documents, JEPA is described as a "salience gate" that predicts retrieval need and modulates encoding strength. But our discussion revealed it should be much more:

- **Part of a unified Aspirational Model** that operates in three temporal modes: encoding gate (present), prospective trigger (future), consolidation bias (past)
- **Paired with an SSM** as the JEPA-gated SSM primitive — the shared dynamics that all cognitive functions use
- **Not a standalone component** but one half of a primitive that's instantiated multiple times

**What to modify**: Reframe JEPA not as a single gate but as the predictive half of the JEPA-gated SSM primitive. The Aspirational Model is one instance of this primitive. The Disturbance Detector is another. The Intuition Module is another. The Self-Model is another.

The documents describe one SSM as "working memory." But our discussion arrived at a different architecture: **shared SSM weights (the transition function), separate SSM states (the memory) per cognitive function.** The Disturbance Detector has its own state. Intuition has its own state. Aspiration has its own state. They all use the same dynamics but maintain different representations.

**What to modify**: Distinguish between SSM weights (shared, loaded once) and SSM states (instance-specific, tiny). The current document implies one SSM doing one thing. The architecture needs many state vectors using one set of dynamics.

### Gap 5: No Prospective Memory

The Aspirational Model should set future triggers — "when you encounter information about X, alert me." This is your mental alarm system. The architecture currently has no equivalent. The Gate should check pending aspirations on every query and fire when conditions match.

The documents mention gestational training with an Oracle but don't model the developmental progression: infant (Oracle provides all signal) → child (Oracle critiques agent's decisions) → adolescent (agent self-regulates, Oracle consulted for edge cases) → adult (agent runs independently).

## 1. Problem Statement

### 1.1 What the Current Architecture Gets Right

The existing architecture correctly identifies that memory is not a text buffer. The separation of a fast, deterministic retrieval loop from a slow, model-driven consolidation loop is the correct mapping of the brain's solution. WaveDB as hippocampal index, the graph as sparse pointer structure, GLiNER2 for extraction, Bonsai for verification, and the GNN consolidator for dream-state processing — these are all sound.

### 1.2 What the Current Architecture Misses

The architecture treats its neural components — Mamba SSM, JEPA Predictor, Gate, Aspirational Model, Self-Model, MoE SSM — as **separate models with separate purposes**. This has three consequences:

| Problem | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Proliferation of models** | Each cognitive function requires its own model. Adding a new function (e.g., disturbance detection) means adding a new model. The architecture doesn't scale cognitively. |
| **No unified dynamics** | The SSM encodes state. The JEPA predicts relevance. The Gate routes queries. These are treated as independent components when they are, in the brain, aspects of a single computational primitive repeated across cortex. |
| **Missing cognitive functions** | The architecture has no disturbance detector (curiosity trigger), no intuition module (rapid cost/benefit gating), no prospective memory (future triggers), and no developmental staging. These aren't optional — they're how a mind decides what to encode, what to pursue, and when it's ready to operate independently. |

### 1.3 The Deeper Issue

The architecture describes *what* the system does but not *how* the cognitive functions relate to each other. The Mamba SSM is "working memory." The JEPA is a "salience gate." The Aspirational Model is "what the agent wants to know." These are descriptions of function, not descriptions of mechanism. And because they're described as separate components, the architecture implies they're implemented separately — different models, different weights, different training procedures.

The brain does not work this way. The canonical cortical microcircuit — the same cell types, the same laminar structure, the same local connectivity — is repeated across the entire neocortex. What differs between regions is input sources, output targets, and inhibitory interneuron composition. The circuit is the same. The **configuration** makes it different.

This amendment proposes the same unification for the architecture.

### 2.2 The Critical Distinction: Shared Weights, Separate States

This is the architectural insight that prevents representational collapse:

| What's Shared | What's Instance-Specific |
|---|---|
| SSM **weights** (how state evolves) | SSM **state** (what the state IS) — 512 floats, ~2 KB |
| JEPA **weights** (how to predict) | JEPA **input/target** (what's being predicted) |
| — | Gate **weights** (inhibit/excite policy per function) — ~500K params |
| — | Input/output **projections** (mapping to/from shared space) — ~100K params |

The SSM weights are the laws of physics for this cognitive universe. The SSM state is the current position within it. Every instance obeys the same laws but occupies a different position.

This is not a metaphor. It's an implementation constraint: the SSM and JEPA weights are loaded once in GPU memory. Every instance calls the same forward pass with its own state vector and its own gate. Adding a new cognitive function costs ~1M parameters, not ~500M.

### 2.3 Why This Doesn't Collapse

A single SSM state vector cannot simultaneously represent world model predictions, compressed outcome history, goal states, and knowledge boundary estimates. These are different kinds of information with different temporal dynamics. Jamming them into one state vector would produce representational collapse — the system would confuse what it expects with what it wants with what it remembers.

The architecture prevents this through three mechanisms:

1. **Separate state spaces**: Each instance has its own 512-dimensional state vector. The Disturbance Detector's state encodes "what I expect to perceive next." The Intuition Module's state encodes "compressed history of pursuit outcomes." These are different representations in physically separate tensors.

2. **Input/output projections**: The input projection maps instance-specific inputs into the shared SSM's representational space. The output projection maps back. These are learned and instance-specific. They act as representational lenses — the same SSM dynamics, focused through different projections for different cognitive functions.

3. **Instance-specific gates**: Each gate learns its own inhibit/excite policy. The Disturbance Detector's gate learns "is this prediction error large enough to flag?" The Intuition Module's gate learns "is the predicted reward/effort ratio high enough to pursue?" Same gate architecture, different learned thresholds.

### 2.4 Biological Fidelity

This maps directly onto the canonical cortical microcircuit:

| Biological Component | Architectural Equivalent |
|---|---|
| Pyramidal cell recurrent dynamics | SSM state evolution |
| Predictive coding (top-down predictions) | JEPA predictor |
| Inhibitory interneurons (PV, SST, VIP) | Gate (threshold, modulation) |
| Neuromodulators (dopamine, acetylcholine) | Adaptive threshold adjustment |
| Canonical microcircuit (repeated across cortex) | The JEPA-gated SSM primitive itself |
| Different cortical regions (V1, A1, PFC) | Different instances with different state vectors |
| Different input sources (LGN → V1, MGN → A1) | Different input projections |
| Different inhibitory interneuron ratios | Different gate configurations |

The major evolutionary expansion in the human brain was not excitatory neurons — it was inhibitory interneurons. Humans didn't just get more neurons. We got more **stops**. More "don't fire." More "not yet." More "this pattern doesn't match." The JEPA-gated SSM captures this: the gate is the inhibitory expansion, and different cognitive functions are different configurations of inhibition over the same recurrent predictive dynamics.

### 3.1 Disturbance Detector (New)

**What it replaces**: Nothing. This is a new cognitive function absent from the current architecture.

**What it does**: Compares incoming perception to the world model's prediction. When the prediction error exceeds an adaptive threshold, a disturbance is registered. The disturbance carries directional information about its unknown source — like a gunshot in the distance, or a flash of color outside the visible spectrum.

**Why it matters**: Without a Disturbance Detector, the system only retrieves what it already knows to look for. It cannot detect that incoming information implies something beyond its current model. It has no curiosity. The Disturbance Detector is the trigger for all exploratory behavior — the thing that makes the system *want* to know what it doesn't already know.

**Gate configuration**: `error > adaptive_threshold → fire`. The threshold adapts based on recent noise levels. In a high-noise environment (many small prediction errors), the threshold rises to prevent false positives. In a low-noise environment, even small anomalies register.

**Implementation sketch**:

```python
class DisturbanceDetector(JEPAGatedSSM):
    """
    Detects patterns in incoming content that cannot be fully explained
    by the agent's current world model.
    """
    
    def detect(self, perception: Embedding, world_model: GraphState) -> list[Disturbance]:
        # SSM state encodes: what do I expect to perceive?
        predicted = self.predictor(self.state)
        
        # Compute prediction error
        error = distance(perception, predicted)
        
        # Gate: is this error large enough to flag?
        decision = self.gate(self.state, predicted, context={
            "error": error,
            "noise_level": self.recent_error_stats.std_dev
        })
        
        if not decision.excite:
            return []  # Error is within expected bounds. No disturbance.
        
        # Disturbance detected. Extract its structure.
        disturbances = []
        for region in self.decompose_error(error, perception, predicted):
            direction = self.infer_direction(region, world_model)
            signature = self.classify_pattern(region)
            
            disturbances.append(Disturbance(
                residual=region,
                direction=direction,
                pattern_signature=signature,
                location=region.location_in_model
            ))
        
        return disturbances
```

### 3.2 Intuition Module (New)

**What it replaces**: Nothing. This is a new cognitive function absent from the current architecture.

**What it does**: When a disturbance is detected, the Intuition Module performs rapid, pre-conscious cost/benefit analysis. It consults a compressed history of past disturbance → pursuit → outcome triples and predicts whether pursuing this disturbance is likely to be worth the effort. The output is a valence signal — exciting, terrifying, or neutral — with a confidence estimate.

**Why it matters**: Without an Intuition Module, every disturbance would be pursued indiscriminately, or a hardcoded rule would decide. The Intuition Module learns from experience which disturbances lead to rewarding discoveries and which lead to dead ends or threats. It's what makes the system's curiosity *wise* rather than merely *active*.

**Gate configuration**: `predicted_reward / predicted_effort > adaptive_threshold → pursue`. The threshold adapts based on sunk cost, novelty, and recent reward rate. When progress stalls in a highly novel domain, the threshold *rises* (easier to excite) — this is the "push beyond the previously intuited limit" mechanism. When sunk cost is high and rewards are sparse, the threshold *falls* (harder to excite) — this is the "cut your losses" mechanism.

**Implementation sketch**:

```python
class IntuitionModule(JEPAGatedSSM):
    """
    Compressed outcome history. Maps disturbance signatures to expected valence.
    """
    
    def evaluate(self, disturbance: Disturbance, exploration_state: Embedding) -> IntuitiveSignal:
        # SSM state encodes: compressed history of pursuit outcomes
        history_state = self.state
        
        # JEPA predicts: if I pursue this disturbance, what state will I reach?
        predicted_outcome = self.predictor(
            current=exploration_state,
            direction=disturbance.direction,
            history=history_state
        )
        
        # Effort: distance from current state to predicted outcome
        effort = distance(exploration_state, predicted_outcome)
        
        # Reward: estimated value of the predicted outcome state
        reward = self.estimate_reward(predicted_outcome, history_state)
        
        # Gate: pursue or inhibit?
        context = GateContext(
            sunk_cost=self.compute_sunk_cost(exploration_state),
            novelty=disturbance.novelty,
            recent_reward_rate=self.recent_reward_rate
        )
        decision = self.gate(self.state, predicted_outcome, context)
        
        return IntuitiveSignal(
            valence=reward / max(effort, EPSILON),
            confidence=decision.confidence,
            decision=decision.excite,
            source="compressed_history" if self.has_history(disturbance) else "no_history"
        )
    
    def record_outcome(self, disturbance_signature, outcome):
        """After pursuit concludes, update compressed history."""
        self.state = self.ssm.step(outcome.embedding, self.state)
        self.recent_reward_rate = self.update_reward_rate(outcome)
```

### 3.3 Aspirational Model (Expanded)

**What it replaces**: The current Aspirational Model, which only scores directional relevance during ingestion.

**What it expands to**: A unified model of "what the agent wants" operating in three temporal modes:

| Mode | Function | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Present** — encoding gate | Modulates encoding strength based on aspirational match | "I'm curious about this → encode strongly" |
| **Future** — prospective memory | Sets triggers that fire when conditions are met | "Alert me when you encounter information about X" |
| **Past** — consolidation bias | Weights replay priority during dream state | "This aligns with what I care about → strengthen" |

**Why it matters**: The current Aspirational Model is scoped too narrowly. It only operates during ingestion. But wanting operates in all three temporal directions. The same dopaminergic signal that gates encoding also maintains goal representations in working memory (prospective intention) and tags memories for replay priority during consolidation. The Aspirational Model should reflect this unity.

**Gate configuration**: `valence > threshold → commit`. The threshold varies by mode: lower for encoding (default curious), higher for prospective triggers (only commit to important future states), intermediate for consolidation bias.

**Prospective memory implementation**:

```python
class AspirationalModel(JEPAGatedSSM):
    """
    What the agent wants. Unified across temporal modes.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__(config)
        self.pending_triggers: list[ProspectiveTrigger] = []
    
    def encode_aspiration(self, goal_state: Embedding, 
                          condition: Optional[dict] = None) -> str:
        """
        If condition is None: aspiration applies to all future ingestion (encoding gate).
        If condition is set: aspiration is a prospective trigger (future mode).
        """
        aspiration_id = generate_id()
        
        if condition:
            self.pending_triggers.append(ProspectiveTrigger(
                id=aspiration_id,
                goal_state=goal_state,
                condition=condition,
                created_at=now()
            ))
        
        return aspiration_id
    
    def check_triggers(self, current_context: dict) -> list[ProspectiveTrigger]:
        """Called before every fast loop. Returns any triggers that match."""
        fired = [t for t in self.pending_triggers if t.condition_matches(current_context)]
        for t in fired:
            self.pending_triggers.remove(t)
        return fired
    
    def score_encoding(self, content: Embedding) -> float:
        """Present mode: should this be encoded, and at what strength?"""
        match_score = cosine_similarity(content, self.state)
        decision = self.gate(self.state, content, mode="encoding")
        return match_score * decision.excite_score
    
    def replay_priority(self, edge: Edge) -> float:
        """Past mode: how important is this edge to consolidate?"""
        match_score = cosine_similarity(edge.embedding, self.state)
        decision = self.gate(self.state, edge.embedding, mode="consolidation")
        return edge.utility_score * (1 + match_score) * decision.excite_score
```

### 3.4 Self-Model (Refactored)

**What it replaces**: The current Self-Model, which uses ad-hoc logic over graph statistics.

**What it becomes**: An instance of the JEPA-gated SSM that learns its own knowledge boundary thresholds from experience rather than using hardcoded heuristics.

**Gate configuration**: `graph_density < threshold → "I don't know"`. The threshold is learned, not set. During gestational training, the Oracle provides feedback: "You should have known this" or "You were right to say you don't know." The gate adapts.

### 4.3 Reconsolidation Counting

The architecture now models the biological consolidation process explicitly:

```python
class Edge:
    # ... existing fields ...
    
    reconsolidation_count: int = 0       # How many times reactivated
    ltp_phase: str = "early"             # "early" | "late"
    consolidation_window_start: Optional[datetime] = None
    
    def on_traverse(self):
        """Called every time this edge is traversed in retrieval."""
        self.reconsolidation_count += 1
        self.last_accessed = now()
        
        # Three retrievals across 15+ days → late-phase LTP
        if (self.reconsolidation_count >= 3 and 
            self.consolidation_window_start and
            (now() - self.consolidation_window_start).days >= 15):
            self.ltp_phase = "late"
            self.utility_decay_rate *= 0.3  # 70% reduction in decay
    
    def on_first_traverse(self):
        """First retrieval starts the consolidation clock."""
        if self.consolidation_window_start is None:
            self.consolidation_window_start = now()
```

This replaces the current flat utility score decay with a biologically-grounded two-phase model. Edges that have been retrieved three times across 15+ days are considered consolidated — they decay 70% slower than unconsolidated edges. This is the architectural equivalent of the transition from hippocampal-dependent to neocortical-independent memory.

### 4.4 Developmental Stages

The architecture now models its own maturation:

```python
class DevelopmentalStage(Enum):
    INFANT = "infant"          # Oracle provides all training signal
    CHILD = "child"            # Oracle critiques agent's decisions
    ADOLESCENT = "adolescent"  # Agent self-regulates, Oracle for edge cases
    ADULT = "adult"            # Agent runs independently

class DevelopmentalTracker:
    """
    Tracks which stage each component is in and manages transitions.
    """
    
    def __init__(self):
        self.stages = {
            "extraction": DevelopmentalStage.INFANT,
            "retrieval": DevelopmentalStage.INFANT,
            "consolidation": DevelopmentalStage.INFANT,
            "disturbance_detector": DevelopmentalStage.INFANT,
            "intuition": DevelopmentalStage.INFANT,
            "aspiration": DevelopmentalStage.INFANT,
            "self_model": DevelopmentalStage.INFANT,
        }
    
    def evaluate_transition(self, component: str, metrics: dict) -> bool:
        """
        Check if a component is ready to advance to the next stage.
        
        Example thresholds:
        - extraction: F1 > 0.85 on held-out data → CHILD
        - retrieval: recall > 0.80 on ConvoMem single-session → CHILD
        - intuition: gate decisions match Oracle > 0.75 → CHILD
        - self_model: "I don't know" precision > 0.80 → ADOLESCENT
        """
        current = self.stages[component]
        
        if current == DevelopmentalStage.INFANT:
            if metrics.get("oracle_mimicry", 0) > self.INFANT_THRESHOLD:
                self.stages[component] = DevelopmentalStage.CHILD
                return True
        
        elif current == DevelopmentalStage.CHILD:
            if metrics.get("oracle_consultation_rate", 1.0) < self.CHILD_THRESHOLD:
                self.stages[component] = DevelopmentalStage.ADOLESCENT
                return True
        
        elif current == DevelopmentalStage.ADOLESCENT:
            if metrics.get("independent_accuracy", 0) > self.ADULT_THRESHOLD:
                self.stages[component] = DevelopmentalStage.ADULT
                return True
        
        return False
```

This matters for Phase 1 because it defines what "done" means for each component. The extraction models are in INFANT stage — they need Oracle-generated training data. They graduate to CHILD when they can extract entities and relations with acceptable accuracy. They graduate to ADOLESCENT when they can handle novel entity types without Oracle consultation. They graduate to ADULT when they can be deployed without any Oracle dependency.

**Savings: ~0.78 GB VRAM** — nearly half the Mind layer's footprint, with more cognitive functions.

### 5.2 Cognitive Scalability

Adding a new cognitive function:

| Architecture | Cost |
|---|---|
| **v7.1** | New model (~100M-500M params), new training procedure, new VRAM allocation |
| **v8** | New state vector (2 KB) + new gate (~500K params) + new projections (~100K params). ~1M total. |

The v8 architecture scales cognitively. Want to add an "Embarrassment Detector" that flags when the agent should feel uncertain about its answer? One new instance. ~1M parameters. No new model to train — just a new gate and projections, trained on Oracle-provided examples of "you should have been less confident here."

### 5.3 Training Efficiency

The shared SSM and JEPA weights are trained once during gestational training. Instance-specific gates are trained separately on smaller, function-specific datasets:

| Component | Training Data Required | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Shared SSM+JEPA | Oracle-generated cognitive state sequences | 10M+ examples |
| Disturbance Detector gate | Oracle-labeled "is this a disturbance?" pairs | 100K examples |
| Intuition gate | Oracle-labeled "should I pursue?" pairs | 100K examples |
| Aspiration gate | Oracle-labeled "should I commit?" pairs | 50K examples |
| Self-Model gate | Oracle-labeled "should I say I don't know?" pairs | 50K examples |

The shared weights are the large investment. The gates are cheap to train and can be iterated rapidly.

## 6. Implementation Impact on Current Phases

### Phase 1 (Current — Extraction Training): No Change

GLiNER2, GLiNER-Decoder, and Bonsai relation extraction training proceed as planned. The JEPA-gated SSM primitive doesn't affect extraction — it affects how extracted information is processed downstream.

**What to be aware of**: The extraction pipeline should produce structured output that the Disturbance Detector can consume. This means preserving not just entities and relations, but also the *prediction* of what entities and relations were expected. The Disturbance Detector needs both the perception and the prediction to compute the residual.

### Phase 2 (Memory Dynamics): Modified

Instead of training a single JEPA and a single SSM as separate components, train the **shared** SSM and JEPA weights. The retrieval gate becomes the first instance-specific gate. This is functionally similar to the current Phase 2 plan but architecturally cleaner — the shared weights are trained once, and the gate is the first of many.

### Phase 3 (GNN Consolidator): Modified

Add reconsolidation counting to the consolidation loop. The GNN's salience scoring should incorporate `reconsolidation_count` and `ltp_phase` as features. Edges in late-phase LTP should have their utility decay rate reduced automatically.

### Phase 5 (New): Instance-Specific Gate Training

Train the Disturbance Detector gate, Intuition Module gate, Aspirational Model gate, and Self-Model gate. This is where the curiosity system comes online. The Oracle generates training examples for each gate. The gates learn to mimic the Oracle's decisions. The developmental tracker evaluates when each gate is ready to advance from INFANT to CHILD.

## 9. Theorcrafting: Where This Goes

### 9.1 The Subconscious Becomes the Primary Intelligence

As the Disturbance Detector, Intuition Module, and Aspirational Model mature, they handle an increasing fraction of cognitive work. The system doesn't just retrieve answers — it anticipates questions, prepares context, and forms aspirations before the user finishes asking. The LLM becomes a specialized tool for tasks that require genuine reasoning. The subconscious becomes the default mode of interaction.

### 9.2 Curiosity as a Learnable Drive

The Disturbance Detector + Intuition Module + Aspirational Model cascade is a curiosity system. It can be tuned. An agent configured for scientific research gets a low disturbance threshold (notice everything) and a high intuition threshold (pursue only the most promising). An agent configured for safety monitoring gets a high disturbance threshold (ignore noise) and a low intuition threshold (pursue anything potentially threatening). The same architecture, different gate configurations, radically different behavior.

### 9.3 The End of the Monolithic Model

The current AI paradigm is a single massive model that knows everything. The JEPA-gated SSM paradigm is a small, shared processing layer that knows nothing, connected to personal knowledge graphs that grow with their users. The model is a commodity. The knowledge is the value. The subconscious is the moat.

### 9.4 Transferrable Cognitive Configurations

If domain knowledge is transferrable (as The Ponder Engine argues), cognitive configurations should be too. A "scientific researcher" gate configuration — low disturbance threshold, high intuition threshold, strong encoding for anomalies — can be exported and imported just like a domain graph. Different tasks get different cognitive styles, not just different knowledge.
