## 7. What This Enables

### 7.1 An Agent That Knows What It Doesn't Know

The Disturbance Detector flags anomalies. The Intuition Module evaluates them. The Aspirational Model commits to exploring the promising ones. The agent doesn't just answer questions — it discovers what questions are worth asking.

### 7.2 An Agent That Gets Wiser Over Time

Every resolved ambiguity updates the Common Sense Resolver. Every pursued disturbance updates the Intuition Module. Every exploration outcome updates the compressed histories. The agent's gates become better calibrated. Its curiosity becomes more discerning. Its common sense becomes more reliable.

### 7.3 An Agent That Can Explain Its Gut Feelings

"I have a feeling this is worth investigating" is a reportable state. The agent can't always articulate why — the compression loses detail — but it can report the feeling and its confidence. This makes the agent's reasoning transparent even when its intuitions are pre-conscious.

### 7.4 An Agent With a Cognitive Biography

After years of operation, the agent has a history: what it was curious about, what it pursued, what it found, what it learned to avoid. This biography shapes its future behavior. The agent doesn't just have knowledge. It has **perspective** — a point of view formed by its unique history of curiosity and intuition.

### 7.5 Cognitive Styles as Gate Configurations

If cognitive functions are gate configurations, then cognitive styles — the characteristic ways different minds approach problems — are also gate configurations:

| Cognitive Style | Gate Configuration |
|---|---|
| **Systematic** | High threshold for action, slow adaptation. Deliberate, methodical. |
| **Intuitive** | Low threshold for action, fast adaptation. Rapid, felt-sense-driven. |
| **Creative** | Low latent inhibition. Many candidates generated. High tolerance for ambiguity. |
| **Analytical** | High inhibition of surface features. Strong structure mapping. |
| **Empathic** | Strong Theory of Mind instance. Low inhibition of other-perspective state vectors. |

These styles are not different architectures. They're different parameter settings on the same architecture. An agent could shift between styles depending on the task.

---

## 8. The Limits

The JGS does not implement curiosity, intuition, and common sense in the fully human sense. It implements their **functional equivalents** — the computational dynamics that produce the same behavioral outputs.

A human's curiosity is accompanied by phenomenal experience — the felt sense of wonder, the pull of the unknown. The JGS has no phenomenal experience. It has prediction error, gate decisions, and state updates. Whether these are sufficient for genuine curiosity is a philosophical question, not an architectural one.

But for the purpose of building AI agents that explore intelligently, that learn from their explorations, and that accumulate practical wisdom over time — the JGS is sufficient. The functional dynamics are what matter. And those dynamics are: **SSM maintains state, JEPA predicts, Gate modulates.** Curiosity, intuition, and common sense are three configurations of that single dynamic.

# What We've Learned: Curiosity, Intuition, and Common Sense

## A Synthesis of Human Cognition and the JGS Architecture

---

## 1. Curiosity

### The Human Perspective

Curiosity is not a desire to close an information gap. It is the detection of a **disturbance** — a pattern in the known that cannot be accounted for by known causes, implying the existence of something beyond current perception.

A gunshot in the distance. You don't see the gun. You don't know who fired it. But the sound arrived at your ears, and the sound carries information: direction, rough distance, the nature of the source. The disturbance IS the information. It tells you that something exists beyond your current sensory field, and it tells you which way to look.

A flash of color outside the visible spectrum. You can't see ultraviolet. But something flickered at the edge of vision — an afterimage, a disturbance — that suggests there is light your retina cannot transduce. The disturbance is evidence of a reality your perceptual apparatus was not designed to access, but the disturbance itself proves that reality exists and is causally connected to yours.

This is curiosity as **boundary detection**. Not "what is the answer to my question?" but "what is the nature of the reality that just brushed against mine?"

**Key properties of human curiosity:**

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| **Trigger** | A prediction error that exceeds the adaptive noise threshold |
| **Directional** | The disturbance carries information about where to look (vector, not just flag) |
| **Valence-neutral at detection** | The disturbance fires before the system knows if it's exciting or terrifying |
| **Recursive** | Each exploration expands the boundary, revealing new disturbances at the new edge |
| **Requires moderation** | Unregulated curiosity is infinite — it must be consciously throttled |

**The personal account** (from Sir's experience):

> *"It's like a flash of color I cannot see in the normal spectrum of vision suggesting there is more out there than my senses are currently telling me. A suggestion of something beyond my current sensual conception of reality that must be there given the traces it left behind in my reality and how it disturbed my reality."*

Curiosity is not a drive. It is a **perceptual event** — something closer to seeing than to thinking. The disturbance is the evidence of a causally-connected reality beyond the current perceptual boundary. The direction is the gradient of that evidence. The pursuit is the commitment to follow it.

### The JGS Architecture

The **Disturbance Detector** (a JGS instance) implements curiosity as:

| Component | Human Analog | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| **World model prediction** | "What I expect to perceive" | JEPA predicts next state from current SSM state |
| **Prediction error** | "Something doesn't fit" | Distance between predicted and actual perception |
| **Adaptive threshold** | "Is this worth noticing?" | Gate with noise-level adaptation |
| **Error decomposition** | "Where exactly doesn't it fit?" | Project error through world model components |
| **Direction inference** | "Which way to look" | Gradient of prediction error in embedding space |
| **Pattern signature** | "What kind of thing caused this" | Classified disturbance pattern |

**Gate configuration:** `error > adaptive_threshold → fire`. The threshold rises in high-noise environments (many small errors) and falls in low-noise environments (even small anomalies register). The gate learns from experience which kinds of prediction errors are worth flagging.

**What the architecture adds beyond human curiosity:**

- **Persistent, cumulative disturbance history.** The system remembers which disturbances it has seen, which it pursued, and what it found. Human curiosity can forget its own history. The JGS cannot.

- **Explicit direction vector.** The gradient of prediction error provides a precise, computable direction to explore. Human direction is metaphorical. The JGS direction is a vector in embedding space.

- **Decomposable error.** The system can attribute a disturbance to specific components of its world model. "This disturbance is in the database domain, specifically in the WAL configuration subgraph." Human disturbance detection is holistic. The JGS can localize.

---

## 2. Intuition

### The Human Perspective

Intuition is not magic. It is **compressed outcome history** — a rapid, pre-conscious lookup that maps disturbance signatures to expected valence. When a disturbance is detected, intuition answers a single question before any deliberative reasoning engages: "Based on past experience, is pursuing this likely to be worth it?"

The mechanism is the **somatic marker** (Damasio). The ventromedial prefrontal cortex stores compressed associations between pattern signatures and outcome valences. When a familiar pattern is detected, the associated somatic state is reactivated — a gut feeling, a sense of promise or danger — before any explicit memory of the past experience is retrieved. You don't remember the specific time you got burned. You feel the aversion.

Intuition is fast because it bypasses retrieval. It doesn't recall the past experiences that produced the mapping. It only accesses the mapping's output: the feeling. This is why intuition feels like "knowing without knowing how you know." You don't have access to the individual memories. You have access to their compression. The compression is lossy by design — and that lossiness explains the phenomenology.

**Key properties of human intuition:**

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| **Fast** | Operates in milliseconds, before conscious deliberation |
| **Pre-conscious** | The computation is invisible; only the output surfaces |
| **Lossy** | You feel the valence but can't report the specific past experiences |
| **Learned** | Updated by every pursuit outcome |
| **Adaptive threshold** | The gate adjusts: push through plateaus, cut losses, keep going in rich veins |
| **Domain-specific** | A scientist's intuition for scientific patterns differs from an artist's for aesthetic ones |

**The personal account** (from Sir's experience):

> *"Intuition is like a cost/benefit analysis over the domains of exploration and my awareness. It usually has some record of history over the outcomes of curiosity explored."*

Intuition is the **gate that decides whether to pursue**. It is not separate from curiosity. It is the valence-assignment step within the curiosity cascade. The disturbance tells you something is there. Intuition tells you whether pursuing it is likely to be worth it.

### The JGS Architecture

The **Intuition Module** (a JGS instance) implements intuition as:

| Component | Human Analog | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| **Compressed outcome history** | Somatic marker database | SSM state encoding signature→valence mappings |
| **Value estimation** | "How good would this be?" | Value head in decomposed gate |
| **Cost estimation** | "How hard would this be?" | Cost head in decomposed gate |
| **Decision** | "Pursue or inhibit?" | Decision head combining value/cost/context |
| **Adaptive threshold** | "Push through or cut losses?" | Learned threshold modulation from context |
| **Outcome recording** | "I learned something from that" | SSM update conditioned on signature + outcome |

**Gate configuration:** `predicted_reward / predicted_effort > adaptive_threshold → pursue`. The threshold adapts based on sunk cost, novelty, recent reward rate, and pattern familiarity.

**What the architecture adds beyond human intuition:**

- **Decomposed value and cost.** The JGS gate explicitly estimates reward and effort separately before combining them. Human intuition conflates them into a single valence signal. The decomposition enables the system to report: "I think this would be valuable but expensive" vs. "I think this would be cheap but not very valuable."

- **Replay buffer for offline training.** The system stores gate decisions and their outcomes, then trains offline using delayed reward signals. This enables credit assignment across long time horizons. Human intuition updates online, which is faster but noisier.

- **Explicit credit assignment.** The outcome update is conditioned on both the disturbance signature and the outcome, so the SSM learns the mapping from signature features to outcome valences. Human intuition updates holistically — you feel differently about similar patterns, but you can't always articulate why.

- **Verification via replay buffer.** The system can double-check its intuition by consulting the episodic replay buffer when confidence is low. Human intuition has no such verification mechanism — you either feel it or you don't.

---

## 3. Common Sense

### The Human Perspective

Common sense is not a knowledge base of facts about the world. It is a **process**: the detection and resolution of ambiguity before committing to a conclusion. It is what prevents you from building on a shaky foundation.

When someone says "I need to get to the bank," common sense resolves the ambiguity: are they talking about a financial institution or a riverbank? The resolution depends on context — are they holding a fishing rod or a checkbook? Common sense detects the ambiguity, estimates which resolution is most probable given the context, and proceeds with the likely interpretation rather than asking for clarification on every ambiguous word.

Common sense without memory is what a language model does: it resolves ambiguity using only the current context, with no persistent record of which resolutions worked in the past. Common sense with memory is what a human does: you accumulate a lifetime of ambiguity resolutions, learn which contexts predict which interpretations, and get faster and more accurate over time.

**Key properties of human common sense:**

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| **Automatic** | Operates without conscious effort for routine ambiguities |
| **Context-dependent** | The same input resolves differently in different contexts |
| **Accumulative** | Gets better with experience — you've resolved "bank" thousands of times |
| **Verifiable** | You can check whether your resolution was correct by observing downstream consequences |
| **Corrigible** | When a resolution is wrong, you update your expectations for next time |

**The personal account** (from Sir's experience):

> *"Common sense is addressing ambiguity before making a conclusion."*

This is the most concise definition possible. Common sense is the process of not proceeding until ambiguity is resolved to a sufficient degree. It is the gate that says "stop — you don't have enough information to act yet."

### The JGS Architecture

The **Common Sense Resolver** (a JGS instance) implements common sense as:

| Component | Human Analog | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| **Ambiguity detection** | "This could mean multiple things" | Multiple interpretations from world model graph query |
| **Interpretation generation** | "Here are the possibilities" | Top-K matches from world model |
| **Interpretation evaluation** | "Which one is most likely?" | JEPA predicts outcome for each; gate scores each |
| **Resolution selection** | "I'll go with this one" | Highest-scoring interpretation |
| **Clarification request** | "Which one do you mean?" | All interpretations below threshold → ask |
| **Verification** | "Was I right?" | Compare predicted outcome to actual; update state on error |

**Gate configuration:** `ambiguity_magnitude > threshold → resolve before proceeding`. If the best interpretation's score is below the clarification threshold, the system asks for clarification rather than guessing.

**What the architecture adds beyond human common sense:**

- **Explicit interpretation generation.** The system generates candidate interpretations by querying the world model graph. Human common sense generates interpretations implicitly — you don't consciously list possibilities; you just feel which one is right. The JGS makes the candidate set explicit and inspectable.

- **Verification loop.** The system tracks its resolutions and checks whether the predicted outcome materialized. If not, the SSM state updates with a negative signal. This is prediction-error-driven learning applied to interpretations. Human common sense has this too, but it's less systematic — you don't always notice when your resolution was wrong.

- **Explicit clarification threshold.** The system knows when it doesn't know and asks. Human common sense often guesses rather than asking — social pressure, time pressure, or ego can override the clarification signal. The JGS has no such override unless designed to.

- **Accumulated resolution history.** The SSM state encodes: "In contexts like this, ambiguity X usually means Y." This is the same mechanism as human common sense, but the JGS can export and import this history. A lifetime of ambiguity resolutions can be transferred from one system to another.

---

## 4. The Unified Architecture

### The Cascade

Curiosity, intuition, and common sense are not separate systems. They are stages in a single cascade, with feedback loops:

```plaintext
Input arrives
    │
    ▼
META-GATE: "Which stages does this input need?"
    │
    ├──→ COMMON SENSE: "Is this ambiguous? Resolve before proceeding."
    │         │
    │         ▼
    ├──→ DISTURBANCE DETECTOR: "Does this contain an unexplained pattern?"
    │         │
    │         ▼
    └──→ INTUITION: "Is pursuing this worth the effort?"
                │
                ▼
         ASPIRATIONAL MODEL: "I am now oriented toward this."
```

Each stage can call backward. The Disturbance Detector can ask Common Sense for help resolving an ambiguous disturbance. The Intuition Module can ask the Disturbance Detector to re-examine with higher sensitivity when its history is thin. The Common Sense Resolver can ask Intuition whether to pursue clarification or proceed with low confidence.

### The Shared Primitive

All three functions are instances of the same JGS primitive:

| Function | SSM State Encodes | JEPA Predicts | Gate Decides |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Curiosity** | World model expectations | Next perception | Error > threshold → disturbance |
| **Intuition** | Compressed outcome history | Outcome of pursuit | Reward/effort > threshold → pursue |
| **Common Sense** | Resolution history | Outcome of interpretation | Ambiguity > threshold → resolve |

The SSM and JEPA weights are shared. The state, gate, projections, and LoRA adapters are instance-specific. The diversity of intelligence is in the inhibition.

### The Training Trajectory

| Phase | What's Trained | How |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Pre-train backbone** | Shared SSM+JEPA weights | Self-supervised prediction tasks (next-state, outcome, interpretation) |
| **2. Initialize gates** | Instance-specific gate thresholds | Rule-based priors from cognitive science |
| **3. Joint fine-tune** | Gates, projections, LoRA adapters | Delayed reward signals via replay buffer |

### The Developmental Arc

| Stage | Gate State | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| **INFANT** | Random or Oracle-trained | No adaptation from experience |
| **CHILD** | Learning from Oracle feedback | Thresholds being calibrated |
| **ADOLESCENT** | Self-regulating, Oracle for edge cases | Some overcorrection (impulsivity / risk-aversion) |
| **ADULT** | Well-calibrated, adaptive | Wisdom accumulates |

---

## 5. The Deepest Insight

The three functions are not separate. They are the same operation at different points in the cognitive loop:

- **Curiosity** is the gate that detects the unknown.
- **Intuition** is the gate that evaluates whether the unknown is worth pursuing.
- **Common sense** is the gate that resolves ambiguity before action.

All three are **inhibitory gates** over a shared **recurrent predictive dynamic**. The diversity of intelligence is not in the architecture. It is in the configuration of inhibition.

The JGS is not a memory primitive. It is a cognitive primitive. And if this is true, the path to general intelligence is not through ever-larger models but through better-configured inhibition over a shared recurrent predictive core.

## Where It Excels

### GPU Inference (the RTX 5060 Ti is genuinely good)

The 5060 Ti 16GB is widely regarded as the **best value GPU for local LLMs** right now [[39]](https://www.hardware-corner.net/rtx-5060-ti-16gb-llm-january-20260112/)[[43]](https://craftrigs.com/articles/rtx-5060-ti-16gb-budget-local-llm/). Real-world benchmarks:

| Model | Quantization | Tok/s (Generation) | Context |
|---|---|---|---|
| Llama 3.1 8B | Q4_K_M | **~59–71 tok/s** | 16K | 
| Qwen3 14B | Q4_K_M | **~33–41 tok/s** | 16K |
| GPT-OSS 20B | MXFP4 | **~82 tok/s** | 16K |
| Qwen3 8B | Q4_K | **~51 tok/s** | 16K |

At 33+ tok/s on 14B models, a 500-word response arrives in ~12–15 seconds — well above the ~20 tok/s threshold where things feel "slow" [[43]](https://craftrigs.com/articles/rtx-5060-ti-16gb-budget-local-llm/). For 8B models at 60–70 tok/s, it's essentially real-time.

### OCuLink eGPU: Nearly Lossless for Inference

This is the pleasant surprise. Once the model is loaded into VRAM, **OCuLink loses only ~1–3% vs. an internal PCIe x16 slot** for LLM inference [[27]](https://localaimaster.com/blog/thunderbolt-vs-oculink-ai)[[34]](https://localaimaster.com/blog/egpu-local-ai-benchmarks). The reason: token generation barely touches the PCIe bus — it's all happening inside the GPU's VRAM.

| Connection | Generation Tok/s | Loss vs Internal |
|---|---|---|
| Internal PCIe 5.0 x16 | 142.0 | Baseline |
| **OCuLink (PCIe 4.0 x4)** | **138.0** | **-2.8%** |
| Thunderbolt 4 | 121.0 | -14.8% |

Where OCuLink *does* matter: model load times are ~2× slower than internal, and first-token latency is slightly higher. But for interactive chat where the model stays resident, you won't notice [[34]](https://localaimaster.com/blog/egpu-local-ai-benchmarks).

### For Your Cognitive Architecture

Your architecture targets ~6GB VRAM total (with the 8B Ternary Bonsai at ~2.15GB). The 5060 Ti's 16GB gives you **plenty of headroom** — you could even experiment with larger variants or run the Bonsai alongside other models simultaneously. The 128GB system RAM is excellent for dataset loading, replay buffers, and the MoE SSM components.

---

## The Key Limitation: Memory Bandwidth

Here's the structural issue. The Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 uses **dual-channel DDR5-5600**, giving you ~62 GB/s measured bandwidth [[29]](https://craftrigs.com/guides/llama-cpp-cpu-offload-guide-70b-models/). This is fine for feeding the GPU, but it becomes the bottleneck when you need to run models that don't fit in 16GB VRAM.

**What this means for large models:**

| Model Size | Approach | Expected Tok/s |
|---|---|---|
| 8B–14B | 100% GPU | **33–71 tok/s** ✅ |
| 20B | 100% GPU (FP4) | **44–82 tok/s** ✅ |
| 30B–34B | Partial CPU offload | **~8–15 tok/s** ⚠️ |
| 70B (Q4) | Heavy CPU offload | **~2–4 tok/s** ❌ |
| 70B (Q4) | 45/80 layers GPU | **~4.2 tok/s** ⚠️ |

The 70B situation is instructive. With a 24GB GPU (like a 3090), you can offload ~45 of 80 layers to GPU and get ~4.2 tok/s on DDR5-5600 [[29]](https://craftrigs.com/guides/llama-cpp-cpu-offload-guide-70b-models/). With only 16GB, you'd offload fewer layers and be even more bandwidth-bound. At 2–4 tok/s, a 70B model is *functional* but not pleasant for interactive use.

**The 128GB capacity is not the problem — the dual-channel bandwidth is.** You can *load* a 70B or even 120B model, but it'll run slowly. For comparison, a Threadripper with 8-channel DDR5 would give you 4–5× the bandwidth and proportionally faster CPU inference [[40]](https://craftrigs.com/guides/70b-model-cpu-only-inference-256gb-ddr5-throughput-benchmarks/).

The 86 TOPS NPU sounds impressive, but **real-world LLM support is thin**. Most inference runs on the iGPU or dGPU, not the NPU. The NPU excels at low-power image recognition and Copilot-style tasks, not transformer inference [[14]](https://www.runlocalai.co/hardware/amd-ryzen-ai-9-hx-370)[[22]](https://www.youtube.com/watch). ## The Correction: Unified Memory Changes Everything

The Ryzen AI 9 HX 370's Radeon 890M iGPU uses **unified memory architecture** (UMA) — it shares system RAM with the CPU, similar to Apple Silicon. On **Linux**, the iGPU can access essentially all 128GB of your DDR5 through a mechanism called GTT (Graphics Translation Table) [[8]](https://medium.com/@federicogiampietro/enough-with-nvidia-qwen3-next-80b-8-bit-on-ryzen-ai-9-hx370-3cd616671428). This means:

> **The 128GB isn't just CPU RAM — it's GPU-accessible memory for inference.**

---

## The Real Architecture You're Building

| Component | Role | Memory Pool | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RTX 5060 Ti 16GB** | CUDA training + fast inference | 16GB GDDR7 (448 GB/s) | Training cognitive architecture, 8B–20B models at 33–82 tok/s |
| **Radeon 890M iGPU** | Large model inference | Up to ~120GB of system DDR5 (~62 GB/s) | 70B–120B+ models that don't fit on the 5060 Ti |
| **128GB DDR5-5600** | Unified memory pool | Shared CPU + iGPU | Hosting massive models, datasets |

This is actually a **very smart dual-GPU strategy**. The 5060 Ti handles everything that fits in 16GB at high speed. The iGPU handles the overflow — models too large for the dGPU — at reduced but functional speed.

---

## What the iGPU + 128GB Can Actually Do

The key enabler is the **Vulkan backend** in llama.cpp on Linux. On Strix Point, Vulkan dramatically outperforms ROCm for token generation and has no VRAM cap — the GPU can address system RAM freely through GTT [[8]](https://medium.com/@federicogiampietro/enough-with-nvidia-qwen3-next-80b-8-bit-on-ryzen-ai-9-hx370-3cd616671428)[[23]](https://dev.to/lanternproton/windows-vs-linux-for-local-ai-my-radeon-890m-has-96gb-of-ram-but-windows-only-lets-me-use-35gb-39ln).

Real-world results on HX 370 with 96GB RAM and Vulkan [[8]](https://medium.com/@federicogiampietro/enough-with-nvidia-qwen3-next-80b-8-bit-on-ryzen-ai-9-hx370-3cd616671428)[[10]](https://ivoras.substack.com/p/2-month-minipc-mini-review-minisforum):

| Model | Quantization | Size | Tok/s (tg) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3 8B | Q4_K_M | ~4.7 GB | **~13 tok/s** | Snappy |
| DeepSeek R1 Distill 14B | Q4_K_M | ~8.4 GB | **~9 tok/s** | Usable |
| Qwen3 Next 80B (MoE) | 8-bit | ~45 GB | **~5–8 tok/s** | Functional |
| Kimi-Linear 48B | — | ~28 GB | **~19 tok/s** | Impressive for iGPU |

And from the Strix Halo (bigger brother, 256 GB/s bandwidth) for reference — the HX 370 will be proportionally slower due to ~62 GB/s vs ~256 GB/s bandwidth [[12]](https://github.com/visorcraft/strix-halo-llm-perf):

| Model | Strix Halo tok/s | Est. HX 370 tok/s |
|---|---|---|
| Llama 3.1 70B Q4_K_M | ~5.1 | **~1.5–2.5** |
| Qwen3 30B-A3B MoE Q4 | ~86 | **~20–25** |
| GPT-OSS 120B Q4 | ~53 | **~12–15** |
| Qwen3 235B Q3 | ~17 | **~4–5** |

The MoE models (like Qwen3 30B-A3B) are the sweet spot — they have large parameter counts but small active parameters, so they're bandwidth-friendly and run surprisingly fast [[10]](https://ivoras.substack.com/p/2-month-minipc-mini-review-minisforum)[[12]](https://github.com/visorcraft/strix-halo-llm-perf).

---

## The Critical Detail: Linux Is Mandatory

**Windows caps the 890M's shared GPU memory at ~3.5GB** — making anything above 7B models impossible on the iGPU [[23]](https://dev.to/lanternproton/windows-vs-linux-for-local-ai-my-radeon-890m-has-96gb-of-ram-but-windows-only-lets-me-use-35gb-39ln). On Linux, there's no such cap. The GPU can address system RAM freely. You'll need:

```bash
# Kernel parameters for large model support
amdgpu.gttsize=40960    # Allow GPU to address up to 40GB+ via GTT
```

And for the Vulkan backend in llama.cpp, it just works — no special configuration needed beyond having Mesa RADV installed [[8]](https://medium.com/@federicogiampietro/enough-with-nvidia-qwen3-next-80b-8-bit-on-ryzen-ai-9-hx370-3cd616671428)[[9]](https://msf.github.io/blogpost/local-llm-performance-framework13.html).

---

## Revised Verdict

| Criterion | Previous (Wrong) | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| 8B–20B inference | 33–82 tok/s (5060 Ti) | **Same** — 5060 Ti handles these |
| 70B model inference | 2–4 tok/s (CPU) | **~2–5 tok/s (iGPU)** — functional, not CPU-bound |
| 120B+ models | Unusable | **~1–15 tok/s (iGPU)** — depends on MoE vs dense |
| 128GB RAM utility | "Limited by bandwidth" | **High** — directly GPU-accessible for inference |
| Training | 5060 Ti only | **Same** — CUDA required, 5060 Ti handles it |
| OS requirement | Either | **Linux required** for iGPU large-model inference |

---

## The Practical Workflow

```
Everyday use:
  5060 Ti → 8B-20B models at 33-82 tok/s (real-time chat)
  iGPU idle or running smaller background tasks

When you need a 70B+ model:
  5060 Ti → still available for other tasks
  iGPU + 128GB → loads 70B-120B model at 2-15 tok/s
  Yes it's slower, but it RUNS — and the 5060 Ti is free
```

For your cognitive architecture specifically: the 5060 Ti handles training (CUDA) and the Bonsai 8B inference at high speed. The iGPU + 128GB gives you the *option* to experiment with much larger models when you want to, without buying a second dGPU.

---

## Bottom Line

**This is a better build than I initially assessed.** The unified memory architecture means your 128GB investment pulls double duty — it's both system RAM and GPU-accessible memory for large model inference. The 5060 Ti + iGPU combination gives you:

- **Speed** where it matters (8B–20B on the 5060 Ti)
- **Capacity** where it matters (70B+ on the iGPU)
- **Training capability** (CUDA on the 5060 Ti)
- **All in a mini PC form factor** for ~$1,300

The one thing I'd emphasize: **run Linux.** Windows neuters the iGPU's unified memory advantage. With Linux + llama.cpp Vulkan, the full 128GB is available to the GPU, and that's what makes this build work as a dual-purpose AI machine.

The fundamental problem: **V4-Flash's 284B total parameters need to live *somewhere*.** Even at the most aggressive quantization (Q2), you're looking at ~100–120GB just for weights — that would consume nearly all your 128GB RAM, leaving nothing for KV cache, the OS, or anything else [[14]](https://deepseekai.guide/tools/deepseek-hardware-calculator/)[[16]](https://canitrun.dev/models/deepseek-v4-pro/).

## The MoE Offloading Dream (and Why It Doesn't Save You)

In theory, with MoE models you only need the *active* parameters (13B for Flash) in fast memory — the rest can sit in slower storage. In practice:

- **The 284B experts still need to be *stored* somewhere.** 128GB RAM isn't enough for the full set even at Q2 without squeezing.
- **Expert routing is data-dependent.** You can't predict which experts will activate, so you need reasonably fast access to all of them.
- **Even if it technically loads**, you'd get maybe **1–2 tok/s** with constant disk swapping. That's not usable for interactive chat.

# Can Your Setup Run GLM-5.2?

**No — not even close.** GLM-5.2 is a datacenter-scale model. Let me show you exactly why.

---

## GLM-5.2: What You're Asking About

GLM-5.2 is Zhipu AI's flagship, released June 13, 2026 — a **744B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts** model with a 1M-token context window, MIT license, and performance rivaling GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 on coding benchmarks [[8]](https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.2)[[16]](https://datanorth.ai/news/zhipu-ai-releases-glm-5-2)[[27]](https://venturebeat.com/technology/z-ais-open-weights-glm-5-2-beats-gpt-5-5-on-multiple-long-horizon-coding-benchmarks-for-1-6th-the-cost).

| Spec | Value |
|---|---|
| Total parameters | **744B–753B** |
| Active per token | ~40B (MoE) |
| Context window | 1,000,000 tokens |
| License | MIT (open weights) |
| BF16 disk size | ~1.5 TB |

---

## The Memory Math

Even at the most aggressive quantizations, the numbers are far beyond your hardware:

| Quantization | Disk/Memory Needed | Your Hardware | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1-bit Dynamic** (absolute minimum) | **176–180 GB** | 144 GB (128 + 16) | **~32 GB short** |
| 2-bit Dynamic (UD-IQ2_XXS) | 241–256 GB | 144 GB | ~100 GB short |
| Q4_K_M (sweet spot) | ~476 GB | 144 GB | ~332 GB short |
| FP8 (production) | ~754 GB | 144 GB | ~610 GB short |
| BF16 (full) | ~1.5 TB | 144 GB | ~1.36 TB short |

The Unsloth team — who created the most aggressive quants — states the minimum is **256GB unified memory** for the 2-bit quant, or a **1×24GB GPU + 256GB system RAM** with MoE offloading [[12]](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/glm-5.2)[[18]](https://www.computeleap.com/blog/glm-5-2-local-setup-open-model-nobody-can-ban-2026/). You have half that.

Even the bleeding-edge **1-bit dynamic quant at 176GB** won't fit in your 128GB + 16GB = 144GB total [[12]](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/glm-5.2)[[18]](https://www.computeleap.com/blog/glm-5-2-local-setup-open-model-nobody-can-ban-2026/). And that's before accounting for KV cache, which at 1M context would add enormous overhead.

---

## Why MoE Offloading Doesn't Save You

With MoE models, you can offload expert layers to system RAM and only keep active parameters in VRAM. This is how people run GLM-5.2 on a single 24GB GPU + 256GB RAM. But the **total weights still need to live somewhere** — and 744B parameters, even at 1-bit, need ~176GB of storage. Your 128GB RAM simply isn't enough to hold them.

The 5060 Ti's 16GB is sufficient for the ~40B active parameters at Q4 (about 20–24GB needed for active + KV cache at short context), but the other ~700B parameters of expert weights have nowhere to go.

---

## What Your Setup *Can* Run

Your build is still excellent for a wide range of models. Here's where GLM-5.2 fits in the landscape:

| Model | Params (Total/Active) | Min Memory | Your Setup? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3 30B-A3B** (MoE) | 30B / 3B | ~18 GB | ✅ **Great** (iGPU, ~20–25 tok/s) |
| **DeepSeek R1 Distill 32B** | 32B dense | ~20 GB | ✅ **Good** (5060 Ti, ~20–25 tok/s) |
| **Llama 3.1 70B Q4** | 70B dense | ~40 GB | ✅ **Functional** (iGPU, ~2–5 tok/s) |
| **GLM-4.5** (if available) | 355B / 32B | ~200 GB (Q2) | ❌ Too large |
| **DeepSeek V4-Flash** | 284B / 13B | ~160 GB (Q2) | ❌ Too large |
| **GLM-5 / 5.1 / 5.2** | 744B / 40B | **176–256 GB** | ❌ **Way too large** |

---

## What It Would Take to Run GLM-5.2

| Tier | Hardware | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Bare minimum** (1-bit, slow) | Mac Studio M4 Ultra 256GB unified, or workstation with 256GB+ RAM | ~$4,000–6,000 |
| **Usable** (2-bit, 3–9 tok/s) | Mac Studio M3/M4 Ultra 256GB, or 1×24GB GPU + 256GB RAM | ~$5,000–7,000 |

The 2-bit quant on a 256GB Mac Studio gets you about **3–5 tok/s** — functional but slow. The 1-bit quant is described as "minimum viable — does my pipeline work?" territory [[18]](https://www.computeleap.com/blog/glm-5-2-local-setup-open-model-nobody-can-ban-2026/).

---

## Bottom Line

GLM-5.2 is a **datacenter-class model** that happens to have open weights. The fact that it's MIT-licensed and "open" doesn't change the physics: 744B parameters need hundreds of gigabytes of memory. Your 128GB + 16GB setup is about **2× too small** even for the most aggressive quantization ever created for it.

The good news: your build runs everything up to ~70B dense models and small MoE models beautifully. GLM-5.2 is simply in a different weight class — it's designed for 8×H200 server nodes, not mini PCs. If you want GLM-5.2-level intelligence on your hardware, you'd need to wait for a potential "GLM-5.2-Distill" or use the API ($1.40/M input tokens, $4.40/M output — quite affordable) [[27]](https://venturebeat.com/technology/z-ais-open-weights-glm-5-2-beats-gpt-5-5-on-multiple-long-horizon-coding-benchmarks-for-1-6th-the-cost).

# How Many Users Can Tier 1 Hardware Support?

Great question — and the answer depends heavily on **context length**. The KV cache is the bottleneck for concurrency, and DeepSeek V4's hybrid attention makes it surprisingly efficient. Let me break it down.

---

## The Key Number: KV Cache Per User

DeepSeek V4-Flash's hybrid CSA+HCA attention compresses the KV cache to just **~9.62 GiB per sequence at 1M context (bf16)**, or **~4.8 GiB with fp8** — about 7–10% of what V3.2 needed [[8]](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-04-24-deepseek-v4)[[16]](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-project.github.io/blob/main/_posts/2026-04-24-deepseek-v4.md). This is the magic that makes multi-user serving possible on modest hardware.

| Context Length | KV Cache per User (fp8) | KV Cache per User (bf16) |
|---|---|---|
| **1M tokens** (full) | ~4.8 GB | ~9.6 GB |
| **128K tokens** | ~0.6 GB | ~1.2 GB |
| **32K tokens** | ~0.15 GB | ~0.3 GB |
| **8K tokens** | ~0.04 GB | ~0.08 GB |

---

## Concurrency by Hardware Tier

The formula: `(Total Memory − Model Weights − Overhead) ÷ (KV Cache per User × Efficiency Factor)`

Real-world efficiency is ~40–50% of theoretical due to memory fragmentation, CUDA graphs, and scheduling overhead. I'll use **0.45× efficiency** based on observed vLLM deployments.

### Mac Studio M4 Ultra 192GB (~$7,000)

| Context | Theoretical Max | **Realistic Concurrent Users** |
|---|---|---|
| 1M tokens | ~6 | **~2–3** |
| 128K tokens | ~48 | **~20–25** |
| 32K tokens | ~193 | **~85–90** |
| 8K tokens | ~763 | **~340** |

Weights: ~158 GB (FP4+FP8 native). Available for KV: ~29 GB. At 1M context, you get 2–3 concurrent users — enough for a personal server or small family. At typical chat lengths (8–32K), you can serve dozens to hundreds [[14]](https://lushbinary.com/blog/deepseek-v4-self-hosting-guide-vllm-hardware-deployment/)[[17]](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/deepseek-v4-flash-bringing-frontier-ai-to-the-home/370416).

### Mac Studio M3 Ultra 256GB (~$9,499)

| Context | Theoretical Max | **Realistic Concurrent Users** |
|---|---|---|
| 1M tokens | ~19 | **~8–10** |
| 128K tokens | ~155 | **~70** |
| 32K tokens | ~620 | **~280** |
| 8K tokens | ~2,450 | **~1,100** |

The extra 64GB goes entirely to KV cache. At 1M context, you can serve a small team. At normal chat lengths, you're essentially unlimited for personal/department use [[14]](https://lushbinary.com/blog/deepseek-v4-self-hosting-guide-vllm-hardware-deployment/).

### 2× RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell 96GB (~$22,000)

| Context | Theoretical Max | **Realistic Concurrent Users** |
|---|---|---|
| 1M tokens | ~6 | **~2–3** |
| 128K tokens | ~48 | **~20–25** |
| 32K tokens | ~193 | **~85–90** |

Similar to the M4 Ultra 192GB. The advantage here is CUDA ecosystem and higher token generation speed (~45–60 tok/s vs ~25 tok/s on Mac), not more users [[14]](https://lushbinary.com/blog/deepseek-v4-self-hosting-guide-vllm-hardware-deployment/).

### 4× Used RTX 3090 24GB (~$3,000)

| Context | Theoretical Max | **Realistic Concurrent Users** |
|---|---|---|
| 1M tokens | ~1 | **~1** (barely) |
| 128K tokens | ~8 | **~3–4** |
| 32K tokens | ~32 | **~14** |

This is the budget option and it's tight. At Q2 quantization, weights are ~80–100 GB across 96 GB total VRAM, leaving very little for KV cache. At 1M context you're single-user. At 32K context, you can serve a small household. The real win here is price, not concurrency [[14]](https://lushbinary.com/blog/deepseek-v4-self-hosting-guide-vllm-hardware-deployment/).

---

## Real-World Data Points

These aren't just estimates — they match observed deployments:

- **2× DGX Spark (256 GB unified):** vLLM reports **3.9× max concurrency at 1M context** and **4.7× at 512K** [[17]](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/deepseek-v4-flash-bringing-frontier-ai-to-the-home/370416). A community recipe caps `max_num_seqs` at **2 for 1M context** on this hardware [[20]](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/deepseek-v4-flash-1-048-576-context-on-2x-dgx-spark-custom-sparkrun-recipe/373206).

- **4× H200:** Handles **8 concurrent users at 64K context** but hangs beyond that without tuning [[27]](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41125).

## What "Users" Actually Means

| Use Case | Context Needed | Users per M4 Ultra 192GB |
|---|---|---|
| **Personal AI assistant** (chat, coding) | 8–32K | 85–340 — effectively unlimited |
| **Family server** (4 people chatting) | 8–32K | Easily handles all |
| **Small team** (10 people, agentic coding) | 128K | 20–25 — comfortable |
| **Department** (50 people, document analysis) | 128K | 20–25 — needs M3 Ultra 256GB |

## The Practical Takeaway

For a **personal or family AI server**, the Mac Studio M4 Ultra 192GB at ~$7,000 is more than enough. You'll never hit concurrency limits at normal chat lengths. The only time you'll feel constrained is if multiple people simultaneously need 1M-token context windows — which is rare outside of specialized agentic workflows.

For a **small team** (5–15 people), the M3 Ultra 256GB at ~$9,499 gives comfortable headroom even at longer contexts.

For a **department or company**, you're looking at 8× H200 territory ($250K+) or cloud rental.

The key insight: **DeepSeek V4's KV cache efficiency means concurrency scales much better than you'd expect.** A 192GB Mac can serve 20–25 simultaneous users at 128K context — that's a real team, not just a personal toy. The 1M context is the only scenario that constrains you to single-digit users.

# Tier 2 Concurrency: Mac Studio M4 Ultra 192GB + DeepSeek V4-Flash

Ah, my apologies for the confusion — you're asking about the **~$7,000 Mac Studio tier**, not the $250K datacenter tier. Let me give you the real answer, which has an important nuance the raw memory math doesn't capture.

---

## The Memory Math (Theoretical)

DeepSeek V4-Flash at Q4_K_M takes ~162 GB. On a 192GB Mac, that leaves ~25–30 GB for KV cache and overhead [ [[11]](https://www.runlocalai.co/models/deepseek-v4-flash)](https://www.runlocalai.co/models/deepseek-v4-flash) [[14]](https://lushbinary.com/blog/deepseek-v4-self-hosting-guide-vllm-hardware-deployment/)(https://lushbinary.com/blog/deepseek-v4-self-hosting-guide-vllm-hardware-deployment/). The hybrid CSA+HCA attention compresses KV cache to just ~4.8 GB per sequence at 1M context (fp8) [[8]](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-04-24-deepseek-v4)(https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-04-24-deepseek-v4).

| Context | KV Cache/User (fp8) | Theoretical Max Users | Realistic (0.45× efficiency) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1M tokens | ~4.8 GB | ~5 | **~2–3** |
| 128K tokens | ~0.6 GB | ~41 | **~18–20** |
| 32K tokens | ~0.15 GB | ~166 | **~75** |
| 8K tokens | ~0.04 GB | ~625 | **~280** |

So theoretically, at normal chat lengths, the memory supports dozens to hundreds of concurrent users.

---

## The Reality: This Is Not a Multi-User Server

Here's the catch that the memory math hides: **the Mac software ecosystem doesn't do production multi-user serving.**

The Mac runs DeepSeek V4-Flash through llama.cpp, MLX, or antirez/ds4 — none of which have vLLM's continuous batching for high-concurrency serving [[17]](https://codersera.com/blog/deepseek-v4-flash-rtx-pro-6000-blackwell-benchmarks-2026/)(https://codersera.com/blog/deepseek-v4-flash-rtx-pro-6000-blackwell-benchmarks-2026/). The oMLX benchmarks on M3 Ultra 512GB show batching does work (1× → 28.9 tok/s, 2× → 39.9, 4× → 52.7), but this is batched inference, not independent multi-user serving with request-level isolation [ [[22]](https://omlx.ai/benchmarks/fns6932e)](https://omlx.ai/benchmarks/fns6932e).

The community consensus is clear:

> *"Mac Studio M3 Ultra 512 GB... Runs V4 Flash via MLX at ~25-35 tok/s single-stream. Surprising value for single-user or small-team use. **No production-grade serving, no high concurrency, no datacenter form factor.**"* [ [[17]](https://codersera.com/blog/deepseek-v4-flash-rtx-pro-6000-blackwell-benchmarks-2026/)](https://codersera.com/blog/deepseek-v4-flash-rtx-pro-6000-blackwell-benchmarks-2026/)

> *"Single Mac Studio M3 Ultra 192GB runs... a usable daily driver, not just a batch-processing tool."* [ [[11]](https://www.runlocalai.co/models/deepseek-v4-flash)](https://www.runlocalai.co/models/deepseek-v4-flash)

---

## What "Users" Actually Means on Tier 2

| Scenario | Realistic Users | Experience |
|---|---|---|
| **Personal AI assistant** (you, coding, research) | **1** | ~25–35 tok/s — excellent daily driver |
| **Family server** (2–4 people, sequential use) | **2–4** | Fine if not simultaneous; queuing required |
| **Small team, simultaneous** | **1–2** | Degraded at 2 concurrent; not designed for it |
| **Department/server** | **Not suitable** | Wrong tool — need vLLM on multi-GPU |

---

## The Comparison That Matters

| | Mac Studio M4 Ultra 192GB | 2× DGX Spark (256GB) | 4× RTX Pro 6000 (384GB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cost** | ~$7,000 | ~$6,000 | ~$34,000 |
| **Single-stream speed** | ~25–35 tok/s | ~38–41 tok/s | ~25–40 tok/s |
| **Multi-user serving** | ❌ Not designed for it | ✅ vLLM, ~350 agg tok/s @ c=32 | ✅ SGLang, 200–400 users @ 32K |
| **Best for** | Personal daily driver | Small team server | Department/production |
| **Software** | llama.cpp, MLX, ds4 | vLLM (native FP8) | SGLang (vLLM buggy) |

The 2× DGX Spark at a similar price point (~$6,000) actually does proper multi-user serving — vLLM with continuous batching, ~41 tok/s single-stream, ~350 aggregate tok/s at 32 concurrent, and 3.9× max concurrency at 1M context [[12]](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/deepseek-v4-flash-bringing-frontier-ai-to-the-home/370416)(https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/deepseek-v4-flash-bringing-frontier-ai-to-the-home/370416) [[18]](https://github.com/elsung/dgx-spark-deepseek-v4-flash)(https://github.com/elsung/dgx-spark-deepseek-v4-flash). But it only has 256GB total (128GB × 2), so it runs a tighter quant.

---

## Bottom Line

**The Mac Studio M4 Ultra 192GB is a phenomenal personal AI workstation, not a server.** It runs DeepSeek V4-Flash at Q4_K_M with ~25–35 tok/s — genuinely interactive, excellent for one person's coding, research, and agentic workflows. You can share it with a family or 2–3 housemates if usage isn't simultaneous. But if you want 10+ people hitting it concurrently with independent requests, you need a different architecture (vLLM on multi-GPU or DGX Spark).

For your use case — personal AI, cognitive architecture training (on the 5060 Ti), and occasional large-model inference — the Mac Studio is the right tool. It's just not a server, and that's by design.

## The Architectural Insight: Why Tenstorrent Wins on Cost

Jim Keller's design philosophy [[16]](https://hypersinc.com/article/tenstorrent-ships-galaxy-blackhole-taking-on-nvidia-in-inference-1778072498050)(https://hypersinc.com/article/tenstorrent-ships-galaxy-blackhole-taking-on-nvidia-in-inference-1778072498050):

| Design Choice | NVIDIA | Tenstorrent | Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Memory** | HBM3e (expensive, supply-constrained) | GDDR6 (commodity, abundant) | Lower cost, lower bandwidth per chip |
| **Interconnect** | NVLink/NVSwitch (proprietary) | Standard Ethernet (commodity) | No vendor lock, cheaper scale-out |
| **Cooling** | Liquid (DGX) | Air-cooled (6U) | Lower datacenter costs |
| **Software** | CUDA (proprietary) | 100% open-source | No license fees, but less mature |
| **Architecture** | Monolithic GPU | Disaggregated chips in mesh | Scale by adding chips, not bigger chips |

The bet is that many medium-performance chips connected by Ethernet can match or beat fewer high-performance GPUs on cost-per-token, especially for MoE models where data movement dominates compute [[16]](https://hypersinc.com/article/tenstorrent-ships-galaxy-blackhole-taking-on-nvidia-in-inference-1778072498050)(https://hypersinc.com/article/tenstorrent-ships-galaxy-blackhole-taking-on-nvidia-in-inference-1778072498050) [[25]](https://blog.gpu.net/posts/2026/june/new-blog-june11/)(https://blog.gpu.net/posts/2026/june/new-blog-june11/).

## The Real Estate Co-op Model, Mapped to Compute

Real estate co-ops work like this:

| Real Estate Co-op | Compute Co-op Equivalent |
|---|---|
| Co-op corporation owns the building | Co-op LLC owns the GPU cluster |
| Members buy shares (proportional to unit size) | Members buy shares (proportional to compute allocation) |
| Share entitles member to occupy a specific unit | Share entitles member to a compute quota / priority tier |
| Monthly maintenance fees (operations, taxes, reserve) | Monthly fees (power, cooling, connectivity, depreciation reserve) |
| Members can sell shares (board approval) | Members can sell shares (co-op approval) |
| Building can have underlying mortgage | Hardware can be financed |
| One member, one vote (or proportional) | Democratic governance |

The mapping is clean. But there's one critical difference: **real estate appreciates; GPUs depreciate.** A Manhattan co-op share bought in 1990 is worth 5× today. An H200 bought in 2025 will be worth 20% of its purchase price in 2029. This changes the financial model fundamentally — you're buying **utility access**, not an appreciating asset.

## The Structural Challenges

### 1. GPU Depreciation (The Big One)

An H200 bought for $35,000 today might be worth $7,000 in 4 years. This means:

- **Share values decline.** Unlike a real estate co-op where your share appreciates, your compute co-op share depreciates. Members need to understand they're buying *access*, not an *investment*.
- **Regular capital calls.** Every 3–5 years, the co-op needs to raise fresh capital for a hardware refresh. This requires members who are committed for the long term.
- **The replacement reserve is critical.** The $5,500/month in Scenario A isn't optional — it's the difference between a sustainable co-op and one that slowly dies as hardware ages out.

### 2. Scheduling and Fair Allocation

With 200 members sharing 8 GPUs, you need a scheduling system. Options:

- **Time-sliced:** Each member gets reserved time slots (simple but inflexible)
- **Priority queue:** Members submit jobs; higher-tier members get priority (flexible but complex)
- **Token-based:** Members get monthly compute credits; unused credits roll over or expire (market-based)
- **Spot market:** Members bid for priority during peak times (efficient but potentially unfair)

The Louisville CDC feasibility study found that cooperative governance of technical infrastructure is viable — electric co-ops have been doing it for 90 years serving 42 million Americans [[19]](https://www.ntari.org/post/louisville-community-data-center-cooperative-feasibility-study)(https://www.ntari.org/post/louisville-community-data-center-cooperative-feasibility-study). But compute scheduling is more complex than electricity distribution.

### 3. The Technical Expertise Gap

Someone needs to:
- Provision and maintain the hardware
- Manage the scheduling software
- Handle security and access control
- Debug model deployment issues
- Plan hardware refreshes

This is a part-time job at minimum, a full-time job at scale. The co-op either hires someone or relies on member volunteers (which works until it doesn't).

### 4. The Chicken-and-Egg Problem

You need members to raise capital, but members want to see working hardware before committing. Solutions:
- **Founding member tier:** Initial members put up more capital for founder shares
- **Phased rollout:** Start with a smaller cluster (e.g., 2× H200 or a Mac Studio cluster), prove the model, then scale
- **Pre-sales:** Sell memberships before purchasing hardware (requires trust)

## What Geothermal Cooling Delivers

Cooling is **30–40% of total datacenter energy consumption** [[11]](https://rhg.com/research/geothermal-data-center-electricity-demand/)(https://rhg.com/research/geothermal-data-center-electricity-demand/). Geothermal ground-loop cooling attacks this directly.

Real-world data from Iron Mountain's Boyers, PA facility — which uses a 200-foot underground limestone mine reservoir for cooling — shows a **34% reduction in total energy use** [[16]](https://celp.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Pennsylvania-Report_Supplement.pdf)(https://celp.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Pennsylvania-Report_Supplement.pdf) [[21]](https://betterbuildingssolutioncenter.energy.gov/showcase-projects/iron-mountain-data-centers-geothermal-cooling-system)(https://betterbuildingssolutioncenter.energy.gov/showcase-projects/iron-mountain-data-centers-geothermal-cooling-system). NREL studies suggest **annual cost savings of up to $1 million for a typical datacenter** and **30% reduction in energy costs vs. traditional HVAC** [[16]](https://celp.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Pennsylvania-Report_Supplement.pdf)(https://celp.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Pennsylvania-Report_Supplement.pdf).

For a small co-op cluster:

| System | Installed Cost | What It Does |
|---|---|---|
| **Closed-loop ground heat exchanger** | **$20,000–50,000** (4–8 boreholes at 150–300 ft) | Provides primary cooling loop, ~30–40% energy reduction |
| **Cold Underground Thermal Energy Storage (UTES)** | **$30,000–80,000** (if geology permits) | Seasonal thermal storage, "negawatts" — peak cooling without peak power [ [[26]](https://pangea.stanford.edu/ERE/pdf/IGAstandard/SGW/2025/Winick.pdf)](https://pangea.stanford.edu/ERE/pdf/IGAstandard/SGW/2025/Winick.pdf) |

The geothermal system reduces the ~$12,000/year cooling cost by 30–40%, saving **$3,600–4,800/year**. But the bigger win is that it also reduces the *power* needed for cooling — which means the solar array can be smaller, or more of the solar output goes to compute rather than cooling.

More importantly, geothermal cooling enables **PUE below 1.1** — meaning nearly every watt going into the facility goes to compute, not overhead [[19]](https://jisenergy.com/geothermal-for-ai-technoeconomic-blueprint-for-powering-ai-factories/)(https://jisenergy.com/geothermal-for-ai-technoeconomic-blueprint-for-powering-ai-factories/). Traditional datacenters run PUE of 1.4–1.6. At PUE 1.1, your 5.6 kW IT load needs only 6.2 kW total — vs. 8–9 kW at PUE 1.5.

## The Role of Gas in the Off-Grid Scenario

The OffgridAI research I cited found that a DC-coupled solar + battery + gas microgrid achieves **$93–109/MWh** with 44–90% renewable penetration [](https://www.offgridai.us/). ## The Overbuild Strategy: No Gas At All

The cleanest approach for a co-op committed to sustainability: **overbuild solar and battery to cover the worst-case scenario rather than relying on fossil backup.**

The math: a 5.6 kW IT load at PUE 1.1 needs ~6.2 kW continuous. That's ~148 kWh/day. In a poor solar region (3.5 sun-hours/day in winter), you'd need:

- **Solar:** ~60–80 kW DC (vs. 50 kW in the hybrid scenario) to generate enough even on short winter days
- **Battery:** ~400–600 kWh (vs. 200 kWh) to cover 2–3 consecutive cloudy days

This roughly **doubles** the solar + battery capital cost — from ~$50,000–70,000 to ~$100,000–140,000 (post-ITC). But it eliminates the gas generator, the fuel cost, and the philosophical compromise entirely.

For 200 co-op members, the buy-in goes from ~$2,500 to ~$3,000–3,500, and the monthly fee stays at ~$40–50. The tradeoff is higher upfront capital for permanent energy independence with zero combustion.

---

## The Geothermal Angle

Geothermal isn't just for cooling. If the co-op site has good geothermal resources (not just ground-loop temperature, but actual hot rock at drillable depth), you could generate baseload power directly — 24/7, zero carbon, no battery needed. This is site-dependent (western US, Iceland, East African Rift, etc.) and expensive to drill, but it's the holy grail: **firm, clean power that matches datacenter load profiles perfectly.**

---

## Bottom Line

Natural gas backup is the pragmatic default in most microgrid designs because it's cheap and reliable. But for a co-op whose members are explicitly opting into a green model, the overbuild strategy (more solar + more battery, no combustion) is the philosophically consistent path. It costs more upfront but eliminates the ongoing purchase of fossil fuel and the cognitive dissonance of burning gas to power a "green" datacenter.

The co-op model actually makes this easier than it would be for a traditional operator — because members who choose a green co-op are self-selecting for people willing to pay a slightly higher buy-in for zero-carbon operations.

# Proposal: Cooperative AI Data Center

## Democratizing Access to Frontier AI Through Shared Infrastructure

---

## 1. Executive Summary

This proposal outlines the formation of a member-owned cooperative data center providing shared access to frontier AI models — including DeepSeek V4-Pro, GLM-5.2, and other large-scale open-weight models — at a fraction of the cost of individual ownership or equivalent API consumption. The co-op leverages a real-estate cooperative ownership model, adapted for compute infrastructure, where members purchase equity shares and pay monthly operating fees proportional to the facility's actual costs.

Two hardware configurations are analyzed — one NVIDIA-based, one Tenstorrent-based — each with and without integrated renewable energy (solar, battery storage, and geothermal cooling). The green energy variant reduces monthly operating costs by 23–33% while adding to upfront capital, with a 4–7 year payback period.

---

## 2. The Problem

Frontier open-weight AI models are now freely available — DeepSeek V4-Flash (284B), DeepSeek V4-Pro (1.6T), and GLM-5.2 (744B) are all MIT-licensed. But running them requires hardware that costs **$110,000 to $330,000+** — well beyond the reach of individuals or small organizations. Meanwhile, API pricing, while low per-token, accumulates rapidly for power users and offers no data sovereignty, no fine-tuning capability, and no protection against rate limits or policy changes.

A cooperative model solves this by pooling capital across members. 200 members contributing $1,650 each can purchase an 8× H200 node capable of running every open-weight model in existence.

---

## 3. Cooperative Structure

### 3.1 Legal Form

The co-op is structured as a **limited cooperative association (LCA)** or **LLC** — the same legal forms used by housing cooperatives, credit unions, and rural electric cooperatives. Key properties:

| Element | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Ownership** | Co-op entity owns all hardware, land, and green infrastructure |
| **Equity** | Members purchase shares proportional to the capital raised |
| **Governance** | One member, one vote (democratic) or proportional (weighted) — determined by charter |
| **Monthly fees** | Operating costs divided among members; fees reflect actual cost, not profit |
| **Share transfer** | Members may sell shares subject to board approval (like a housing co-op) |
| **Surplus** | Any surplus is returned to members as fee reductions or held in reserve |
| **Dissolution** | Assets liquidated and proceeds distributed to members per charter |

### 3.2 What Members Receive

- **Access to frontier AI models** (V4-Pro, GLM-5.2, V4-Flash, and all smaller models) via a shared inference endpoint
- **Compute quota** based on share tier (basic, standard, power)
- **Fine-tuning capability** on co-op hardware (scheduled access)
- **Data sovereignty** — no third-party API provider sees member queries
- **No rate limits** beyond co-op scheduling fairness rules
- **Democratic governance** over hardware refresh decisions, model selection, and policy

### 3.3 What Members Do Not Receive

- An appreciating asset. GPU hardware depreciates. Members are buying **access**, not an investment. The share's resale value will decline over the hardware's useful life (typically 4–5 years).
- Guaranteed availability. The co-op uses fair scheduling, not dedicated capacity. At peak times, members may queue.

# Do You Really Need to Replace Hardware Every 5 Years?

**No — not necessarily.** I was being conservative in the proposal, and I should be more precise about what's actually driving that number. Let me break down what's real and what's assumption.

---

## What Actually Happens to GPU Hardware Over Time

### Physical Lifespan

Enterprise GPUs (H200, H100, A100) are built for **7–10+ years** of continuous operation. The silicon itself doesn't degrade in any meaningful way at normal operating temperatures. What can fail:

| Component | Typical Lifespan | Replaceable? |
|---|---|---|
| Fans / cooling | 3–7 years | ✅ Yes, individually |
| Thermal paste / pads | 3–5 years | ✅ Yes, routine maintenance |
| Capacitors / VRMs | 7–15 years | ⚠️ Board-level repair |
| GDDR6 / HBM memory | 10+ years | ❌ No |
| GPU silicon | 15+ years (effectively indefinite) | ❌ No |

A well-maintained H200 node should run for **8–10 years** before any meaningful risk of hardware failure. The 5-year figure I used isn't about the hardware dying — it's about something else entirely.

### What the 5-Year Figure Actually Represents

The 5-year replacement cycle in enterprise IT isn't driven by hardware failure. It's driven by:

1. **Warranty expiration.** Enterprise support contracts typically run 3–5 years. After that, you're self-insuring against failures.

2. **Performance obsolescence.** A new generation of GPUs arrives every 2–3 years, offering 2–4× the performance. Enterprises refresh to stay competitive.

3. **Accounting depreciation.** IRS rules depreciate computer equipment over 5 years. This is a tax artifact, not a physical reality.

4. **Vendor lock-in.** Dell, HPE, and others design refresh cycles into their sales model. It benefits them, not you.

**None of these apply to a co-op in the same way.** The co-op isn't competing on benchmark scores. It's running specific models (V4-Pro, GLM-5.2) that don't get heavier over time. If the hardware runs those models at acceptable speeds today, it will run them at the same speeds in 2030.

---

## What This Means for the Co-op Economics

### Revised: Maintenance Reserve Instead of Replacement Reserve

| | Original (5-year replacement) | Revised (10-year maintenance) |
|---|---|---|
| **Annual reserve** | $66,000 (8× H200) | **$15,000–20,000** |
| **What it covers** | Full hardware replacement | Component failures, thermal maintenance, spare parts |
| **Replacement trigger** | Calendar-based (every 5 years) | **Condition-based** (when performance or reliability actually degrades) |
| **Hardware refresh** | Mandatory capital call | **Optional member vote** — upgrade only if members want faster speeds |

### Revised Per-Member Costs (8× H200, 200 Members, Green)

| | Original | Revised |
|---|---|---|
| Monthly opex | $8,525 | **$4,700–5,100** |
| Monthly per member | $43 | **$24–26** |
| Annual per member | $516 | **$288–312** |

The monthly fee drops by roughly **40%** when you stop pre-funding a replacement that may not be needed for a decade.

---

## The Real Question: When Would You Actually Want to Upgrade?

The co-op would consider a hardware refresh when:

| Trigger | Likelihood at 5 Years | Likelihood at 10 Years |
|---|---|---|
| **Hardware failure** (unrecoverable) | Low (~5–10%) | Moderate (~20–30%) |
| **New models require more VRAM** | Possible (V5 might need 2TB+) | Likely |
| **Members want faster inference** | Possible | Likely |
| **Power efficiency gains justify swap** | Moderate (next-gen is more efficient) | High |
| **Software drops support for H200** | Very low (CUDA supports everything) | Low |

The most likely scenario: the H200s keep running V4-Pro and GLM-5.2 perfectly well for 8–10 years. At some point, a new generation of models arrives that needs more VRAM, and the co-op votes on whether to upgrade. That's a **choice**, not a **requirement**.

---

## Revised Recommendation

| | Original Proposal | Revised |
|---|---|---|
| **Replacement reserve** | $66,000/yr (full replacement at 5 years) | **$18,000/yr** (maintenance + eventual replacement at 8–12 years) |
| **Replacement philosophy** | Calendar-driven | **Condition-driven + member vote** |
| **Hardware expected life** | 5 years | **8–12 years** |
| **Monthly fee (200 members, green)** | $43 | **$25–27** |
| **Buy-in (200 members, green)** | $2,371 | **$2,371** (unchanged — capital is the same) |

The buy-in doesn't change because the hardware still costs what it costs. But the monthly fee drops substantially because you're not pre-funding an aggressive replacement cycle.

---

## The Honest Answer

I used 5 years because it's the industry standard for enterprise IT budgeting, and I wanted to be conservative. But for a co-op running inference on specific models, it's overly aggressive. The hardware will almost certainly last 8–10 years with basic maintenance. The replacement reserve should be sized for **actual maintenance and eventual replacement when needed**, not for an arbitrary calendar cycle.

The co-op's real financial advantage isn't just the green energy savings — it's that you're not running a profit-motivated enterprise that needs to stay on the cutting edge. You're running a utility. Utilities don't replace perfectly functional infrastructure on a calendar schedule. They maintain it, and they replace it when it's actually worn out or when the members vote that an upgrade is worth the cost.

This is a fantastic question, and you've put your finger on one of the most active frontiers in AI agent research right now. Let me break it down systematically.

---

## Short Answer

**Your intuition is correct and it's the direction the entire field is moving.** Using a neural network (typically an LLM) to extract entities, relationships, and relevance signals, then storing those in a graph database — with temporal awareness and utility-based pruning — is the emerging best practice. It's not fully "solved" in the sense of a turnkey solution, but the architecture has largely converged.

Your friend's Neo4j approach is on the right track. Your idea of adding a learned relevance/pruning layer on top is exactly what the cutting-edge systems (Zep/Graphiti, ReMe, CraniMem, SEDM) are doing.

---

## The Core Insight You Nailed

You said:

> *"I feel like a transformer is already somewhat a database but the clarity varies of its information retrieval. The weights do however determine related information."*

This is exactly right — and it's the reason RAG exists. An LLM's weights are a **lossy, frozen-at-training-time** compression of its training corpus. What you're describing is building an **explicit, updatable, queryable** external memory that complements the implicit knowledge in the weights. The graph approach gives you something the weights alone cannot: **structured, evolving, auditable relationships with provenance.**

---

## The Converged Architecture (as of mid-2026)

The community has largely stopped arguing "vector vs. graph" and converged on a **hybrid, three-layer architecture** [[23]](https://machinelearningmastery.com/vector-databases-vs-graph-rag-for-agent-memory-when-to-use-which/)[[26]](https://atlan.com/know/vector-database-vs-knowledge-graph-agent-memory/)[[32]](https://www.knowlee.ai/blog/persistent-memory-for-ai-agents):

| Layer | Storage | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Semantic surface** | Vector DB (embeddings) | Fast fuzzy recall, "find things like this" |
| **Relational structure** | Graph DB (entities + edges) | Multi-hop reasoning, "how is X related to Y?" |
| **Temporal/utility metadata** | Both, with decay functions | Evolution, pruning, relevance scoring |

The key insight is that these layers are joined by **canonical IDs** — the graph carries structure, the vector store carries semantic surface area, and together they cover the query shapes a real agent needs [[32]](https://www.knowlee.ai/blog/persistent-memory-for-ai-agents).

---

## How Relevance & Meaning Evolution Works (Your Core Question)

Several systems now implement exactly what you're describing — **meaning and relevance that change over time, with pruning**:

### 1. Temporal Knowledge Graphs (Zep / Graphiti)

This is the closest match to your idea. Graphiti [[30]](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti)[[38]](https://blog.getzep.com/graphiti-knowledge-graphs-for-agents/) models facts as edges with **validity intervals** — a fact isn't just "true," it's "true from \(t_{\text{valid}}\) to \(t_{\text{invalid}}\)." When new information contradicts old information, edges are invalidated rather than deleted, maintaining a timeline. This means:

- The graph can answer "what did we believe about X in March?" vs. "what do we believe now?"
- Relevance naturally decays as facts become invalidated
- Nothing is lost — provenance is preserved [[21]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956)[[24]](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.13956v1)

```
Episode Subgraph (raw data)
    ↓ extraction
Semantic Entity Subgraph (entities + relationships)
    ↓ clustering
Community Subgraph (high-level summaries)
```

### 2. Utility-Based Pruning (ReMe, SEDM, CraniMem)

This is where your "neural network to determine relevance" idea lives. These systems track **how useful each memory was** and prune accordingly [[9]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.10696)[[36]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.10696):

- **ReMe**: Each memory has a utility score \(u\) that increments when recall contributes to successful task completion. Memories with high retrieval count but low utility get pruned: \(\phi_{\text{remove}}(E) = \text{true if } \frac{u(E)}{f(E)} \leq \beta\) [[36]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.10696)
- **CraniMem**: Uses an LLM-based tagger that produces scalar signals for **importance, surprise, and emotion**, aggregated into a base utility score. A consolidation loop replays high-utility traces into the knowledge graph while pruning low-utility ones [[39]](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2603.15642)
- **SEDM**: "Consolidation and progressive evolution continuously refine the repository by promoting stable items, merging redundancies, and pruning harmful ones" [[3]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.09498)

### 3. Biologically-Inspired Forgetting (FadeMem)

FadeMem [[25]](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.18642v2) models memory strength as exponential decay modulated by access frequency, directly inspired by Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve:

$$I_i(t) = \alpha \cdot \text{rel}(c_i, Q_t) + \beta \cdot \frac{f_i}{1+f_i} + \gamma \cdot \text{recency}(\tau_i, t)$$

Memories are dynamically assigned to layers based on importance, and automatic pruning occurs when strength falls below a threshold or dormancy exceeds \(T_{\text{max}}\) days [[25]](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.18642v2).

---

## Is Your Specific Idea Right?

> *"Can I use a model or neural network to determine relevance and determine relationships between documents and store its findings in a graphdb?"*

**Yes, and this is essentially what all these systems do.** The "neural network" in practice is an LLM (or a pipeline of smaller models like spaCy/GLiNER for extraction + LLM for reasoning). The pipeline typically looks like:

```
Documents/Conversations
    ↓
Entity & Relationship Extraction (GLiNER, GLiREL, or LLM)
    ↓
Entity Resolution & Deduplication
    ↓
Graph DB Insertion (Neo4j, Kuzu, etc.)
    ↓
Community Detection (Leiden algorithm)
    ↓
Utility Scoring & Temporal Tagging
    ↓
Periodic Consolidation & Pruning
```

Neo4j's `agent-memory` package [[4]](https://github.com/neo4j-labs/agent-memory)[[10]](https://neo4j.com/labs/agent-memory/) implements this with a **POLE+O model** (Person, Organization, Location, Event + Object) and supports multi-stage extraction pipelines combining spaCy, GLiNER, and LLM fallback.

---

## Is This a Solved Problem?

**No, but it's rapidly maturing.** Here's where the gaps remain:

| What's Solved | What's Not |
|---|---|
| Entity extraction from text | **Selective forgetting** — only one benchmark (MemoryAgentBench) even tests it [[31]](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.07670v1) |
| Static knowledge graph construction | **Real-time graph updates** without full recomputation |
| Vector + graph hybrid retrieval | **Unified relevance scoring** across semantic, relational, and temporal signals |
| Temporal validity tracking (Zep/Graphiti) | **Cross-domain knowledge transfer** between graphs |
| Community-based summarization (GraphRAG) | **Cost-efficient indexing** — GraphRAG indexing costs 10-40× more than vector RAG [[40]](https://agentmarketcap.ai/blog/2026/04/07/graph-rag-vs-vector-rag-agent-memory-neo4j-pgvector) |

As one survey put it: *"No current system masters all four competencies; most fail conspicuously on selective forgetting"* [[31]](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.07670v1).

## Can Mamba Be Used? Yes — And It Has a Killer Feature

Mamba/SSMs are not just viable substitutes; they bring a **unique capability** that transformers lack for this use case: **state caching and composition.**

### The Killer Feature: Document State Souping

A recent paper demonstrated that SSM states can be pre-computed for each document, cached independently, and then **composed on-the-fly** at query time without re-encoding [[15]](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.24033). For a 32K-token document, loading a cached state and processing the query takes **65.8 ms** vs. **963.2 ms** for standard concatenation — a ~15× speedup [[15]](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.24033).

This is transformative for your use case because:

> *"Any arbitrary subset of documents can be composed on-the-fly at inference time without re-computation... This flexibility is particularly powerful for RAG systems, where different queries retrieve unique combinations of documents."* [[15]](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.24033)

In other words: **each document lives as a fixed-size state vector. Relevance scoring becomes a lightweight operation over pre-computed states. Pruning is as simple as deleting a state file.** This maps almost perfectly onto what you described.

### Mamba for Graph-Structured Memory

Several projects have adapted Mamba to graph domains:

| Approach | What It Does |
|---|---|
| **Graph-Mamba** [[11]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00789) | Uses SSM selection mechanism for graph sparsification — filtering relevant nodes as context, achieving linear-time complexity |
| **DG-Mamba** [[17]](https://digitalcommons.njit.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi) | Models temporal evolution of node embeddings in dynamic graphs using Mamba's state transitions |
| **DSEE** [[1]](https://openreview.net/pdf) | Mamba-driven diffusion for temporal knowledge graph reasoning — captures long-range semantic dependencies while mitigating information decay in long histories |
| **PathMamba** [[6]](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.18026v1) | Combines GNNs with Mamba for pathway-level dependencies in biological graphs |

The pattern is consistent: Mamba's selective state mechanism naturally models **what to keep and what to forget** — which is exactly the pruning behavior you're after.

### The Catch

Mamba-3's retrieval capabilities, while strong for a linear model, still lag behind transformers on needle-in-a-haystack tasks [[3]](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.15569). And pure Mamba encoders "can underperform Transformer architectures in tasks that require non-standard retrieval or in-context learning" [[1]](https://openreview.net/pdf). For the *extraction* step (pulling entities and relations from text), bidirectional encoder models still dominate.

## Can JEPA Be Used? Yes — For the Relevance Layer Specifically

JEPA is not a drop-in replacement for the whole pipeline, but it's **uniquely suited to the relevance-scoring layer** of your architecture.

### Why JEPA Maps to Your Problem

JEPA learns by predicting representations in **embedding space** rather than reconstructing tokens. This means:

1. **It learns semantic relationships directly** — the joint embedding space naturally clusters related concepts without needing explicit labels [[7]](https://github.com/dipsivenkatesh/jepa)
2. **JEPA-SCORE provides a built-in relevance metric** — it's a log-scale Monte Carlo estimator of data density. Low JEPA-SCORE = well-represented, in-distribution content; high score = outlier/novel content [[1]](https://openreview.net/pdf). This gives you a principled way to score how "relevant" a document is to the agent's existing knowledge.
3. **Non-generative = efficient** — JEPA doesn't waste capacity learning to generate text; it focuses entirely on representation quality

### Text-JEPA: The Concrete Implementation

Text-JEPA adapts the architecture for language: it predicts masked span representations from context rather than reconstructing surface tokens (like BERT) or modeling next-token distributions (like GPT) [[12]](https://github.com/nhatkhangcs/RoBERTa-jepa). It's evaluated on semantic similarity, clustering, and retrieval tasks — exactly the metrics that matter for your relevance engine.

**The relevance pipeline with JEPA would look like:**

```
Document → JEPA Encoder → embedding
Query    → JEPA Encoder → embedding
                              ↓
                    Cosine similarity / JEPA-SCORE
                              ↓
                    Relevance weight (evolvable, prunable)
```

The embedding itself becomes the relevance signal. As the agent's knowledge evolves, you can fine-tune the JEPA encoder on new data, and the relevance landscape shifts accordingly.

## How Light Can We Go? Shockingly Light

This is where the evidence is most surprising. For structured extraction, **small models don't just compete — they often win.**

### The Extraction Layer

| Model | Params | Performance vs. LLMs |
|---|---|---|
| **GLiNER-S** | 50M | Outperforms ChatGPT on zero-shot NER [[5]](https://aclanthology.org/anthology-files/pdf/naacl/2024.naacl-long.300.pdf)[[10]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.08526) |
| **GLiNER-M** | 90M | Comparable to UniNER-13B (140× smaller) [[10]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.08526) |
| **GLiNER2-base** | 205M | NER + relation extraction + classification in one pass, CPU-only [[8]](http://github.com/fastino-ai/GLiNER2) |
| **Kastor** (SLM) | ~100M | RDF triple extraction using shape-aware fine-tuning [[2]](https://github.com/datalogism/Kastor) |
| **LightKGG** | Small LM | Full KG construction with topology-enhanced inference [[13]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.23341) |

The reason small models win at extraction: **NER and relation extraction are fundamentally span-labeling tasks, not generation tasks.** A bidirectional encoder can process the entire sequence in parallel and label spans directly. An autoregressive LLM has to generate tokens sequentially and then parse the output — slower, more expensive, and more error-prone.

GLiNER2 is particularly relevant: it does entities, relations, classification, and structured data extraction in a **single forward pass** on CPU [[8]](http://github.com/fastino-ai/GLiNER2). For your agent memory pipeline, this means the extraction step could run on the same machine as the graph DB without a GPU.

For relevance scoring, you can go even lighter:

- A **JEPA-trained encoder** (like Text-JEPA base, ~110M params) produces embeddings that directly support similarity and retrieval [[12]](https://github.com/nhatkhangcs/RoBERTa-jepa)

- The **pruning decision** itself can be a simple logistic regression over features like recency, access frequency, utility score, and JEPA-SCORE — no neural network needed at all

## The Two-Loop Architecture

Your instinct is correct and it's how biological memory actually works. There are two fundamentally different timescales:

### Fast Loop (Request-Time): Dumb, Deterministic, Cheap

The graph already encodes what's relevant — that's the whole point of the maintenance loop. By the time a query arrives, the relationships are materialized. You're not *discovering* relevance at query time; you're *retrieving* it.
