## What Lives Where

| Layer | Location | Contents | Size |
|-------|----------|----------|------|
| **Mint Account** | On-chain | `supply=1`, `decimals=0`, mint authority | ~82 bytes |
| **Metadata Account** | On-chain (PDA) | `name`, `symbol`, `uri`, creators, royalties | ~200–700 bytes |
| **Token Account** | On-chain | `amount=1`, `owner=you`, `mint=<mint_address>` | 165 bytes |
| **Metadata JSON** | Off-chain (Arweave/IPFS) | `description`, `image` URI, `attributes[]`, `animation_url` | ~1–10 KB |
| **The actual image** | Off-chain (Arweave/IPFS) | PNG, GIF, MP4, etc. | KB to MB |

The on-chain Metadata Account stores a **URI string** (max 200 characters) — nothing more. That URI points to a JSON file. That JSON file contains another URI pointing to the actual image [ [[1]](https://solana.com/docs/tokens/metaplex)](https://solana.com/docs/tokens/metaplex)[ [[2]](https://www.quicknode.com/guides/solana-development/nfts/solana-nft-metadata-deep-dive)](https://www.quicknode.com/guides/solana-development/nfts/solana-nft-metadata-deep-dive)[ [[10]](https://www.solana-nft-creator.com/solana-nft-storage-ipfs-arweave/)](https://www.solana-nft-creator.com/solana-nft-storage-ipfs-arweave/).

---

## Why This Architecture?

**Cost.** Storing 1 MB on Solana costs roughly **~7 SOL** in rent-exempt reserve (at ~6960 lamports per byte). A single 100 KB image would cost ~0.7 SOL just to exist. Multiply that by a 10,000-piece collection and you're looking at 7,000 SOL in storage alone.

Instead, the on-chain footprint per NFT is about **400 bytes** (~0.0028 SOL), and the heavy content lives on Arweave (one-time payment, permanent) or IPFS (requires pinning) [ [[10]](https://www.solana-nft-creator.com/solana-nft-storage-ipfs-arweave/)](https://www.solana-nft-creator.com/solana-nft-storage-ipfs-arweave/)[ [[14]](https://www.alchemii.io/blog/what-is-metaplex-token-metadata)](https://www.alchemii.io/blog/what-is-metaplex-token-metadata).

---

## The Three Accounts That Make an NFT

When you mint an NFT, three on-chain accounts are created:

```
1. Mint Account
   └─ PDA seeds: none (generated keypair or PDA)
   └─ Owner: Token Program
   └─ Data: { mint_authority, supply: 1, decimals: 0, freeze_authority }

2. Token Account (Associated Token Account)
   └─ PDA seeds: [owner_pubkey, Token_Program_ID, mint_pubkey]
   └─ Owner: Token Program
   └─ Data: { mint, owner, amount: 1 }

3. Metadata Account
   └─ PDA seeds: ["metadata", Metadata_Program_ID, mint_pubkey]
   └─ Owner: Metadata Program
   └─ Data: { name, symbol, uri, creators, royalties, ... }
```

Plus optionally a **Master Edition Account** (for NFTs that can have numbered prints) [ [[1]](https://solana.com/docs/tokens/metaplex)](https://solana.com/docs/tokens/metaplex)[ [[5]](https://github.com/metaplex-foundation/metaplex-program-library/blob/ecb0dcd82274b8e70dacd171e1a553b6f6dab5c6/token-metadata/program/src/state/metadata.rs)](https://github.com/metaplex-foundation/metaplex-program-library/blob/ecb0dcd82274b8e70dacd171e1a553b6f6dab5c6/token-metadata/program/src/state/metadata.rs)[ [[9]](https://github.com/metaplex-foundation/metaplex-program-library/blob/6cb5e8ce4f4ca59629ea8adde7a78caef9c28a89/token-metadata/program/src/state.rs)](https://github.com/metaplex-foundation/metaplex-program-library/blob/6cb5e8ce4f4ca59629ea8adde7a78caef9c28a89/token-metadata/program/src/state.rs).

---

## What "Owning" the NFT Means

Your wallet holds **no image, no JSON, no metadata**. It holds:

- A **Token Account** where `amount == 1` and `owner == your_pubkey`
- The **private key** that proves you control that pubkey

When a marketplace or wallet displays your NFT, it:

1. Finds all Token Accounts where `owner == your_pubkey` and `amount > 0`
2. For each, fetches the Metadata Account PDA at `["metadata", program_id, mint]`
3. Reads the `uri` field from that Metadata Account
4. Fetches the JSON from Arweave/IPFS
5. Reads the `image` field from that JSON
6. Fetches and renders the actual image

If step 4 or 6 fails (dead gateway, unpinned IPFS content), your NFT displays as a **broken image** — even though you still "own" it on-chain [ [[2]](https://www.quicknode.com/guides/solana-development/nfts/solana-nft-metadata-deep-dive)](https://www.quicknode.com/guides/solana-development/nfts/solana-nft-metadata-deep-dive)[ [[14]](https://www.alchemii.io/blog/what-is-metaplex-token-metadata)](https://www.alchemii.io/blog/what-is-metaplex-token-metadata)[ [[20]](https://solanastreaming.com/blog/where-to-get-solana-token-metadata)](https://solanastreaming.com/blog/where-to-get-solana-token-metadata).

---

## Storage Options Compared

| Option | Permanence | Cost Model | Risk |
|--------|-----------|------------|------|
| **Arweave** | Permanent (designed for 200+ years) | One-time payment in SOL (via Irys/Bundlr) | None, if paid |
| **IPFS + Pinata** | As long as pinned | Recurring pinning fee | Content lost if unpinned |
| **IPFS + NFT.Storage** | Free tier, long-term | Free (Filecoin backing) | Service could sunset |
| **Centralized (AWS/S3)** | As long as you pay | Monthly | Domain expires → NFT breaks |
| **Fully on-chain** | As long as Solana exists | ~7 SOL/MB | Prohibitively expensive |

Arweave is the dominant choice in the Solana ecosystem because Metaplex's tooling integrates with it directly, and you pay once in SOL [ [[10]](https://www.solana-nft-creator.com/solana-nft-storage-ipfs-arweave/)](https://www.solana-nft-creator.com/solana-nft-storage-ipfs-arweave/)[ [[12]](https://www.metaplex.com/docs/smart-contracts/core-candy-machine/preparing-assets)](https://www.metaplex.com/docs/smart-contracts/core-candy-machine/preparing-assets)[ [[15]](https://nft-bowl.com/blog/articles/nft-metadata-on-chain-vs-off-chain/)](https://nft-bowl.com/blog/articles/nft-metadata-on-chain-vs-off-chain/).

---

## The Bottom Line

> Your wallet stores **zero content**. The blockchain stores a **32-byte mint address** and a **200-character URI string**. Everything else — the JSON description, the image, the animation — lives on a separate storage network. The NFT is a **bearer instrument** whose value depends on the persistence of that external storage.
so the nft lives on the block chain and the solana keypair links me to it?

Almost — but with an important nuance about what "the NFT" actually is.

---

## The Ownership Link

Your keypair links you to a **Token Account** on-chain, and that Token Account says `amount: 1` for a specific **Mint**. That's the ownership proof:

```
Your Private Key ──signs──▶ Your Public Key
                                    │
                                    │ matches
                                    ▼
                           Token Account
                           ┌──────────────────────┐
                           │ owner: YOUR_PUBKEY   │  ◀── this is the link
                           │ mint:  NFT_MINT_123  │
                           │ amount: 1            │
                           └──────────────────────┘
```

So yes — the keypair is the **sole link** between you and the on-chain record that says "this person owns this NFT."

---

## But "The NFT" Is Three Things, Not One

This is where the nuance matters:

| Component | On-chain? | What it is |
|-----------|-----------|------------|
| **Ownership record** | ✅ Yes | Token Account: `owner=you, mint=NFT_MINT, amount=1` |
| **Identity record** | ✅ Yes | Metadata PDA: `name, uri → points to JSON` |
| **The thing itself** | ❌ No | Image/JSON on Arweave or IPFS |

So when someone says "the NFT lives on the blockchain," they're being imprecise. What lives on-chain is:

- **Proof that you own it** (the Token Account)
- **A label describing it** (the Metadata Account with a URI pointer)

The actual image — the thing you'd look at and call "the NFT" — is on a separate storage network, tethered to the chain by a URL string.

```
│   │  CLAIM TICKET #42   │   ◀── Token Account │
│   │  Owner: You         │                     │
│   │  Item: Painting X   │                     │
│   └─────────────────────┘                     │
│                                               │
│   The ticket is NOT the painting.             │
│   But whoever holds the ticket                │
│   owns the painting.                          │
│                                               │
│   Your keypair = the hand that holds          │
│   the ticket.                                 │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The painting is in the vault (Arweave). The ticket is on-chain (Token Account). Your keypair is the hand holding the ticket. Transfer the ticket → transfer the painting. Lose the keypair → you can still see the painting hanging in the vault, but you can never claim it again.

---

## So, Precisely:

> The **ownership record** lives on-chain. The **content** lives off-chain. Your **keypair** is the cryptographic proof that you control the public key named as `owner` on that ownership record. The three together — record, content, and key — are what people colloquially call "the NFT."
but for the digital representation it lives on the solana block chain

You're right to push back — I blurred a crucial distinction. Let me be more precise.

---

## The NFT *Is* the On-Chain Token

The **non-fungible token** itself — the scarce digital asset, the thing that is uniquely identified, owned, and transferred — lives entirely on Solana. It is the combination of:

```
Mint Account (on-chain)          ← "This token exists, supply = 1"
    +
Token Account (on-chain)         ← "You own it"
    +
Metadata Account (on-chain)      ← "It's called this, here's its URI"
```

That is the NFT. That is the digital representation. It is a set of bytes in accounts on the Solana ledger, secured by the network's consensus, transferred by transactions, and linked to your keypair. It is **cryptographically scarce** in a way no off-chain file can be.

---

## The Image Is Not the NFT

What I was calling "the thing itself" — the JPEG, the PNG, the GIF — is **associated media**. It's what the token *points to*, not what the token *is*.

```
NFT (on-chain)                    Image (off-chain)
─────────────────────────         ───────────────────
Scarce                           Infinitely copyable
Transferred via transaction      Transferred via HTTP
Ownership is cryptographically   Ownership is meaningless
  provable
Lives as long as Solana does     Lives as long as someone pays
                                   for storage
```

The image is decoration. The **token** is the asset. If Arweave goes dark tomorrow, you still own the NFT — the on-chain records are intact. The image just won't render. The token hasn't vanished.

---

## The Analogy, Corrected

It's less like a coat check and more like a **certificate of authenticity**:

> You buy a signed, numbered print from an artist. The physical print hangs on your wall. The certificate of authenticity sits in your drawer. If your house burns down, the certificate survives — and you still "own" print #7/100, even though the physical object is gone. The certificate *is* the ownership. The print was just the thing you looked at.

In the digital realm, the certificate (the on-chain token) is the only thing that can't be copied. The image can be right-click-saved by anyone. **The token is the scarce thing.** And it lives on Solana.

---

So yes — you're correct. The digital representation, the actual NFT, lives on the Solana blockchain. The image is just what your wallet renders when it follows the URI pointer.
and my wallet/key pair for solana is what would give me access to the nft

Yes. Your keypair is the **sole access control mechanism**.

---

## The Chain of Authority

```
Your Private Key
      │
      │ signs a transaction that says "transfer NFT #42 to Alice"
      ▼
Solana Runtime verifies:
  "Does the signature match the public key listed as `owner`
   on the Token Account for NFT #42?"
      │
      ├─ Match ✅ → transfer executes, Alice now owns it
      │
      └─ No match ❌ → transaction rejected
```

Without that private key, the on-chain Token Account will forever say `owner: your_pubkey` — and no one can change it. The NFT is frozen in place. Viewable by anyone, but movable by no one.

---

## What the Keypair Actually Gates

| Action | Requires your keypair? |
|--------|------------------------|
| View the NFT's metadata | No — anyone can read the chain |
| View the image | No — anyone can follow the URI |
| Transfer the NFT | **Yes** |
| List it for sale | **Yes** |
| Burn it | **Yes** |
| Update metadata (if authority) | **Yes** |

So the keypair doesn't give you "access" in the sense of unlocking hidden content. It gives you **control** — the exclusive right to change the `owner` field on that Token Account. And in a system where ownership *is* the asset, that right is everything.
What programming language is used to program dao in solana

# Programming Languages for Solana DAOs

The on-chain DAO program itself is written in **Rust**, almost always using the **Anchor framework**. Here's the full picture:

---

## The Core: Rust + Anchor

Solana programs (smart contracts) compile to **BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) bytecode** — the runtime doesn't care about the source language. But in practice, **Rust is the only first-class citizen** [ [[2]](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/40/what-are-the-frameworks-and-development-environments-for-solana)](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/40/what-are-the-frameworks-and-development-environments-for-solana)[ [[8]](https://solana.com/docs/programs/rust)](https://solana.com/docs/programs/rust)[ [[13]](https://www.c-sharpcorner.com/article/solanas-language-support-and-simplified-development-with-anchor-framework/)](https://www.c-sharpcorner.com/article/solanas-language-support-and-simplified-development-with-anchor-framework/):

| Language | Status | Reality |
|----------|--------|---------|
| **Rust** | ✅ Primary | 99%+ of programs, full SDK, all tooling |
| **C** | ⚠️ Possible | Technically compiles to BPF, no real ecosystem |
| **C++** | ⚠️ Possible | Same as C — possible but nobody does it |

**Anchor** sits on top of Rust and provides the DSL, macros, and tooling that make development practical. It's the equivalent of Hardhat/Truffle for Ethereum — and it's what the vast majority of Solana developers use [ [[5]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor)[ [[10]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/developer-content/blob/main/content/courses/onchain-development/intro-to-anchor.md)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/developer-content/blob/main/content/courses/onchain-development/intro-to-anchor.md)[ [[15]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/)](https://www.anchor-lang.com/).

---

## The Standard DAO Implementation: SPL Governance

The canonical DAO program on Solana is **SPL Governance**, maintained by the Solana Program Library. It's written entirely in **Rust** and provides the core primitives: Realms, Proposals, Voting, and Treasury management [ [[3]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/blob/governance-v3.1.0/governance/program/src/state/realm.rs)](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/blob/governance-v3.1.0/governance/program/src/state/realm.rs)[ [[6]](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance)](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance)[ [[9]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance)](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance):

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           SPL Governance (Rust)              │
│                                              │
│  Realm ──▶ Governance ──▶ Proposal ──▶ Vote │
│    │            │              │             │
│    │       Token Gov     Program Gov         │
│    │       Mint Gov                          │
│                                              │
│  Plugins (custom voter weight, etc.)         │
│    └─ Also written in Rust/Anchor            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Most DAOs don't write their own governance program from scratch — they deploy an instance of SPL Governance (or use the shared instance) and configure it with their token and parameters [ [[6]](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance)](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance)[ [[12]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/blob/master/governance/README.md)](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/blob/master/governance/README.md).

---

## The Client Side: TypeScript

While the on-chain program is Rust, the **client** that users interact with is typically written in **TypeScript** using the `@solana/spl-governance` SDK [ [[1]](https://www.splgovernance.com/docs.html)](https://www.splgovernance.com/docs.html)[ [[6]](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance)](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance):

```typescript
import { GovernanceSDK } from '@solana/spl-governance';

const sdk = new GovernanceSDK({
  connection,
  wallet: yourWallet,
});

// Create a DAO, submit proposals, cast votes, etc.
```

The most popular UI for Solana DAOs — **Realms** ([realms.today](https://realms.today)) — is built with this TypeScript SDK [ [[14]](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/blob/master/governance/README.md)](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/blob/master/governance/README.md).

---

## Customization: Plugins in Rust/Anchor

If a DAO needs custom behavior (quadratic voting, NFT-gated voting, multi-token governance), it writes a **plugin** — which is just another Solana program. These plugins are written in **Rust with Anchor**, because they need to implement the SPL Governance plugin interface and compile to BPF [ [[1]](https://www.splgovernance.com/docs.html)](https://www.splgovernance.com/docs.html)[ [[6]](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance)](https://github.com/Mythic-Project/solana-program-library/tree/master/governance):

```rust
// Example: custom voter weight plugin
#[program]
pub mod quadratic_voting {
    use super::*;
    
    pub fn calculate_voter_weight(ctx: Context<...>, args: ...) -> Result<u64> {
        // sqrt of token balance for quadratic voting
        let weight = (args.token_balance as f64).sqrt() as u64;
        Ok(weight)
    }
}
```

---

## The Bottom Line

| Layer | Language | Framework |
|-------|----------|-----------|
| On-chain DAO program | **Rust** | Anchor |
| Governance plugins | **Rust** | Anchor |
| Client SDK / UI | **TypeScript** | `@solana/spl-governance` |
| Alternative (rare) | C / C++ | None (raw BPF) |

If you're building a DAO on Solana, you're writing Rust. There's no practical alternative.
so how is the sol cryptocurrency spent when interacting with a dao on a solana block chain

# How SOL Flows During DAO Interactions

Every interaction with a Solana DAO is a **transaction**, and every transaction consumes SOL. But the *who*, *when*, and *why* differ depending on the action. Here's the full picture.

---

## The Two Kinds of SOL Consumption

| Type | What it pays for | Refundable? |
|------|-----------------|-------------|
| **Transaction fee** | Processing your instruction (signature verification, compute) | ❌ No — burned + paid to validator |
| **Rent deposit** | Storing new account data on-chain | ✅ Yes — reclaimable when account is closed |

Both are denominated in **lamports** (1 SOL = 10⁹ lamports).

---

## Transaction Fee Breakdown

Every transaction costs at minimum **5,000 lamports per signature** (0.000005 SOL) plus an optional priority fee [[3]](https://solana.com/docs/core/fees)[[5]](https://solana.com/docs/core/fees/fee-structure):

$$\text{Total fee} = \underbrace{5{,}000 \times n_\text{sigs}}_{\text{base fee}} + \underbrace{\left\lceil\frac{\text{CU price} \times \text{CU limit}}{1{,}000{,}000}\right\rceil}_{\text{priority fee (optional)}}$$

| Component | Recipient |
|-----------|-----------|
| Base fee (50%) | 🔥 Burned |
| Base fee (50%) | Validator |
| Priority fee (100%) | Validator |

The fee is **deducted before execution begins** and is **not refunded even if the transaction fails** [[3]](https://solana.com/docs/core/fees)[[16]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/developer-content/blob/main/docs/core/fees.md).

---

## Who Pays, Action by Action

### 1. Creating a Realm (DAO)

```plaintext
User's wallet pays:
  ├─ Transaction fee (~5,000 lamports)
  └─ Rent deposit for new Realm account (~1-2 SOL worth of lamports)
```

The Realm account stores the DAO's configuration (community mint, council mint, authorities) and must be rent-exempt. This is a one-time cost paid by the DAO creator [[4]](https://docs.realms.today/developer-resources/spl-governance)[[18]](https://docs.realms.today/developer-resources/sdk/sdk-dao-creation).

### 2. Creating a Governance

```
User's wallet pays:
  ├─ Transaction fee
  └─ Rent deposit for Governance account
  └─ Rent deposit for native treasury PDA (DAO wallet)
```

The Governance account defines voting rules. A **native treasury PDA** is also created — this is the DAO's SOL wallet, a Program-Derived Address controlled by the Governance program [[4]](https://docs.realms.today/developer-resources/spl-governance)[[20]](https://paragraph.com/@xentoshi/spl-governance-a-technical-overview).

### 3. Depositing Tokens to Get Voting Power

```
User's wallet pays:
  ├─ Transaction fee
  └─ Rent deposit for TokenOwnerRecord account (if first deposit)
```

To vote, a member deposits governance tokens into the Realm. This creates a **TokenOwnerRecord** that tracks their voting weight. The deposited tokens themselves stay in a Token Account owned by the Realm [[6]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/blob/master/governance/README.md)[[8]](https://www.splgovernance.com/docs.html).

### 4. Creating a Proposal

```plaintext
User's wallet pays:
  ├─ Transaction fee
  └─ Rent deposit for Proposal account
  └─ (Optional) Proposal deposit — refundable
```

The proposal creator pays to create the Proposal account. Additionally, if the number of active proposals exceeds `deposit_exempt_proposal_count`, a **proposal deposit** is required. This deposit is held in a PDA and can be **reclaimed** once the proposal is no longer active — it's a spam-prevention mechanism, not a fee [[2]](https://docs.rs/spl-governance/latest/spl_governance/instruction/enum.GovernanceInstruction.html)[[12]](https://docs.rs/crate/spl-governance/latest/source/src/instruction.rs)[[18]](https://docs.realms.today/developer-resources/sdk/sdk-dao-creation).

### 5. Casting a Vote

```plaintext
Voter's wallet pays:
  └─ Transaction fee only (~5,000 lamports)
```

Voting is the cheapest action. No new accounts are created — the vote is recorded in the existing Proposal account. Just the base transaction fee [[6]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/blob/master/governance/README.md)[[8]](https://www.splgovernance.com/docs.html).

### 6. Executing a Passed Proposal

```
Anyone's wallet pays:
  └─ Transaction fee

The DAO's native treasury PDA signs:
  └─ Transfers SOL from treasury
  └─ Invokes other programs
```

This is the critical moment. Once a proposal passes and the hold-up time elapses, **anyone** can trigger execution. The executor pays the transaction fee, but the **Governance PDA signs on behalf of the DAO** — meaning the DAO treasury itself authorizes the spending of its own SOL [[2]](https://docs.rs/spl-governance/latest/spl_governance/instruction/enum.GovernanceInstruction.html)[[4]](https://docs.realms.today/developer-resources/spl-governance)[20]:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ExecuteTransaction                                  │
│                                                      │
│  Fee payer: Alice (anyone, pays ~5,000 lamports)     │
│  Signer: Governance PDA (the DAO itself)              │
│                                                      │
│  Instruction: Transfer 100 SOL from                  │
│    native_treasury_PDA → developer_wallet            │
│                                                      │
│  The PDA "signs" via invoke_signed —                  │
│  no private key exists for it.                       │
│  The program derives the PDA from seeds,             │
│  verifies it matches, and authorizes the transfer.   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The DAO treasury's SOL is spent **by the program itself**, using the PDA's signing authority. The human executor just pays the network fee to submit the transaction [[2]](https://docs.rs/spl-governance/latest/spl_governance/instruction/enum.GovernanceInstruction.html)[[4]](https://docs.realms.today/developer-resources/spl-governance).

---

## The Full SOL Flow Diagram

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────┐
                    │     USER'S WALLET        │
                    │     (your keypair)       │
                    └──────────┬──────────────┘
                               │
            pays transaction fees for:
                               │
        ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
        ▼                      ▼                      ▼
   Create Realm          Create Proposal          Cast Vote
   Create Governance     Insert Transaction      Execute (optional)
   Deposit Tokens        Add Signatory
                         Sign Off
                               │
                        ┌──────┴──────┐
                        ▼              ▼
                   Fee: ~5,000    Fee: ~5,000
                   + rent         (no rent)
                   deposits
                        │              │
                        ▼              ▼
                 ┌────────────────────────────┐
                 │       VALIDATORS           │
                 │  50% base fee (burned)     │
                 │  50% base fee + priority   │
                 └────────────────────────────┘


                    ┌─────────────────────────┐
                    │    DAO NATIVE TREASURY   │
                    │    (Governance PDA)      │
                    └──────────┬──────────────┘
                               │
            spends SOL when proposal executes:
                               │
        ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
        ▼                      ▼                      ▼
   Pay contributor       Fund development       Upgrade program
   Transfer to vault     Buy NFT for DAO        Anything programmed
```

---

## Practical Cost Examples

| Action | Approximate SOL Cost | Who Pays |
|--------|---------------------|----------|
| Create Realm + Governance + Treasury | ~0.02–0.05 SOL | DAO creator |
| Deposit tokens for voting power | ~0.002 SOL | Member |
| Create a proposal | ~0.002–0.01 SOL | Proposal author |
| Cast a vote | ~0.000005 SOL | Voter |
| Execute passed proposal (simple transfer) | ~0.00001 SOL | Executor (anyone) |
| Execute passed proposal (complex, many accounts) | ~0.0001–0.001 SOL | Executor (anyone) |

The DAO treasury's own SOL is only spent when a proposal **explicitly instructs** it — e.g., "transfer 100 SOL to address X." The treasury doesn't pay network fees for governance actions; individual users do [[4]](https://docs.realms.today/developer-resources/spl-governance)[[20]](https://paragraph.com/@xentoshi/spl-governance-a-technical-overview).

---

## The Key Insight

> **Your personal SOL pays for the *act of governing* (creating, voting, executing). The DAO treasury's SOL pays for the *outcome of governing* (grants, investments, payments).** The two pools of SOL are separate, and the Governance PDA is the cryptographic bridge that lets the DAO spend its own money without any human holding its private key — because no such key exists.
What does PDA mean?

# PDA: Program Derived Address

A **Program Derived Address** is a public key on Solana that has **no corresponding private key**. It is derived deterministically from a program's ID and a set of seeds, and only that program can "sign" for it.

---

## The Core Idea

```
Normal Address (EOA):                    PDA:

  Private Key ──▶ Public Key              No private key exists
       │                                       │
       │ can sign                              │ can't sign
       ▼                                       ▼
  "I authorize this"                    Program derives it from seeds
                                        and says "I authorize this
                                        on the PDA's behalf"
```

A PDA is not generated from a keypair. It's **computed**:

$$\text{PDA} = \text{SHA-256}(\text{seeds} \ || \ \text{program\_id} \ || \ \text{"ProgramDerivedAddress"} \ || \ \text{bump})$$

The bump is a single byte (255 down to 1) iterated until the resulting hash is **not** a valid point on the Ed25519 curve — guaranteeing no private key can exist for it (https://solana.com/docs/core/pda)(https://www.quicknode.com/guides/solana-development/anchor/program-derived-addresses)(https://www.helius.dev/blog/an-introduction-to-pdas-on-solana).

---

## Why They Exist

| Problem | PDA Solution |
|---------|--------------|
| A DAO treasury needs to hold SOL, but no single person should control it | Treasury is a PDA — only the governance program can spend from it |
| A program needs to store state for each user | Derive a PDA per user: `seeds = [b"user", user_pubkey]` |
| An escrow needs to hold funds until conditions are met | Escrow PDA — only the escrow program can release funds |
| A program needs deterministic, collision-resistant addresses | PDAs are deterministic: same seeds + program = same address, every time |

---

## How a PDA "Signs"

A PDA can't produce an Ed25519 signature — there's no private key. Instead, during **Cross-Program Invocation (CPI)**, the owning program calls:

```rust
invoke_signed(
    instruction,
    account_infos,
    &[&[b"seed1", b"seed2", &[bump]]]  // seeds used to derive the PDA
);
```

The runtime then:

1. Re-derives the PDA from the provided seeds + program ID
2. Verifies it matches the address being "signed" for
3. If it matches → treats the program as having signed

This is the cryptographic primitive that makes DAO treasuries, escrow accounts, and program-controlled state possible (https://solana.com/docs/core/pda)[](https://www.helius.dev/blog/an-introduction-to-pdas-on-solana).

---

## Concrete Example: DAO Treasury

```
Governance Program ID: "GovER5LTHms3bLBqWub97yVrMmEogzX7xNjdXpPPCVZw"

Treasury PDA = find_program_address(
    seeds = [b"treasury", realm_pubkey.as_ref()],
    program_id = Governance_Program_ID
)

Result: some 32-byte address like "7zBW...xY9"
         + bump byte (e.g., 255)

This address:
  ✅ Can receive SOL (anyone can credit any account)
  ✅ Can hold SOL
  ❌ Cannot be signed for by any private key
  ✅ Can be "signed" for by the Governance program via invoke_signed
```

When a passed proposal says "send 100 SOL to Alice," the Governance program calls `invoke_signed` with the treasury PDA's seeds, and the runtime authorizes the transfer — because the program proved it *derives* that address (https://docs.realms.today/developer-resources/spl-governance)(https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library/blob/master/governance/README.md).

---

## PDA vs. EOA at a Glance

| | EOA (normal address) | PDA |
|---|---|---|
| Created from | Keypair generation | `find_program_address(seeds, program_id)` |
| Has private key? | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Can sign transactions? | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Can sign via CPI? | N/A | ✅ Yes (via `invoke_signed`) |
| Deterministic? | ❌ Random | ✅ Same seeds → same address |
| Off-curve? | ❌ Must be on-curve | ✅ Must be off-curve |

---

> **PDA = a public key that is mathematically guaranteed to have no private key, derived from a program's ID and seeds, enabling programs to own and control assets without any human holding the keys.**

# How to Acquire SOL

There are fundamentally **five ways** to acquire SOL, each serving a different need. Here they are, from most common to most niche.

---

## 1. Buy on a Centralized Exchange (Fiat → SOL)

The standard path for most people. You trade government-issued money (USD, EUR, etc.) for SOL through a regulated platform [[1]](https://coinbureau.com/guides/how-to-buy-solana)(https://coinbureau.com/guides/how-to-buy-solana)[ [[4]](https://finance.yahoo.com/personal-finance/investing/article/how-to-buy-solana-170411361.html)](https://finance.yahoo.com/personal-finance/investing/article/how-to-buy-solana-170411361.html)[ [[13]](https://cryptonewssol.com/how-to-guides/how-to-buy-solana/)](https://cryptonewssol.com/how-to-guides/how-to-buy-solana/).

| **Binance** | 0.1% (0.075% with BNB) | Lowest fees, global |


## 2. Buy Directly in a Wallet (On-Ramp)

# Anchor: The Complete Educational Overview

Anchor is the **standard development framework** for building Solana programs. It's not a separate language — it's a set of Rust macros, tooling, and conventions layered on top of raw Solana development that eliminates boilerplate and enforces security by default [ [[1]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/introduction)](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/introduction)[ [[10]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/)](https://www.anchor-lang.com/).

---

## Why Anchor Exists

Raw Solana development requires you to manually:

- Serialize/deserialize every account by hand
- Verify account ownership, discriminators, and constraints yourself
- Construct CPIs with raw `AccountInfo` arrays
- Derive PDAs and manage bump seeds manually
- Write your own TypeScript client from scratch

Anchor automates all of this. The framework's philosophy is: **"make the safe thing the easy thing."** If you write idiomatic Anchor, you get security checks for free [[1]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/introduction)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/introduction)[ [[8]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/developer-content/blob/main/content/courses/onchain-development/intro-to-anchor.md)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/developer-content/blob/main/content/courses/onchain-development/intro-to-anchor.md).

---

## The Four Core Macros

Every Anchor program is built around four macros. They form a layered architecture:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  ANCHOR PROGRAM                      │
│                                                      │
│  declare_id!("ABC123...")     ← on-chain address     │
│                                                      │
│  #[program]                   ← instruction handlers  │
│  pub mod my_program {                               │
│      pub fn do_thing(ctx: Context<DoThing>, ...) {}  │
│  }                                                   │
│                                                      │
│  #[derive(Accounts)]         ← account validation    │
│  pub struct DoThing<'info> {                        │
│      #[account(init, payer = user, space = ...)]     │
│      pub my_account: Account<'info, MyData>,        │
│      #[account(mut)]                                 │
│      pub user: Signer<'info>,                       │
│      pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,    │
│  }                                                   │
│                                                      │
│  #[account]                   ← data structure        │
│  pub struct MyData {                                │
│      pub authority: Pubkey,                         │
│      pub value: u64,                                │
│  }                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 1. `declare_id!` — The Program's Identity

```rust
declare_id!("ABC123def456...");
```

This is the program's on-chain address. It's a 32-byte Ed25519 public key. Anchor uses this to:
- Set the `owner` field on any account the program creates
- Verify that accounts passed to instructions belong to this program
- Derive PDAs that are tied to this program [ [[2]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure)](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure)[ [[5]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/program-structure.mdx)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/program-structure.mdx)

### 2. `#[program]` — Instruction Handlers

```rust
#[program]
pub mod my_program {
    use super::*;

    pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>, data: u64) -> Result<()> {
        ctx.accounts.my_account.data = data;
        msg!("Changed data to: {}!", data);
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

Each **public function** inside this module becomes an on-chain instruction. The first parameter is always `Context<T>` where `T` is the accounts struct. Additional parameters are the instruction's arguments — serialized automatically [ [[2]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure)](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure) [[5]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/program-structure.mdx)(https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/program-structure.mdx) [[8]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/developer-content/blob/main/content/courses/onchain-development/intro-to-anchor.md)(https://github.com/solana-foundation/developer-content/blob/main/content/courses/onchain-development/intro-to-anchor.md).

### 3. `#[derive(Accounts)]` — Account Validation

This is where Anchor's power really shows. The struct defines **which accounts an instruction needs** and **what rules they must satisfy** [[2]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure)(https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure) [[7]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts) [[15]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md)(https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md):

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct Initialize<'info> {
    #[account(init, payer = user, space = 8 + 32 + 8)]
    pub my_account: Account<'info, MyData>,

    #[account(mut)]
    pub user: Signer<'info>,

    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}
```

Before your instruction logic runs, Anchor **automatically validates** every constraint. If any check fails, the transaction is rejected before a single line of your code executes.

### 4. `#[account]` — Data Structure Definition

```rust
#[account]
pub struct MyData {
    pub authority: Pubkey,  // 32 bytes
    pub value: u64,         // 8 bytes
}
```

This macro does three things automatically [ [[2]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure)](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure) [[17]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management):

| Feature | What it does |
|---------|-------------|
| **Discriminator** | Prepends an 8-byte hash of the struct name — prevents account type confusion |
| **Owner assignment** | Sets the account owner to your program ID on creation |
| **Serialization** | Implements `AccountSerialize`/`AccountDeserialize` for reading/writing |

The discriminator is a critical security feature. Without it, an attacker could pass a different account type and your program would misinterpret the bytes. Anchor's 8-byte discriminator makes this impossible [[2]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure)(https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/program-structure) [[17]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management).

---

## Account Types

Anchor provides strongly-typed wrappers around raw `AccountInfo`. Each type performs specific validation [[7]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts)[ [[15]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md):

| Type | Checks Performed | Use Case |
|------|-----------------|----------|
| `Account<'info, T>` | Owner = program ID, discriminator matches `T`, deserializes into `T` | Your program's data accounts |
| `Signer<'info>` | `is_signer == true` | Authority, fee payer |
| `SystemAccount<'info>` | Owner = System Program | SOL wallets, native transfers |
| `Program<'info, T>` | `executable == true` | Invoking other programs |
| `UncheckedAccount<'info>` | **None** — raw access | Edge cases, manual validation |
| `LazyAccount<'info, T>` | Same as `Account` but deserializes on-demand | Large accounts, save compute |

---

## Account Constraints — The Security Layer

Constraints are declared inside the `#[account(...)]` attribute. They are Anchor's most important security primitive [ [[7]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts)](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts) [[15]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md)(https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md) [[17]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management):

### Initialization Constraints

```rust
#[account(
    init,              // Create account via CPI to System Program
    payer = user,      // Who pays the rent
    space = 8 + 32 + 8 // discriminator + fields
)]
pub my_account: Account<'info, MyData>,
```

`init` triggers a CPI to the System Program to allocate space, assign ownership to your program, and set the discriminator — all atomically [[7]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts) [[17]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management).

### PDA Constraints

```rust
#[account(
    init,
    payer = user,
    space = 8 + 32,
    seeds = [b"vault", user.key().as_ref()],
    bump
)]
pub vault: Account<'info, Vault>,
```

Anchor derives the PDA from the seeds, verifies the provided account matches, and stores the canonical bump in `ctx.bumps.vault` for later use in CPIs [ [[3]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx) [[7]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts).

### Ownership & Relationship Constraints

```rust
#[account(
    mut,
    has_one = authority,                              // my_account.authority == authority.key()
    constraint = my_account.value < 100,              // custom check
    constraint = my_account.is_active @ ErrorCode::Inactive  // with custom error
)]
pub my_account: Account<'info, MyData>,
pub authority: Signer<'info>,
```

`has_one` checks that a field in the account data matches a provided account's public key — essential for authorization. `constraint` allows arbitrary boolean expressions [[7]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts)[ [[15]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md).

### Lifecycle Constraints

```rust
#[account(
    mut,
    close = destination,   // Transfer lamports to destination, zero out data
)]
pub my_account: Account<'info, MyData>,

#[account(
    mut,
    realloc = 8 + 32 + 16,  // New total size
    realloc::payer = user,  // Who pays for additional space
    realloc::zero = true,   // Zero-initialize new bytes
)]
pub my_account: Account<'info, MyData>,
```

`close` reclaims rent by transferring lamports and zeroing data. `realloc` resizes accounts — critical for dynamic state [ [[17]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management)](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management).

---

## PDA Handling in Anchor

Anchor makes PDAs ergonomic. The `seeds` and `bump` constraints handle derivation and validation [ [[3]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx)[ [[7]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts)](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/accounts):

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct ProcessVault<'info> {
    #[account(
        mut,
        seeds = [b"vault", owner.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
    )]
    pub vault: SystemAccount<'info>,
    pub owner: Signer<'info>,
}
```

The bump is accessible in instruction logic:

```rust
pub fn process(ctx: Context<ProcessVault>) -> Result<()> {
    let bump = ctx.bumps.vault;  // The canonical bump byte
    // Use in CPI signer seeds...
}
```

**Seeds can be:**
- Static byte strings: `b"vault"`
- Account public keys: `user.key().as_ref()`
- Instruction arguments: `#[account(seeds = [b"order", order_id.to_le_bytes().as_ref()], bump)]`

The seeds are also exported to the IDL, so the TypeScript client can derive PDAs automatically [ [[3]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx).

---

## Cross-Program Invocations (CPIs)

Anchor provides two CPI patterns [ [[4]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/cpi)](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/concepts/cpi) [[9]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/cpi)(https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/cpi)[ [[16]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/advanced/declare-program)](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/advanced/declare-program):

### Pattern 1: Direct CPI (same-program or known dependency)

```rust
use anchor_lang::system_program::{transfer, Transfer};

pub fn sol_transfer(ctx: Context<SolTransfer>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
    let cpi_context = CpiContext::new(
        ctx.accounts.system_program.to_account_info(),
        Transfer {
            from: ctx.accounts.pda_account.to_account_info(),
            to: ctx.accounts.recipient.to_account_info(),
        },
    );

    transfer(cpi_context, amount)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

### Pattern 2: CPI with PDA Signer

When a PDA needs to "sign" the CPI:

```rust
pub fn sol_transfer(ctx: Context<SolTransfer>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
    let seeds: &[&[u8]] = &[b"pda", ctx.accounts.recipient.key().as_ref()];
    let bump = ctx.bumps.pda_account;
    let signer_seeds: &[&[&[u8]]] = &[&[seeds, &[bump]].concat()];

    let cpi_context = CpiContext::new(
        ctx.accounts.system_program.to_account_info(),
        Transfer {
            from: ctx.accounts.pda_account.to_account_info(),
            to: ctx.accounts.recipient.to_account_info(),
        },
    ).with_signer(signer_seeds);

    transfer(cpi_context, amount)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

The runtime re-derives the PDA from the provided seeds, verifies it matches, and treats the program as having signed [[9]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/cpi)(https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/basics/cpi) [[18]](https://solana.com/docs/intro/quick-start/cross-program-invocation)(https://solana.com/docs/intro/quick-start/cross-program-invocation).

### Pattern 3: `declare_program!` — Dependency-Free CPIs

For external programs where you don't want a crate dependency:

```rust
declare_program!(external_program);
// Generates: cpi, client, accounts, program, constants, events, types, errors modules

pub fn call_external(ctx: Context<CallExternal>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
    external_program::cpi::some_instruction(
        CpiContext::new(
            ctx.accounts.external_program.to_account_info(),
            external_program::cpi::accounts::SomeAccounts {
                // ...
            },
        ),
        amount,
    )?;
    Ok(())
}
```

This generates type-safe CPI helpers from the external program's IDL — no crate dependency needed [ [[16]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/advanced/declare-program)](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/advanced/declare-program).

---

## The IDL and Auto-Generated TypeScript Client

Anchor generates an **Interface Description Language (IDL)** — a JSON file describing every instruction, account type, error code, and PDA seed in your program [[1]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/introduction)(https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/introduction) [[3]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx)(https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx):

```json
{
  "address": "ABC123...",
  "instructions": [
    {
      "name": "initialize",
      "discriminator": [33, 223, 61, 208, ...],
      "accounts": [
        { "name": "my_account", "writable": true, "pda": { "seeds": [...] } },
        { "name": "user", "signer": true, "writable": true }
      ],
      "args": [{ "name": "data", "type": "u64" }]
    }
  ],
  "accounts": [
    { "name": "MyData", "type": { "fields": [...] } }
  ],
  "errors": [
    { "code": 6000, "name": "Unauthorized", "msg": "..." }
  ]
}
```

From this IDL, Anchor's TypeScript SDK generates a fully typed client [ [[1]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/introduction)](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/introduction)[ [[11]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/quickstart/solpg)](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/quickstart/solpg):

```typescript
// Auto-generated from IDL — fully typed
const txHash = await program.methods
  .initialize(new BN(42))
  .accounts({
    myAccount: myAccountPda,  // PDA auto-derived if seeds are in IDL
    user: wallet.publicKey,
    systemProgram: SystemProgram.programId,
  })
  .rpc();

// Fetch deserialized account data
const myData = await program.account.myData.fetch(myAccountPda);
console.log(myData.value.toString()); // "42"
```

The client automatically:
- Derives PDAs from seeds declared in the IDL
- Serializes arguments with correct types
- Constructs the transaction message
- Deserializes returned account data [ [[3]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx)](https://github.com/solana-foundation/anchor/blob/master/docs/content/docs/basics/pda.mdx) [[11]](https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/quickstart/solpg)(https://www.anchor-lang.com/docs/quickstart/solpg)

---

## Error Handling

Anchor provides a custom error system:

```rust
#[error_code]
pub enum ErrorCode {
    #[msg("Unauthorized access")]
    Unauthorized,           // code 6000
    #[msg("Value too large")]
    ValueTooLarge,          // code 6001
    #[msg("Account is inactive")]
    AccountInactive,        // code 6002
}
```

These integrate with constraints:

```rust
#[account(
    constraint = my_account.authority == signer.key() @ ErrorCode::Unauthorized
)]
```

Anchor's built-in constraint violations also have specific error codes (e.g., `ConstraintSeeds = 2006`, `ConstraintHasOne = 2001`), making client-side error handling precise [[15]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md)(https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-com/blob/main/apps/web/public/programs-anchor.md).

---

## State Management Patterns

### Creating Accounts

```rust
#[account(init, payer = user, space = 8 + MyData::INIT_SPACE)]
pub my_account: Account<'info, MyData>,
```

With `#[derive(InitSpace)]` for automatic space calculation:

```rust
#[account]
#[derive(InitSpace)]
pub struct MyData {
    pub authority: Pubkey,   // 32 bytes
    pub value: u64,          // 8 bytes
    // INIT_SPACE = 40, automatically computed
}
```

### Updating Accounts

```rust
#[account(mut, has_one = authority)]
pub my_account: Account<'info, MyData>,
pub authority: Signer<'info>,
```

### Closing Accounts (Reclaiming Rent)

```rust
#[account(mut, close = destination)]
pub my_account: Account<'info, MyData>,
#[account(mut)]
pub destination: SystemAccount<'info>,  // receives the lamports
```

### Conditional Initialization

```rust
#[account(init_if_needed, payer = user, space = 8 + 32)]
pub maybe_account: Account<'info, MaybeData>,
```

⚠️ Use `init_if_needed` carefully — it can mask account state issues. Always validate the account after initialization [ [[17]](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management)](https://solana-foundation-anchor.mintlify.app/guides/state-management).

# Building Hierarchical Permissions in a Solana DAO with Anchor

**Yes — and Anchor is the ideal framework for it.** The combination of Anchor's constraint system, PDA derivation, and CPI support gives you everything needed to build sophisticated role hierarchies. There are three proven architectural patterns, ranging from simple to fully composable.

---

## The Core Insight

On Solana, permissions aren't enforced by a central server checking a database row. They're enforced by **on-chain account state** that Anchor validates **before your instruction logic runs**. The pattern is:

```plaintext
User signs transaction
    │
    ▼
Anchor constraints check: "Does a PDA exist that proves this user has role X?"
    │
    ├─ PDA exists, role matches ✅ → instruction executes
    └─ No PDA or wrong role ❌ → transaction rejected before any code runs
```

This is fundamentally different from Web2 middleware. The permission proof is a **cryptographically verifiable on-chain account**, not a session token [[2]](https://github.com/NandaCardinaly/solana-rbac-onchain)[[6]](https://dev.to/originalb/implementing-role-based-access-control-rbac-on-solana-4p79).

---

## Pattern 1: Embedded Role PDA (Single Program)

The simplest approach — your DAO program manages roles directly. Each member gets a `UserRole` PDA derived from their wallet address [[6]](https://dev.to/originalb/implementing-role-based-access-control-rbac-on-solana-4p79):

```rust
#[account]
pub struct UserRole {
    pub authority: Pubkey,     // 32 bytes — the member's wallet
    pub role: u8,              // 1 byte  — 0=Member, 1=Contributor, 2=Admin, 3=SuperAdmin
    pub bump: u8,              // 1 byte
}

impl UserRole {
    pub const SPACE: usize = 8 + 32 + 1 + 1;  // discriminator + fields
}
```

### The Role Hierarchy

```rust
pub mod roles {
    pub const MEMBER: u8       = 0;  // Can vote, view proposals
    pub const CONTRIBUTOR: u8  = 1;  // Can create proposals
    pub const ADMIN: u8        = 2;  // Can manage roles, execute proposals
    pub const SUPER_ADMIN: u8  = 3;  // Can transfer DAO ownership, upgrade program
}
```

### Assigning a Role (Admin-gated)

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
#[instruction(role: u8)]
pub struct AssignRole<'info> {
    #[account(
        init,
        payer = admin,
        space = UserRole::SPACE,
        seeds = [b"user_role", target_user.key().as_ref()],
        bump
    )]
    pub user_role: Account<'info, UserRole>,

    /// CHECK: The user receiving the role — no signature needed
    pub target_user: UncheckedAccount<'info>,

    #[account(
        seeds = [b"user_role", admin.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = admin_role.role >= roles::ADMIN @ ErrorCode::Unauthorized,
        constraint = admin_role.role > role @ ErrorCode::CannotAssignEqualOrHigher,
        // ↑ Hierarchical constraint: you can only assign roles below your own
    )]
    pub admin_role: Account<'info, UserRole>,

    #[account(mut)]
    pub admin: Signer<'info>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}
```

The critical line is:

```rust
constraint = admin_role.role > role @ ErrorCode::CannotAssignEqualOrHigher
```

This enforces the hierarchy: an Admin (2) can assign Contributor (1) or Member (0), but never another Admin or SuperAdmin. A SuperAdmin (3) can assign anyone [[6]](https://dev.to/originalb/implementing-role-based-access-control-rbac-on-solana-4p79).

### Enforcing Permissions in Instructions

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct CreateProposal<'info> {
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"user_role", proposer.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = user_role.role >= roles::CONTRIBUTOR @ ErrorCode::Unauthorized
    )]
    pub user_role: Account<'info, UserRole>,

    #[account(mut)]
    pub proposer: Signer<'info>,
    // ... proposal accounts
}
```

The constraint fires **before** `create_proposal` executes. If the user lacks the role, the transaction fails atomically — no partial state changes, no gas wasted on execution [[6]](https://dev.to/originalb/implementing-role-based-access-control-rbac-on-solana-4p79)[[10]](https://github.com/tobi-techy/Anchor-Pinocchio-Security-Example).

---

## Pattern 2: Permission Bitmask (Fine-Grained)

Instead of a single `role: u8`, use a **bitmask** for granular permissions. This is how production systems like LazorKit and the on-chain API key manager work [13][14]:

```rust
pub mod permissions {
    pub const VIEW_PROPOSALS: u16  = 1 << 0;  // 0b00000001
    pub const CAST_VOTE: u16       = 1 << 1;  // 0b00000010
    pub const CREATE_PROPOSAL: u16 = 1 << 2;  // 0b00000100
    pub const EXECUTE: u16         = 1 << 3;  // 0b00001000
    pub const MANAGE_ROLES: u16    = 1 << 4;  // 0b00010000
    pub const MANAGE_TREASURY: u16 = 1 << 5;  // 0b00100000
    pub const UPGRADE_PROGRAM: u16 = 1 << 6;  // 0b01000000
    pub const TRANSFER_OWNERSHIP: u16 = 1 << 7; // 0b10000000
}

#[account]
pub struct MemberPermissions {
    pub authority: Pubkey,
    pub permissions: u16,   // bitmask — 2 bytes, essentially zero compute cost
    pub bump: u8,
}
```

### Checking Permissions

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct ExecuteProposal<'info> {
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"member_perms", executor.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = member_perms.permissions & permissions::EXECUTE != 0
            @ ErrorCode::MissingExecutePermission
    )]
    pub member_perms: Account<'info, MemberPermissions>,

    #[account(mut)]
    pub executor: Signer<'info>,
    // ...
}
```

A single bitwise AND replaces string comparisons or role-number checks. This costs **essentially zero compute units** and allows combining permissions arbitrarily — a member could have `CAST_VOTE | CREATE_PROPOSAL` without having `EXECUTE` [[13]](https://paragraph.com/@theauroraai/solana-api-key-management-anchor).

### Predefined Role Templates

You can still offer familiar role names by composing bitmasks:

```rust
pub mod role_templates {
    use super::permissions::*;
    
    pub const MEMBER: u16       = VIEW_PROPOSALS | CAST_VOTE;
    pub const CONTRIBUTOR: u16  = MEMBER | CREATE_PROPOSAL;
    pub const ADMIN: u16        = CONTRIBUTOR | EXECUTE | MANAGE_ROLES | MANAGE_TREASURY;
    pub const SUPER_ADMIN: u16  = ADMIN | UPGRADE_PROGRAM | TRANSFER_OWNERSHIP;
}
```

This gives you both the simplicity of named roles and the flexibility of granular permissions [[13]](https://paragraph.com/@theauroraai/solana-api-key-management-anchor).

---

## Pattern 3: Dedicated RBAC Program (CPI-Composable)

For a DAO spanning multiple programs, extract permissions into a **standalone RBAC program** that any other program can query via CPI. This is the most scalable pattern [[1]](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/23922/solana-anchor-authorization-best-practice-for-a-modular-multi-program-system-sh)[[2]](https://github.com/NandaCardinaly/solana-rbac-onchain)[4].

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 RBAC Program                         │
│                                                      │
│  Resources: "dao:v1", "treasury:v1", "program:v1"   │
│  Roles per resource: admin, editor, viewer           │
│  Assignments: (user_pubkey, resource, role)          │
│                                                      │
│  check_permission(user, resource, permission) → ✅/❌ │
└──────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┘
           │ CPI
    ┌──────┼──────┬──────────────┐
    ▼      ▼      ▼              ▼
┌──────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌──────────┐
│DAO   │ │Trea│ │Proposal│ │Upgrade   │
│Core  │ │sury│ │Program │ │Program   │
└──────┘ └────┘ └────────┘ └──────────┘
```

### The RBAC Program's Core Instruction

```rust
// In the RBAC program — callable via CPI by any other program
pub fn check_permission(
    ctx: Context<CheckPermission>,
    resource: String,
    required_permission: u16,
) -> Result<()> {
    let assignment = &ctx.accounts.assignment;
    
    require!(
        assignment.resource == resource,
        ErrorCode::WrongResource
    );
    require!(
        assignment.permissions & required_permission == required_permission,
        ErrorCode::InsufficientPermissions
    );
    require!(
        !assignment.is_revoked,
        ErrorCode::PermissionRevoked
    );
    
    // If we reach here, permission is valid.
    // No return value needed — success = permission granted.
    Ok(())
}
```

### Calling It From Your DAO Program

```rust
// In your DAO program
pub fn execute_proposal(ctx: Context<ExecuteProposal>, ...) -> Result<()> {
    // CPI to RBAC program to verify permissions
    rbac_program::cpi::check_permission(
        CpiContext::new(
            ctx.accounts.rbac_program.to_account_info(),
            rbac_program::cpi::accounts::CheckPermission {
                assignment: ctx.accounts.permission_assignment.to_account_info(),
                authority: ctx.accounts.executor.to_account_info(),
            },
        ),
        "dao:v1".to_string(),
        permissions::EXECUTE,
    )?;
    
    // Permission verified — proceed with execution
    // ...
}
```

The key advantage: the RBAC program owns the permission state. Your DAO program, treasury program, and upgrade program all query the same source of truth. Revoke a user's admin role in one place, and it propagates everywhere instantly [[1]](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/23922/solana-anchor-authorization-best-practice-for-a-modular-multi-program-system-sh)[[2]](https://github.com/NandaCardinaly/solana-rbac-onchain).

### Sol Cerberus: RBAC as a Macro Annotation

The Sol Cerberus project takes this even further — it reduces permission checking to a single attribute on your instruction [4]:

```rust
#[program]
pub mod my_dao {
    use super::*;

    #[rule(DAO, Execute)]  // ← That's it. Permission checked automatically.
    pub fn execute_proposal(ctx: Context<Execute>, ...) -> Result<()> {
        // Business logic here — permissions already verified
    }
}
```

The `#[rule(Resource, Permission)]` macro expands into the full CPI flow at compile time. You define roles, resources, and permissions once, then annotate instructions [[4]](https://github.com/AnderUstarroz/sol-cerberus-website/blob/main/docs/index.md).

---

## Integrating with SPL Governance

You don't have to choose between custom RBAC and SPL Governance — they compose. SPL Governance handles the **voting and proposal lifecycle**; your custom RBAC program handles **who can do what within the DAO's operations** [[1]](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/23922/solana-anchor-authorization-best-practice-for-a-modular-multi-program-system-sh)[[8]](https://github.com/rohit-sekhri51/capstone-dao-notebox):

```plaintext
SPL Governance                    Your RBAC Program
─────────────────                ──────────────────
Realm creation                   Role assignment
Token-weighted voting            Permission bitmasks
Proposal lifecycle               Resource scoping
Vote counting                    CPI permission checks
Proposal execution               Hierarchical constraints
Treasury management              Session keys / expiry
```

A passed SPL Governance proposal can execute an instruction that calls your RBAC program to grant a role — the DAO votes on who gets what permissions, and the RBAC program enforces them day-to-day [[8]](https://github.com/rohit-sekhri51/capstone-dao-notebox).

---

## Advanced: Multi-Tier Hierarchy with LazorKit's Model

LazorKit demonstrates a production-grade three-tier hierarchy for smart wallets that maps directly to DAO needs [[14]](https://github.com/lazor-kit/lazorkit-protocol/tree/17c1c82486db57252badac8726326833d9e96ecc)[[15]](https://github.com/lazor-kit/lazorkit-protocol/tree/aa0beba093f42e714495b9e5445d109cd98e7fdd):

| Role | Can execute | Can manage roles | Can transfer ownership | Can create sessions |
|------|------------|-----------------|------------------------|---------------------|
| **Owner (0)** | ✅ | ✅ (all) | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Admin (1)** | ✅ | ✅ (Spenders only) | ❌ | ✅ |
| **Spender (2+)** | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |

Key design decisions:

- **Anti-lockout**: Cannot remove the last Admin/Owner — prevents accidental DAO paralysis
- **No self-escalation**: A Spender cannot grant themselves Admin; an Admin cannot become Owner
- **Explicit transfer**: Ownership transfer requires the current Owner's signature — no silent takeover
- **Session keys**: Temporary permissions with expiry, so routine operations don't need the master key every time [[14]](https://github.com/lazor-kit/lazorkit-protocol/tree/17c1c82486db57252badac8726326833d9e96ecc)[[15]](https://github.com/lazor-kit/lazorkit-protocol/tree/aa0beba093f42e714495b9e5445d109cd98e7fdd)

---

## Security Considerations

From the Solana security patterns research [[1]](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/23922/solana-anchor-authorization-best-practice-for-a-modular-multi-program-system-sh)[[10]](https://github.com/tobi-techy/Anchor-Pinocchio-Security-Example):

| Vulnerability | Mitigation |
|--------------|------------|
| **Missing signer check** | Always use `Signer<'info>`, never `UncheckedAccount` for authority |
| **PDA seed collision** | Include all relevant identifiers in seeds; order matters |
| **CPI authority escalation** | Use `Program<'info, T>` not `UncheckedAccount` for CPI targets |
| **Account reuse** | Verify source ≠ destination when transferring |
| **Replay attacks** | Bind signatures to specific instructions and accounts |
| **Trusting CPI caller** | Never trust `invoke`r program ID — always re-check signers |
| **Centralized upgrade authority** | Use a multisig for program upgrade authority |

The golden rule from the StackExchange discussion [[1]](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/23922/solana-anchor-authorization-best-practice-for-a-modular-multi-program-system-sh):

> **"Authorization is not inferred from programs, only proofs."** A program cannot trust the caller. The only things that can be trusted are Accounts, Signatures, and PDAs derived from known seeds.

---

## The Bottom Line

| Approach | Best for | Complexity |
|----------|----------|------------|
| **Embedded role PDA** | Single-program DAO, quick to implement | Low |
| **Permission bitmask** | Fine-grained control, many permission types | Medium |
| **Dedicated RBAC program** | Multi-program DAO, composable permissions | Medium-High |
| **Sol Cerberus** | Fastest integration, `#[rule]` macro | Low (to use) |
| **SPL Governance + custom RBAC** | Full DAO with voting + granular ops | High |

All of these are built in **Rust with Anchor**. The framework's constraint system, PDA management, and CPI support are exactly the primitives that make hierarchical permissions both possible and safe. The pattern is production-proven — LazorKit, Sol Cerberus, and multiple treasury programs use it in production today [[2]](https://github.com/NandaCardinaly/solana-rbac-onchain)[[4]](https://github.com/AnderUstarroz/sol-cerberus-website/blob/main/docs/index.md)[[7]](https://github.com/ussyalfaks/treasury_vault_program)[[14]](https://github.com/lazor-kit/lazorkit-protocol/tree/17c1c82486db57252badac8726326833d9e96ecc).
what do RBAC mean?

# RBAC: Role-Based Access Control

**RBAC** stands for **Role-Based Access Control**. It's a security model where permissions are assigned to **roles**, and users are assigned to those roles — rather than granting permissions directly to individual users.

---

## The Core Idea

```
❌ Direct Permission Assignment (ACL):     ✅ Role-Based (RBAC):

  Alice → can_create_proposals              Alice → assigned role: Admin
  Alice → can_execute                       Bob   → assigned role: Contributor
  Alice → can_manage_treasury               Carol → assigned role: Member
  Bob   → can_create_proposals
  Bob   → can_vote                          Role: Admin
  Carol → can_vote                            ├─ can_create_proposals
                                               ├─ can_execute
  (6 assignments to manage)                   ├─ can_manage_treasury
                                               └─ can_vote

                                            Role: Contributor
                                              ├─ can_create_proposals
                                              └─ can_vote

                                            Role: Member
                                              └─ can_vote

                                            (3 roles, 3 user assignments)
```

When Alice leaves the DAO, you remove one assignment — not six permissions. When a new permission is added, you update the role — not every user.

---

## The Three Components

| Component | What it is | Example |
|-----------|------------|---------|
| **User** | Who is acting | Alice's wallet `7EcDh...` |
| **Role** | A named set of permissions | `Admin`, `Contributor`, `Member` |
| **Permission** | A specific action allowed | `can_execute_proposals`, `can_manage_roles` |

The relationship:

$$\text{User} \rightarrow \text{Role} \rightarrow \{\text{Permission}_1, \text{Permission}_2, ...\}$$

---

## In the Solana DAO Context

RBAC is the model we were just discussing. The `UserRole` PDA on-chain is the physical representation of the "User → Role" assignment. The `permissions` bitmask inside that account is the "Role → Permissions" mapping. The Anchor constraint:

```rust
constraint = user_role.role >= roles::ADMIN
```

is the enforcement point — the runtime RBAC check that happens before any business logic executes.

---

> **RBAC = don't manage what each person can do. Manage what each role can do, and assign people to roles.** It's the standard model for access control in operating systems, databases, cloud platforms, and now — via Anchor PDAs — Solana programs.

# How Clients Find and Connect to Solana Nodes

There are actually **two completely different answers** to this question — one for regular users and applications, and one for validators joining the network. The discovery problem is solved differently at each level.

---

## For Users and Applications: You Don't Discover — You're Told

A wallet like Phantom, a dApp, or the Solana CLI **does not search the network for nodes**. It connects to a URL that is either hardcoded, configured, or provided by an RPC service. There is no discovery protocol at the application layer [[6]](https://solana.com/docs/rpc)(https://solana.com/docs/rpc) [[19]](https://blog.triton.one/what-is-solana-rpc-nodes-endpoints-and-data-access/)(https://blog.triton.one/what-is-solana-rpc-nodes-endpoints-and-data-access/).

### The Three Ways an App Gets an RPC URL

| Method | Example | Who uses it |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| **Public endpoint (hardcoded)** | `https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com` | Wallets, CLI tools, hobby projects |
| **RPC provider API key** | `https://solana-mainnet.g.alchemy.com/v2/your-key` | Production dApps |
| **Private node** | `https://my-validator.example.com:8899` | Validator operators, institutions |

```typescript
// The simplest possible connection — a hardcoded URL
const connection = new Connection("https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com");

// Or using the convenience helper that returns the same hardcoded URL
const connection = new Connection(clusterApiUrl("mainnet-beta"));
```

The Solana Foundation operates public endpoints for each network [ [[6]](https://solana.com/docs/rpc)](https://solana.com/docs/rpc):

| Network | Public RPC Endpoint |
|---------|-------------------|
| Mainnet | `https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com` |
| Devnet | `https://api.devnet.solana.com` |
| Testnet | `https://api.testnet.solana.com` |
| Local | `http://localhost:8899` |

These are **shared, rate-limited infrastructure** — not suitable for production. For anything serious, developers use dedicated RPC providers (Helius, Triton, QuickNode, Alchemy) that give them a specific URL with an API key [ [[19]](https://blog.triton.one/what-is-solana-rpc-nodes-endpoints-and-data-access/)](https://blog.triton.one/what-is-solana-rpc-nodes-endpoints-and-data-access/).

---

## How Those RPC Nodes Found Each Other: The Gossip Protocol

This is the real answer to "how would anyone know where a node is located." The RPC nodes you connect to didn't magically appear — they discovered each other through Solana's **gossip protocol**, which is the network's control plane [ [[1]](https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/gossip-protocol-spec.md)](https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/gossip-protocol-spec.md) [[2]](https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/implementation-details.md)(https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/implementation-details.md) [[16]](https://medium.com/rakurai-io/exploring-solana-a-deep-dive-into-its-core-components-7c0d1bce7e28)(https://medium.com/rakurai-io/exploring-solana-a-deep-dive-into-its-core-components-7c0d1bce7e28).

### The Bootstrap Problem

A new validator starting up faces the same question you asked: "where is anyone?" It solves this through **entrypoints** — a small set of well-known bootstrap nodes with DNS names that every validator operator configures [[2]](https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/implementation-details.md)(https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/implementation-details.md)[ [[11]](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/21502/solana-validator-not-finding-peers)](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/21502/solana-validator-not-finding-peers):

```bash
solana-validator \
  --entrypoint entrypoint.mainnet-beta.solana.com:8001 \
  --entrypoint entrypoint2.mainnet-beta.solana.com:8001 \
  --entrypoint entrypoint3.mainnet-beta.solana.com:8001 \
  ...
```

These entrypoint DNS names resolve to IP addresses of stable, long-running validators operated by the Solana Foundation and major infrastructure providers. They are the **seed nodes** — the only hardcoded addresses in the entire system [ [[11]](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/21502/solana-validator-not-finding-peers)](https://solana.stackexchange.com/questions/21502/solana-validator-not-finding-peers).

### The Bootstrap Sequence

```
New validator starts up
    │
    ▼
1. IP ECHO: Connects to entrypoint's TCP echo server (same IP:port as gossip)
   Sends list of its own ports → entrypoint probes them → responds with:
     • The validator's public IP (NAT discovery)
     • The cluster's shred_version (hard-fork identifier)
    │
    ▼
2. GOSSIP JOIN: Sends push messages to entrypoint containing:
     • Its own ContactInfo (pubkey, gossip addr, RPC addr, TPU addr, etc.)
     • A pull request with Bloom filters over its empty CrdsTable
    │
    ▼
3. PEER DISCOVERY: Entrypoint propagates the new node's ContactInfo
   to other nodes via push messages. Other nodes start including
   the new node in their pull requests and active sets.
    │
    ▼
4. FULL PARTICIPATION: Within seconds, the new node has a populated
   CrdsTable with hundreds of peers — all discovered through gossip,
   not hardcoded.
```

The IP Echo step is critical — it solves NAT traversal. A validator behind a firewall doesn't know its own public IP. The entrypoint tells it, and also verifies that its ports are reachable from the outside world [[1]](https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/gossip-protocol-spec.md)(https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/gossip-protocol-spec.md)[ [[2]](https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/implementation-details.md)](https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/implementation-details.md).

### What Gets Gossiped

Every node periodically broadcasts a `ContactInfo` message containing **all** its network addresses [[1]](https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/gossip-protocol-spec.md)(https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/gossip-protocol-spec.md) [[5]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/27eff8408b7223bb3c4ab70523f8a8dca3ca6645/gossip/src/contact_info.rs)(https://github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/27eff8408b7223bb3c4ab70523f8a8dca3ca6645/gossip/src/contact_info.rs):

| Field | Port (default) | Protocol | Purpose |
|-------|---------------|----------|---------|
| `gossip` | 8001 | UDP | Gossip protocol itself |
| `tvu` | 8000 | UDP | Turbine block propagation (data plane) |
| `tpu` | 8856 | UDP/QUIC | Transaction ingestion |
| `rpc` | 8899 | TCP (HTTP) | **JSON-RPC for applications** |
| `rpc_pubsub` | 8900 | TCP (WebSocket) | Subscription push notifications |
| `serve_repair` | 8002 | UDP/QUIC | Block repair requests |

This is how RPC nodes become discoverable: they advertise their `rpc` address via gossip, and other nodes record it. The `getClusterNodes` RPC method simply dumps this gossip table — it returns every node that has advertised itself [[3]](https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getclusternodes)(https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getclusternodes) [[18]](https://solana.com/el/docs/rpc/http/getclusternodes)(https://solana.com/el/docs/rpc/http/getclusternodes).
