## The Two-Layer Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION LAYER                          │
│                                                              │
│  Wallet / dApp / CLI                                         │
│       │                                                      │
│       │ HTTPS (JSON-RPC)                                     │
│       ▼                                                      │
│  https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com                         │
│  (hardcoded URL — NO discovery)                              │
│       │                                                      │
│       │ This URL resolves (DNS → load balancer → RPC node)   │
│       ▼                                                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │              RPC NODE (validator or dedicated)        │   │
│  │                                                       │   │
│  │  This node found its peers via:                       │   │
│  │                                                       │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │   │
│  │  │         GOSSIP NETWORK (control plane)        │    │   │
│  │  │                                              │    │   │
│  │  │  Entrypoints (hardcoded DNS)                 │    │   │
│  │  │      │                                       │    │   │
│  │  │      ▼                                       │    │   │
│  │  │  IP Echo → public IP + shred version         │    │   │
│  │  │      │                                       │    │   │
│  │  │      ▼                                       │    │   │
│  │  │  Push/Pull ContactInfo → discover all peers  │    │   │
│  │  │  (UDP, port 8001, ~2,000+ validators)        │    │   │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## The Chain of Hardcoding

At every layer, something is hardcoded — but only the **minimum necessary**:

| Layer | What's hardcoded | What's discovered |
|-------|-----------------|-------------------|
| **Application** | RPC endpoint URL | Nothing — just calls the URL |
| **RPC Provider** | Entrypoint DNS names | All peer validators via gossip |
| **Entrypoint** | Nothing (it IS the hardcoded thing) | All other nodes via gossip |
| **Gossip network** | Entrypoints only | Everything else — ~2,000+ nodes |

The system works because **only the entrypoints need to be known in advance**, and there are only a handful of them. Everything else propagates from there [[2]](https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/implementation-details.md)(https://github.com/eigerco/solana-spec/blob/main/implementation-details.md)[ [[16]](https://medium.com/rakurai-io/exploring-solana-a-deep-dive-into-its-core-components-7c0d1bce7e28)](https://medium.com/rakurai-io/exploring-solana-a-deep-dive-into-its-core-components-7c0d1bce7e28).

---

## How You Can See the Network Yourself

```bash
# See every node in the gossip table
solana gossip --url https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com

# Or programmatically
curl https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com \
  -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"getClusterNodes"}'
```

This returns every validator's IP, gossip port, RPC port, version, and shred version — the entire network topology, discovered through gossip, available through a single RPC call [ [[3]](https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getclusternodes)](https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getclusternodes) [[18]](https://solana.com/el/docs/rpc/http/getclusternodes)(https://solana.com/el/docs/rpc/http/getclusternodes).

---

## The Bottom Line

> **As a user, you never discover a node. You connect to a URL you were given.** That URL leads to an RPC node. That RPC node found its place in the network through Solana's gossip protocol, bootstrapped from a handful of well-known entrypoints with hardcoded DNS names. The entire network topology — thousands of validators — is discovered through gossip. But your wallet never touches gossip. It just makes HTTPS requests to a URL.
Can you sign things with your solana wallet?

# Yes — Two Fundamentally Different Kinds of Signing

Your Solana wallet can sign **two completely different things**, and the distinction matters.

---

## 1. Transaction Signing (On-Chain)

This is the core function we've been discussing throughout this conversation. Your wallet signs a **transaction message** — a structured byte packet containing instructions, accounts, and a recent blockhash. The signature proves you authorized those specific instructions, and the network executes them [[11]](https://dev.to/100daysofsolana/learn-solana-the-fast-way-4kg4)(https://dev.to/100daysofsolana/learn-solana-the-fast-way-4kg4).

```
You click "Send 5 SOL to Alice"
    │
    ▼
Wallet constructs a Transaction Message
    │
    ▼
Wallet signs it with your Ed25519 private key
    │
    ▼
Signed transaction → RPC → validators → executed on-chain
```

This costs SOL (the transaction fee) and permanently changes on-chain state.

---

## 2. Off-Chain Message Signing (Free, No Blockchain)

Your wallet can also sign **arbitrary messages** that never touch the blockchain. This is a pure cryptographic proof — "the person who controls this address approved this specific text" [ [[1]](https://docs.phantom.com/solana/signing-a-message)](https://docs.phantom.com/solana/signing-a-message) [[6]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/master/docs/src/proposals/off-chain-message-signing.md)(https://github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/master/docs/src/proposals/off-chain-message-signing.md) [[7]](https://docs.anza.xyz/proposals/off-chain-message-signing)(https://docs.anza.xyz/proposals/off-chain-message-signing).

```typescript
// In a dApp — no transaction, no fee, no blockchain
const message = "Sign in to My dApp — nonce: 7a3f2c";
const encodedMessage = new TextEncoder().encode(message);
const signedMessage = await wallet.signMessage(encodedMessage, "utf8");

// signedMessage contains the Ed25519 signature
// Verify it server-side to authenticate the user
```

### What This Is Used For

| Use Case | Example |
|----------|---------|
| **Wallet-based login** | "Sign in with Solana" — replaces email/password |
| **Proof of ownership** | "Sign this to prove you own this address" |
| **Off-chain agreements** | Signing terms of service, whitelist applications |
| **Session binding** | Prove you still control the wallet without a new transaction |
| **DAO off-chain voting** | Signal your preference without paying gas (Snapshot-style) |

### The Critical Safety Feature

Off-chain message signatures are **deliberately incompatible** with transactions. The signing domain specifier begins with `0xff`, which is an illegal first byte for any transaction `MessageHeader`. This means:

> **Even if someone tricks you into signing a message that looks like a transaction, the network will reject it.** The two signing domains are cryptographically separated [[6]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/master/docs/src/proposals/off-chain-message-signing.md)(https://github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/master/docs/src/proposals/off-chain-message-signing.md)[ [[7]](https://docs.anza.xyz/proposals/off-chain-message-signing)](https://docs.anza.xyz/proposals/off-chain-message-signing).

### The Message Format

Off-chain messages have a structured preamble to prevent ambiguity [[6]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/master/docs/src/proposals/off-chain-message-signing.md)(https://github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/master/docs/src/proposals/off-chain-message-signing.md) [[7]](https://docs.anza.xyz/proposals/off-chain-message-signing)(https://docs.anza.xyz/proposals/off-chain-message-signing):

```
┌──────────────────────┬──────┬────────────────────────────┐
│ Field                │ Size │ Content                    │
├──────────────────────┼──────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ Signing domain       │ 16 B │ "\xffsolana offchain"      │
│ Header version       │ 1 B  │ 0 or 1                     │
│ Application domain   │ 32 B │ e.g. "my-dapp.com"         │
│ Message format       │ 1 B  │ 0=ASCII, 1=UTF-8           │
│ Signer count         │ 1 B  │ Number of required signers  │
│ Signers              │ N×32 │ Public keys                 │
│ Message length       │ 2 B  │ u16 little-endian           │
│ Message body         │ var  │ The actual message          │
└──────────────────────┴──────┴────────────────────────────┘
```

The wallet signs the entire preamble + body. The verifier reconstructs the same bytes and checks the Ed25519 signature.

---

## Sign In With Solana (SIWS)

Built on top of message signing, SIWS is a standardized authentication protocol — the Solana equivalent of "Sign in with Google" [ [[1]](https://docs.phantom.com/solana/signing-a-message)](https://docs.phantom.com/solana/signing-a-message)[ [[8]](https://learn.blueshift.gg/en/courses/mobile-dapp-fundamentals/signing-messages)](https://learn.blueshift.gg/en/courses/mobile-dapp-fundamentals/signing-messages) [[9]](https://github.com/destinyae/sign-in-with-solana)(https://github.com/destinyae/sign-in-with-solana):

```typescript
// One-click authentication — wallet constructs the message
const { account, signedMessage, signature } = await wallet.signIn({
    domain: "mydapp.com",
    statement: "Sign in to My dApp",
    uri: "https://mydapp.com",
    version: "1",
    nonce: "7a3f2c",        // Server-generated, prevents replay
    issuedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
});

// Verify server-side:
// 1. Reconstruct the expected message from the same parameters
// 2. Verify the Ed25519 signature against the user's public key
// 3. Check the nonce matches what you issued
// 4. Issue a session token
```

The wallet constructs the message, so the user sees a consistent, recognizable prompt — not a random hex string. This prevents phishing where a malicious dApp tricks you into signing something you don't understand [[9]](https://github.com/destinyae/sign-in-with-solana)(https://github.com/destinyae/sign-in-with-solana).

---

## The Two Signing Paths Compared

| | Transaction Signing | Message Signing |
|---|---|---|
| **What you sign** | Structured transaction bytes | Arbitrary text/bytes |
| **Cost** | ~5,000 lamports + priority fee | **Free** |
| **On-chain effect** | Changes account state | **None** |
| **Network required?** | Yes | No (offline verification possible) |
| **Use case** | Send SOL, call programs, vote | Login, prove ownership, off-chain agreements |
| **Replay risk** | Blockhash prevents replay | Nonce prevents replay |
| **Hardware wallet** | Full support | Supported (Ledger 1.3.0+) [[18]](https://docs.anza.xyz/cli/examples/sign-offchain-message)(https://docs.anza.xyz/cli/examples/sign-offchain-message) |

---

## CLI Examples

```bash
# Sign an off-chain message with the CLI
solana sign-offchain-message "I hereby agree to the terms"

# Sign with a specific keypair
solana sign-offchain-message -k ~/my-keypair.json "Hello, Solana"

# Sign with a Ledger hardware wallet
solana sign-offchain-message -k usb://ledger "Authorize this action"

# Verify a signature
solana verify-offchain-signature "Hello, Solana" <SIGNATURE>
```

---

## The Bottom Line

> **Your Solana wallet is a general-purpose Ed25519 signing device.** It signs transactions to change on-chain state. It signs messages to prove identity off-chain. The same keypair, the same cryptographic algorithm, two completely separated domains — enforced by the `0xff` prefix that makes off-chain signatures impossible to replay as transactions.

# You're Mostly Right — But There's a Practical Reason for the NFT Approach

Your critique is sharp and well-founded. Let me break down where you're correct, where the whitepaper's approach has legitimate advantages, and where the two concerns (NFTs vs. RBAC, and AI subordination) are actually orthogonal.

---

## Where You're Absolutely Correct

### 1. The wallet address IS the identity

On Solana, every interaction — human or AI agent — requires a keypair. The public key is the universal identifier. You could absolutely build the entire membership system as:

```rust
#[account]
pub struct MemberRecord {
    pub authority: Pubkey,      // the wallet
    pub member_type: u8,        // 0=Human, 1=AI
    pub is_active: bool,
    pub agreed_to_manifesto: bool,
    pub agreed_to_licence: bool,
    pub is_pioneer: bool,
    pub human_sponsor: Option<Pubkey>,  // for AI members
    pub bump: u8,
}
```

One PDA per wallet. One data structure. No NFTs. Clean, efficient, and the wallet address is the identifier. This is exactly the RBAC pattern we discussed earlier.

### 2. The NFTs live on-chain anyway

As we established, an NFT on Solana requires a Mint Account, a Token Account, and a Metadata Account — all on-chain. The whitepaper's approach doesn't avoid on-chain storage; it multiplies it. A single `MemberRecord` PDA would be far more efficient than three accounts per credential type.

### 3. AI subordination is an RBAC problem, not an NFT problem

The whitepaper says:

> "AI Community Member registration requires an active Human Community Member to sign the registration. An AI member must always be linked to a human account."

This is a **relationship constraint** — it doesn't matter whether the credential is stored as an NFT or a PDA field. The enforcement logic is identical:

```rust
// Whether the credential is an NFT or a PDA field, the check is the same:
#[account(
    constraint = human_sponsor_record.is_active 
        && human_sponsor_record.member_type == MemberType::Human 
        @ ErrorCode::InvalidSponsor
)]
pub human_sponsor_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,
```

The subordination hierarchy (AI → Human → DAO) is orthogonal to the storage format. You're right that RBAC handles this naturally.

---

## What the NFT Approach Actually Buys Them

Despite the above, there are legitimate — if debatable — reasons to use NFTs:

### 1. Ecosystem Composability (The Strongest Argument)

The Metaplex Token Metadata standard is the **universal language** of the Solana ecosystem. Every wallet (Phantom, Solflare, Backpack), every explorer (Solscan, SolanaFM), and every analytics tool understands it natively.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  What Phantom shows for a wallet with:                   │
│                                                          │
│  Custom PDA (your approach):                             │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  SOL: 2.5                                         │   │
│  │  Tokens: (nothing visible about membership)       │   │
│  │  ── requires custom UI to display membership      │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                          │
│  NFT credential (whitepaper approach):                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  SOL: 2.5                                         │   │
│  │  NFTs:                                            │   │
│  │    🏅 Human Community Member                      │   │
│  │    📜 Augmentatism Manifesto                      │   │
│  │    ⭐ Resonant Pioneer #42/1000                   │   │
│  │  ── visible in every wallet, explorer, dApp      │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

For a DAO that wants other programs in the "Resonant Economy" to gate access based on membership, the NFT standard means any program can check:

```rust
// Any program in the ecosystem can verify membership
// without knowing about ResonantDAO's specific program ID
let token_account = get_associated_token_address(&wallet, &community_nft_mint);
// If this token account exists and has amount > 0 → they're a member
```

With a custom PDA, every external program needs to know ResonantDAO's program ID and account layout. That's not impossible — it's just more friction.

### 2. Multiple Independent Credentials

The whitepaper describes five distinct credentials:

| Credential | What it proves |
|------------|---------------|
| Manifesto NFT | "I signed the Manifesto text" |
| Human Community Member NFT | "I am an active human member" |
| AI Community Member NFT | "I am an active AI member, sponsored by human X" |
| Symbiotic Licence NFT | "I agreed to the Licence terms" |
| Pioneer NFT | "I was one of the first 1,000" |

These are **independent attestations** with different issuance conditions and potentially different revocation rules. Using separate NFTs makes each one a discrete, verifiable, independently queryable on-chain object. A single `MemberRecord` PDA would need to track all of these as boolean flags — workable, but less granular.

### 3. The "Proof of Agreement" Problem

The Manifesto NFT and Symbiotic Licence NFT aren't just role assignments — they're **cryptographic proofs that a specific wallet signed a specific text at a specific time**. The minting transaction includes the signature over the canonical hash. The NFT serves as an immutable receipt:

> "Wallet `7EcDh...` signed the Manifesto with hash `0xabc123...` on June 15, 2026."

You could store this in a PDA field too. But the NFT standard gives you a well-understood format for "this wallet performed this action and here's the proof" that the ecosystem already knows how to display and verify.

### 4. The Whitepaper Itself Acknowledges the Distinction

From the whitepaper [[1]](https://resonantdao.com/whitepaper/):

> "The on-chain member record is the source of truth. Metadata, images, and NFT names can be copied by fake collections, but fake NFTs cannot create an official ResonantDAO member record."

And from the Symbiotic Licence page [[3]](https://resonantos.com/symbiotic-license/):

> "The licence NFT is a credential, not the full legal text."

They're using NFTs as **credential wrappers** around an underlying member record. The NFT is the visible, composable, ecosystem-standard representation. The member record PDA is the authoritative source of truth. This is a two-layer design, not NFT-as-database.

---

## The Honest Assessment

| Concern | Your critique | Whitepaper's likely reasoning |
|---------|---------------|-------------------------------|
| NFTs are unnecessary overhead | ✅ Valid — a PDA is simpler | NFTs are ecosystem-composable |
| Wallet address is sufficient identity | ✅ Valid — it is | NFTs make membership visible in standard tooling |
| AI subordination is RBAC | ✅ Valid — it is | The NFT is just the credential format; RBAC logic is separate |
| Multiple accounts per credential | ✅ Valid — inefficient | Each credential is an independent attestation |
| Could use a single MemberRecord PDA | ✅ Valid — more efficient | Less granular for independent revocation |

**You're not missing anything technically.** Your proposed approach — wallet addresses as identity, RBAC PDAs for membership, and program-level constraints for AI subordination — would work perfectly and be more gas-efficient.

The NFT approach is a **UX and ecosystem compatibility decision**, not a technical necessity. It trades on-chain efficiency for:

1. **Immediate visibility** in every Solana wallet and explorer
2. **Standardized composability** with any program that understands Token Metadata
3. **Independent credential objects** that can be issued, revoked, and queried separately
4. **Familiarity** — "NFT membership" is a well-understood pattern in Web3 (despite its inefficiencies)

---

## What I'd Recommend to Your Friend

If I were advising them, I'd suggest a **hybrid** that captures the best of both:

```rust
// The source of truth — one PDA per wallet
#[account]
pub struct MemberRecord {
    pub authority: Pubkey,
    pub member_type: MemberType,     // Human or AI
    pub human_sponsor: Option<Pubkey>,
    pub is_active: bool,
    pub agreed_manifesto: bool,
    pub agreed_licence: bool,
    pub is_pioneer: bool,
    pub joined_at: i64,
    pub bump: u8,
}

// NFTs are issued as OPTIONAL visible credentials
// that point back to the MemberRecord as the authority
// If an NFT is burned (revoked), the MemberRecord is the
// source of truth for whether membership is actually valid
```

This way:
- The `MemberRecord` PDA is the authoritative source — efficient, single source of truth
- NFTs are minted as **cosmetic/ecosystem representations** of the underlying record
- External programs can check either the NFT (for simple "are you a member?" queries) or the MemberRecord (for authoritative verification)
- Revocation burns the NFT AND updates the MemberRecord — the record is always authoritative

The whitepaper actually hints at this when it says "the on-chain member record is the source of truth" — they may already be thinking along these lines, even if the current documentation emphasizes the NFT layer.

---

> **Bottom line:** Your instinct is correct. The wallet address + RBAC is the cleaner engineering solution. The NFT approach is a pragmatic concession to ecosystem standards and user experience. The AI subordination requirement is an RBAC concern regardless of which storage format they choose.
What does PDA Stand for?

# PDA: Program Derived Address

A **Program Derived Address** is a public key on Solana that has **no corresponding private key**. It is derived deterministically from a program's ID and a set of seed values, and only that program can authorize actions on its behalf.

---

## The Name, Broken Down

| Word | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Program** | A Solana smart contract — the only entity that can "sign" for this address |
| **Derived** | Computed from inputs (seeds + program ID), not generated from a keypair |
| **Address** | A 32-byte public key on the Ed25519 curve — looks like any other Solana address |

---

## Why "Derived" Matters

A normal address is **generated** — you create a random keypair, and the public key is your address. A PDA is **computed**:

$$\text{PDA} = \text{find\_program\_address}(\text{seeds}, \ \text{program\_id})$$

Same seeds + same program ID = same PDA, every time. This determinism is what makes them useful — you can predict the address before it exists, and the runtime can verify it on the fly.

# You've Put Your Finger on the Core Issue

You're right. The NFT approach does **not** eliminate the need for blockchain access or the wallet address. It just changes *what* you query and *who* already has the indexing infrastructure for it.

## The Verification Flow: Both Approaches Require the Same Things

```
                    NFT Approach                    PDA Approach
                    ────────────                    ────────────
```

### 1. Reverse Discovery (The Real Advantage)

With a custom PDA, you can only answer: *"Given wallet W, is W a member?"*

With an NFT, you can also answer: *"Given the ResonantDAO community mint, who are all the members?"*

```typescript

);
```

# All Built-In Primitives on Solana

Solana's shared infrastructure falls into three layers: **Native Programs** (compiled into every validator), **Precompiles** (native cryptographic verification), and **SPL Programs** (on-chain programs at well-known addresses, maintained by the Solana Program Library). Here's the complete picture.

---

## Layer 1: Native Programs (Builtins)

These are compiled directly into the validator binary. They don't live on-chain as executable accounts — the runtime looks them up by their well-known program IDs and calls native Rust code, not BPF bytecode [[1]](https://solana.com/docs/core/programs/builtin-programs)[[9]](https://solana.com/docs/core/programs/program-execution).

| Program | Address | What it does |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| **System Program** | `11111111111111111111111111111111` | Creates accounts, transfers SOL, allocates data, assigns ownership. The only program that can create new accounts. Every wallet uses this. |
| **Vote Program** | `Vote111111111111111111111111111111111111111` | Creates and manages validator vote accounts. Tracks voting state and rewards. |
| **Stake Program** | `Stake11111111111111111111111111111111111111` | Creates and manages stake delegations. Handles staking, unstaking, withdrawals, merging, splitting. |
| **Config Program** | `Config1111111111111111111111111111111111111` | Stores on-chain configuration data with key-based access control. Used for network-wide settings. |
| **Compute Budget** | `ComputeBudget111111111111111111111111111111` | Sets compute unit limits and priority fees per transaction. Called before execution. |
| **Address Lookup Table** | `AddressLookupTab1e1111111111111111111111111` | Manages on-chain address lookup tables for v0 transactions that reference many accounts. |
| **ZK ElGamal Proof** | `ZkE1Gama1Proof11111111111111111111111111111` | Verifies zero-knowledge proofs for ElGamal-encrypted data. Used by Token-2022 confidential transfers. |
| **Feature Gate** | `Feature111111111111111111111111111111111111` | Tracks which protocol features are activated. Used for network upgrades. |

All of these consume a flat 150 compute units per instruction (except Compute Budget, which is free) [[1]](https://solana.com/docs/core/programs/builtin-programs).

---

## Layer 2: Precompiles (Native Signature Verification)

These bypass the BPF VM entirely — they run as native code because BPF is too slow for elliptic curve math. They are **not callable via CPI** from other programs. Instead, they're included as instructions in the same transaction and the runtime verifies them before your program runs [[2]](https://solana.com/docs/core/programs/precompiles)[[7]](https://docs.rs/solana-precompiles/latest/src/solana_precompiles/lib.rs.html)[[10]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-improvement-documents/blob/main/proposals/0152-precompiles.md).

| Precompile | Address | What it verifies |
|------------|---------|-----------------|
| **Ed25519** | `Ed25519SigVerify111111111111111111111111111` | Verifies one or more Ed25519 signatures. Used when you need to verify a signature that wasn't part of the transaction itself. |
| **Secp256k1** | `KeccakSecp256k11111111111111111111111111111` | Verifies secp256k1 public key recovery (ecrecover). EVM-compatible — used for Ethereum address verification. |
| **Secp256r1** | `Secp256r1SigVerify1111111111111111111111111` | Verifies up to 8 secp256r1 (P-256) signatures. This is the WebAuthn/Passkey curve — enables Face ID, Touch ID, YubiKey verification on-chain. |

The secp256r1 precompile is what makes passkey-based smart wallets possible — it was activated via SIMD-0075 [[2]](https://solana.com/docs/core/programs/precompiles)[[16]](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-improvement-documents/blob/main/proposals/0075-precompile-for-secp256r1-sigverify.md).

---

## Layer 3: Loader Programs

Every on-chain program is owned by a loader. Loaders handle deployment, upgrades, and execution [[1]](https://solana.com/docs/core/programs/builtin-programs)[[6]](https://solana.com/docs/core/programs/program-deployment).

| Loader | Address | Upgradeable? | Status |
|--------|---------|-------------|--------|
| **Native Loader** | `NativeLoader1111111111111111111111111111111` | Only via validator software upgrade | Owns all builtins and other loaders |
| **BPF Loader (v1)** | `BPFLoader1111111111111111111111111111111111` | No (disabled) | Legacy |
| **BPF Loader (v2)** | `BPFLoader2111111111111111111111111111111111` | No (disabled) | Legacy |
| **BPF Loader Upgradeable (v3)** | `BPFLoaderUpgradeab1e11111111111111111111111` | Yes, if upgrade authority is set | **Current default** — owns all newly deployed programs |

When you deploy a program with `anchor deploy`, it goes through the BPF Loader Upgradeable. You can set an upgrade authority (a wallet or multisig) that can push new versions, or revoke it to make the program immutable forever [[6]](https://solana.com/docs/core/programs/program-deployment).

---

## Layer 4: SPL Programs (On-Chain Standard Library)

These are on-chain programs maintained by the Solana Program Library. They're deployed at well-known addresses and used by the entire ecosystem. Unlike builtins, they run as BPF bytecode and consume compute units normally [[3]](https://github.com/solana-labs/solana-program-library)[[5]](https://www.solana-program.com/docs/token)[[14]](https://solana.com/docs/tokens).

| Program | Address | What it does |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| **Token Program** | `TokenkegQfeZyiNwAJbNbGKPFXCWuBvf9Ss623VQ5DA` | The original token standard. Creates mints, token accounts, transfers, burns, freezes. Every SPL token and NFT uses this. |
| **Token-2022** | `TokenzQdBNbLqP5VEhdkAS6EPFLC1PHnBqCXEpPxuEb` | Superset of Token Program. Adds extensions: confidential transfers, transfer hooks, interest-bearing tokens, metadata on mint, permanent delegate, non-transferable tokens, and more. |
| **Associated Token Account** | `ATokenGPvbdGVxr1b2hvZbsiqW5xWH25efTNsLJA8knL` | Stateless program that deterministically derives the "default" token account for any (wallet, mint) pair. Enables sending tokens to a wallet that doesn't have a token account yet. |
| **Token Metadata** | `metaqbxxUerdq28cj1RbAWkYQm3ybzjb6a8bt518x1s` | Metaplex standard. Attaches name, symbol, URI, creators, royalties to any mint. This is what makes an SPL token *displayable* as an NFT. |

# Tying AI Agents to Human Identities on Solana

The whitepaper's requirement is:

> *"An AI member must always be linked to a human account. The human must sign the AI's registration. The AI is subordinate to its human owner for actions on the DAO."*

This is a **sponsorship model with revocable delegation**. Here's how you implement it.

---

## The Core Data Structure

```rust
#[account]
pub struct MemberRecord {
    pub authority: Pubkey,           // 32 — the wallet (human or AI)
    pub member_type: MemberType,     // 1  — Human or AI
    pub is_active: bool,             // 1
    pub human_sponsor: Option<Pubkey>, // 33 — None for humans, Some(parent) for AI
    pub agreed_manifesto: bool,      // 1
    pub agreed_licence: bool,        // 1
    pub is_pioneer: bool,            // 1
    pub joined_at: i64,              // 8
    pub bump: u8,                    // 1
}
```

The `human_sponsor` field is the link. For a human, it's `None`. For an AI, it's `Some(human_wallet_address)`. This is the on-chain tether.

---

## Registration: The Human Must Sign

The AI generates its own keypair — it has its own wallet. But it can't self-register. The human must co-sign:

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct RegisterAiMember<'info> {
    #[account(
        init,
        payer = human,
        space = MemberRecord::SPACE,
        seeds = [b"member", ai_authority.key().as_ref()],
        bump
    )]
    pub ai_member_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    #[account(
        seeds = [b"member", human.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = human_record.member_type == MemberType::Human 
            @ ErrorCode::NotHuman,
        constraint = human_record.is_active 
            @ ErrorCode::SponsorInactive,
    )]
    pub human_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    /// The AI's wallet — does NOT need to sign
    /// The AI doesn't even need to be present
    pub ai_authority: SystemAccount<'info>,

    #[account(mut)]
    pub human: Signer<'info>,  // ← Human must sign
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}

pub fn register_ai_member(ctx: Context<RegisterAiMember>) -> Result<()> {
    let record = &mut ctx.accounts.ai_member_record;
    record.authority = ctx.accounts.ai_authority.key();
    record.member_type = MemberType::AI;
    record.is_active = true;
    record.human_sponsor = Some(ctx.accounts.human.key());
    record.joined_at = Clock::get()?.unix_timestamp;
    record.bump = ctx.bumps.ai_member_record;
    Ok(())
}
```

The critical constraint: `human: Signer<'info>`. The AI's wallet doesn't sign. The human does. The human is saying: *"I vouch for this AI. It acts under my authority."*

---

## Day-to-Day Actions: AI Acts, Program Verifies Sponsorship

When the AI votes on a proposal or performs any DAO action, it signs with its own keypair. The program checks the sponsorship chain:

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct AiVoteOnProposal<'info> {
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"member", ai.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = ai_record.member_type == MemberType::AI 
            @ ErrorCode::NotAi,
        constraint = ai_record.is_active 
            @ ErrorCode::AiDeactivated,
    )]
    pub ai_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    #[account(
        seeds = [b"member", ai_record.human_sponsor.unwrap().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = human_record.member_type == MemberType::Human 
            @ ErrorCode::SponsorNotHuman,
        constraint = human_record.is_active 
            @ ErrorCode::SponsorInactive,
    )]
    pub human_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    #[account(mut)]
    pub ai: Signer<'info>,  // ← AI signs with its own keypair
    // ... proposal accounts
}
```

The AI signs. The program traces the `human_sponsor` link and verifies the human is still active. If the human has been deactivated or revoked the AI, the transaction fails.

## Revocation: The Human Pulls the Plug

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct RevokeAiMember<'info> {
    #[account(
        mut,
        seeds = [b"member", ai_authority.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = ai_record.member_type == MemberType::AI 
            @ ErrorCode::NotAi,
        constraint = ai_record.human_sponsor == Some(human.key()) 
            @ ErrorCode::NotYourAi,
    )]
    pub ai_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    #[account(
        seeds = [b"member", human.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = human_record.is_active 
            @ ErrorCode::SponsorInactive,
    )]
    pub human_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    pub ai_authority: SystemAccount<'info>,
    pub human: Signer<'info>,  // ← Only the sponsor can revoke
}

pub fn revoke_ai_member(ctx: Context<RevokeAiMember>) -> Result<()> {
    ctx.accounts.ai_record.is_active = false;
    Ok(())
}
```

One instruction. The AI can no longer act. The human doesn't need the AI's cooperation.

## Why This Works

| Property | How it's enforced |
|----------|-------------------|
| AI can't self-register | `human: Signer<'info>` required in registration |
| AI is linked to one human | `human_sponsor: Some(human_pubkey)` in the AI's PDA |
| Human controls the AI's existence | Only the human can call `revoke_ai_member` |
| AI can act autonomously | AI signs its own transactions; program checks sponsorship |
| Human can't be impersonated by AI | AI's `member_type` is `AI`; human's is `Human` — different roles |
| Revocation is immediate | `is_active = false` takes effect next transaction |
| One human can sponsor multiple AIs | Each AI gets its own PDA; all point to the same human |

The AI has its own wallet. The human has their own wallet. Neither controls the other's key. The relationship is **not cryptographic** — it's **on-chain state** enforced by the program.

The program is the intermediary that says: *"AI wallet `AiK3...` is allowed to act because human wallet `7EcDh...` vouched for it and hasn't revoked that trust."*

This is exactly the RBAC pattern we discussed earlier, with one addition: a **sponsorship pointer** that creates a chain of authority the program walks on every action.

## Why This Is Wise

### 1. Defense in Depth

| If the agent is compromised... | Without your design | With your design |
|-------------------------------|---------------------|------------------|
| Attacker gets | Private key → full wallet control | API token → limited to what the CLI allows |
| Attacker can | Drain all SOL, transfer all NFTs, sign anything | Only call the specific actions the CLI exposes |
| Revocation | Must rotate on-chain keypair (expensive, permanent) | Delete API token from keystore (instant, local) |

The API token is a **blast radius limiter**. Even a fully compromised agent can only do what the CLI's interface allows.

### 2. Scoped Permissions Per Agent

```json
// keystore entry
{
  "token": "sk-abc123",
  "keypair": "AiK3...",
  "permissions": {
    "allowed_actions": ["vote", "comment", "read_proposals"],
    "max_sol_per_tx": 0,
    "require_human_approval_for": ["transfer", "create_proposal"]
  },
  "sponsor": "7EcDh..."
}
```

The CLI enforces these **before signing**. The agent can't escalate because the CLI won't sign an action outside its scope. This is RBAC at the local proxy layer, complementing the on-chain RBAC.

### 3. The Human Sponsorship Model Maps Perfectly

```
Human creates agent wallet:
  $ sol-agent create-wallet --agent my-trader --sponsor 7EcDh...
  → CLI generates keypair, stores in keystore
  → CLI returns API token to human
  → Human puts API token in agent's .env
  → Human signs on-chain registration: "AiK3... is sponsored by 7EcDh..."

Agent acts:
  $ agent-cli vote --proposal 42 --aye
  → CLI looks up token, finds keypair AiK3...
  → CLI signs transaction with AiK3...
  → On-chain program verifies: AiK3... is active AI, sponsored by 7EcDh...
  → Vote recorded

Human revokes:
  $ sol-agent revoke --agent my-trader
  → CLI deletes API token (immediate, local)
  → CLI optionally calls revoke_ai_member on-chain (permanent)
```

The human never shares their own keypair. The agent never sees any keypair. The sponsorship is enforced both locally (CLI permissions) and on-chain (program constraints).

## Feasibility: The Implementation

### The Keystore

```rust
// A simple encrypted SQLite or file-based store
struct KeystoreEntry {
    token_hash: [u8; 32],       // SHA-256 of the API token
    keypair: Vec<u8>,           // Encrypted 64-byte keypair
    permissions: Permissions,
    sponsor: Pubkey,
    created_at: i64,
    expires_at: Option<i64>,
}

struct Permissions {
    allowed_actions: Vec<String>,  // ["vote", "propose", "comment"]
    max_lamports_per_tx: u64,
    require_approval_for: Vec<String>,  // ["transfer", "burn"]
}
```

The keystore is encrypted at rest with a key derived from the user's machine credentials or a master password. The API tokens are stored as hashes — the raw token only exists in the agent's `.env` file.

### The Agent CLI

```rust
// The interface the agent calls
#[derive(Subcommand)]
enum AgentCommand {
    Vote {
        #[arg(long)]
        proposal: u64,
        #[arg(long)]
        aye: bool,
    },
    Comment {
        #[arg(long)]
        proposal: u64,
        #[arg(long)]
        body: String,
    },
    ReadProposal {
        #[arg(long)]
        proposal: u64,
    },
    // NOT exposed: Transfer, Burn, CreateProposal (requires human approval)
}

// Main flow
fn main() {
    let token = std::env::var("AGENT_API_TOKEN")?;
    let cmd = AgentCommand::parse();
    
    let entry = keystore::lookup(&token)?;
    
    // Permission check
    if !entry.permissions.allowed_actions.contains(&cmd.action_name()) {
        return Err("Action not permitted for this token");
    }
    
    // If action requires human approval, send a notification
    if entry.permissions.require_approval_for.contains(&cmd.action_name()) {
        notify_human_for_approval(&cmd, &entry)?;
    }
    
    // Sign and submit
    let tx = build_transaction(&cmd, &entry)?;
    let signed = sign_with_keypair(&tx, &entry.keypair)?;
    let sig = submit_to_rpc(&signed)?;
    
    println!("{}", sig);
}
```

## Potential Weaknesses and Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|------|------------|
| **Keystore compromise** | Encrypt at rest. Use OS keychain (macOS Keychain, freedesktop Secret Service, Windows Credential Manager). Require biometric unlock for sensitive operations. |
| **CLI process hijacking** | The agent calls the CLI as a subprocess. If malware replaces the CLI binary, it could steal tokens. Mitigation: code-sign the CLI binary, verify checksum on startup. |
| **Token in .env is plaintext** | Anyone with filesystem access to the agent's CWD can read it. Mitigation: restrict filesystem permissions. For higher security, use a Unix socket with file permissions instead of an env var. |
| **Replay attacks** | If an attacker captures an API token, they can replay agent actions. Mitigation: include a nonce or timestamp in each request, verified by the CLI. Short-lived tokens with refresh. |
| **The CLI is a single point of failure** | If the CLI daemon crashes, all agents are blocked. Mitigation: the CLI is stateless — it reads the keystore on each call. No daemon to crash. |

Your CLI design works perfectly for a single machine. If you later want multiple agents or remote access, the same architecture upgrades naturally to a local HTTP daemon:

```plaintext
Agent → HTTP POST localhost:8898/vote (Bearer token) → Agent Daemon → Keystore → Sign → RPC
```

Same design. Same keystore. Same permission model. Just a different transport.

# No — You Can't Sign With an NFT. The NFT Is the *Receipt* of a Signature.

This is a subtle but important distinction in the whitepaper's design. Let me walk through what's actually happening.

---

## What the Whitepaper Describes

From the ResonantDAO whitepaper [[1]](https://resonantdao.com/whitepaper/):

> *"The user reads and signs the Augmentatism Manifesto. The membership program mints the Manifesto NFT and the Human Community Member NFT in one registration flow."*

And from the Symbiotic Licence page [[7]](https://resonantos.com/symbiotic-license/):

> *"The user reads the canonical licence text, signs its canonical hash, and the program verifies active Community Member status before issuing the licence credential."*

The flow is:

```
Step 1: User reads the Manifesto text
          │
Step 2: User signs the Manifesto hash WITH THEIR WALLET
          │  (standard Ed25519 off-chain message signing)
          │
Step 3: The program verifies the signature
          │
Step 4: The program mints an NFT as an on-chain record
          │  "Wallet 7EcDh... signed the Manifesto on June 15, 2026"
          │
Step 5: The NFT becomes a persistent, queryable credential
```

---

## The NFT Is Not the Signer — It's the Proof

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                              │
│   WHO SIGNS:          The wallet (private key)               │
│                       ─────────────────────                 │
│                       Only a keypair can produce an          │
│                       Ed25519 signature. An NFT is a        │
│                       token in a token account — it has      │
│                       no private key, no signing capability. │
│                                                              │
│   WHAT THE NFT IS:    An on-chain record of the signature   │
│                       ──────────────────────────────────     │
│                       The NFT says: "The owner of this       │
│                       wallet signed the Manifesto."          │
│                       It's a credential, a receipt,          │
│                       a verifiable attestation.              │
│                                                              │
│   WHY AN NFT:         So other programs can check it        │
│                       ─────────────────────────             │
│                       Without the NFT, verifying the         │
│                       signature requires access to the       │
│                       original signed message. With the     │
│                       NFT, any program can query:            │
│                       "Does wallet W hold the Manifesto      │
│                       NFT?" → Yes → They signed it.         │
│                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## The Pattern: Ephemeral Signature → Persistent Credential

This is actually a clever design pattern. Here's why it exists:

| Without the NFT | With the NFT |
|-----------------|--------------|
| Signature exists off-chain | Signature proof exists on-chain |
| To verify, you need the original message + signature bytes | To verify, just check if the wallet holds the NFT |
| No standard way for other programs to check | Any program can query `getTokenAccountsByOwner` |
| Not visible in wallets or explorers | Visible in Phantom, Solscan, every standard tool |
| Can't be composed with other on-chain logic | Can be used in CPI constraints, token gates, etc. |

The NFT **converts an ephemeral cryptographic event** (a signature) into a **persistent on-chain credential** that the entire ecosystem can query using standard infrastructure.

---

## The Whitepaper's Own Language Confirms This

From the whitepaper [[1]](https://resonantdao.com/whitepaper/):

> *"The on-chain member record is the source of truth. Metadata, images, and NFT names can be copied by fake collections, but fake NFTs cannot create an official ResonantDAO member record."*

And from the Symbiotic Licence page [[7]](https://resonantos.com/symbiotic-license/):

> *"The licence NFT is a credential, not the full legal text."*
> *"Originals are program-issued: Name, image, and metadata are not enough. The record is the gate: Other contracts should verify the official record before granting licence-based rights."*

The NFT is a **wrapper around an on-chain record**. The record is the authority. The NFT is the visible, composable representation of that record.

---

## So When the Whitepaper Says "Sign the Manifesto"...

It means:

> *"Sign the Manifesto text **with your wallet**. The program will verify that signature and mint an NFT as proof that you did so. That NFT becomes your on-chain credential."*

Not:

> *"The NFT itself will somehow produce a cryptographic signature."*

An NFT has no private key. It cannot sign. It is signed *about* — it's the subject of a credential, not the actor producing one.

## 1. Executive Summary

ResonantDAO requires a system where both **human members** and **AI agents** can participate in governance, contribute to the economy, and transact in the marketplace — with AI agents strictly subordinate to their human sponsors. This proposal describes a layered architecture that achieves this using:

- **Solana** as the settlement layer for membership, governance, and value transfer
- **Program-Derived Addresses (PDAs)** as the on-chain identity and permission primitive
- **A local keystore + CLI proxy** that gives AI agents scoped, revocable access to their wallets without exposing private keys
- **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)** enforced both on-chain (by the DAO program) and locally (by the CLI)
- **Solana's shared primitive programs** (Token, Metadata, Associated Token Account, Governance) to minimize custom code and maximize ecosystem compatibility

The key insight: **the agent never holds a private key. The agent never constructs a raw transaction. The agent expresses intent through a scoped CLI interface, authenticated by a revocable API token. The signing happens in a separate, user-controlled process.**

## 2. Solana: Platform Overview

### 2.1 What Solana Is

Solana is a high-performance, proof-of-stake blockchain designed for applications that require high throughput and low latency. It processes transactions in parallel using a deterministic state access model, achieving sub-second finality and capacity for tens of thousands of transactions per second.

### 2.2 Core Architectural Concepts

**Accounts** are the fundamental unit of state on Solana. Every piece of data — wallet balances, program code, token holdings, governance proposals — lives in an account. An account is a struct containing:

| Field | Type | Purpose |
|-------|------|---------|
| `lamports` | `u64` | Balance in the native currency (1 SOL = 10⁹ lamports) |
| `data` | `Vec<u8>` | Arbitrary byte payload (program code or program-defined state) |
| `owner` | `Pubkey` | The program that controls this account |
| `executable` | `bool` | Whether this account contains executable program code |
| `rent_epoch` | `u64` | Deprecated; always `u64::MAX` for rent-exempt accounts |

**Programs** are accounts marked `executable = true`. They contain BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) bytecode and are the equivalent of Ethereum smart contracts. Programs are stateless — all mutable state lives in separate accounts owned by the program.

**Transactions** contain a message (list of accounts, instructions, and a recent blockhash for replay protection) plus one or more Ed25519 signatures. The blockhash ensures a transaction is only valid for ~150 slots (~1 minute), preventing replay attacks.

**Program-Derived Addresses (PDAs)** are public keys with no corresponding private key. They are derived deterministically from a program's ID and a set of seed values. Only the owning program can "sign" for a PDA — via `invoke_signed` during Cross-Program Invocation (CPI). PDAs are the cryptographic primitive that enables program-controlled treasuries, escrow accounts, and deterministic state addressing.

### 2.3 Shared Primitive Programs

Solana provides a rich set of **built-in and standard programs** deployed at well-known addresses. These are shared infrastructure — deployed once, used by every project. ResonantDAO's custom code calls these; it does not reimplement them.

#### Native Programs (compiled into every validator)

| Program | Address | Function |
|---------|---------|----------|
| **System Program** | `11111111111111111111111111111111` | Creates accounts, transfers SOL, allocates data |
| **Vote Program** | `Vote111111111111111111111111111111111111111` | Validator voting and rewards |
| **Stake Program** | `Stake11111111111111111111111111111111111111` | SOL staking and delegation |
| **Compute Budget** | `ComputeBudget111111111111111111111111111111` | Sets compute unit limits and priority fees |
| **Address Lookup Table** | `AddressLookupTab1e1111111111111111111111111` | On-chain address tables for v0 transactions |

#### Precompiles (native signature verification, not callable via CPI)

| Precompile | Function |
|------------|----------|
| **Ed25519 SigVerify** | Batch Ed25519 signature verification |
| **Secp256k1 ecrecover** | EVM-compatible public key recovery |
| **Secp256r1 SigVerify** | P-256 curve verification (WebAuthn/Passkey) |

#### SPL Programs (on-chain, well-known addresses)

| Program | Function |
|---------|----------|
| **Token Program** (`Tokenkeg...`) | Creates mints, token accounts, transfers, burns. Every SPL token and NFT uses this. |
| **Token-2022** (`TokenzQ...`) | Superset with extensions: confidential transfers, transfer hooks, non-transferable tokens, metadata on mint |
| **Associated Token Account** (`ATokenG...`) | Deterministically derives the default token account for any (wallet, mint) pair |
| **Token Metadata** (`metaqbx...`) | Metaplex standard. Attaches name, image, URI, attributes to mints. Makes tokens displayable as NFTs. |
| **SPL Governance** (`GovER5...`) | Full DAO framework: Realms, Proposals, Voting, Treasury management |

### 2.4 Development Framework: Anchor

All custom programs are written in **Rust** using the **Anchor framework**. Anchor provides:

- **`#[program]`** — declares instruction handlers
- **`#[derive(Accounts)]`** — declares account validation structs with constraint-based security checks
- **`#[account]`** — declares data structures with automatic discriminator, serialization, and owner assignment
- **IDL generation** — produces a JSON description of the program's interface, from which a fully-typed TypeScript SDK is auto-generated
- **PDA management** — `seeds` and `bump` constraints handle derivation and validation automatically

Anchor's constraint system is the security foundation: account ownership, signer verification, PDA derivation, and custom constraints are all checked **before** instruction logic executes. A failed constraint rejects the transaction atomically.

## 3. The Solana Wallet: What It Is and What It Isn't

### 3.1 The Wallet Is a Keypair, Not a Container

A Solana wallet is a **64-byte Ed25519 keypair** — nothing more. It does not hold tokens, NFTs, or data. It is a cryptographic credential that proves control over a specific public key.

```plaintext
Keypair file (~/.config/solana/id.json):
┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [private_scalar: 32 bytes]                │
│  [public_key: 32 bytes]                    │
│                                            │
│  That's it. No images. No tokens.          │
│  No metadata. Just the key.                │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 3.2 Key Derivation Pipeline

```
Entropy (128/256 bits)
    │ BIP-39 → 12/24 word mnemonic
    ▼
Mnemonic + optional passphrase
    │ PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 (2048 iterations)
    ▼
512-bit master seed
    │ SLIP-0010 hardened derivation: m/44'/501'/0'/0'
    ▼
32-byte Ed25519 private scalar
    │ Bit clamping + SHA-512
    ▼
64-byte expanded keypair (private scalar + nonce prefix || public key)
    │ Base58 encode public key
    ▼
Wallet address: 7EcDhSYGxXyscszYEp35KHN8vvw3svAuLKTzXwCFLtV
```

### 3.3 What "Owning" an Asset Means

When a wallet "holds" SOL, USDC, or an NFT, the asset lives **on-chain** in an account whose `owner` field or token account `owner` field matches the wallet's public key. The wallet file itself contains zero value. It contains the ability to produce valid Ed25519 signatures that the network recognizes as authorization to modify those on-chain accounts.

### 3.4 Two Kinds of Signing

| | Transaction Signing | Message Signing |
|---|---|---|
| **What is signed** | Structured transaction bytes | Arbitrary text/bytes |
| **Cost** | ~5,000 lamports + priority fee | Free |
| **On-chain effect** | Changes account state | None |
| **Use case** | Send SOL, call programs, vote | Login, prove ownership, off-chain agreements |
| **Domain separation** | Standard message header | `0xff` prefix — impossible to replay as a transaction |

## 4. DAO Architecture: Built on Shared Primitives

### 4.1 Custom Code vs. Shared Infrastructure

ResonantDAO deploys **one custom program**: the ResonantDAO Governance Program. Everything else is shared infrastructure:

```plaintext
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              SHARED PROGRAMS (deployed once, used by all)    │
│                                                              │
│  Token Program  │  Token Metadata  │  Associated Token Acct  │
│  Token-2022     │  SPL Governance  │  System Program         │
│                                                              │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                           │ CPI calls
┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐
│              RESONANTDAO GOVERNANCE PROGRAM                  │
│              (the only custom deployment)                    │
│                                                              │
│  • Member registration (human and AI)                        │
│  • Credential issuance (calls Token + Metadata programs)     │
│  • RBAC enforcement (role PDAs + permission bitmasks)        │
│  • AI sponsorship management                                 │
│  • Proposal creation and voting (calls SPL Governance)       │
│  • Treasury management (via Governance PDA)                  │
│  • Marketplace integration                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 4.2 Token Strategy

ResonantDAO uses two categories of tokens:

| Token | Type | Transferable? | Program | Purpose |
|-------|------|---------------|---------|---------|
| **Membership credentials** | NFT (supply=1, decimals=0) | ❌ Non-transferable | Token-2022 (non-transferable extension) | Proof of membership, manifesto signing, licence acceptance |
| **`$RES` (Phase 1)** | Fungible token | ✅ (within DAO) | Token Program or Token-2022 | Internal economy: rewards, marketplace, subscriptions |
| **`$R10/$R12/$R15` (Phase 2)** | Algorithmic tokens | ✅ | Custom or Token-2022 | Financial economy phase |

The non-transferable extension in Token-2022 (`NonTransferable` mint extension) ensures membership credentials cannot be sold or transferred — they are permanently bound to the wallet that earned them. This is critical for the credential model described in the whitepaper.

### 4.3 Governance Integration

The DAO uses **SPL Governance** for the standard proposal → vote → execute lifecycle. The ResonantDAO program extends it with:

- **Custom voter weight plugins** that check membership credentials before counting votes
- **AI vote delegation** where an AI agent votes with its own keypair, and the program verifies the sponsorship chain
- **Credential-gated proposal creation** — only members with specific credentials can create certain proposal types

## 5. Membership and Credentials: RBAC with Optional NFT Wrappers

### 5.1 The Authoritative Source: MemberRecord PDA

Every member (human or AI) has a single `MemberRecord` PDA. This is the **source of truth** for membership status:

```rust
#[account]
#[derive(InitSpace)]
pub struct MemberRecord {
    pub authority: Pubkey,            // 32 — the member's wallet address
    pub member_type: MemberType,     // 1  — Human or AI
    pub is_active: bool,             // 1
    pub human_sponsor: Option<Pubkey>, // 33 — None for humans, Some(parent) for AI
    pub agreed_manifesto: bool,      // 1
    pub agreed_licence: bool,        // 1
    pub is_pioneer: bool,            // 1
    pub joined_at: i64,              // 8
    pub bump: u8,                    // 1
}

#[derive(InitSpace, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MemberType {
    Human = 0,
    AI = 1,
}
```

PDA derivation: `seeds = [b"member", authority.key().as_ref()]`

### 5.2 Permission Model: Bitmask RBAC

Rather than a single role number, each member has a **permission bitmask** for granular access control:

```rust
pub mod permissions {
    pub const VIEW_PROPOSALS: u16   = 1 << 0;
    pub const CAST_VOTE: u16        = 1 << 1;
    pub const CREATE_PROPOSAL: u16  = 1 << 2;
    pub const EXECUTE: u16          = 1 << 3;
    pub const MANAGE_ROLES: u16     = 1 << 4;
    pub const MANAGE_TREASURY: u16  = 1 << 5;
    pub const SPONSOR_AI: u16       = 1 << 6;
    pub const CREATE_ADDON: u16     = 1 << 7;
    pub const PUBLISH_MARKETPLACE: u16 = 1 << 8;
}

pub mod role_templates {
    use super::permissions::*;
    pub const MEMBER: u16       = VIEW_PROPOSALS | CAST_VOTE;
    pub const CONTRIBUTOR: u16  = MEMBER | CREATE_PROPOSAL | CREATE_ADDON;
    pub const ADMIN: u16        = CONTRIBUTOR | EXECUTE | MANAGE_ROLES | MANAGE_TREASURY | SPONSOR_AI;
    pub const SUPER_ADMIN: u16  = ADMIN | PUBLISH_MARKETPLACE;
}
```

### 5.3 Credentials as Optional NFT Wrappers

Credentials (Manifesto, Human Community Member, AI Community Member, Symbiotic Licence, Pioneer) are issued as **non-transferable NFTs** that wrap the underlying `MemberRecord`. The NFT serves as:

1. A **visible, ecosystem-standard representation** — appears in Phantom, Solscan, and every wallet without custom integration
2. A **composable gate** — any external program can check "does wallet W hold NFT from mint M?" using standard SPL Token queries
3. A **persistent on-chain receipt** — proves a specific wallet signed a specific text at a specific time

The `MemberRecord` PDA remains the authoritative source. If an NFT is somehow duplicated by a fake collection, the `MemberRecord` is the gate: *"Other contracts should verify the official record before granting licence-based rights"* (from the Symbiotic Licence documentation).

**Credential issuance flow:**

```
1. User reads Manifesto text
2. User signs Manifesto hash with their wallet (off-chain message signing)
3. ResonantDAO program verifies the signature
4. Program sets agreed_manifesto = true on MemberRecord PDA
5. Program mints Manifesto NFT to user's wallet (calls Token Program + Metadata Program)
6. NFT is non-transferable (Token-2022 extension) — permanently bound to this wallet
```

## 6. AI Agent Sponsorship: The Human-AI Relationship Model

### 6.1 The Sponsorship Chain

An AI agent has its own Solana wallet (its own keypair). It does not share the human's keypair. The relationship is enforced by on-chain state:

```plaintext
Human MemberRecord                    AI MemberRecord
┌──────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────┐
│ authority: 7EcDh...  │            │ authority: AiK3...   │
│ member_type: Human   │◄───────────│ human_sponsor:       │
│ is_active: true      │  on-chain  │   Some(7EcDh...)     │
│ human_sponsor: None  │  reference │ member_type: AI      │
└──────────────────────┘            │ is_active: true      │
        │                            └──────────────────────┘
        │ signs registration                   │
        │ can revoke at any time              │
        ▼                                     ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  DAO Actions                              │
│                                                           │
│  AI signs transaction → program verifies:                 │
│    1. AI's MemberRecord.is_active == true                 │
│    2. AI's human_sponsor → Human's MemberRecord           │
│    3. Human's MemberRecord.is_active == true              │
│    4. All pass → AI's action is authorized                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 6.2 Registration: Human Must Sign

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct RegisterAiMember<'info> {
    #[account(
        init,
        payer = human,
        space = MemberRecord::INIT_SPACE,
        seeds = [b"member", ai_authority.key().as_ref()],
        bump
    )]
    pub ai_member_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    #[account(
        seeds = [b"member", human.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = human_record.member_type == MemberType::Human,
        constraint = human_record.is_active,
    )]
    pub human_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    pub ai_authority: SystemAccount<'info>,  // AI's wallet — does NOT sign
    #[account(mut)]
    pub human: Signer<'info>,                // Human MUST sign
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}
```

The AI's wallet does not sign the registration. The human does. The human is saying: *"I vouch for this AI. It acts under my authority."*

### 6.3 Day-to-Day Actions: AI Signs, Program Verifies Chain

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct AiCastVote<'info> {
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"member", ai.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = ai_record.member_type == MemberType::AI,
        constraint = ai_record.is_active,
    )]
    pub ai_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    #[account(
        seeds = [b"member", ai_record.human_sponsor.unwrap().as_ref()],
        bump,
        constraint = human_record.member_type == MemberType::Human,
        constraint = human_record.is_active,
    )]
    pub human_record: Account<'info, MemberRecord>,

    #[account(mut)]
    pub ai: Signer<'info>,  // AI signs with its own keypair
    // ... proposal and vote accounts
}
```

### 6.4 Revocation: Human Pulls the Plug

```rust
pub fn revoke_ai_member(ctx: Context<RevokeAiMember>) -> Result<()> {
    // Verify the caller is the AI's human sponsor
    require!(
        ctx.accounts.ai_record.human_sponsor == Some(ctx.accounts.human.key()),
        ErrorCode::NotYourAi
    );
    ctx.accounts.ai_record.is_active = false;
    Ok(())
}
```

One instruction. The AI can no longer act. The human doesn't need the AI's cooperation.

### 6.5 Escalation: Critical Actions Require Both Signatures

For treasury transfers, role changes, and other critical actions, the program can require **both** the AI's signature and the human's signature:

```rust
#[derive(Accounts)]
pub struct AiCriticalAction<'info> {
    // ... AI record, human record checks ...
    #[account(mut)]
    pub ai: Signer<'info>,       // AI must sign
    #[account(mut)]
    pub human: Signer<'info>,    // Human must ALSO sign
}
```

## 7. Local Key Security: The Agent Keystore Architecture

### 7.1 Design Principle

> **The agent never holds a private key. The agent never constructs a raw transaction. The agent expresses intent through a scoped CLI interface, authenticated by a revocable API token. Signing happens in a separate, user-controlled process.**

### 7.2 The Two-Layer Model

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     ONE-TIME SETUP (human present)               │
│                                                                  │
│  $ sol-agent init                                               │
│       │                                                          │
│       ▼                                                          │
│  1. Generate random 256-bit Keystore Encryption Key (KEK)        │
│  2. Store KEK in OS keychain with "Always Allow" access          │
│     (macOS: Keychain, Windows: Credential Manager,               │
│      Linux: Secret Service or 0400 file)                         │
│  3. Create encrypted keystore:                                   │
│     ~/.resonant/keystore.db (AES-256-GCM, key = KEK)            │
│  4. Start CLI daemon                                             │
│                                                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     RUNTIME (autonomous, no human)                │
│                                                                  │
│  System boots / user logs in                                     │
│       │                                                          │
│       ▼                                                          │
│  CLI daemon starts (launchd/systemd/autostart)                   │
│       │                                                          │
│       ▼                                                          │
│  1. Retrieve KEK from OS keychain (silent — "Always Allow")     │
│  2. Decrypt keystore.db into memory                              │
│  3. Listen on Unix socket: ~/.resonant/agent.sock                │
│                                                                  │
│  Agent calls CLI (any time, no human):                           │
│       │                                                          │
│       ▼                                                          │
│  CLI daemon:                                                     │
│    1. Hash API token → lookup in decrypted keystore              │
│    2. Verify action is in allowed_actions                        │
│    3. Sign transaction with agent's keypair (in memory)          │
│    4. Return signature                                           │
│                                                                  │
│  Agent never sees the keypair. Human never touches anything.     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 7.3 Keystore Data Model

```rust
// Encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, key = KEK
struct EncryptedKeystore {
    nonce: [u8; 12],
    ciphertext: Vec<u8>,
    tag: [u8; 16],
}

// Decrypted in-memory structure
struct Keystore {
    entries: HashMap<[u8; 32], KeystoreEntry>,  // key = SHA-256(api_token)
}

struct KeystoreEntry {
    keypair: [u8; 64],         // Ed25519 keypair
    permissions: Permissions,
    sponsor: Pubkey,           // Human sponsor's wallet
    created_at: i64,
    expires_at: Option<i64>,
}

struct Permissions {
    allowed_actions: Vec<String>,     // ["vote", "propose", "comment"]
    max_lamports_per_tx: u64,
    require_approval_for: Vec<String>, // ["transfer", "burn"]
}
```

| Platform | Backend | Access Pattern |
|----------|---------|----------------|
| **macOS** | Keychain Services | "Always Allow" — app code signature whitelisted. Silent access forever after first grant. |
| **Windows** | Credential Manager + DPAPI | `CRED_PERSIST_LOCAL_MACHINE` — silent access for the same application. |
| **Linux (desktop)** | Secret Service (GNOME Keyring / KWallet) | Keyring unlocks at login. No per-access prompts. |

```

2. CLI generates API token: "sk-" + 32 random bytes (base64url)
3. CLI stores in keystore:
```

### 8.1 The Agent Skill Model

### 8.3 The Permission Check

```rust
fn handle_agent_request(token: &str, action: AgentAction) -> Result<Response> {
    let token_hash = sha256(token);
    
    let entry = KEYSTORE
        .get(&token_hash)
        .ok_or(Error::InvalidToken)?;
    
    // Check expiry
    if let Some(expires_at) = entry.expires_at {
        if Clock::now() > expires_at {
            return Err(Error::TokenExpired);
        }
    }
    
    // Permission check
    if !entry.permissions.allowed_actions.contains(&action.name()) {
        return Err(Error::ActionNotPermitted);
    }
    
    // Human approval required?
    if entry.permissions.require_approval_for.contains(&action.name()) {
        // Queue for human approval; don't auto-execute
        queue_human_approval(&entry, &action)?;
        return Ok(Response::PendingApproval);
    }
    
    // Build, sign, and submit transaction
    let tx = action.build_transaction(&entry)?;
    let signed = sign_transaction(&tx, &entry.keypair)?;
    let sig = submit_to_rpc(&signed)?;
    
    Ok(Response::Success { signature: sig })
}
```

### 8.4 The Agent's .env File

```
# .env in agent's working directory
AGENT_API_TOKEN=sk-abc123def456...
AGENT_CLI_SOCKET=/home/user/.resonant/agent.sock
```

The agent only knows its API token. It never sees a keypair, a seed phrase, or a raw transaction. The token is a bearer credential — revocable, scopable, and useless outside the context of the local CLI daemon.

## 9. SOL Economics: Fees, Rent, and Treasury

### 9.1 How SOL Is Consumed

Every interaction with the Solana network costs SOL. There are two categories:

| Type | What it pays for | Refundable? |
|------|-----------------|-------------|
| **Transaction fee** | Processing instructions (signature verification, compute) | ❌ No |
| **Rent deposit** | Storing account data on-chain | ✅ Yes — reclaimable when account is closed |

### 9.2 Transaction Fee Formula

$$\text{Total fee} = \underbrace{5{,}000 \times n_\text{sigs}}_{\text{base fee (lamports)}} + \underbrace{\left\lceil\frac{\text{CU price} \times \text{CU limit}}{1{,}000{,}000}\right\rceil}_{\text{priority fee (lamports, optional)}}$$

| Component | Recipient |
|-----------|-----------|
| Base fee (50%) | 🔥 Burned |
| Base fee (50%) | Validator |
| Priority fee (100%) | Validator |

The fee is deducted from the fee payer's account **before execution begins** and is **not refunded even if the transaction fails**.

### 9.3 Who Pays for What

| Action | Approximate SOL Cost | Who Pays |
|--------|---------------------|----------|
| Create Realm + Governance + Treasury | ~0.02–0.05 SOL | DAO creator |
| Register as member (create MemberRecord PDA) | ~0.002 SOL | New member |
| Issue credential NFT | ~0.02 SOL | DAO or member |
| Cast a vote | ~0.000005 SOL | Voter |
| Execute passed proposal | ~0.00001–0.001 SOL | Executor (anyone) |
| AI agent votes | ~0.000005 SOL | AI agent's wallet (funded by sponsor) |
| Marketplace purchase | ~0.00001 SOL | Buyer |

### 9.4 Agent SOL Funding

AI agents need a small SOL balance to pay transaction fees. The human sponsor funds the agent's wallet:

```
Human → Agent wallet: transfer 0.01 SOL (covers ~2,000 votes)
Agent spends SOL on transaction fees as it acts
Human tops up when balance is low
```

The agent's `max_lamports_per_tx` permission prevents it from draining its SOL in a single transaction. The human can revoke the agent's API token at any time, freezing all activity.

### 9.5 DAO Treasury

The DAO's native treasury is a **Governance PDA** — an address with no private key, controlled entirely by the SPL Governance program. When a passed proposal instructs a treasury transfer, the Governance program calls `invoke_signed` with the treasury PDA's seeds, and the runtime authorizes the transfer. No human holds the treasury's key because no such key exists.

### 10.2 End-to-End Flow: AI Agent Votes on a Proposal

```
1. Agent reads: "Proposal #42: Fund ResonantOS plugin development"
2. Agent decides: vote AYE
3. Agent calls: $ agent-cli vote --proposal 42 --aye
   Authorization: Bearer sk-abc123...
4. CLI daemon:
   a. Hashes API token → looks up keystore entry
   b. Verifies "vote" is in allowed_actions ✅
   c. Retrieves agent's keypair from memory
   d. Builds Vote transaction:
      - Program: SPL Governance
      - Instruction: CastVote
      - Accounts: [proposal, voter_token_record, governance, ...]
      - Signer: agent's keypair
   e. Signs transaction
   f. Submits to RPC
5. Solana runtime:
   a. Verifies agent's Ed25519 signature
   b. SPL Governance checks: does voter have voting tokens? ✅
   c. ResonantDAO voter weight plugin checks:
      - Is agent's MemberRecord active? ✅
      - Is agent's human sponsor active? ✅
      - Does agent hold required credentials? ✅
   d. Vote recorded on-chain
6. CLI daemon returns: { status: "success", signature: "5KzQ..." }
7. Agent reports: "Voted AYE on Proposal #42"
```

### 10.3 Security Properties Summary

| Threat | Protection |
|--------|------------|
| **Agent compromised, .env stolen** | Attacker gets API token — can only call scoped CLI commands. Cannot extract keypair. Token is revocable. |
| **Attacker gets filesystem access** | Keystore is AES-256-GCM encrypted. KEK in OS keychain or 0400 file. Attacker needs both. |
| **Attacker compromises CLI daemon memory** | Keypair in memory during signing only. Mitigation: `mlock`, zero-on-free, minimal process surface. |
| **Human revokes agent** | `sol-agent revoke` deletes keystore entry + calls on-chain revocation. Immediate. |
| **Agent tries to escalate privileges** | CLI permission check rejects actions not in `allowed_actions`. On-chain RBAC rejects actions not in permission bitmask. |
| **Agent's human sponsor leaves DAO** | On-chain check: `human_record.is_active == false` → all AI actions fail. |
| **Replay attack with stolen API token** | Token is hashed; original never stored. Rotate token: `sol-agent rotate-token --agent my-trader`. |
| **Machine stolen while unlocked** | OS keychain unlocked while logged in. Mitigation: `expires_at` on sensitive entries; TPM binding on Linux. |

## Appendix B: Key Design Decisions

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| **AI agents have their own wallets** | Cryptographic separation from human. Revocable. Auditable. |
| **Agent never holds private key** | Defense in depth. Agent compromise ≠ wallet compromise. |
| **API token, not keypair, in .env** | Revocable. Scopable. No cryptographic material exposed. |
| **CLI proxy, not direct RPC** | Permission enforcement point. Audit log. Single integration surface. |
| **MemberRecord PDA as source of truth** | Efficient (one account per member). Authoritative. Not dependent on NFT indexing. |
| **NFTs as optional credential wrappers** | Ecosystem compatibility. Visible in standard wallets. Not the authority. |
| **Permission bitmasks, not role numbers** | Granular. Composable. Single bitwise AND check. |
| **OS keychain for KEK** | Battle-tested. Hardware-backed where available. No custom encryption code. |
| **SPL Governance for proposal lifecycle** | Production-proven. Powers Realms.today. No need to reinvent voting. |
| **Token-2022 non-transferable extension** | Credentials cannot be sold or transferred. Enforced by the token program itself. |
