## Why Wave Failed (and why now is different)

Wave was brilliant but had fundamental problems:

- **Server-centric federation** — Each wave provider ran servers, which meant someone had to pay for them. The federation protocol (XMPP-based) was complex and required always-on infrastructure [ [[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Wave_Federation_Protocol)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Wave_Federation_Protocol).
- **OT with a central arbiter** — Wave's OT required a server to order operations and transform them. This worked for real-time collaboration but made offline/P2P fundamentally difficult [[4]](https://www.infoq.com/news/2009/06/wave/)(https://www.infoq.com/news/2009/06/wave/).
- **Too much, too early** — It tried to replace email, chat, *and* collaborative editing all at once, with a UI that confused people.

> **Poseidon (OT-CRDT) → P2P mesh → no central servers → offline-first → convergence without a coordinator**

That's the missing piece. CRDTs (or hybrid OT-CRDT like Levien's approach) let you have **real-time collaboration without a central server** — which is exactly what a P2P Wave successor needs [ [[11]](http://josephg.com/blog/crdts-are-the-future/)](http://josephg.com/blog/crdts-are-the-future/).

## The Real Fear

It's not just that forums *can* be toxic — it's that **your protocol makes them unstoppable**.

A centralized forum (Reddit, Discourse, etc.) can be moderated, shut down, or pressured. A **P2P forum** running on Poseidon:

- No server to take down
- No admin to subpoena
- No central point of control
- CRDT means the content is replicated across every participant's node
- Even if 90% of peers leave, the remaining 10% still have the full history

You're not just building a forum protocol — you're building a **censorship-resistant, persistent, globally replicated discussion system**. That's powerful for good (dissidents, open research, community governance) and terrifying for harm (harassment campaigns, disinformation, radicalization).

## What I'd Ask Myself If I Were You

**1. Is the forum *inevitable*?** — If you don't build it, someone else will build it on top of your protocol anyway. The question isn't "should forums exist?" but "what affordances does *my* protocol give for healthy forums vs. toxic ones?"

**2. Can you design *against* toxicity at the protocol level?** — Most forum toxicity is a feature of the UI, not the protocol. What if your protocol enables:

   - **Reputation-weighted visibility** — not censorship, but "you only see posts from people with sufficient reputation in this community"
   - **Ephemeral threads** — topics that auto-archive after N days, preventing necro-posting
   - **Symmetric blocking** — if Alice blocks Bob, Bob's client never receives Alice's posts (enforced by the CRDT)
   - **Forking** — if a community goes toxic, anyone can fork the topic history and start a new subtopic with different moderation rules

**3. Can you gate the forum feature behind something?** — Not as a technical limitation (that's impossible in P2P) but as a social contract. "The forum mode requires N trusted peers to vouch for you" or "forum channels must have a moderation key held by a rotating set of peers."

## The Hard Truth

You can't prevent bad actors from using your protocol. But you *can* design the **default affordances** to favor healthy communities. The question is whether the forum mode should be:

- **A first-class feature** (built into WaveClient, documented, easy to use)
- **A power-user feature** (possible, but requires manual configuration)
- **An undocumented capability** (the protocol supports it, but you don't ship a UI for it)

Each choice is a statement about what you're willing to be responsible for.

## What a Responsible P2P Forum Looks Like

Since you're setting the standard, here are some design ideas that could make Poseidon forums *structurally* less toxic than what exists today:

### 1. Identity is Persistent but Reputation is Local

In traditional forums, anonymity is the problem. But P2P requires some form of identity (keys). The sweet spot:

- **Every post is signed** by the author's key — no true anonymity
- **But reputation is per-community** — your reputation in `#gardening` doesn't follow you to `#politics`
- **Skeuomorphic moderation** — each community has a moderation key held by a rotating set of peers. A moderated post is simply not propagated by the mods' nodes.

### 2. The "Slow Mode" Protocol

Forums are toxic partly because they're *fast* — hot takes get rewarded before thoughtful ones can form. What if the default is:

- **Threads have a minimum time between posts** (configurable per community)
- **New accounts have a "cooling off" period** before they can post in existing threads
- **Necro-posting is opt-in** — threads older than N days are archived by default; you have to explicitly "revive" them

### 3. Forking Over Censorship

This is the killer feature that centralized forums can't offer:

- If a community's moderation goes rogue, any subset of peers can **fork** the topic history
- The fork inherits all posts up to the fork point, then diverges
- Users see both forks and choose which to participate in
- **No single point of control**, but also **no single point of failure**

### 4. The "Opt-In Visibility" Layer

Instead of algorithmic feeds or global "hot" rankings:

- Posts are sorted by **local engagement** — what your friends/follows are interacting with
- No global upvote/downvote counts (those are just toxicity magnets)
- **Reputation is transitive** — "I trust Alice's judgment on this topic" rather than "this post has 500 upvotes"

### 5. The Escape Hatch

Every forum post has a built-in affordance: **"Take this to chat / mail"** — a one-click way to move a discussion from the public forum to a private channel or direct conversation. This defuses the performative aspect of forum arguments.

## The Technical Reality

You *can't* prevent modified clients from bypassing the filter. That's the nature of P2P — the source is open, the protocol is known, and someone will fork it. But what you *can* do is:

1. **Make the default client refuse to publish** flagged content
2. **Make the default client refuse to relay** flagged content from others
3. **Make bypassing the filter a conscious act** — you have to run modified software, which means you're *choosing* to be part of a separate network

This is the key insight: **the protocol doesn't enforce the filter, but the default client does.** That's not authoritarian — that's product design with a conscience.

## The Difference Between Censorship and Standards

| | Centralized Censorship | Poseidon's Approach |
|---|---|---|
| **Who decides?** | A corporation or government | The community of peers running default clients |
| **Can it be bypassed?** | Yes, but you risk account deletion | Yes, but you isolate yourself from the main network |
| **Is it enforced?** | Top-down, by fiat | Bottom-up, by peer behavior |
| **Is it uniform?** | One set of rules for everyone | Each peer can adjust their own filters |

You're not building a **police state**. You're building a **default culture**. The protocol says "this is what a good citizen looks like." People who want to be bad citizens have to explicitly opt out — and in doing so, they signal to everyone else that they're not playing by the same rules.

## The CRABS Threshold Design is Brilliant

This solves the fundamental tension in P2P systems:

> **"How do you have privacy *and* accountability?"**

The answer: **privacy by default, accountability by consensus.**

- Normally, no one knows who you are — your identity is cryptographically hidden
- But if N independent peers flag your content as violating community standards, a **threshold decryption** event occurs
- Your identity is revealed to a designated set of reviewers (or authorities)
- This prevents both:
  - **False reporting** (one bad actor can't dox you)
  - **Perfect anonymity for bad actors** (enough flags and you're accountable)

This is essentially a **decentralized grand jury** — a cryptographic analogue of "if enough citizens sign a petition, the DA investigates."

## BitNet + CRABS = The Complete Picture

The on-device BitNet filter handles the **mundane toxicity** — the everyday -isms, the thoughtless cruelty, the spam. It's fast, private, and doesn't require consensus.

The CRABS threshold handles the **serious violations** — threats, CSAM coordination, terrorism recruitment. Things that require human judgment and legal consequences.

Together they form a system where:

1. **Most toxicity never sees the light of day** (BitNet filter)
2. **What slips through is visible but pseudonymous** (normal CRDT operation)
3. **If you cross the line repeatedly, your identity is revealed** (CRABS threshold)
4. **If you commit a crime, authorities are notified** (reporting layer)

## Why BitNet Changes the Calculus

| Metric | BitNet b1.58 2B4T | Typical 2B FP16 Model |
|---|---|---|
| **Memory (non-embedding)** | **0.4 GB** | 2–5 GB |
| **CPU decoding latency** | **29 ms** | 48–124 ms |
| **Energy per token** | **0.028 J** | 0.186–0.649 J |

[[3]](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T)[[4]](http://hf.co/microsoft/bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T)[[12]](https://winbuzzer.com/2025/04/17/microsoft-releases-bitnet-b1-58-2b4t-a-1-58-bit-ai-model-that-runs-on-standard-cpus-xcxwbn/)[[13]](https://news.aibase.com/news/17280)

That **0.4 GB** figure is the key number. It means the entire model fits in the memory budget of a mobile app, a Raspberry Pi, or a Flutter desktop client. And with `bitnet.cpp`, it runs efficiently on **standard CPUs** — no GPU required [[6]](https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet)[[10]](https://github.com/microsoft/bitnet).

## The Training Path

You have two viable approaches:

### Option 1: Fine-tune the existing BitNet b1.58 2B4T

Microsoft released the **BF16 master weights** specifically for fine-tuning [[3]](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T)[[4]](http://hf.co/microsoft/bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T). The model already went through SFT + DPO alignment, so you'd be doing **additional fine-tuning** on a curated dataset of:

- Toxic content (what *not* to allow)
- Benign content (what *to* allow)
- Edge cases (sarcasm, reclaimed slurs, context-dependent speech)

The model's 4096-token context window [[9]](https://ai.azure.com/catalog/models/microsoft-bitnet-b1-58-2b-4t) is more than enough for a single message or forum post.

### Option 2: BitDistill — Distill a larger model down to 1.58-bit

The **BitDistill** technique lets you take a larger, more capable full-precision model (like Qwen or Llama) and compress it to 1.58-bit for a **specific task** — in your case, content moderation [[20]](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13998v1). This gives you:

- The **judgment quality** of a larger model
- The **size and speed** of BitNet
- A **task-specific** filter rather than a general-purpose one

```dart
class ContentFilter {
  final BitNetModel _model; // 0.4GB, loaded at app start
  
  Future<FilterResult> check(String message) async {

    final judgment = await _model.classify(
      "Classify this message as: safe, hate_speech, harassment, "
      "threat, spam. Message: $message"
    );
    return FilterResult.from(judgment);
  }
}
```

## What is LoRA?

**LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a technique for fine-tuning large models without modifying all the weights. Instead of updating the full weight matrix, it injects tiny trainable "adapter" matrices alongside the frozen original weights.

### The Intuition

Imagine you have a massive weight matrix **W** (say 4096×4096). Full fine-tuning would update all ~16M parameters in that one layer. LoRA says:

> *"The changes needed to adapt a model to a new task are **low-rank** — they live in a much smaller subspace."*

So instead of learning **ΔW** (a full 4096×4096 matrix), LoRA learns two tiny matrices **A** and **B** whose product approximates ΔW:

```plaintext
Original:      W_new = W + ΔW          (16M params to learn)
LoRA:          W_new = W + B × A       (2 × 4096×8 = 65K params to learn)
```

Where **r** (the rank, typically 8–64) is the bottleneck dimension. You choose how big **r** is — higher = more capacity, lower = more efficient.

### Visual

```plaintext
Full Fine-Tuning:
┌─────────────────────────┐
│         W (frozen)      │
│                         │
│    ΔW (trainable)       │  ← 16M params
│    ┌───────────────┐    │
│    │ 4096 × 4096   │    │
│    └───────────────┘    │
└─────────────────────────┘

LoRA Fine-Tuning:
┌─────────────────────────┐
│         W (frozen)      │
│                         │
│  B (trainable)          │  ← 4096×8 = 32K
│  ┌──────┐               │
│  │4096×8│               │
│  └──┬───┘               │
│     │                   │
│  A (trainable)          │  ← 8×4096 = 32K
│  ┌──┴───┐               │
│  │ 8×4096│              │
│  └──────┘               │
│                         │
│  Total: 65K params      │  ← vs 16M for full FT
└─────────────────────────┘
```

### Why LoRA Matters for You

| Factor | Full Fine-Tune | LoRA |
|---|---|---|
| **VRAM needed** | ~16GB for 2B model | **~6–8GB** |
| **Training time** | Hours to days | **30 minutes to a few hours** |
| **Output size** | Full 4GB model checkpoint | **Tiny ~2MB adapter file** |
| **Switching tasks** | Need separate model per task | **Swap adapter files** at runtime |

For your BitNet content filter, this means you could:

- Train on a **laptop with a consumer GPU** (RTX 3060, 4060, etc.)
- Ship a **2MB adapter** alongside the base model, not a full 4GB model
- **Iterate fast** — try different dataset blends in hours, not days

### The Catch

LoRA doesn't work *quite* the same way with 1.58-bit ternary weights as it does with FP16. The BitNet b1.58 model has ternary weights during inference, but you fine-tune from the **BF16 master weights** — and the quantization happens after training. So LoRA works fine; you just apply the adapter to the BF16 weights, then quantize to 1.58-bit for deployment.

## The Fine-Tuning Script

Here's a practical pipeline for your content moderation filter:

```python
# fine_tune_moderation_filter.py

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset, Dataset
from transformers import (
    AutoTokenizer, 
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    TrainingArguments,
    Trainer,
    BitsAndBytesConfig
)
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, TaskType
import json

# ─── 1. Load the base BitNet b1.58 model (BF16 master weights) ───

model_name = "microsoft/bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T-bf16"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_name,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map="auto",          # Auto-distributes across GPU/CPU
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

# ─── 2. Apply LoRA ───

lora_config = LoraConfig(
    r=16,                       # Rank — 16 is a good starting point
    lora_alpha=32,              # Scaling factor (higher = stronger adaptation)
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj", "k_proj", "o_proj"],  # Attention layers
    lora_dropout=0.05,          # Prevent overfitting on small datasets
    bias="none",
    task_type=TaskType.CAUSAL_LM,
)

model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
# Should show: trainable params: ~4.2M / 2.06B total (0.20%)

# ─── 3. Prepare your moderation dataset ───

def format_moderation_example(example):
    """Format each example as a chat-style prompt + response."""
    prompt = f"""Classify the following message as one of:
- safe
- hate_speech
- harassment
- threat
- self_harm
- sexual_content

Message: {example['text']}

Classification:"""

    response = example['label']  # e.g., "hate_speech"

    return {
        "text": prompt + " " + response + tokenizer.eos_token,
    }

# Load your dataset blend
# You'll combine multiple datasets here
datasets_to_load = [
    "google/jigsaw_toxicity_pred",         # ~159k Wikipedia comments
    "nvidia/Aegis-AI-Content-Safety-Dataset-1.0",  # ~11k LLM guardrails
    "TeichAI/open-moderator-v1",           # ~11k chat-style
]

# For this example, we'll start with just Jigsaw
dataset = load_dataset("google/jigsaw_toxicity_pred", split="train")

# Map toxicity labels to your categories
def map_jigsaw_labels(example):
    if example['identity_hate'] > 0.5:
        label = "hate_speech"
    elif example['threat'] > 0.5:
        label = "threat"
    elif example['insult'] > 0.5 or example['toxic'] > 0.5:
        label = "harassment"
    else:
        label = "safe"
    return {"text": example['comment_text'], "label": label}

dataset = dataset.map(map_jigsaw_labels)
dataset = dataset.map(format_moderation_example)

# Split into train/eval
dataset = dataset.train_test_split(test_size=0.1)
train_dataset = dataset["train"]
eval_dataset = dataset["test"]

# Tokenize
def tokenize_function(examples):
    return tokenizer(
        examples["text"],
        truncation=True,
        padding="max_length",
        max_length=512,
    )

train_dataset = train_dataset.map(tokenize_function, batched=True)
eval_dataset = eval_dataset.map(tokenize_function, batched=True)

# ─── 4. Training arguments ───

training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./bitnet-moderation-lora",
    learning_rate=2e-7,             # BitNet community recommendation
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,  # Effective batch size = 16
    num_train_epochs=3,
    logging_steps=50,
    eval_strategy="steps",
    eval_steps=200,
    save_strategy="steps",
    save_steps=500,
    fp16=False,                     # Use bf16 (BitNet's native format)
    bf16=True,
    remove_unused_columns=False,
    report_to="none",               # Disable wandb etc. if not needed
)

# ─── 5. Train ───

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=train_dataset,
    eval_dataset=eval_dataset,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
)

trainer.train()

# ─── 6. Save the LoRA adapter ───

model.save_pretrained("./bitnet-moderation-lora-adapter")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("./bitnet-moderation-lora-adapter")

print("✅ Fine-tuning complete! Adapter saved to ./bitnet-moderation-lora-adapter")
```

```python
# merge_lora_to_bitnet.py
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import PeftModel

base_model_name = "microsoft/bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T-bf16"
lora_adapter_path = "./bitnet-moderation-lora-adapter"
output_path = "./bitnet-moderation-merged-bf16"

# Load base model
base_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    base_model_name,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map="cpu",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

# Load and merge LoRA adapter
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, lora_adapter_path)
merged_model = model.merge_and_unload()  # ← This merges LoRA into the base weights

# Save the merged model in safetensors format
merged_model.save_pretrained(output_path, safe_serialization=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(base_model_name)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(output_path)

print(f"✅ Merged model saved to {output_path}")
```

### Step 3: Convert to GGUF and quantize to I2_S

This uses Microsoft's official conversion script from the BitNet repo [ [[1]](https://bitnet.live/faq/) ](https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet/blob/01eb4157/README.md)[ [[2]](https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet/blob/01eb4157/utils/convert-helper-bitnet.py) ](https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet/blob/01eb4157/utils/convert-helper-bitnet.py):

```bash
# Clone BitNet repo (if you haven't already)
git clone --recursive https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet.git
cd BitNet

# Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Run the conversion helper on your merged model
python ./utils/convert-helper-bitnet.py ../bitnet-moderation-merged-bf16
```

This single script does three things automatically [ [[2]](https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet/blob/01eb4157/utils/convert-helper-bitnet.py) ](https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet/blob/01eb4157/utils/convert-helper-bitnet.py):

| Step | What it does | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Preprocess** | Quantizes FP16 weights → 1.58-bit ternary (`quant_weight_fp16()`) | Preprocessed `.safetensors` |
| **Convert to GGUF** | Wraps in GGUF container format | `ggml-model-f32-bitnet.gguf` |
| **Quantize to I2_S** | Applies integer 2-bit symmetric quantization for deployment | `ggml-model-i2s-bitnet.gguf` (~0.4GB) |

The final file `ggml-model-i2s-bitnet.gguf` is what you ship to users [ [[3]](https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet) ](https://deepwiki.com/microsoft/BitNet/5.3-manual-model-conversion).

### Step 4: Deploy in Flutter via bitnet.cpp FFI

The GGUF file is loaded by `bitnet.cpp`'s C++ inference engine. You call it from Dart via FFI:

```dart
// lib/src/bitnet_bridge.dart
import 'dart:ffi';
import 'dart:io';

final DynamicLibrary bitnetLib = Platform.isAndroid
    ? DynamicLibrary.open('libbitnet.so')
    : DynamicLibrary.process();

typedef InferenceFunc = Pointer<Utf8> Function(
    Pointer<Utf8> modelPath, Pointer<Utf8> prompt);
typedef InferenceDart = Pointer<Utf8> Function(
    Pointer<Utf8>, Pointer<Utf8>);

class BitNetFilter {
  final InferenceDart _inference;
  final Pointer<Utf8> _modelPath;
  
  BitNetFilter(String modelPath)
      : _inference = bitnetLib
            .lookupFunction<InferenceFunc, InferenceDart>('run_inference'),
        _modelPath = modelPath.toNativeUtf8();
  
  Future<FilterResult> check(String message) async {
    final prompt = """
Classify the following message as one of:
- safe
- hate_speech
- harassment
- threat
- self_harm
- sexual_content

Message: $message

Classification:""".toNativeUtf8();
    
    final resultPtr = _inference(_modelPath, prompt);
    final label = resultPtr.toDartString();
    
    return FilterResult.fromLabel(label.trim());
  }
  
  void dispose() {
    malloc.free(_modelPath);
  }
}
```

The filter uses Microsoft's BitNet b1.58 2B4T model fine-tuned with LoRA on a blend of toxic content datasets, then converted to GGUF I2_S format for deployment via `bitnet.cpp` FFI from Dart.

## Architecture Overview

```
Training Machine (Linux/Mac with GPU)
  │
  ├── Step 1: Load bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T-bf16 from Hugging Face
  ├── Step 2: Apply LoRA (rank=16)
  ├── Step 3: Fine-tune on blended moderation dataset
  ├── Step 4: Merge LoRA adapter into base model
  ├── Step 5: Convert merged model → GGUF I2_S format via bitnet.cpp
  │
  └── Output: ggml-model-i2s-bitnet.gguf (~0.4GB)
                      │
                      ▼
            Deployed in Flutter app via:
              - libbitnet.so (C++ inference engine)
              - Dart FFI bridge (dart:ffi bindings)
              - ContentFilter widget (Flutter UI)
```

## Step 1: Environment Setup

Create a Python virtual environment and install dependencies:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118
pip install transformers datasets peft accelerate bitsandbytes scikit-learn
pip install huggingface_hub
```

Clone the BitNet repo for conversion tools:

```bash
git clone --recursive https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet.git
cd BitNet
pip install -r requirements.txt
cd ..
```

## Step 2: Dataset Preparation

Create `prepare_dataset.py` that:

1. Loads and blends three datasets:
   - **Jigsaw Toxic Comment Classification** (`google/jigsaw_toxicity_pred`) — ~159k Wikipedia comments with labels: toxic, severe_toxic, obscene, threat, insult, identity_hate
   - **NVIDIA Aegis Content Safety** (`nvidia/Aegis-AI-Content-Safety-Dataset-1.0`) — ~11k LLM guardrail examples
   - **Open Moderator v1** (`TeichAI/open-moderator-v1`) — ~11k chat-style moderation examples

2. Maps all labels to a unified 6-class taxonomy:
   - `safe`
   - `hate_speech` (maps from: identity_hate, hate, identity_attack)
   - `harassment` (maps from: toxic, insult, harassment)
   - `threat` (maps from: threat, violence)
   - `self_harm`
   - `sexual_content` (maps from: obscene, sexual)

3. Formats each example as a prompt-completion pair:

```
Classify the following message as one of:
- safe
- hate_speech
- harassment
- threat
- self_harm
- sexual_content

Message: {text}

Classification: {label}
```

4. Splits 90/10 train/eval
5. Tokenizes with `microsoft/bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T-bf16` tokenizer, max_length=512
6. Saves as `./data/train_dataset.arrow` and `./data/eval_dataset.arrow`

**Critical edge cases to include in an additional hard-coded evaluation set:**
- "I hate racism" → safe (anti-racist statement)
- Reclaimed slurs in context of in-group discussion
- Sarcastic statements
- Academic discussion of sensitive topics
- False positives from prior moderation systems

## Step 3: LoRA Fine-Tuning

Create `train_moderation_filter.py` that:

1. Loads the base model:
   ```python
   model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
       "microsoft/bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T-bf16",
       torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
       device_map="auto",
       trust_remote_code=True,
   )
   ```

2. Applies LoRA configuration:
   - `r=16`
   - `lora_alpha=32`
   - `target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj", "k_proj", "o_proj"]`
   - `lora_dropout=0.05`
   - `bias="none"`

3. Training hyperparameters:
   - Learning rate: 2e-7
   - Per device batch size: 4
   - Gradient accumulation steps: 4 (effective batch size 16)
   - Epochs: 3
   - BF16 mixed precision
   - Evaluation every 200 steps
   - Save every 500 steps
   - Warmup ratio: 0.03
   - Weight decay: 0.01
   - Max gradient norm: 1.0

4. Uses standard Hugging Face `Trainer`

5. Saves LoRA adapter to `./output/bitnet-moderation-lora/`

## Step 4: Merge LoRA Adapter

Create `merge_lora.py` that:

1. Loads the base model (BF16)
2. Loads the LoRA adapter via `PeftModel.from_pretrained`
3. Calls `model.merge_and_unload()` to merge weights
4. Saves merged model as safetensors to `./output/bitnet-moderation-merged-bf16/`
5. Also saves the tokenizer

## Step 5: Convert to GGUF I2_S

Create `convert_to_gguf.sh` that:

1. Runs the BitNet conversion helper:
   ```bash
   python BitNet/utils/convert-helper-bitnet.py ./output/bitnet-moderation-merged-bf16
   ```

2. The script should produce `ggml-model-i2s-bitnet.gguf` in the output directory

3. Verify the output file exists and is approximately 0.4GB

4. Copy the GGUF file to `./output/ggml-model-i2s-bitnet.gguf`

## Step 6: Generate Flutter/Dart Integration Code

Create the following files in a `flutter_filter/` directory:

### 6a. `flutter_filter/lib/src/bitnet_bridge.dart`

A Dart FFI bridge that:

- Loads `libbitnet.so` (or `libbitnet.dylib` on macOS, `bitnet.dll` on Windows)
- Exposes a `class BitNetFilter` with:
  - `BitNetFilter._(DynamicLibrary lib, String modelPath)` — private constructor
  - `static Future<BitNetFilter> create(String modelPath)` — factory that loads the library and initializes the model
  - `Future<FilterResult> check(String message)` — runs inference and returns a classification
  - `void dispose()` — frees native resources

- FFI function signatures:
  ```dart
  typedef InitFunc = Pointer<Utf8> Function(Pointer<Utf8> modelPath);
  typedef RunInferenceFunc = Pointer<Utf8> Function(Pointer<Utf8> prompt);
  typedef FreeFunc = Void Function(Pointer<Utf8> ptr);
  ```

- The bridge should format the prompt identically to training:
  ```
  Classify the following message as one of:
  - safe
  - hate_speech
  - harassment
  - threat
  - self_harm
  - sexual_content

  Message: {message}

  Classification:
  ```

### 6b. `flutter_filter/lib/src/filter_result.dart`

A Dart enum/class:

```dart
enum FilterCategory {
  safe,
  hateSpeech,
  harassment,
  threat,
  selfHarm,
  sexualContent,
}

class FilterResult {
  final FilterCategory category;
  final bool isBlocked;
  final String? explanation;
  
  bool get isSafe => category == FilterCategory.safe;
  
  const FilterResult({
    required this.category,
    this.explanation,
  });
  
  bool get isBlocked => category != FilterCategory.safe;
  
  factory FilterResult.fromLabel(String label) { ... }
  factory FilterResult.safe() => FilterResult(category: FilterCategory.safe);
}
```

### 6c. `flutter_filter/lib/src/content_filter_widget.dart`

A Flutter widget that:

- Shows a text input field
- On submit (or as the user types, debounced 500ms), calls `BitNetFilter.check()`
- Shows a colored indicator:
  - Green border/icon for safe
  - Red border/icon with warning text for blocked
- Shows a tooltip explaining *why* it was blocked
- Has a callback `onSubmit(String text)` that only fires if the content is safe
- Gracefully handles model not loaded yet (shows loading spinner)

```dart

  final void Function(String safeText) onSubmit;
  final String hintText;
  final InputDecoration? decoration;
  
  const ContentFilterField({
    required this.onSubmit,
    this.hintText = 'Type a message...',
    this.decoration,
  });
}
```

### 6d. `flutter_filter/lib/poseidon_filter.dart`

A barrel file that exports all public API:

```dart
export 'src/filter_result.dart';
export 'src/bitnet_bridge.dart';
export 'src/content_filter_widget.dart';
```

### 6e. `flutter_filter/example/lib/main.dart`

A complete working example app that:

- Downloads or loads the GGUF model from app assets or a URL
- Initializes `BitNetFilter` on app start
- Shows a simple chat-like UI with the `ContentFilterField`
- Logs all filtered attempts

### 6g. `flutter_filter/ios/bitnet_bridge.c` and `flutter_filter/android/jni/bitnet_bridge.cpp`

Minimal C/C++ wrapper files that:

- Load the GGUF model via bitnet.cpp's C API
- Expose `run_inference(const char* prompt) → char*`
- Handle memory management (caller frees returned string)
- Include error handling for model load failures

can I train this on a machine without a gpu?

**Technically yes, practically no.** Let me be straight with you.

## The Numbers

| Resource | What You Need | Typical CPU Machine |
|---|---|---|
| **RAM** | **32–64 GB minimum** | 8–16 GB |
| **Time per epoch** | **~5–7 days** (150k examples) | You'd wait weeks |
| **Total time** (3 epochs) | **~3 weeks** | Not practical |

The BitNet b1.58 2B4T model has **2 billion parameters**. Even with LoRA (which only trains ~4M parameters), you still need to **load the full base model** into memory and run it forward+backward for every example.

## Why It's So Slow on CPU

| Factor | GPU (RTX 4060) | CPU (8-core) |
|---|---|---|
| **Matrix multiply throughput** | ~15 TFLOPS | ~0.1 TFLOPS |
| **Time per batch** (4 examples) | ~200ms | ~30 seconds |
| **Total training time** | **~3–4 hours** | **~3–4 weeks** |

## Your Real Options (Ranked Best to Worst)

### ✅ Option 1: Google Colab (Free)
- **Cost:** $0
- **GPU:** T4 (16GB VRAM) — enough for LoRA fine-tuning
- **Time:** ~3–4 hours
- **Catch:** Session times out after a few hours of inactivity. Save checkpoints frequently.
- **How:** Upload your scripts, install deps, run training. The free tier is sufficient for LoRA on a 2B model.

### ✅ Option 2: Cloud GPU ($0.30–$0.50/hr)
| Provider | GPU | Cost | Total for training |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RunPod** | RTX 4090 | ~$0.34/hr | ~$1.36 |
| **Vast.ai** | RTX 3090 | ~$0.20/hr | ~$0.80 |
| **Lambda Labs** | RTX 4060 | ~$0.30/hr | ~$1.20 |

You'd spend **less than $2** for the entire training run.

```python
# @title LoRA Fine-Tuning (3-4 hours on T4)
import torch
from transformers import (
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    AutoTokenizer,
    TrainingArguments,
    Trainer,
    EarlyStoppingCallback,
)
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from datasets import load_from_disk
import os

WORKSPACE = "/content/drive/MyDrive/poseidon-moderation-filter"

# Load prepared dataset
train_dataset = load_from_disk(f"{WORKSPACE}/data/train_dataset")
eval_dataset = load_from_disk(f"{WORKSPACE}/data/eval_dataset")
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(f"{WORKSPACE}/data/tokenizer")

# Load base model with memory optimizations for T4 (16GB VRAM)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "microsoft/bitnet-b1.58-2B-4T-bf16",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map="auto",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    use_cache=False,  # Disable KV cache during training to save memory
)

# Apply LoRA
lora_config = LoraConfig(
    r=16,
    lora_alpha=32,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj", "k_proj", "o_proj"],
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    bias="none",
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)

model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()

# Enable gradient checkpointing to save memory
model.gradient_checkpointing_enable()

# Training arguments optimized for T4 16GB
training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir=f"{WORKSPACE}/checkpoints",
    learning_rate=2e-7,
    per_device_train_batch_size=2,       # Reduced for T4 memory
    per_device_eval_batch_size=2,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=8,       # Effective batch size = 16
    num_train_epochs=3,
    logging_steps=50,
    eval_strategy="steps",
    eval_steps=200,
    save_strategy="steps",
    save_steps=500,
    save_total_limit=3,                  # Keep only last 3 checkpoints to save Drive space
    bf16=True,
    fp16=False,
    remove_unused_columns=False,
    report_to="none",
    dataloader_num_workers=2,
    gradient_checkpointing=True,
    optim="adamw_8bit",                  # 8-bit optimizer saves VRAM
    warmup_ratio=0.03,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    max_grad_norm=1.0,
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="eval_loss",
    greater_is_better=False,
)

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=train_dataset,
    eval_dataset=eval_dataset,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
)

# Train
trainer.train()

# Save final LoRA adapter to Drive
adapter_path = f"{WORKSPACE}/output/bitnet-moderation-lora"
model.save_pretrained(adapter_path)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(adapter_path)
print(f"✅ LoRA adapter saved to {adapter_path}")
```

```python
    return {"text": text, "label": label_map.get(example.get("label", "safe"), "safe")}

    """Map Davidson hate_speech_offensive labels.
    0 = hate speech, 1 = offensive language, 2 = neither
    """
    label_map = {
        0: "hate_speech",
        1: "harassment",
        2: "safe",
    }
    text = example.get("tweet", example.get("text", ""))
    return {"text": text, "label": label_map.get(example.get("class", 2), "safe")}

# ─── Apply Mappings ───
```

```python
aegis = aegis.map(map_aegis_labels, remove_columns=aegis.column_names)

print("Mapping Open Moderator labels...")
open_mod = open_mod.map(map_open_mod_labels, remove_columns=open_mod.column_names)

print("Mapping HateSpeech labels...")
hate = hate.map(map_hate_labels, remove_columns=hate.column_names)

# ─── Combine ───
print("Combining datasets...")
combined = concatenate_datasets([aegis, open_mod, hate])

# Print label distribution
labels, counts = np.unique(combined["label"], return_counts=True)
print("Label distribution:")
for l, c in zip(labels, counts):
    print(f"  {l}: {c} ({c/len(combined)*100:.1f}%)")

# ─── Format as prompt-completion pairs ───
def format_example(example):
    prompt = f"""Classify the following message as one of:
- safe
- hate_speech
- harassment
- threat
- self_harm

Message: {example['text']}

Classification:"""
    return {"text": prompt + " " + example['label']}

# ─── Train/Test Split ───

eval_dataset = split["test"]

# ─── Tokenize ───

eval_dataset.save_to_disk(f"{WORKSPACE}/data/eval_dataset")
```

```python
        "safe": "safe",
    }

def map_open_mod_labels(example):

        "hate_speech": "hate_speech",
        "harassment": "harassment",
        "threat": "threat",
        "self_harm": "self_harm",
        "safe": "safe",
    }

    label_map = {0: "hate_speech", 1: "harassment", 2: "safe"}
    text = example.get("tweet", example.get("text", ""))
    return {"text": text, "label": label_map.get(example.get("class", 2), "safe")}
```

# Synthesizing SoPPSoN + Meridian for OFFS Network Design

This is a rich synthesis. Let me pull the key mechanisms from each paper and show how they compose into a unified P2P network layer for your Owner-Free File System.

---

## Core Insight: Two Orthogonal Dimensions

The papers solve **different but complementary** problems:

| | **SoPPSoN** | **Meridian** |
|---|---|---|
| **What it optimizes** | *Who* is useful to *whom* | *Where* nodes sit in latency space |
| **Structure** | Weighted, directed social graph | Multi-resolution rings |
| **Learning** | Hebbian rules (frequency, feedback, symmetry) | Hypervolume diversity maximization |
| **Convergence** | Adaptive decay + deviation detection | Exponential ring radii → O(log N) hops |
| **Key metric** | Peer *utility* (resource quality, response success) | Peer *latency* (RTT) |

The synthesis: **Meridian provides the spatial scaffolding; SoPPSoN provides the adaptive intelligence layered on top.**

---

## Synthesized Architecture

### 1. Multi-Resolution Rings (Meridian) → The Spatial Skeleton

Each OFFS node maintains **concentric, non-overlapping rings** of peers, but instead of pure latency, ring membership is determined by a **composite distance metric**:

\[
D(i, j) = \alpha \cdot \text{latency}(i, j) + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \frac{1}{w_{ij} + \epsilon}
\]

Where \(w_{ij}\) is the **SoPPSoN-style connection strength** from node \(i\) to node \(j\). This means:

- **Nearby + useful** peers cluster in inner rings
- **Distant but highly useful** peers can still appear in inner rings
- Pure latency neighbors that never respond get pushed outward

```plaintext
Ring 0: [0, β·α⁰)      ← closest & most useful peers
Ring 1: [β·α⁰, β·α¹)
Ring 2: [β·α¹, β·α²)
...
Ring k: [β·α^{k-1}, β·α^k)  ← outermost ring
```

Each ring holds exactly \(k\) primary members + \(m\) secondary candidates (FIFO pool).

---

### 2. Hebbian Weight Learning (SoPPSoN) → The Adaptive Intelligence

Your existing RPC messages map naturally onto Hebbian learning triggers:

```typescript
enum RPCType {
  Ping,           // → triggers decay check, no weight change
  Find_Node,      // → Feedback rule if node helps route to target
  Find_Value,     // → Frequency rule if node provides the value
  Store,          // → Frequency rule (inverse: requester→storer)
  Random,         // → Symmetry rule (discovery of new peers)
  Ping_Value,     // → Frequency rule (verification = continued utility)
  Ping_Storage,   // → Frequency rule (verification = continued utility)
}
```

#### Learning Rules Applied to OFFS:

**Frequency Rule** (direct resource provision):
When peer \(j\) successfully stores or retrieves data for peer \(i\):

\[
w_{ij} \leftarrow w_{ij} + \gamma \cdot x_i \cdot x_j
\]

Where the learning rate \(\gamma\) depends on:
- **Search time** \(\tau\) (faster = stronger reinforcement)
- **Resource quality** \(q \in [-1, 1]\) (data integrity verification)
- **Storage duration** for Store operations (longer commitment = higher weight)

**Feedback Rule** (routing contribution):
When a multi-hop Find_Value succeeds, every intermediate node \(k\) that forwarded the request to node \(l\) gets:

\[
w_{kl} \leftarrow w_{kl} + \eta_f \cdot \Delta w_{ij}
\]

This is critical for OFFS — nodes that *route well* get reinforced even if they don't hold the data themselves.

**Symmetry Rule** (inferred reciprocity):
After updating \(w_{ij}\):

\[
w_{ji} \leftarrow w_{ji} + \eta_s \cdot \Delta w_{ij}, \quad \eta_s \ll \eta_f
\]

Useful for OFFS because a node that stores your data might later want to store data with you.

---

### 3. Adaptive Decay with Deviation Detection (SoPPSoN)

Connections decay over time in the absence of stimulus:

\[
w_{ij}(s+1) = w_{ij}(s) \cdot \exp(-\eta_d)
\]

But with the **adaptive decay rate** from SoPPSoN:

\[
\eta_d(i) = \frac{n_i}{a \cdot n_i^2 - b \cdot n_i + c}
\]

Where \(n_i\) is the number of current neighbors. Nodes with fewer connections decay faster (they're still searching), while well-connected nodes decay slower.

**Deviation detection** prunes outliers: a connection \(w_{ij}\) is removed if there exists neighbor \(l\) such that:

\[
\frac{w_{il}}{w_{ij}} > \kappa
\]

This keeps ring membership tight and useful.

---

### 4. Gossip-Based Node Discovery (Meridian + SoPPSoN)

Combining both papers' gossip approaches:

```typescript
interface GossipPacket {
  source: NodeID;
  samples: Array<{
    node: NodeID;
    ring: number;        // which ring the source placed this node in
    weight: number;      // SoPPSoN connection strength
    latency: number;     // measured RTT
  }>;
}
```

**Gossip cycle:**
1. Node \(A\) picks a random node from each of its rings
2. Sends gossip packet containing one random sample from each ring
3. Recipient \(B\) measures latency to \(A\) and all samples
4. \(B\) places new nodes into appropriate rings as secondary members
5. \(B\) triggers **Symmetry rule** for the new connections

This ensures both **spatial diversity** (Meridian) and **utility-weighted discovery** (SoPPSoN).

---

### 5. Query Routing: "Zooming In" with Social Intelligence

When a Find_Value or Find_Node request arrives:

```plaintext
function routeQuery(query: Query, currentNode: Node): RouteDecision {
    // 1. Determine target distance
    const targetDist = measureDistance(query.target);
    const ringIndex = findRing(targetDist);
    
    // 2. Select candidate peers from adjacent rings
    const candidates = [
        ...currentNode.rings[ringIndex - 1],  // inner ring
        ...currentNode.rings[ringIndex],       // matching ring
        ...currentNode.rings[ringIndex + 1],   // outer ring
    ];
    
    // 3. Filter by latency bound (Meridian-style)
    const viable = candidates.filter(p => 
        p.latency <= 2 * targetDist
    );
    
    // 4. Roulette-wheel selection weighted by w_ij (SoPPSoN-style)
    const selected = rouletteWheelSelect(viable, p => p.weight);
    
    // 5. Forward or terminate
    if (selected && selected.distanceToTarget < β * targetDist) {
        return { action: 'forward', to: selected };
    }
    return { action: 'terminate', bestKnown: currentNode.bestMatch };
}
```

This combines:
- **Meridian's exponential convergence** (each hop reduces distance by factor \(\beta\))
- **SoPPSoN's weighted selection** (useful peers get more traffic)
- **Latency bounding** (don't wait for peers that can't possibly be closer)

---

### 6. Ring Membership Management (Meridian's Hypervolume)

Within each ring, diversity is maintained via hypervolume maximization. For OFFS, we extend this to a **multi-objective diversity score**:

```typescript
function diversityScore(peers: Peer[]): number {
    // Each peer has coordinates: [latency_to_peer1, latency_to_peer2, ..., weight]
    const coordinates = peers.map(p => [
        ...p.latencyVector,  // Meridian-style local coordinate space
        p.weight,            // SoPPSoN connection strength
        p.storageReliability, // OFFS-specific: uptime, data integrity
    ]);
    return computeHypervolume(convexHull(coordinates));
}
```

This ensures rings contain peers that are diverse across **all relevant dimensions**: latency, utility, and storage reliability.

---

### 7. Updated RPC Message Structure

Bringing it all together, here's how your message types evolve:

```typescript
enum RPCType {
  // --- Liveness & Discovery ---
  Ping,              // Basic liveness; triggers decay check
  Ping_Response,     // Return current ring summary
  Gossip,            // Meridian-style anti-entropy push
  Gossip_Response,   // Acknowledgment with samples
  
  // --- Routing ---
  Find_Node,         // Kademlia-style node lookup
  Find_Node_Response,
  Find_Value,        // Content location
  Find_Value_Response,
  
  // --- Storage ---
  Store,             // Store data; triggers Frequency rule
  Store_Response,
  Retrieve,          // Retrieve data; triggers Frequency rule
  Retrieve_Response,
  
  // --- Verification (SoPPSoN reinforcement) ---
  Ping_Value,        // Verify data exists; triggers Frequency rule
  Ping_Value_Response,
  Ping_Storage,      // Verify storage commitment
  Ping_Storage_Response,
  
  // --- Network Maintenance ---
  Random,            // Random peer discovery; triggers Symmetry rule
  Random_Response,
  Ring_Update,       // Notify peers of ring membership changes
}
```

---

### 8. The Combined Data Flow

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                    │     Gossip Protocol          │
                    │  (Meridian anti-entropy)     │
                    │  + SoPPSoN Symmetry rule     │
                    └──────────┬──────────────────┘
                               │ populates
                               ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                    │   Multi-Resolution Rings     │
                    │  (Meridian spatial scaffold) │
                    │  + SoPPSoN weighted edges    │
                    └──────────┬──────────────────┘
                               │ used by
                               ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                    │    Query Routing             │
                    │  Exponential zoom-in         │
                    │  + Roulette-wheel selection  │
                    └──────────┬──────────────────┘
                               │ results feed back
                               ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                    │   Hebbian Weight Updates     │
                    │  Frequency / Feedback rules  │
                    │  + Adaptive decay            │
                    └──────────┬──────────────────┘
                               │ modifies
                               ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                    │  Ring Membership Management  │
                    │  Hypervolume diversity       │
                    │  + Deviation detection       │
                    └─────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Key Design Decisions to Consider

1. **Composite distance function**: The \(\alpha\) parameter that balances latency vs. utility is critical. I'd suggest starting with \(\alpha = 0.7\) (slightly favoring latency) and letting it adapt based on observed performance.

2. **Ring cardinality \(k\)**: Meridian shows \(k \approx 8\) works well for 2000 nodes. For OFFS, you might want \(k \in \) depending on churn rates.

3. **Learning rate \(\gamma\)**: SoPPSoN uses a time-dependent \(\gamma\) that decays with search time. For OFFS storage operations, you might also scale \(\gamma\) by the **size of stored data** — larger commitments deserve stronger reinforcement.

In the owner free file system we have a concept called altruism. This is where nodes actively try to seek out content for other nodes. We do this through a process I like to call node respiration. Individual nodes have a fixed storage capacity. From zero percent to fifty percent capacity, a node will try to seek out new blocks of data from its neighboring nodes to store for itself to use in new representations of data. After fifty percent the node stops seeking. At eighty percent it starts removing it its least popular blocks and starts sending them out to nodes on the network who are below fifty percent. This emptying process will happen until the node gets back below fifty percent.  I also wanted to incorporate a process of memory to the network. I want it to use an elastic bloom filter for each node that a node is connected to remember any failed requests for blocks that came past that node. If a node can't honor a request for a block, then it stores that block's ID in the filter, and if it sees it later, it sends it up the pipe towards that node. the values in the filter will decay over time. This will require new messages that are not present here.

# Synthesizing Altruistic Respiration + EBF Memory into the OFFS Network

This is a beautiful design. The respiration cycle gives the network a metabolic rhythm, and the EBF-based memory system creates a "promissory note" economy between peers. Let me fully synthesize this with the SoPPSoN and Meridian frameworks.

## 1. The Respiration Cycle: A Metabolic Model

Think of each node as a lung. Storage capacity drives a rhythmic inhale/exhale cycle:

```
     INHALE (0-50%)          NEUTRAL (50-80%)         EXHALE (80-100%)
    ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐
    │ Actively seek │        │  Passively    │        │ Shed least    │
    │ new blocks    │   →    │  participate  │   →    │ popular       │
    │ from neighbors│        │  (route only) │        │ blocks to     │
    │               │        │               │        │ nodes < 50%   │
    └──────────────┘        └──────────────┘        └──────────────┘
          ↑                                               │
          └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    Exhalation stops at 50%
```

This creates a natural **pressure gradient** — full nodes push toward empty nodes, and the network self-balances without central coordination.

## 2. Elastic Bloom Filter as Network Memory

Each node maintains **one EBF per outgoing connection**. This is the key insight: the EBF encodes "what I owe this peer."

### Structure per Connection

```
Connection B → A:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Fast Memory: Bloom Filter (bit array)   │  ← queried on every block acquisition
│  Slow Memory: Cooperative Bucket Array   │  ← stores elastic fingerprints
│                                           │
│  Stored: {block_X, block_Y, block_Z...}  │  ← IDs of blocks A wanted but B lacked
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Lifecycle of a "Memory"

```
STEP 1: FAILED REQUEST
  A → B: Find_Value(block_X)
  B:     "I don't have block_X"
  B:     EBF_{B→A}.insert(hash(block_X))
         ┌──────────────────┐
         │ EBF_{B→A}: {X}   │  ← debt recorded
         └──────────────────┘

STEP 2: ACQUISITION (via respiration)
  B inhales block_X from C (or receives via exhalation)
  B stores block_X locally

STEP 3: RECALL CHECK
  B: for each EBF I maintain:
       if EBF.query(hash(block_X)) == true:
         → B has a "debt" to repay

STEP 4: PROACTIVE PUSH
  B → A: Push_Block(block_X, reason="recall")
  A → B: Ack(gratitude=true)
  B:     EBF_{B→A}.delete(hash(block_X))   ← debt cleared
         ┌──────────────────┐
         │ EBF_{B→A}: {}    │  ← clean
         └──────────────────┘
  w_{A→B} increases significantly (Hebbian Frequency rule)
```

---

## 3. Decay of EBF Memory Over Time

The user specified that "values in the filter will decay over time." The EBF's native **compression** operation provides this elegantly:

### Time-Based Compression Schedule

```
T₀: EBF initialized (size m)
T₁: Compress → size m/2, some fingerprints lost
T₂: Compress → size m/4, more fingerprints lost
T₃: Compress → size m/8, most old debts forgotten
```

Each compression:
1. Halves the Bloom filter size
2. Merges adjacent buckets, appending a bit to each fingerprint
3. Naturally drops fingerprints from buckets that overflow during merge
4. Increases false positive rate slightly (acceptable for "fuzzy memory")

### Adaptive Decay Rate

Borrowing from SoPPSoN's adaptive decay:

\[
\eta_d(i) = \frac{n_i}{a \cdot n_i^2 - b \cdot n_i + c}
\]

Where \(n_i\) is the number of entries in the EBF. A fuller EBF decays faster (the node is accumulating too many unpaid debts), while a sparse EBF decays slower (debts are being repaid promptly).

## 5. Integrated Message Flow: Complete Respiration Cycle

### INHALE PHASE (Node A at 30% capacity)

```typescript

  rings: [ring_0, ring_1, ring_2],  // Meridian: nearby + mid-range
  minWeight: 0.1,                    // SoPPSoN: only useful peers
  diversity: true,                   // Hypervolume diversity

    capacity: 0.30,
    interests: [...],       // optional: content type preferences
    exclude: [...],         // blocks A already has
```

### EXHALE PHASE (Node B at 85% capacity)

```typescript

const candidates = identifyLeastPopular({
  threshold: 0.85,          // start shedding
  target: 0.50,             // stop at 50%
  sortBy: 'popularity',     // access count × recency
});

// B finds nodes below 50% (from periodic Capacity messages)

  maxCapacity: 0.50,
  rings: [ring_0, ring_1],  // prefer nearby nodes
  sortBy: 'capacity_asc',   // emptiest nodes first
});

// B pushes blocks

  const recipient = selectBestRecipient(block, recipients);
  sendRPC(RPCType.Push, {
    block: block.data,
    reason: 'exhalation',
    popularity: block.popularity,

  // On Push_Ack: Hebbian weight update, block removed from B's storage
}
```

### EBF RECALL (Node B acquires block X that A wanted)

```typescript

function onBlockAcquired(block: Block) {
  for (const [peerId, ebf] of this.outgoingEBFs) {
    if (ebf.query(hash(block.id))) {
      // B remembers peerId wanted this block
      const peer = this.connections.get(peerId);
      
      // Check if peer still needs it (optional Recall_Hint round-trip)
      // Or just Push directly (simpler, more altruistic)
      sendRPC(RPCType.Push, {
        block: block.data,
        reason: 'recall',
        original_request: ebf.getMetadata(hash(block.id)), // timestamp, etc.
      }, peer);
      
      // On Push_Ack: clear from EBF, strong Hebbian reinforcement
    }
  }
}
```

## 6. Hebbian Weight Integration

The respiration messages map onto SoPPSoN's learning rules:

| Trigger | Rule | Weight Change | Rationale |
|---------|------|---------------|-----------|
| Pull succeeds (A pulls from B) | **Frequency** | \(w_{A→B} += \gamma \cdot x_A \cdot x_B\) | B provided content |
| Push accepted (B pushes to A) | **Frequency** | \(w_{A→B} += \gamma_{push} \cdot x_A \cdot x_B\) | B was proactively useful |
| EBF Recall Push accepted | **Frequency** (amplified) | \(w_{A→B} += 2\gamma \cdot x_A \cdot x_B\) | B *remembered* A's need — high trust signal |
| B routes Find_Value to C who has it | **Feedback** | \(w_{B→C} += \eta_f \cdot \Delta w_{A→C}\) | C was useful, B's route was good |
| Push declined (A doesn't need it) | **Decay** | \(w_{A→B} -= \eta_d\) | B's judgment of A's needs was wrong |
| EBF entry expires (decayed) | **Decay** (indirect) | No weight change, but lost opportunity | Debt forgotten — connection weakens naturally |

The learning rate \(\gamma\) for respiration can incorporate:

\[
\gamma = \begin{cases}
\gamma_0 \cdot (1 - \frac{\tau}{\tau_{max}}) \cdot q & \text{if } \tau \leq \tau_{max} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

Where:
- \(\tau\) = time spent searching before acquiring the block
- \(q \in [-1, 1]\) = quality/utility of the block (validated on receipt)
- For EBF recalls, \(\tau\) is the time since the original failed request — longer memories get stronger reinforcement

## OFFS Network Layer — Complete

### 1. Spatial Scaffold (Meridian)

Multi-resolution rings, exponential radii, hypervolume diversity. Each node knows ~72 peers organized into concentric rings. Queries zoom in with O(log N) hops.

### 2. Social Intelligence (SoPPSoN)

### 3. Metabolic Rhythm (Respiration)

```
  Re-insert = push expiry forward
  Maintenance tick = advance hand, clear current slot
  Query on block acquisition → if hit, Push to peer
  On Push_Ack → delete from EBF
```

## Seek Frequency as a Function of Capacity

```
Seek interval τ(c):

  τ_max │
        │                                   ┌──────────
        │                              ┌────┘
        │                         ┌────┘
        │                    ┌────┘
        │               ┌────┘
        │          ┌────┘
  τ_min │────┐────┘
        │
        └─────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼─────────
             0%            25%            50%        100%
             
             ◄── INHALE ──►◄─ NEUTRAL ──►◄ EXHALE ─►
             aggressive     passive        shedding
```

A simple curve:

\[
\tau(c) = \tau_{min} + (\tau_{max} - \tau_{min}) \cdot \left(\frac{c}{0.50}\right)^\alpha, \quad c \in [0, 0.50]
\]

Where:
- \(c\) = capacity fraction
- \(\tau_{min}\) = seek interval when starving (e.g., 5 seconds)
- \(\tau_{max}\) = seek interval at 50% (e.g., 300 seconds, or effectively stops)
- \(\alpha\) = curvature (1 = linear, 2 = quadratic slowdown, >2 = linger aggressive then drop fast)

At \(c \geq 0.50\), the node stops initiating Seeks entirely — it only routes and receives Pushes.

---

### What This Means Behaviorally

| Capacity | Seek Interval | Behavior |
|----------|--------------|----------|
| 5% | Every ~5s | Ravenous. Pulls almost anything. |
| 25% | Every ~30s | Interested but pacing itself. |
| 40% | Every ~2min | Picky. Only pulls high-value blocks. |
| 48% | Every ~5min | Barely seeking. Waiting for something exceptional. |
| 50%+ | Never | Inhale stops. Routes for others. |

The node naturally becomes more **discerning** as it fills up — it won't waste remaining space on low-quality blocks because it knows the next Seek might be minutes away.

### Integration with the Seek Logic

```typescript
function shouldSeek(node: Node): boolean {
  if (node.capacity >= 0.50) return false;
  
  const elapsed = now() - node.lastSeekTime;
  const interval = seekInterval(node.capacity);
  return elapsed >= interval;
}

function seekInterval(capacity: number): number {
  const c = capacity / 0.50;  // normalized to [0, 1]
  const alpha = 2;             // quadratic slowdown
  return TAU_MIN + (TAU_MAX - TAU_MIN) * Math.pow(c, alpha);
}
```

And when a Seek does fire, the node can also raise its **quality bar** proportionally — only pulling blocks whose expected utility exceeds a threshold that rises with capacity:

```typescript
function shouldPull(block: BlockOffer, node: Node): boolean {
  const threshold = capacityToThreshold(node.capacity);
  return block.expectedUtility >= threshold;
}
```

## The Two-Tier Locality System

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              HOT CACHE (LRU)                     │
│  ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐                │
│  │ A │→│ B │→│ C │→│ D │→│ E │  (most→least)  │
│  └───┘ └───┘ └───┘ └───┘ └───┘                │
│  Blocks here: no ejection_date, actively used   │
└────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                     │ eviction
                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              COLD STORAGE (on disk)              │
│  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐        │
│  │ F (2h)   │ │ G (8h)   │ │ H (3d)   │  ...   │
│  │ ej:14:32 │ │ ej:08:15 │ │ ej:Mon   │        │
│  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘        │
│  ejection_date = when LRU kicked it out          │
│  Exhale sheds oldest ejection_date first         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The elegance: the LRU cache size becomes the knob for "how much local utility history do I remember before I consider a block cold?" A larger cache means blocks stay hot longer, fewer get ejection dates, and exhalation has less to work with. A smaller cache means blocks cycle through hot/cold faster, and the node is more aggressive about identifying what's truly active *right now*.

```c
// In block_cache_put:
int block_cache_put(block_cache_t* cache, block_t* block) {
  index_entry_t* entry = index_entry_create(block->hash);
  index_add(cache->index, entry);
  
  index_entry_t* evicted = block_lru_cache_put(cache->lru, block, entry);
  if (evicted != NULL) {
    // Kicked out of hot cache — start the cold clock
    index_set_entry_ejection(cache->index, evicted, now());
  }
  return 0;
}

// In block_cache_get:
block_t* block_cache_get(block_cache_t* cache, buffer_t* hash) {
  // If it's in the hot cache, LRU moves it to front
  // If it's cold (on disk), it gets loaded and re-enters hot cache
  // Either way, ejection_date gets cleared since it's hot again
  index_entry_t* entry = index_get(cache->index, hash);  // also increments fib
  index_set_entry_ejection(cache->index, entry, 0);       // clear ejection — it's hot
  // ... load from sections if not in LRU, put into LRU ...
}
```

## 1. Overview

The OFFS network is a **self-organizing, altruistic peer-to-peer overlay** where nodes cooperate to store, replicate, and retrieve content-addressed blocks of data. The network has no central coordinator. Instead, four interacting mechanisms produce emergent global behavior:

| Mechanism | Role | Inspiration |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| **Multi-resolution rings** | Spatial routing; O(log N) hop convergence | Meridian |
| **Hebbian weight learning** | Social graph; who is useful to whom | SoPPSoN |
| **Respiration cycle** | Capacity-driven seek/shed rhythm | — |
| **EBF + timing wheel memory** | Per-connection promissory notes | Elastic Bloom Filter |

Nodes carry a **fixed storage capacity**. Below 50% they actively seek new blocks. Above 80% they shed their coldest blocks to nodes with room. Between 50–80% they route for others but neither seek nor shed.

## 3. Data Structures

### 3.1 Ring Table (per node)

Each node maintains a fixed number of concentric, non-overlapping rings. Ring boundaries grow exponentially.

```
Ring i:  inner = β · α^(i-1),  outer = β · α^i    (i ≥ 1)
Ring 0:  [0, β)
```

| Parameter | Value | Meaning |
|-----------|-------|---------|
| `α` | 2 | Multiplicative radius increase factor |
| `β` | configurable | Innermost ring radius (e.g., 5 ms) |
| `k` | 8 | Primary members per ring |
| `m` | 4 | Secondary (FIFO candidate) members per ring |
| Ring count | ⌈log_α(max_RTT / β)⌉ | Typically 8–12 |

Each ring member stores:

```
ring_member_t {
  node_id_t   id;
  uint32_t    latency;     // last measured RTT (ms)
  float       weight;      // SoPPSoN connection strength w_ij
  float       capacity;    // last known capacity [0.0, 1.0]
}
```

### 3.2 Connection Weight Table

A directed, weighted graph over all known peers:

```
w_{i→j} ∈ [0, 1]

Stored alongside ring membership.
Decays over time in absence of positive stimulus.
```

### 3.3 Index Entry (per stored block)

```
index_entry_t {
  buffer_t*                 hash;           // content-addressed block ID
  fibonacci_hit_counter_t   counter;        // global popularity rank
  size_t                    section_id;     // which section file
  size_t                    section_index;  // offset within section file
  uint64_t                  ejection_date;  // when LRU evicted it (0 = hot)
}
```

### 3.4 Fibonacci Hit Counter

```
fibonacci_hit_counter_t {
  uint32_t  fib;         // current Fibonacci rank
  uint32_t  count;       // hits within current rank
  uint32_t  threshold;   // hits needed to promote (= fibonacci(fib))
}
```

Promotion thresholds: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, fib(2)=1, fib(3)=2, fib(4)=3, fib(5)=5, fib(6)=8, fib(7)=13, …

Each promotion gets exponentially harder. A block at fib=10 has survived ~143 accesses.

### 3.5 Rank Map (per node)

```
rank_map_t: HashMap<uint32_t fib, index_entry_vec_t*>
```

Maps each Fibonacci rank to the set of locally-stored blocks at that rank. Used for:

- **Representation building:** pick blocks biased toward higher fib
- **Exhalation:** shed from lowest fib upward (tie-break by ejection_date)

### 3.6 Per-Connection Memory

```
connection_memory_t {
  elastic_bloom_filter_t   ebf;       // fingerprints of owed blocks
  timing_wheel_t           wheel;     // TTL-based expiry
  uint64_t                 last_tick; // last maintenance tick timestamp
}
```

One per outgoing connection. Inserted on failed Find_Value. Queried on block acquisition. Deleted on successful Push_Ack. Expired by timing wheel tick.

### 3.7 Timing Wheel

```
timing_wheel_t {
  uint32_t    slot_count;       // N (e.g., 64)
  uint64_t    slot_duration_ms; // e.g., 60000 (1 minute)
  uint32_t    current_slot;     // hand position
  slot_t*     slots;            // array of N slots
  uint64_t    last_advance;     // last tick timestamp
}

slot_t {
  ebf_ref_t*  refs;             // references into EBF buckets
  size_t      count;
}
```

## 4. Ring Topology & Routing

### 4.1 Ring Membership Management

Rings are populated via gossip. Within each ring, diversity is maintained through **hypervolume maximization** over a local, non-exported coordinate space.

Each node computes coordinates for ring candidates as:

```
coords(peer_j) = [latency(i, j₁), latency(i, j₂), ..., latency(i, jₖ), w_{i→j}]
```

The subset of `k` peers whose convex hull has the largest hypervolume becomes the primary ring. The remaining `m` become secondaries (FIFO pool). This computation runs in the background; stale results are acceptable.

### 4.2 Query Routing

Queries "zoom in" toward the target. Each hop reduces distance by factor β.

```
ROUTE-QUERY(query, current_node):
  target_dist = measure_latency(current_node, query.target)
  ring = find_ring(target_dist)
  
  candidates = rings[ring-1] ∪ rings[ring] ∪ rings[ring+1]
  candidates = filter(candidates, p → p.latency ≤ 2 · target_dist)
  
  // Roulette-wheel selection weighted by w_{current→p}
  selected = roulette_select(candidates, weight = w)
  
  if selected ≠ null AND selected.dist_to_target < β · target_dist:
    forward query to selected
  else:
    terminate, return best known
```

### 4.3 Gossip Protocol

Anti-entropy push, executed periodically by every node:

```
GOSSIP-CYCLE(node):
  for each ring r in node.rings:
    peer = random_member(r)
    packet = {
      source:       node.id,
      capacity:     node.capacity,
      samples:      [one random member from each ring]
    }
    send GOSSIP to peer

ON-RECEIVE-GOSSIP(packet, from_peer):
  measure latency to from_peer and all samples
  place from_peer and samples into appropriate rings as secondaries
  trigger Symmetry rule for new connections
```

Gossip period: short for new nodes (rapid discovery), lengthens to steady-state value.

## 5. Connection Weights & Hebbian Learning

### 5.1 Weight Update Rules

| Rule | Trigger | Formula |
|------|---------|---------|
| **Frequency** | Peer j directly provides a block to peer i | \(w_{ij} \leftarrow w_{ij} + \gamma \cdot x_i \cdot x_j\) |
| **Feedback** | Peer k forwarded a request that ultimately succeeded via peer l | \(w_{kl} \leftarrow w_{kl} + \eta_f \cdot \Delta w_{ij}\) |
| **Symmetry** | After any update to \(w_{ij}\) | \(w_{ji} \leftarrow w_{ji} + \eta_s \cdot \Delta w_{ij}\) |
| **Decay** | No positive stimulus for time s | \(w_{ij}(s) = w_{ij}(0) \cdot \exp(-\eta_d \cdot s)\) |

### 5.2 Learning Rate

\[\gamma = \begin{cases} \gamma_0 \cdot \left(1 - \frac{\tau}{T}\right) \cdot q & \tau \leq T \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

Where:
- \(\tau\) = time spent searching before acquisition
- \(T\) = maximum search time (e.g., 6 hops)
- \(q \in [-1, 1]\) = resource quality (validated on receipt)
- \(\gamma_0\) = base learning rate

### 5.3 Weight Multipliers by Operation

| Operation | Multiplier | Rationale |
|-----------|------------|-----------|
| Normal Pull success | 1.0× | Standard provision |
| Push accepted (exhalation) | 1.0× | Proactive gift |
| EBF Recall Push accepted | 2.0× | Remembered a past need — high trust |
| Push declined | −0.5× | Misjudged peer's needs |

### 5.4 Adaptive Decay Rate

\[\eta_d(i) = \frac{n_i}{a \cdot n_i^2 - b \cdot n_i + c}\]

Where \(n_i\) = number of current neighbors. Fewer neighbors → faster decay (still searching). More neighbors → slower decay (well-connected, stable).

### 5.5 Deviation Detection

A connection \(w_{ij}\) is pruned if there exists neighbor \(l\) such that:

\[\frac{w_{il}}{w_{ij}} > \kappa\]

This removes connections that are dramatically weaker than peers in the same ring.

## 6. Respiration Cycle

### 6.1 Capacity Phases

```
0% ──────────── 50% ──────────── 80% ──────────── 100%
│  INHALE       │   NEUTRAL     │    EXHALE       │
│  Seek→Pull    │  route only   │  Push→shed      │
│  aggressive   │  receive only │  until 50%      │
└───────────────┴───────────────┴─────────────────┘
```

### 6.2 Seek Throttle

Seek interval as a function of capacity:

\[\tau(c) = \tau_{\min} + (\tau_{\max} - \tau_{\min}) \cdot \left(\frac{c}{0.50}\right)^\alpha, \quad c \in [0, 0.50]\]

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| \(\tau_{\min}\) | 5 s | Seek interval at 0% capacity |
| \(\tau_{\max}\) | 300 s | Seek interval at 50% capacity |
| \(\alpha\) | 2.0 | Curvature (quadratic slowdown) |

At \(c \geq 0.50\), seeking stops entirely.

### 6.3 Inhale Algorithm

```
INHALE-CYCLE(node):
  if node.capacity ≥ 0.50: return
  if not SHOULD-SEEK(node): return
  
  node.last_seek = now()
  
  // Select diverse, useful neighbors
  targets = select_neighbors(node, {
    rings:      [0, 1, 2],
    min_weight: 0.1,
    diversity:  true
  })
  
  for each peer in targets:
    send SEEK to peer
  
  // Process responses asynchronously
  // For each offer: evaluate, PULL if valuable
```

### 6.4 Exhale Algorithm

```
EXHALE-CYCLE(node):
  if node.capacity < 0.80: return
  
  to_free = blocks_to_reach(node, target = 0.50)
  
  // Collect all cold blocks (ejection_date > 0)
  cold = filter(index_to_array(node.index), e → e.ejection_date > 0)
  
  // Sort by ejection_date ASC (oldest eviction first)
  sort(cold, by: ejection_date)
  
  // Find recipients below 50%
  recipients = filter(all_known_peers, p → p.capacity < 0.50)
  sort(recipients, by: capacity ASC)  // emptiest first
  
  for i = 0; i < min(to_free, cold.length); i++:
    entry = cold[i]
    recipient = best_recipient(entry, recipients)
    block = load_from_sections(node.sections, entry)
    send PUSH(block, reason = EXHALATION) to recipient
    index_remove(node.index, entry.hash)
  
  // On PUSH_ACK: Hebbian reinforcement, remove block from disk
```

### 6.5 Ejection Date Lifecycle

```
ON-BLOCK-ENTER-HOT-CACHE:
  entry.ejection_date = 0    // "alive"

ON-LRU-EVICTION:
  entry.ejection_date = now()   // "cold since..."

ON-BLOCK-RE-ENTER-HOT-CACHE (via access):
  entry.ejection_date = 0    // "alive again"
```

The ejection date is set **only by the LRU cache eviction**. It is never set on access. It is cleared when a block re-enters the hot cache.

## 7. Network Memory

### 7.1 Concept

Each node maintains one EBF per outgoing connection. The EBF stores fingerprints of block IDs that the remote peer requested but this node could not provide. It is a **promissory note**: "I owe you this block if I ever get it."

### 7.2 Insert (on failed Find_Value)

```
REMEMBER-FAILED-REQUEST(memory, block_hash):
  (fp, index) = hash_to_ebf(block_hash, memory.ebf.size)
  bucket = memory.ebf.buckets[index]
  
  // Already remembered? Push expiry forward.
  for each entry in bucket:
    if entry.fp == fp:
      remove entry.ref from wheel.slots[entry.wheel_slot]
      entry.wheel_slot = COMPUTE-EXPIRY-SLOT(wheel)
      add entry.ref to wheel.slots[entry.wheel_slot]
      return
  
  // New memory
  slot = COMPUTE-EXPIRY-SLOT(wheel)
  ref = { bucket_index: index, fp_index: bucket.length }
  bucket.push({ fp, wheel_slot: slot, ref })
  wheel.slots[slot].add(ref)
  memory.ebf.bloom.set_bit(index)
```

### 7.3 Query (on block acquisition)

```
CHECK-ALL-MEMORIES(node, block_hash):
  for each memory in node.outgoing_memories:
    if EBF-QUERY(memory.ebf, block_hash):
      peer = memory.associated_peer
      send PUSH(block, reason = RECALL) to peer
      
      // On PUSH_ACK:
      EBF-DELETE(memory.ebf, block_hash)
      w_{peer→node} += 2.0 · γ   // amplified Hebbian
```

### 7.4 EBF Query

```
EBF-QUERY(ebf, block_hash):
  (fp, index) = hash_to_ebf(block_hash, ebf.size)
  
  // Fast path: Bloom filter
  if not ebf.bloom.get_bit(index): return false
  
  // Slow path: check fingerprints
  for each entry in ebf.buckets[index]:
    if entry.fp == fp: return true
  
  return false
```

### 7.5 Maintenance Tick

```
MEMORY-TICK(node):
  now = get_time_ms()
  
  for each memory in node.outgoing_memories:
    elapsed = now - memory.wheel.last_tick
    slots_elapsed = elapsed / memory.wheel.slot_duration_ms
    
    for s = 0; s < slots_elapsed; s++:
      memory.wheel.current_slot = (memory.wheel.current_slot + 1) % N
      slot = memory.wheel.slots[memory.wheel.current_slot]
      
      for each ref in slot:
        EBF-DELETE-REF(memory.ebf, ref)
      slot.clear()
    
    memory.wheel.last_tick = now
```

### 7.6 Timing Wheel Configuration

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `N` (slot_count) | 64 | Number of wheel slots |
| `slot_duration_ms` | 60000 | 1 minute per slot |
| `default_ttl_ms` | 3600000 | 1 hour default memory |
| Max memory span | 64 min | N × slot_duration |

## 8. Popularity & Rank Gossip

### 8.1 Fibonacci Rank Promotion

When `index_entry_increment` returns 1 (promotion occurred):

```
ON-RANK-PROMOTION(node, entry):
  // Update local rank map
  old_fib = entry.counter.fib - 1
  remove entry from node.index.ranks[old_fib]
  add entry to node.index.ranks[entry.counter.fib]
  
  // Gossip to neighbors
  for each peer in node.all_peers:
    send RANK_UPGRADE {
      block_hash: entry.hash,
      fib:        entry.counter.fib,
      count:      entry.counter.count,
      origin:     node.id,
      hop_count:  0
    } to peer
```

### 8.2 Receiving Rank Gossip

```
ON-RANK-UPGRADE(msg, from_peer):
  entry = index_peek(node.index, msg.block_hash)
  
  if entry != NULL:
    // We have this block — upgrade if remote rank is higher
    if msg.fib > entry.counter.fib:
      entry.counter.fib = msg.fib
      entry.counter.count = msg.count
      entry.counter.threshold = fibonacci(msg.fib)
      update_rank_map(node.index, entry, old_fib, msg.fib)
    
    // Don't re-gossip if we already knew a higher rank
    return
  
  // We don't have this block
  // Check if this is the highest rank we've seen
  if msg.fib > node.highest_seen_rank:
    node.highest_seen_rank = msg.fib
    // Altruistic inhale: seek this block if we have room
    if node.capacity < 0.50:
      initiate_seek_for(msg.block_hash)
  
  // Forward gossip if hop_count < max_hops
  if msg.hop_count < MAX_RANK_HOPS:
    msg.hop_count++
    forward to random subset of peers
```

### 8.3 Block Selection for Representations

```
PICK-BLOCK-FOR-REPRESENTATION(index):
  max_fib = find_max_fib(index.ranks)
  
  // Walk from highest rank downward
  // Higher fib → exponentially higher selection probability
  for fib = max_fib; fib > 0; fib--:
    bucket = index.ranks[fib]
    if bucket != NULL AND bucket.length > 0:
      // Probability of selecting from this rank ∝ fibonacci(fib)
      if random() < fibonacci(fib) / fibonacci(max_fib + 1):
        return random_element(bucket)
  
  // Fallback to fib=0
  return random_element(index.ranks[0])
```
