## 10. Request Algorithms

### 10.1 Ping

```
HANDLE-PING(msg, socket):
  // Update last-seen for source
  // Trigger decay check on w_{self→source}
  
  response = {
    ring_summary: [one random member from each ring]
  }
  send PING_RESPONSE to socket

HANDLE-PING-RESPONSE(msg, socket):
  // Measure latency to source
  // Update ring placement for source
  // Place summary members into rings as secondaries
```

### 10.2 Find_Node

```
HANDLE-FIND-NODE(msg, socket):
  target = msg.target_id
  
  // Find k closest nodes in routing table to target
  closest = find_closest_nodes(target, k = 8)
  
  send FIND_NODE_RESPONSE { closest } to socket
```

### 10.3 Find_Value

```
HANDLE-FIND-VALUE(msg, socket):
  block_hash = msg.block_hash
  entry = index_peek(self.index, block_hash)
  
  if entry != NULL:
    // We have it
    send FIND_VALUE_RESPONSE {
      found:  true,
      holder: self.id,
      fib:    entry.counter.fib
    } to socket
    
    // Increment local counter (may trigger rank promotion)
    index_increment(self.index, entry)
    return
  
  // We don't have it — check if we can route
  // Route using ROUTE-QUERY algorithm (Section 4.2)
  next_hop = ROUTE-QUERY(msg, self)
  
  if next_hop != NULL:
    forward FIND_VALUE to next_hop
  else:
    // Dead end — remember the failed request
    REMEMBER-FAILED-REQUEST(self.memories[msg.source], block_hash)
    
    send FIND_VALUE_RESPONSE {
      found: false
    } to socket
```

### 10.4 Store

```
HANDLE-STORE(msg, socket):
  block = msg.block_data
  block_hash = hash(block)
  
  // Check capacity
  if self.capacity >= 1.0:
    send STORE_RESPONSE { success: false, reason: "full" } to socket
    return
  
  // Write to sections
  (section_id, section_index) = sections_write(self.sections, block)
  
  // Create index entry
  entry = index_entry_from(block_hash, section_id, section_index, 0, counter={0})
  index_add(self.index, entry)
  
  // Put into hot cache (may evict another block → sets its ejection_date)
  evicted = block_lru_cache_put(self.lru, block, entry)
  if evicted != NULL:
    index_set_entry_ejection(self.index, evicted, now())
  
  // Hebbian: storer is useful to store-requester
  w_{msg.source→self} += γ_store
  
  send STORE_RESPONSE { success: true } to socket
```

### 10.5 Seek (Inhale)

```
HANDLE-SEEK(msg, socket):
  requester_capacity = msg.capacity
  
  // Only respond if we have blocks to offer
  // Select a sample of our blocks, biased toward higher fib
  offers = []
  for i = 0; i < MAX_OFFERS; i++:
    entry = PICK-BLOCK-FOR-REPRESENTATION(self.index)
    if entry not already in msg.exclude_hashes:
      offers.push({
        hash: entry.hash,
        fib:  entry.counter.fib,
        size: get_block_size(entry)
      })
  
  send SEEK_RESPONSE { offers } to socket

HANDLE-SEEK-RESPONSE(msg, socket):
  // Evaluate each offer
  for each offer in msg.offers:
    if SHOULD-PULL(offer, self):
      send PULL { block_hash: offer.hash } to msg.source
```

### 10.6 Pull

```
HANDLE-PULL(msg, socket):
  block_hash = msg.block_hash
  entry = index_find(self.index, block_hash)
  
  if entry == NULL:
    send PULL_RESPONSE { rejection: "not_found" } to socket
    return
  
  block = load_from_sections(self.sections, entry)
  
  // Increment local counter
  index_increment(self.index, entry)
  
  send PULL_RESPONSE { block_data: block } to socket

HANDLE-PULL-RESPONSE(msg, socket):
  if msg has block_data:
    // Store locally
    HANDLE-STORE-like logic
    // Hebbian: provider was useful
    w_{self→msg.source} += γ_pull
  else:
    // Rejection — slight decay on provider
    w_{self→msg.source} -= η_reject
```

### 10.7 Push (Exhalation or Recall)

```
HANDLE-PUSH(msg, socket):
  block = msg.block_data
  block_hash = hash(block)
  
  // Accept if we have room
  if self.capacity < 1.0:
    // Store (same as STORE path)
    (section_id, section_index) = sections_write(self.sections, block)
    entry = index_entry_from(block_hash, section_id, section_index, 0, counter={0})
    index_add(self.index, entry)
    
    evicted = block_lru_cache_put(self.lru, block, entry)
    if evicted != NULL:
      index_set_entry_ejection(self.index, evicted, now())
    
    send PUSH_ACK { accepted: true } to socket
    
    // Hebbian reinforcement
    if msg.reason == RECALL:
      w_{self→msg.source} += 2.0 · γ   // amplified
    else:
      w_{self→msg.source} += γ_push
  else:
    send PUSH_ACK { accepted: false } to socket
    w_{self→msg.source} -= η_reject

HANDLE-PUSH-ACK(msg, socket):
  if msg.accepted:
    // Block successfully transferred — remove locally
    index_remove(self.index, block_hash)
    delete_from_sections(self.sections, entry)
    
    // If this was a recall, clear the EBF entry
    if recall_context:
      EBF-DELETE(self.memories[msg.source], block_hash)
  else:
    // Recipient rejected — try another peer
    retry_push_with_different_recipient()
```

### 10.8 Random

```
HANDLE-RANDOM(msg, socket):
  // Return a random peer from across all rings
  random_peer = select_completely_random_peer(self)
  send RANDOM_RESPONSE { peer } to socket
  
  // Symmetry rule: new connection discovered
  w_{self→random_peer} initialized if new
```

### 10.9 Ping_Value

```
HANDLE-PING-VALUE(msg, socket):
  block_hash = msg.block_hash
  entry = index_peek(self.index, block_hash)
  
  if entry != NULL:
    // Value exists — this is continued utility
    // Extend ejection_date? No — only LRU does that.
    // But reinforce Hebbian weight
    w_{self→msg.source} += γ_ping_value
    send PING_VALUE_RESPONSE { exists: true, fib: entry.counter.fib } to socket
  else:
    send PING_VALUE_RESPONSE { exists: false } to socket
```

### 10.10 Ping_Storage

```
HANDLE-PING-STORAGE(msg, socket):
  // Verify storage commitment is still honored
  // Check that sections file is intact, block is readable
  entry = index_peek(self.index, msg.block_hash)
  
  if entry != NULL AND verify_block_integrity(entry):
    w_{self→msg.source} += γ_ping_storage
    send PING_STORAGE_RESPONSE { healthy: true } to socket
  else:
    send PING_STORAGE_RESPONSE { healthy: false } to socket
```

### 10.11 Recall_Hint

```
HANDLE-RECALL-HINT(msg, socket):
  block_hash = msg.block_hash
  
  // Do we still need this block?
  if index_peek(self.index, block_hash) == NULL AND self.capacity < 0.50:
    send RECALL_ACCEPT to socket
  else:
    send RECALL_DECLINE to socket

HANDLE-RECALL-ACCEPT(msg, socket):
  // Sender wants it — push the block
  entry = index_find(self.index, msg.block_hash)
  block = load_from_sections(self.sections, entry)
  send PUSH(block, reason = RECALL) to msg.source

HANDLE-RECALL-DECLINE(msg, socket):
  // Recipient no longer needs it — clear the debt
  EBF-DELETE(self.memories[msg.source], msg.block_hash)
```

# OFFS Network Layer — Design Specification

**Version:** 1.0  
**Date:** 2026-05-09

## 1. Introduction

The Owner-Free File System (OFFS) network is a self-organizing, altruistic peer-to-peer overlay. Nodes cooperate to store, replicate, and retrieve content-addressed blocks without central coordination. The network exhibits emergent behavior through four interacting mechanisms:

| Mechanism | Purpose | Origin |
|-----------|---------|--------|
| Multi-resolution rings | Spatial routing, O(log N) convergence | Meridian |
| Hebbian weight learning | Social graph, peer utility tracking | SoPPSoN |
| Respiration cycle | Capacity-driven seek/shed rhythm | Original |
| EBF + timing wheel memory | Per-connection promissory notes | Elastic Bloom Filter |

Nodes have a fixed storage capacity. Below 50% they actively seek new blocks. Above 80% they shed their coldest blocks to nodes with room. Between 50–80% they route for others but neither seek nor shed. The seek rate slows quadratically as capacity approaches 50%.

```
                               │

│                        ROUTING LAYER                             │

```

## 3. Data Structures

### 3.1 Ring Table

Each node maintains concentric, non-overlapping rings of peers organized by latency.

```plaintext
Ring i:  inner = β · α^(i-1),  outer = β · α^i    (i ≥ 1)
Ring 0:  [0, β)
```

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `α` | 2 | Multiplicative radius increase |
| `β` | 5 ms | Innermost ring radius |
| `k` | 8 | Primary members per ring |
| `m` | 4 | Secondary (FIFO candidate) members per ring |
| Ring count | ⌈log_α(max_RTT / β)⌉ | Typically 8–12 |

Each ring member:

```c
typedef struct {
  node_id_t   id;
  uint32_t    latency;     // last measured RTT (ms)
  float       weight;      // Hebbian connection strength w_ij
  float       capacity;    // last known capacity [0.0, 1.0]
} ring_member_t;
```

### 3.2 Connection Weights

Directed, weighted edges over all known peers:

```plaintext
w_{i→j} ∈ [0, 1]
```

Stored alongside ring membership. Decays in absence of positive stimulus. Updated by Hebbian learning rules.

### 3.3 Index Entry

```c
typedef struct {
  refcounter_t               refcounter;
  PLATFORMLOCKTYPE(lock);
  fibonacci_hit_counter_t     counter;        // global popularity rank
  buffer_t*                   hash;            // content-addressed block ID
  size_t                      section_id;      // which section file
  size_t                      section_index;    // offset within section file
  uint64_t                    ejection_date;   // when LRU evicted it (0 = hot)
} index_entry_t;
```

### 3.4 Fibonacci Hit Counter

```c
typedef struct {
  uint32_t  fib;         // current Fibonacci rank
  uint32_t  count;       // hits within current rank
  uint32_t  threshold;   // hits needed to promote (= fibonacci(fib))
} fibonacci_hit_counter_t;
```

Promotion thresholds:

| fib | threshold | cumulative hits to reach |
|-----|-----------|------------------------|
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 | 2 |
| 3 | 2 | 4 |
| 4 | 3 | 7 |
| 5 | 5 | 12 |
| 6 | 8 | 20 |
| 7 | 13 | 33 |
| 8 | 21 | 54 |
| 9 | 34 | 88 |
| 10 | 55 | 143 |

Each promotion is exponentially harder. A block at fib=10 has survived ~143 accesses. This cannot be gamed by rapid repeated requests.

### 3.5 Rank Map

```c
typedef HASHMAP(uint32_t, index_entry_vec_t) rank_map_t;
```

Maps each Fibonacci rank to the set of locally-stored blocks at that rank. Used for representation building (pick blocks biased toward higher fib) and exhalation (shed from lowest fib upward, tie-break by ejection_date).

### 3.6 Per-Connection Memory

One per outgoing connection:

```c
typedef struct {
  elastic_bloom_filter_t   ebf;       // fingerprints of owed blocks
  timing_wheel_t           wheel;     // TTL-based expiry
  uint64_t                 last_tick; // last maintenance tick
} connection_memory_t;
```

### 3.7 Timing Wheel

```c
typedef struct {
  uint32_t    slot_count;       // N (default: 64)
  uint64_t    slot_duration_ms; // per-slot duration (default: 60000)
  uint32_t    current_slot;     // hand position
  slot_t*     slots;            // array of N slots
  uint64_t    last_advance;     // last tick timestamp
} timing_wheel_t;

typedef struct {
  ebf_ref_t*  refs;             // references into EBF buckets
  size_t      count;
} slot_t;
```

## 4. Ring Topology & Routing

### 4.1 Ring Membership Management

Rings are populated via gossip. Within each ring, diversity is maintained through **hypervolume maximization** over a local, non-exported coordinate space.

Each node computes coordinates for ring candidates:

```plaintext
coords(peer_j) = [latency(i, j₁), latency(i, j₂), ..., latency(i, jₖ), w_{i→j}]
```

The subset of `k` peers whose convex hull has the largest hypervolume becomes the primary ring. The remaining `m` become secondaries (FIFO pool). This computation runs in the background; stale results are acceptable.

### 4.2 Query Routing Algorithm

Queries "zoom in" toward the target. Each hop reduces distance by factor β.

```
ROUTE-QUERY(query, current_node):
  target_dist = measure_latency(current_node, query.target)
  ring = find_ring(target_dist)
  
  candidates = rings[ring-1] ∪ rings[ring] ∪ rings[ring+1]
  candidates = filter(candidates, p → p.latency ≤ 2 · target_dist)
  
  // Roulette-wheel selection weighted by w_{current→p}
  selected = roulette_select(candidates, weight = w)
  
  if selected ≠ null AND selected.dist_to_target < β · target_dist:
    forward query to selected
  else:
    terminate, return best known
```

### 4.3 Gossip Protocol

Anti-entropy push, executed periodically by every node:

```
GOSSIP-CYCLE(node):
  for each ring r in node.rings:
    peer = random_primary_member(r)
    packet = {
      source:       node.id,
      capacity:     node.capacity,
      samples:      [one random member from each ring]
    }
    send GOSSIP to peer

ON-RECEIVE-GOSSIP(packet, from_peer):
  measure latency to from_peer and all samples
  place from_peer and samples into appropriate rings as secondaries
  trigger Symmetry rule for new connections
```

Gossip period: short for new nodes (rapid discovery), lengthens to steady-state value.

## 5. Connection Weights & Hebbian Learning

### 5.1 Weight Update Rules

| Rule | Trigger | Formula |
|------|---------|---------|
| **Frequency** | Peer j directly provides a block to peer i | `w_ij ← w_ij + γ · x_i · x_j` |
| **Feedback** | Peer k forwarded a request that succeeded via peer l | `w_kl ← w_kl + η_f · Δw_ij` |
| **Symmetry** | After any update to `w_ij` | `w_ji ← w_ji + η_s · Δw_ij` |
| **Decay** | No positive stimulus for time s | `w_ij(s) = w_ij(0) · exp(-η_d · s)` |

### 5.2 Learning Rate

```
γ = γ₀ · (1 - τ/T) · q       if τ ≤ T
γ = 0                          otherwise
```

Where:
- `τ` = time spent searching before acquisition
- `T` = maximum search hops (default: 6)
- `q ∈ [-1, 1]` = resource quality (validated on receipt)
- `γ₀` = base learning rate (default: 0.1)

### 5.3 Weight Multipliers by Operation

| Operation | Multiplier | Rationale |
|-----------|------------|-----------|
| Normal Pull success | 1.0× | Standard provision |
| Push accepted (exhalation) | 1.0× | Proactive gift |
| EBF Recall Push accepted | 2.0× | Remembered a past need — high trust |
| Push declined | −0.5× | Misjudged peer's needs |

### 5.4 Adaptive Decay Rate

```plaintext
η_d(i) = n_i / (a · n_i² - b · n_i + c)
```

Where `n_i` = number of current neighbors. Fewer neighbors → faster decay (still searching). More neighbors → slower decay (well-connected, stable).

### 5.5 Deviation Detection

A connection `w_ij` is pruned if there exists neighbor `l` such that:

```
w_il / w_ij > κ      (default κ = 10⁻⁸)
```

This removes connections that are dramatically weaker than peers in the same ring.

## 6. Respiration Cycle

### 6.1 Capacity Phases

```
0% ──────────── 50% ──────────── 80% ──────────── 100%
│  INHALE       │   NEUTRAL     │    EXHALE       │
│  Seek→Pull    │  route only   │  Push→shed      │
│  aggressive   │  receive only │  until 50%      │
└───────────────┴───────────────┴─────────────────┘
```

### 6.2 Seek Throttle

Seek interval as a function of capacity:

```
τ(c) = τ_min + (τ_max - τ_min) · (c / 0.50)^α       c ∈ [0, 0.50]
τ(c) = ∞                                               c ≥ 0.50
```

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `τ_min` | 5 s | Seek interval at 0% capacity |
| `τ_max` | 300 s | Seek interval at 50% capacity |
| `α` | 2.0 | Curvature (quadratic slowdown) |

Behavior at key points:

| Capacity | Seek Interval | Behavior |
|----------|--------------|----------|
| 5% | ~5 s | Ravenous — pulls almost anything |
| 25% | ~30 s | Interested but pacing |
| 40% | ~2 min | Picky — only high-value blocks |
| 48% | ~5 min | Barely seeking |
| 50%+ | Never | Inhale stops entirely |

### 6.3 Inhale Algorithm

```plaintext
INHALE-CYCLE(node):
  if node.capacity ≥ 0.50: return
  if not SHOULD-SEEK(node): return
  
  node.last_seek = now()
  
  // Select diverse, useful neighbors via Meridian rings + SoPPSoN weights
  targets = select_neighbors(node, {
    rings:      [0, 1, 2],
    min_weight: 0.1,
    diversity:  true
  })
  
  for each peer in targets:
    send SEEK to peer
  
  // Process responses asynchronously
  // For each offer: evaluate, PULL if valuable
```

### 6.4 Exhale Algorithm

```plaintext
EXHALE-CYCLE(node):
  if node.capacity < 0.80: return
  
  to_free = blocks_to_reach(node, target = 0.50)
  
  // Collect all cold blocks (ejection_date > 0, i.e., not in hot cache)
  cold = filter(index_to_array(node.index), e → e.ejection_date > 0)
  
  // Sort by ejection_date ASC (oldest eviction first)
  sort(cold, by: ejection_date ascending)
  
  // Find recipients below 50%
  recipients = filter(all_known_peers, p → p.capacity < 0.50)
  sort(recipients, by: capacity ascending)   // emptiest first
  
  for i = 0; i < min(to_free, cold.length); i++:
    entry = cold[i]
    recipient = best_recipient(entry, recipients)
    block = load_from_sections(node.sections, entry)
    send PUSH(block, reason = EXHALATION) to recipient
    index_remove(node.index, entry.hash)
  
  // On PUSH_ACK: Hebbian reinforcement, remove block from disk
```

### 6.5 Ejection Date Lifecycle

The ejection date is set **only by the LRU cache eviction**. It is never set on access. It is cleared when a block re-enters the hot cache.

```
ON-BLOCK-ENTER-HOT-CACHE:
  entry.ejection_date = 0              // "alive"

ON-LRU-EVICTION:
  entry.ejection_date = now()          // "cold since..."

ON-BLOCK-RE-ENTER-HOT-CACHE (via access):
  entry.ejection_date = 0              // "alive again"
```

The ejection date measures **local utility** — how long since this node last used the block. The Fibonacci rank measures **global popularity** — how widely requested the block is across the network. These are orthogonal signals:

| Signal | Scope | Drives |
|--------|-------|--------|
| Fibonacci rank (fib) | Global (gossiped) | What to seek, what to use in representations, what to replicate |
| Ejection date | Local (per-node) | What to shed when space is tight |

## 7. Network Memory

### 7.1 Concept

Each node maintains one EBF per outgoing connection. The EBF stores fingerprints of block IDs that the remote peer requested but this node could not provide. It is a **promissory note**: "I owe you this block if I ever get it."

### 7.2 Insert (on failed Find_Value)

```plaintext
REMEMBER-FAILED-REQUEST(memory, block_hash):
  (fp, index) = hash_to_ebf(block_hash, memory.ebf.size)
  bucket = memory.ebf.buckets[index]
  
  // Already remembered? Push expiry forward.
  for each entry in bucket:
    if entry.fp == fp:
      remove entry.ref from wheel.slots[entry.wheel_slot]
      entry.wheel_slot = COMPUTE-EXPIRY-SLOT(wheel)
      add entry.ref to wheel.slots[entry.wheel_slot]
      return
  
  // New memory
  slot = COMPUTE-EXPIRY-SLOT(wheel)
  ref = { bucket_index: index, fp_index: bucket.length }
  bucket.push({ fp, wheel_slot: slot, ref })
  wheel.slots[slot].add(ref)
  memory.ebf.bloom.set_bit(index)
```

### 7.3 Query (on block acquisition)

```
CHECK-ALL-MEMORIES(node, block_hash):
  for each memory in node.outgoing_memories:
    if EBF-QUERY(memory.ebf, block_hash):
      peer = memory.associated_peer
      send PUSH(block, reason = RECALL) to peer
      
      // On PUSH_ACK:
      EBF-DELETE(memory.ebf, block_hash)
      w_{peer→node} += 2.0 · γ   // amplified Hebbian
```

### 7.4 EBF Query

```plaintext
EBF-QUERY(ebf, block_hash):
  (fp, index) = hash_to_ebf(block_hash, ebf.size)
  
  // Fast path: Bloom filter
  if not ebf.bloom.get_bit(index): return false
  
  // Slow path: check fingerprints
  for each entry in ebf.buckets[index]:
    if entry.fp == fp: return true
  
  return false
```

### 7.5 Maintenance Tick

```
MEMORY-TICK(node):
  now = get_time_ms()
  
  for each memory in node.outgoing_memories:
    elapsed = now - memory.wheel.last_tick
    slots_elapsed = elapsed / memory.wheel.slot_duration_ms
    
    for s = 0; s < slots_elapsed; s++:
      memory.wheel.current_slot = (memory.wheel.current_slot + 1) % N
      slot = memory.wheel.slots[memory.wheel.current_slot]
      
      for each ref in slot:
        EBF-DELETE-REF(memory.ebf, ref)
      slot.clear()
    
    memory.wheel.last_tick = now
```

### 7.6 Timing Wheel Configuration

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `N` (slot_count) | 64 | Number of wheel slots |
| `slot_duration_ms` | 60000 | 1 minute per slot |
| `default_ttl_ms` | 3600000 | 1 hour default memory |
| Max memory span | 64 min | N × slot_duration |

## 8. Popularity & Rank Gossip

### 8.1 Fibonacci Rank Promotion

When `index_entry_increment` returns 1 (promotion occurred):

```plaintext
ON-RANK-PROMOTION(node, entry):
  // Update local rank map
  old_fib = entry.counter.fib - 1
  remove entry from node.index.ranks[old_fib]
  add entry to node.index.ranks[entry.counter.fib]
  
  // Gossip to neighbors
  for each peer in node.all_peers:
    send RANK_UPGRADE {
      block_hash: entry.hash,
      fib:        entry.counter.fib,
      count:      entry.counter.count,
      origin:     node.id,
      hop_count:  0
    } to peer
```

### 8.2 Receiving Rank Gossip

```plaintext
ON-RANK-UPGRADE(msg, from_peer):
  entry = index_peek(node.index, msg.block_hash)
  
  if entry != NULL:
    // We have this block — upgrade if remote rank is higher
    if msg.fib > entry.counter.fib:
      old_fib = entry.counter.fib
      entry.counter.fib = msg.fib
      entry.counter.count = msg.count
      entry.counter.threshold = fibonacci(msg.fib)
      update_rank_map(node.index, entry, old_fib, msg.fib)
    // Don't re-gossip if we already knew a higher rank
    return
  
  // We don't have this block
  // Check if this is the highest rank we've seen
  if msg.fib > node.highest_seen_rank:
    node.highest_seen_rank = msg.fib
    // Altruistic inhale: seek this block if we have room
    if node.capacity < 0.50:
      initiate_seek_for(msg.block_hash)
  
  // Forward gossip if hop_count < max_hops
  if msg.hop_count < MAX_RANK_HOPS:
    msg.hop_count++
    forward to random subset of peers
```

### 8.3 Block Selection for Representations

```
PICK-BLOCK-FOR-REPRESENTATION(index):
  max_fib = find_max_fib(index.ranks)
  
  // Walk from highest rank downward
  // Higher fib → exponentially higher selection probability
  for fib = max_fib; fib > 0; fib--:
    bucket = index.ranks[fib]
    if bucket != NULL AND bucket.length > 0:
      if random() < fibonacci(fib) / fibonacci(max_fib + 1):
        return random_element(bucket)
  
  // Fallback to fib=0
  return random_element(index.ranks[0])
```

## 10. Request Algorithms

### 10.1 Ping

```
HANDLE-PING(msg, socket):
  // Update last-seen for source
  // Trigger decay check on w_{self→source}
  
  response = {
    ring_summary: [one random member from each ring]
  }
  send PING_RESPONSE to socket

HANDLE-PING-RESPONSE(msg, socket):
  // Measure latency to source
  // Update ring placement for source
```

## 11. Complete Lifecycle of a Block

```plaintext
BLOCK X IS BORN
  │  Node A creates it, stores locally
  │  index_add(index, entry)  → fib=0, count=0
  │  ranks[0].push(entry)
  │  ejection_date = 0 (hot)
  │
  ├── BLOCK X GETS REQUESTED
  │     index_get(index, hash) → _index_increment
  │     count hits threshold → fib promotes to 1
  │     ranks[0].splice(entry), ranks[1].push(entry)
  │     A gossips: "block_X is rank 1"
  │
  ├── BLOCK X BECOMES POPULAR (fib climbs to 5+)
  │     Each promotion gossiped
  │     Other nodes seek it out (altruistic inhale)
  │     Replication spreads
  │
  ├── BLOCK X IN HOT CACHE GETS EVICTED
  │     block_lru_cache_put evicts block X
  │     index_set_entry_ejection(index, entry, now())
  │     ejection_date = 2026-05-09 14:32:00
  │
  ├── NODE A FILLS UP (capacity > 80%)
  │     Exhale scans entries with ejection_date > 0
  │     Sort by ejection_date ASC (oldest first)
  │     Block X at fib=7 with ejection_date 3 weeks ago → SHED
  │     Block Y at fib=0 with ejection_date 5 min ago → KEPT (still locally useful)
  │
  ├── NODE B FAILS TO FIND BLOCK X
  │     B→C: Find_Value(block_X) → "not found"
  │     C: EBF_{C→B}.insert(hash(X)), wheel slot = 42
  │     30 min later: C inhales block_X from D
  │     C: EBF_{C→B}.query(hash(X)) → true
  │     C→B: Push(block_X, reason=recall)
  │     B→C: Push_Ack
  │     C: EBF_{C→B}.delete(hash(X))
  │     w_{B→C} += 2γ  (amplified Hebbian)
  │
  └── BLOCK X FADES
        Requests slow, fib stalls
        Eventually exhaled from most nodes
        Only kept by nodes with spare capacity
        If never requested again → naturally expires
```

If using meridian and I'm searching for a block will the search request reach every node in the network?

Short answer: **no.** Meridian does not flood. Each hop queries a small constant number of peers (the ring members at that distance), and the query converges in O(log N) hops. The total nodes touched per query is roughly `k × O(log N)` — not the whole network.

But that answer exposes a deeper issue with how Find_Value works in OFFS.

---

## The Problem

Meridian routes toward a **network location** (latency coordinates). It answers: "which node is closest to target T in terms of RTT?" The convergence guarantee relies on the metric being distance in latency space.

Find_Value asks a different question: "who holds block hash H?" The block hash is a cryptographic identifier, not a network coordinate. There's no inherent mapping from hash → network location that Meridian can zoom in on.

If you route Find_Value using Meridian's spatial algorithm blindly, you'll converge to the node that's **network-closest to you**, not the node that holds the block. The block could be on a node 200 ms away while you're busy zooming in on your local neighborhood.

---

## Options for Find_Value Routing

### Option A: DHT Overlay (Structured)

Hash blocks onto a node ID space. Each node is responsible for a range of block hashes. Find_Value routes through the DHT (like Kademlia or Chord) toward the responsible node. Meridian is used only for the *underlay* — when the DHT says "contact node X," Meridian finds the fastest path to X.

```
Find_Value(block_H):
  target_node = DHT_lookup(block_H)     // which node is responsible?
  route = Meridian_route(target_node)   // fastest path to that node
  forward Find_Value along route
```

**Pro:** Guaranteed to find the block if it exists. O(log N) hops.
**Con:** Rigid placement. Blocks live where the DHT says, not where they're useful. Works against respiration and altruism.

### Option B: Gossip Flood (Unstructured)

Find_Value floods to a subset of peers with a TTL. Each recipient checks locally, forwards if not found.

```
Find_Value(block_H, ttl=6):
  if I have block_H → respond
  else → forward to k random peers with ttl-1
```

**Pro:** Simple. Block lives wherever it was placed. Works with respiration.
**Con:** O(k^ttl) messages. High overhead. No latency awareness.

### Option C: Social Routing (SoPPSoN-Weighted)

Route Find_Value toward peers that have been **historically useful** for similar content. The Hebbian weights encode "who has helped me before." The rank gossip tells you "who has popular blocks."

```
Find_Value(block_H):
  // Check local index first
  if I have it → done
  
  // Route toward peers with high weights and high-capacity
  candidates = top_weighted_peers(k=8)
  for each peer in candidates:
    forward Find_Value to peer
  
  // Peers that have served similar content before are more likely
  // to either have it or know who does
```

**Pro:** Exploits the social graph. Self-reinforcing. Works with respiration.
**Con:** No formal guarantee of finding the block. Cold-start: new nodes have no weight history.

### Option D: Hybrid — What OFFS Should Use

Combine all three. The network already has the pieces:

```
Find_Value(block_H, ttl=6):
  // 1. Check local
  if index_peek(self, block_H) → respond immediately
  
  // 2. Check EBF memories — do I know who wanted this?
  for each memory in self.outgoing_memories:
    if EBF_QUERY(memory, block_H):
      // I owe this to someone, but maybe they already have it
      // or someone near them does
  
  // 3. Route via Meridian rings + SoPPSoN weights
  //    Select peers that are:
  //    - In the right latency ring (spatial proximity)
  //    - Have high w_{self→peer} (proven useful)
  //    - Have high capacity (more likely to hold diverse blocks)
  //    - Have high max_fib (connected to popular content)
  
  candidates = select_peers({
    rings:       relevant_rings,
    min_weight:  0.1,
    min_capacity: 0.0,  // even full nodes might know who has it
    sort_by:     composite_score  // weight × (1 + max_fib/10) × (1 - capacity/2)
  })
  
  // 4. Forward to best candidates
  for each peer in candidates (limit k):
    forward Find_Value(block_H, ttl-1) to peer
  
  // 5. On failure (ttl exhausted, no result):
  //    Remember in EBF for recall later
  REMEMBER-FAILED-REQUEST(self.memories[source], block_H)
```

The key insight: **Find_Value doesn't need to reach every node. It needs to reach a node that either has the block or is on a path toward it.** The SoPPSoN weights create exactly those paths — they encode the flow of successful requests. Popular blocks (high fib) have wide replication and many weighted paths pointing toward them. Obscure blocks have fewer paths but also fewer requesters.

---

## The Convergence Argument (Informal)

For a block at fib=7 (globally popular, widely replicated):

- Many nodes hold it
- Many nodes have strong weights pointing toward holders
- Rank gossip has propagated awareness
- Find_Value will find it in 2–3 hops with very high probability

For a block at fib=0 (new, single copy):

- Only one node holds it
- Only that node's immediate peers have weights pointing to it
- Find_Value may need more hops or may miss it
- But: if it's fib=0, it's not being requested much anyway
- And: the EBF memory system ensures that failed requests become future recalls

The network doesn't guarantee finding every block every time. It guarantees that **the more a block is wanted, the easier it is to find.** This is the right tradeoff for an owner-free system — popularity drives availability, and the altruistic respiration cycle continuously redistributes blocks toward the nodes that need them.

## The Problem Negative Information Solves

Without it, a forwarded Find_Value can:

1. **Loop:** A → B → C → A (cycle)
2. **Echo:** A forwards to B and C; both B and C forward to D; D gets the same query twice
3. **Self-loop:** A forwards to B; B's best candidate for the block happens to be A

Quasar's solution: each message carries a **visited set** encoded as a bloom filter. Before forwarding to a peer, check the filter. If the peer is present, skip it — that gravity well is "negated."

---

## Adapted for OFFS Find_Value

### Message Structure

```c
typedef struct {
  rpc_header_t  header;
  buffer_t*     block_hash;        // what we're looking for
  uint8_t       ttl;               // remaining hops
  buffer_t*     visited_bloom;     // bloom filter of visited node IDs
  size_t        visited_count;     // approximate count (for false positive estimation)
} find_value_msg_t;
```

### Forwarding Algorithm

```plaintext
HANDLE-FIND-VALUE(msg, socket):
  block_hash = msg.block_hash
  
  // 1. Check local — do I have it?
  entry = index_peek(self.index, block_hash)
  if entry != NULL:
    send FIND_VALUE_RESPONSE { found: true, holder: self.id, fib: entry.counter.fib }
    index_increment(self.index, entry)   // may trigger rank promotion
    return
  
  // 2. TTL exhausted?
  if msg.ttl == 0:
    REMEMBER-FAILED-REQUEST(self.memories[msg.source], block_hash)
    send FIND_VALUE_RESPONSE { found: false }
    return
  
  // 3. Add self to visited set
  bloom_insert(msg.visited_bloom, self.id)
  msg.visited_count++
  msg.ttl--
  
  // 4. Select candidate peers
  candidates = select_peers({
    rings:       relevant_rings_for_distance,
    min_weight:  0.1,
    sort_by:     composite_score,   // weight × capacity_factor × fib_factor
    limit:       FORWARD_FANOUT     // e.g., 3-4
  })
  
  // 5. Filter out visited peers (negative information)
  fresh = []
  for each peer in candidates:
    if not bloom_contains(msg.visited_bloom, peer.id):
      fresh.push(peer)
  
  // 6. Forward to remaining candidates
  for each peer in fresh:
    forward msg to peer
  
  // 7. If no candidates survived filtering
  if fresh is empty:
    REMEMBER-FAILED-REQUEST(self.memories[msg.source], block_hash)
    send FIND_VALUE_RESPONSE { found: false }
```

## Bloom Filter Sizing

The visited set stays small. Even with fanout 3 and TTL 6, worst case nodes visited is bounded:

| TTL | Fanout | Max nodes visited (no overlap) |
|-----|--------|-------------------------------|
| 6 | 3 | 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 + 81 + 243 = 364 |
| 6 | 4 | ~1,365 |
| 4 | 3 | 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = 40 |

In practice, overlap is high (multiple paths hit same nodes), so actual visited count is much lower. A **256-byte (2048-bit) bloom filter** with ~200 insertions gives a false positive rate around 0.1% — effectively zero practical impact. Even if a false positive skips a node, another copy of the message from a different path will likely reach it.

```c
#define VISITED_BLOOM_BYTES  256    // 2048 bits
#define VISITED_BLOOM_HASHES 4      // k hash functions
```

---

## Why This Is Better Than a Simple List

| | Node ID List | Bloom Filter |
|---|---|---|
| Size growth | O(nodes_visited × 20 bytes) | Fixed 256 bytes |
| Lookup | O(n) scan | O(k) = 4 hashes |
| False negatives | None | None (bloom filters have no false negatives) |
| False positives | None | ~0.1% at 200 entries |
| Serialization | Variable length | Fixed length |

The fixed size matters — the message doesn't bloat as it propagates.

---

## Full Quasar-Style Gravity Wells for OFFS?

Quasar's other mechanism — proactive dissemination of attenuated bloom filters to create "gravity wells" — could also apply to OFFS, but selectively:

### What Quasar Does

Each node maintains per-neighbor attenuated bloom filters:
- Level 0: "groups I belong to"
- Level 1: "groups my neighbors belong to"  
- Level 2: "groups reachable within 2 hops"
- ...

A message for group G checks these filters level-by-level. A match at level L means "G is reachable L hops away via this neighbor." The message takes a directed walk into that gravity well.

### What OFFS Could Do

Instead of groups, advertise **high-fib blocks**:

```plaintext
Level 0: "high-fib blocks I hold" (e.g., fib ≥ 5)
Level 1: "high-fib blocks my neighbors hold"
Level 2: "high-fib blocks reachable within 2 hops"
```

This is feasible because:
- High-fib blocks are few (a node might have 10–50 blocks at fib ≥ 5)
- They're exactly the blocks people are looking for
- The bloom filters stay small and accurate

Low-fib blocks don't get gravity wells — they rely on the visited-filtered forwarding to find them. This is the right tradeoff: **popular blocks get proactive routing infrastructure, obscure blocks get reactive search.**

### Gravity Well Insertion (on rank promotion to fib ≥ 5)

```plaintext
ON-RANK-PROMOTION(node, entry):
  if entry.counter.fib >= GRAVITY_WELL_THRESHOLD:   // e.g., 5
    // Update my own level-0 filter
    node.home_filter[0].insert(entry.hash)
    
    // Propagate to neighbors (they update their level-1 filters)
    for each neighbor in node.overlay_neighbors:
      send FILTER_UPDATE { level: 0, added: entry.hash } to neighbor
```

### Using Gravity Wells in Find_Value

```plaintext
HANDLE-FIND-VALUE(msg, socket):
  // ... local check, TTL check, visited insertion as before ...
  
  // Check gravity wells first (directed walk)
  for level = 0 to K:
    for each neighbor in self.overlay_neighbors:
      filter = get_attenuated_filter_for(neighbor)
      if filter[level].contains(msg.block_hash):
        // Check negative information
        if not bloom_contains(msg.visited_bloom, neighbor.id):
          // Found a gravity well — directed walk
          forward msg to neighbor
          return   // only need one directed walk per hop
  
  // No gravity well matched — fall back to weighted random walk
  candidates = select_weighted_peers(...)
  fresh = filter_visited(candidates, msg.visited_bloom)
  for each peer in fresh:
    forward msg to peer
```

This gives you two-tier routing:
1. **Directed walk** when a gravity well exists (popular blocks, fast convergence)

## Elastic Attenuated Bloom Filter (EABF) per Connection

### Structure

```
EABF_{self → peer}:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Level 0: blocks at distance 0 via this peer │  ← "peer wants this" (failed Find_Value)
  │                                              │  ← "peer has this" (peer accepted Store)
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Level 1: blocks at distance 1 via this peer │  ← "peer's neighbor has this"
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Level 2: blocks at distance 2 via this peer │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Level 3: blocks at distance 3 via this peer │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
            Timing Wheel (TTL decay per entry)
```

Each level is an elastic bloom filter. The whole structure decays via the timing wheel — entries that aren't refreshed eventually evaporate.

---

## Two Paths Populate the EABF

### Path 1: Failed Find_Value (Retroactive)

```
A → B: Find_Value(block_X)
B:     "Not found"

B inserts into EABF_{B→A}:
  Level 0 ← hash(block_X)    // "A wants this; if I get it, it's 0 hops to A"
  Timing wheel slot ← now() + TTL
```

Same as before, but now it's level 0 of the attenuated structure.

### Path 2: Successful Store (Proactive)

This is the new piece. When a Store succeeds, every node along the path inserts the block hash into the EABF for the neighbor they forwarded to, at the level corresponding to remaining distance.

```
Store path: A → B → C → D (D accepted)

D (holder):
  // I have it locally — record in my own level-0 for all connections?
  // Actually, D doesn't need to record anything for itself.
  // But D could insert into EABF_{D→C} level 0: "C knows I have this"
  EABF_{D→C}.level[0] ← hash(block_X)

C (forwarded to D, 1 hop from holder):
  EABF_{C→D}.level[1] ← hash(block_X)   // "D has it, 1 hop away via D"
  EABF_{C→B}.level[0] ← hash(block_X)   // "B knows I routed this"

B (forwarded to C, 2 hops from holder):
  EABF_{B→C}.level[2] ← hash(block_X)   // "reachable 2 hops away via C"
  EABF_{B→A}.level[0] ← hash(block_X)   // "A knows I routed this"

A (originator, 3 hops from holder):
  EABF_{A→B}.level[3] ← hash(block_X)   // "reachable 3 hops away via B"
```

More systematically:

```plaintext
ON-STORE-SUCCESS(path, block_hash):
  // path = [A, B, C, D] where D is the holder
  // path_len = 4
  
  holder_idx = path_len - 1
  
  for i = 0; i < holder_idx; i++:
    forwarder = path[i]
    forwardee = path[i + 1]
    distance_to_holder = holder_idx - i
    
    // The forwarder inserts into the EABF for the forwardee:
    // "block_X is (distance_to_holder - 1) hops beyond forwardee"
    insert_into_eabf(
      eabf:   EABF_{forwarder → forwardee},
      level:  distance_to_holder - 1,
      hash:   block_hash,
      ttl:    compute_ttl(distance_to_holder)  // farther = shorter TTL?
    )
```

## Using EABFs for Find_Value Routing

Now when a Find_Value arrives, the node checks its EABFs level-by-level — a directed walk into the strongest, closest gravity well:

```plaintext
HANDLE-FIND-VALUE(msg, socket):
  block_hash = msg.block_hash
  
  // 1. Local check (unchanged)
  entry = index_peek(self.index, block_hash)
  if entry != NULL:
    // ... respond, increment fib, return
  
  // 2. TTL check, visited set update (unchanged)
  
  // 3. GRAVITY WELL SEARCH (new — uses EABFs)
  //    Check all EABFs, level 0 first (closest), then level 1, etc.
  for level = 0 to MAX_EABF_LEVEL:
    for each neighbor in self.overlay_neighbors:
      eabf = get_eabf(self, neighbor)
      
      if eabf_contains(eabf, level, block_hash):
        // Check negative information
        if not bloom_contains(msg.visited_bloom, neighbor.id):
          // Gravity well found! Directed walk.
          forward msg to neighbor
          return   // one directed walk per hop is sufficient
  
  // 4. No gravity well — fall back to weighted random walk
  candidates = gather_weighted_candidates(msg)
  forward_via_roulette(msg, candidates)
```

The critical property: **level 0 hits are preferred over level 1, which are preferred over level 2.** The search naturally converges toward the holder, taking the shortest known path at each hop.

## TTL Scaling by Level

Farther entries should decay faster — long paths are more volatile:

```c
uint64_t compute_ttl(uint8_t distance) {
  // Level 0 (direct): full TTL
  // Level 3+: shorter TTL, path is more likely to change
  return BASE_TTL_MS / (1 + distance * DISTANCE_DECAY_FACTOR);
  // e.g., BASE_TTL_MS = 3600000, DISTANCE_DECAY_FACTOR = 0.5
  // Level 0: 60 min, Level 1: 40 min, Level 2: 30 min, Level 3: 24 min
}
```

---

## Hebbian Updates + EABF Population Happen Together

The Store response handler does both:

```plaintext
HANDLE-STORE-RESPONSE(msg, socket):
  if not msg.accepted: return
  
  τ = msg.latency
  γ = γ₀ · max(0, 1 - τ / T) · q_store
  Δw = γ
  
  // ── HEBBIAN UPDATES (unchanged) ──
  // Frequency, Feedback, Symmetry rules applied along path
  
  // ── EABF POPULATION (new) ──
  // Every node along the path records where the block went
  holder_idx = msg.path_len - 1
  for i = 0; i < holder_idx; i++:
    if self.id == msg.path[i]:
      forwardee = msg.path[i + 1]
      distance = holder_idx - i
      
      eabf_insert(
        &self.eabfs[forwardee],
        level: distance - 1,
        hash:  msg.block_hash,
        ttl:   compute_ttl(distance - 1)
      )
```

## Re-insertion Refreshes TTL (Same as Before)

If the same block is stored again along a similar path, or if a Find_Value fails again for the same block, the existing entry gets its TTL pushed forward:

```plaintext
eabf_insert(eabf, level, hash, ttl):
  existing = eabf_find_entry(eabf, level, hash)
  if existing:
    // Push expiry forward in timing wheel
    move_to_future_slot(eabf.wheel, existing)
    return
  
  // New entry
  slot = compute_expiry_slot(eabf.wheel, ttl)
  eabf.levels[level].insert(hash)
  eabf.wheel.slots[slot].add(ref_to_entry)
```

## Why This Is Better Than Separate Structures

| | Plain EBF (retroactive only) | EABF (retroactive + proactive) |
|---|---|---|
| Failed Find_Value | "A wanted X" | "A wanted X" (level 0) |
| Successful Store | Not recorded | "X is L hops via neighbor N" (level L) |
| Find_Value routing | Only weighted random walk | Directed walk into gravity wells first |
| Cold start for new block | No routing info exists | Populated immediately after first Store |
| Block moves/deletes | Stale entry until TTL expires | Same, but higher levels decay faster |
| Memory per connection | O(1) bloom filter | O(K) bloom filters (K small, e.g., 4) |

## What Actually Creates Traffic

The EABF is **local state**. It's never transmitted. The only thing that goes over the wire is the block data (128 KB) and the path array in the Store message (~80 bytes of node IDs). The EABF entries are a side effect computed locally from that path.

So the real question splits into two:

| Concern | Source | Magnitude |
|---------|--------|-----------|
| CPU cost of EABF insertions | Local hash + bloom operations | Microseconds per block |
| CPU cost of timing wheel ticks | Local expiration | ~100 µs every 60 seconds |
| Network traffic from EABF | None — it's never sent | Zero |
| Network traffic from Store operations | 128 KB blocks × replication factor | This is the real cost |

---

## CPU: EABF Insertion Cost

One insertion into one EABF level:

```plaintext
hash block ID (XXH3, 128-bit)     ~100 ns
k=4 bloom filter hashes           ~100 ns
k=4 bloom filter bit sets         ~50 ns
timing wheel slot append          ~50 ns
                                 ─────
Total per insertion:             ~300 ns
```

For a file producing 120 new blocks, with path length 3, and replication factor 3:

```plaintext
120 blocks × 3 replicas × 3 hops × 300 ns = ~324 µs
```

That's **one-third of a millisecond** of CPU time for an entire file's worth of EABF insertions. It's lost in the noise of the disk I/O for writing the blocks.

---

## CPU: Timing Wheel Maintenance

Assume a well-connected node with 50 peers, 4-level EABFs, ~200 entries per level:

```plaintext
Total EABF entries: 50 × 4 × 200 = 40,000
Entries per wheel slot: 40,000 / 64 ≈ 625
Cost to expire one entry: ~200 ns (clear bloom bits, splice from bucket)
Cost per tick: 625 × 200 ns ≈ 125 µs
Ticks per minute: 1
```

**125 microseconds of CPU per minute.** That's 0.0002% of one core.

---

## Network: What Actually Matters

The EABF itself adds zero bytes to any message. The path array in the Store message is:

```
path_len ≤ 6 nodes × 20 bytes (node ID) = 120 bytes
```

Compared to a 131,072 byte block, that's 0.09%. Irrelevant.

The real network cost is the block replication itself:

```plaintext
120 new blocks × 128 KB × 3 replicas = ~46 MB
```

That's the actual churn. But it's the *point* of the system — you're storing data on the network. The EABF just makes future lookups for that data efficient, at effectively zero marginal cost.

---

## One Thing to Clarify: Are EABFs Gossiped?

In pure Quasar, the attenuated bloom filters *are* gossiped to propagate gravity wells. In our adaptation, we have two choices:

### Option A: Local Only (What I Described Above)

EABFs are populated by Store path recording and used only for local forwarding decisions. No gossip. The numbers above apply.

**Pro:** Zero network overhead for the memory system.
**Con:** Gravity wells only extend as far as the Store paths that happened to pass through this node. No proactive multi-hop awareness.

### Option B: Gossiped (Quasar-Style)

Each node periodically sends its level-0 EABF to neighbors, who merge it into their level-1, and so on. This creates true multi-hop gravity wells for popular blocks.

**Pro:** Find_Value gets directed walks from farther away. Better for popular blocks.
**Con:** Additional gossip traffic. But still small — a 512-byte bloom filter per neighbor per gossip cycle.

Even with Option B, the overhead is modest. A 512-byte filter × 50 neighbors × every 30 seconds = ~6.8 Kbps. That's less than a single 128 KB block transfer every 2.5 minutes.

---

## Bottom Line

The EABF memory system is not a churn concern. The CPU cost is measured in microseconds, the network cost is either zero (local only) or a few Kbps (gossiped). The block data transfers dominate by orders of magnitude, and those are the intended workload — not overhead.

## Updated Ping Response

```c
typedef struct {
  rpc_header_t  header;
  uint64_t      echo_time;         // requester's timestamp, echoed back
  float         capacity;          // cached, updated on block add/remove
  uint8_t       phase;             // cached, updated on threshold crossing
} ping_response_msg_t;
```

The handler does:

```c
void handle_ping(msg, socket) {
  ping_response_msg_t resp = {
    .echo_time = msg.timestamp,
    .capacity  = self.cached_capacity,   // just reads a float
    .phase     = self.cached_phase,       // just reads an enum
  };
  send_response(socket, &resp);
}
```

No locks, no scans, no allocations. The cached values are updated atomically when blocks are added or removed, and when capacity crosses the 50% or 80% thresholds. The ping path stays hot and predictable.

## What's Missing

### 1. Seek / Offer (Inhale)

A node below 50% doesn't know *which* blocks to ask for. It needs to browse.

```
A (30% capacity) → B: Seek(interests?, exclude_hashes[])
B → A: Offer([{hash, fib, size}, ...])
A → B: Pull(hash)  →  B responds with StoreBlock (the data)
```

This is distinct from FindBlock. FindBlock says "I want X." Seek says "what do you have that I might want?" Without it, inhaling nodes have no way to discover new blocks except by already knowing their hashes.

**Proposed names: `SeekBlock` / `OfferBlocks`**

Or fold Pull into FindBlock with a mode — but that's muddy. Cleaner to keep them separate.

### 2. Rank Gossip

When a block's fib promotes, the node tells its peers. This drives altruistic replication.

```
A → B: RankUpgrade(block_hash, fib=7, count=3, hop_count=0)
```

Fire-and-forget, no response needed. Without it, popularity signals don't propagate and the network can't self-organize around popular content.

**Proposed name: `RankBlock`** — "I'm telling you this block's rank changed."

### 3. Recall Hint (Optional)

We could skip the hint round-trip and just Push directly when an EABF level-0 hits. But the hint lets the recipient decline if they already got the block elsewhere, avoiding wasted transfers.

```
B → A: RecallHint(block_hash)
A → B: RecallAccept  or  RecallDecline
```

**Proposed: fold into StoreBlock with `reason=RECALL` and let the recipient NACK if unwanted.** One less message type, but the sender might waste bandwidth pushing a 128 KB block that gets rejected. The hint is a ~50 byte probe that prevents that. Tradeoff: simplicity vs. bandwidth. For 128 KB blocks, the hint is probably worth it.

# OFFS Network Layer — Implementation Specification

## Overview

Implement the P2P network layer for the Owner-Free File System. The network is a self-organizing overlay combining Meridian (multi-resolution latency rings), SoPPSoN (Hebbian weight learning), Quasar (negative information routing), and Elastic Attenuated Bloom Filters with timing wheels for per-connection memory.

Nodes have fixed storage capacity. Below 50% they actively seek blocks (inhale). Above 80% they shed coldest blocks to nodes with room (exhale). Between 50-80% they route only. Seek rate slows quadratically as capacity approaches 50%.

Handler: read cached capacity/phase (no locks, no scans). Echo timestamp. Must be fast — Meridian uses this for RTT.

### 1.2 PingCapacity / PingCapacityResponse
```

  - message_id: uint64
  - source: node_id (20 bytes)
  - capacity: float32
  - phase: uint8
  - samples: []struct {
      node_id: 20 bytes
      ring:    uint8 (which ring the source placed this node in)
      weight:  float32
      latency: uint32 (ms)

    }

  - message_id: uint64
  - capacity: float32
  - phase: uint8
  - samples: []struct { ... } (same structure)
```
This is the gossip/anti-entropy message. Handler: measure latency to source and all samples. Place source and samples into appropriate rings as secondary members. Trigger Symmetry rule for new connections.

### 1.3 PingBlock / PingBlockResponse
```
PingBlock:
  - message_id: uint64
  - block_hash: 32 bytes

PingBlockResponse:
  - message_id: uint64
  - exists: bool
  - fib: uint32 (0 if not found)
  - healthy: bool (false if not found)
```
Handler: check index for block_hash. If found, verify block integrity in sections. Reinforce Hebbian weight w_{self→source} on success.

### 1.4 FindBlock / FindBlockResponse
```
FindBlock:
  - message_id: uint64
  - block_hash: 32 bytes
  - ttl: uint8 (remaining hops, decremented each forward)
  - visited_bloom: []byte (256 bytes = 2048 bits, bloom filter of visited node IDs)
  - visited_count: uint16 (approximate, for false positive estimation)
  - path: []node_id (max 6, nodes this request has traversed)
  - path_len: uint8
  - start_time: uint64 (when original requester began search)
  - original_source: node_id (who originally asked, for EBF memory on failure)

FindBlockResponse:
  - message_id: uint64
  - found: bool
  - holder: node_id (if found)
  - fib: uint32 (block's current fib rank)
  - path: []node_id (complete path from requester to holder)
  - path_len: uint8
  - latency: uint64 (total search time ms, for Hebbian learning rate)
```
Handler algorithm:
1. Check local index. If found → respond, increment fib, return.
2. If TTL=0 → insert block_hash into EABF_{self→original_source}.level with timing wheel TTL, respond not found.
3. Add self to path and visited_bloom. Decrement TTL.
4. Check all EABFs level 0→K for gravity well match. If found and neighbor not in visited_bloom → directed walk forward to that neighbor.
5. No gravity well → gather candidates from rings [ring_for_distance-1, ring_for_distance, ring_for_distance+1], filter by visited_bloom and min_weight > 0.01.
6. Roulette-wheel select FORWARD_FANOUT (3) candidates weighted by w_{self→candidate}. Forward to each.
7. If no candidates → same as TTL=0 failure path.

Response handler: if found, apply Hebbian rules along path (Frequency: requester→holder, Feedback: each forwarder→forwardee, Symmetry: reverse of each). Also populate EABFs along path (see Section 4).

### 1.5 FindNode / FindNodeResponse
```
FindNode:
  - message_id: uint64
  - target_id: node_id

FindNodeResponse:
  - message_id: uint64
  - closest_nodes: []node_id (up to 8)
```
Handler: return k=8 closest nodes in routing table to target_id by XOR distance.

### 1.6 StoreBlock / StoreBlockResponse
```
StoreBlock:
  - message_id: uint64
  - block_hash: 32 bytes
  - block_size: uint32
  - block_fib: uint32
  - replicas_needed: uint8 (how many more nodes must accept)
  - max_hops: uint8
  - visited_bloom: []byte (256 bytes)
  - visited_count: uint16
  - path: []node_id (max 6)
  - path_len: uint8
  - start_time: uint64
  - carry_data: bool
  - block_data: []byte (only if carry_data=true, 128KB typical)

StoreBlockResponse:
  - message_id: uint64
  - accepted: bool
  - holder: node_id (if accepted)
  - replicas_remaining: uint8 (if not accepted)
  - path: []node_id
  - path_len: uint8
  - latency: uint64
```
Handler algorithm:
1. Check SHOULD-ACCEPT: not already stored, room available, not in exhale phase (capacity < 0.80). Accept with probability = 1.0 - capacity/0.80.
2. If accept → write to sections, create index entry, put in hot cache (eviction sets ejection_date), check all EABFs for recall obligations, respond accepted. If replicas_needed > 0 after decrement, continue forwarding from here.
3. If decline and max_hops=0 → respond not accepted.
4. If decline → add self to path and visited_bloom, decrement max_hops.
5. Gather candidates from rings , filter by visited_bloom, skip peers in exhale phase, skip peers with consecutive_fails ≥ MAX_FAILS, skip peers we're rate-limiting.
6. Compute composite storage score S(j) = w_{self→j} × (1 - capacity_j) × 1/(1 + latency/β) × availability_j.
7. Roulette-wheel select FORWARD_FANOUT candidates weighted by S(j). Forward to each.

Response handler: if accepted, apply Hebbian rules along path and populate EABFs along path (see Section 4).

### 1.7 SeekingBlocks / SeekingBlocksResponse
```
SeekingBlocks:
  - message_id: uint64
  - capacity: float32 (requester's capacity)
  - exclude_hashes: [][]byte (blocks requester already has)

SeekingBlocksResponse:
  - message_id: uint64
  - offers: []struct {
      hash: 32 bytes
      fib:  uint32
      size: uint32
    }
```
Handler: select up to MAX_OFFERS blocks from local index using PICK-BLOCK-FOR-REPRESENTATION (walk ranks from highest fib downward, probability ∝ fibonacci(fib)). Exclude hashes in exclude_hashes list. Return offers.

Response handler: evaluate each offer. If SHOULD-PULL (block not already stored, capacity < 0.50, fib exceeds local threshold), send FindBlock for that hash.

### 1.8 RankBlock (fire-and-forget, no response)
```
RankBlock:
  - block_hash: 32 bytes
  - fib: uint32
  - count: uint32
  - origin: node_id
  - hop_count: uint8
```
Handler:
1. If we have this block and msg.fib > local.fib → upgrade local entry's fib, count, threshold. Update rank_map. Do not re-gossip.
2. If we don't have this block and msg.fib > highest_seen_rank → set highest_seen_rank. If capacity < 0.50, initiate Seek for this block.
3. If hop_count < MAX_RANK_HOPS (6), increment hop_count and forward to random subset of peers.

### 1.9 RecallBlock / RecallAccept / RecallDecline
```
RecallBlock:
  - message_id: uint64
  - block_hash: 32 bytes

RecallAccept:
  - message_id: uint64

RecallDecline:
  - message_id: uint64
```
Handler for RecallBlock: if we don't have the block and capacity < 0.50 → send RecallAccept, else → send RecallDecline.
Handler for RecallAccept: load block from sections, send StoreBlock with reason=RECALL.
Handler for RecallDecline: delete block_hash from EABF_{self→source}.

```
  - type: uint8 (which RPC type was rejected)
  - retry_after_ms: uint32
  - current_limit: float32 (tokens/second currently available)
```

## 2. Core Data Structures

### 2.1 Ring Table
```c
Ring i: inner = β × α^(i-1), outer = β × α^i  (i ≥ 1)
Ring 0: [0, β)

Constants: α=2, β=5ms, k=8 primary per ring, m=4 secondary per ring
Ring count: ceil(log_α(max_RTT / β)), typically 8-12

ring_member_t {
  node_id: 20 bytes
  latency: uint32 (ms)
  weight: float32 (Hebbian w_ij)
  capacity: float32 [0,1]
  phase: uint8 (INHALE/NEUTRAL/EXHALE)
  last_gossip_time: uint64
  availability: float32 [0,1] (EWMA)
  consecutive_fails: uint32
}
```

### 2.2 EABF (Elastic Attenuated Bloom Filter) per connection
```
EABF_{self→peer}:
  levels: [0..K] of elastic_bloom_filter (K=3, i.e., 4 levels)
  wheel: timing_wheel (64 slots × 60s = 64 min span)

Level 0: blocks at distance 0 via this peer (peer wants/has this)
Level 1: blocks at distance 1 via this peer (peer's neighbor has this)
Level 2: blocks at distance 2
Level 3: blocks at distance 3

Each level: 512-byte bloom filter with elastic fingerprint bucket array in slow memory.
```

### 2.3 Timing Wheel
```
timing_wheel_t {
  slot_count: 64
  slot_duration_ms: 60000
  current_slot: uint32
  slots: [64]slot_t
  last_advance: uint64
}

slot_t {
  refs: []ebf_ref_t (references into EABF buckets)
}

ebf_ref_t {
  level: uint8
  bucket_index: uint32
  fp_index: uint32
}
```

### 2.4 Token Buckets (per peer, per RPC type)
```
token_bucket_t {
  base_rate: float32
  max_rate: float32
  burst_size: float32
  tokens: float32
  last_refill: uint64
  total_accepted: uint64
  total_rejected: uint64
}

peer_rate_limits_t {
  peer_id: node_id
  weight: float32
  buckets: map[rpc_type]token_bucket_t
}

Default rates:
  FindBlock:  base=5/s,  max=50/s,  burst=20, cost=1
  StoreBlock: base=0.5/s, max=5/s,   burst=3,  cost=1
  SeekingBlocks: base=1/s, max=10/s, burst=5,  cost=1
  PingCapacity: base=10/s, max=10/s, burst=10, cost=0.1
  Ping: base=10/s, max=10/s, burst=10, cost=0.1
```

### 2.5 Peer Availability
```
peer_availability_t {
  availability: float32 (EWMA [0,1])
  last_seen: uint64
  consecutive_fails: uint32
  first_seen: uint64
}
```
Updated on every ping success/timeout. EWMA with α=0.1. New peers start at 0.5.

## 3. Hebbian Learning Rules

Apply on successful FindBlockResponse and StoreBlockResponse:

```
τ = response.latency (total search time ms)
T = MAX_SEARCH_TIME_MS (6 hops × avg hop latency, e.g., 60000)
q = 1.0 (quality, validated on receipt)
γ = γ₀ × max(0, 1 - τ/T) × q
Δw = γ

γ₀ = 0.1
η_f = 0.25 (feedback constant)
η_s = 0.05 (symmetry constant)

FREQUENCY RULE: w_{requester→holder} += Δw
  (if no prior connection, create with initial strength = Δw)

FEEDBACK RULE: for i = 1 to path_len-2:
  w_{path[i]→path[i+1]} += η_f × Δw

SYMMETRY RULE: for i = 0 to path_len-2:
  w_{path[i+1]→path[i]} += η_s × Δw

Weight multipliers:
  Normal FindBlock success: 1.0×
  StoreBlock accepted (exhalation): 1.0×
  StoreBlock accepted (recall): 2.0×
  Push declined: -0.5×
```

---

## 4. EABF Population on Successful Store

When StoreBlock succeeds along path [A, B, C, D] where D is holder:

```
For each node i in path (except holder):
  forwardee = path[i+1]
  distance = (holder_index - i)
  
  Insert into EABF_{path[i]→forwardee}:
    level: distance - 1
    hash: block_hash
    ttl: BASE_TTL_MS / (1 + (distance-1) × 0.5)
      Level 0: 60 min, Level 1: 40 min, Level 2: 30 min, Level 3: 24 min

If entry already exists at that level → push timing wheel expiry forward (refresh).
```

---

## 5. Respiration Cycle

### 5.1 Seek Throttle
```
τ(c) = τ_min + (τ_max - τ_min) × (c/0.50)^α    for c ∈ [0, 0.50]
τ(c) = ∞                                          for c ≥ 0.50

τ_min = 5000ms, τ_max = 300000ms, α = 2.0
```

### 5.2 Inhale Cycle (runs when capacity < 50% and seek interval elapsed)
```
1. Select diverse neighbors from rings [0,1,2] with min_weight > 0.1
2. Send SeekingBlocks to selected peers
3. Process responses: for each offer, if SHOULD-PULL → send FindBlock
```

### 5.3 Exhale Cycle (runs when capacity ≥ 80%)
```
1. to_free = blocks needed to reach 50% capacity
2. Collect all cold blocks: entries with ejection_date > 0
3. Sort by ejection_date ASC (oldest eviction first)
4. Find recipients: peers with capacity < 0.50, sort by capacity ASC
5. For each block in cold[0..to_free]:
   - Load from sections
   - Send StoreBlock(reason=EXHALATION) to best recipient
   - On acceptance: index_remove locally, delete from sections
   - On rejection: try next recipient
```

### 5.4 Ejection Date Lifecycle
```
Block enters hot cache: ejection_date = 0
LRU evicts block: ejection_date = now()
Block re-enters hot cache via access: ejection_date = 0
```

---

## 6. Ring Membership Management

Run periodically in background:
1. For each ring, compute local coordinates for all primary+secondary members:
   coords(peer_j) = [latency(self, j₁), latency(self, j₂), ..., latency(self, jₖ), w_{self→j}]
2. Find subset of k peers with maximal hypervolume convex hull → new primaries
3. Remaining m peers → secondaries (FIFO pool)
4. If a peer is unreachable during computation, drop and replace from secondaries

---

## 7. Gossip Cycle

Run periodically (short period for new nodes, lengthens to steady state):
1. For each ring, pick random primary member
2. Send PingCapacity with source=self, capacity, phase, and one random sample from each ring
3. On receiving PingCapacity: measure latency to source and all samples, place into rings as secondaries, trigger Symmetry rule

---

## 8. Timing Wheel Maintenance Tick

Run every 60 seconds:
1. Advance hand by elapsed slots
2. For each expired slot across all EABFs:
   - Delete each ref's fingerprint from its EABF bucket
   - If bucket becomes empty, clear corresponding bloom filter bit

---

## 9. Rate Limiting

On every incoming message:
1. Get or create peer_rate_limits for source
2. Apply capacity_multiplier: if type is StoreBlock and capacity ≥ 0.80 → multiplier = 0.05; if 0.50-0.80 → linear taper; otherwise 1.0
3. Try consume token from appropriate bucket
4. If rejected → send RateLimited response with retry_after_ms and current_limit
5. Sender-side: before forwarding, check local copy of remote limits. Skip peers in backoff or with insufficient burst.

---

## 10. Block Selection for Representations

```
PICK-BLOCK-FOR-REPRESENTATION(index):
  max_fib = find_max_fib(index.ranks)
  for fib = max_fib down to 1:
    bucket = index.ranks[fib]
    if bucket not empty:
      if random() < fibonacci(fib) / fibonacci(max_fib + 1):
        return random_element(bucket)
  return random_element(index.ranks[0])
```

| REPLICATION_FACTOR | 3 | Additional nodes for new blocks |

| m_ring | 4 | Secondary ring members |
| LATENCY_NORM_MS | 50 | β for storage score |
| MAX_OFFERS | 20 | Max blocks in SeekingBlocksResponse |

## 12. Implementation Notes

- All message handlers must be non-blocking. Use async I/O.
- EABF slow memory (fingerprint buckets) can live on disk; fast memory (bloom bits) in RAM.
- Timing wheel ticks should not block message processing.
- Capacity and phase are cached atomics updated on block add/remove and threshold crossing.
- Hebbian weight updates and EABF insertions happen in the response path, not the request path.
- Token bucket refill happens on consume attempt, not on a timer.
- Ring hypervolume computation is background, best-effort; stale results are acceptable.
- Path arrays in messages are bounded by MAX_PATH; overflow is a protocol error.

```markdown
Implement the P2P network layer for the Owner-Free File System. The network is a self-organizing overlay combining Meridian (multi-resolution latency rings), SoPPSoN (Hebbian weight learning), Quasar (negative information routing), and Elastic Attenuated Bloom Filters with timing wheels for per-connection memory.
```

```markdown
# Meridian: A Lightweight Framework for Network Positioning without Virtual Coordinates

**Bernard Wong, Aleksandrs Slivkins, Emin Gün Sirer**

Dept. of Computer Science, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853

{bwong, slivkins, egs}@cs.cornell.edu

## Abstract

Selecting nodes based on their position in the network is a basic building block for many distributed systems. This paper describes a peer-to-peer overlay network for performing position-based node selection. Our system, Meridian, provides a lightweight, accurate and scalable framework for keeping track of location information for participating nodes. The framework consists of an overlay network structured around multi-resolution rings, query routing with direct measurements, and gossip protocols for dissemination. We show how this framework can be used to address three commonly encountered problems in large-scale distributed systems without having to compute absolute coordinates; namely, closest node discovery, central leader election, and locating nodes that satisfy target latency constraints. We show analytically that the framework is scalable with logarithmic convergence when Internet latencies are modeled as a growth-constrained metric, a low-dimensional Euclidian metric, or a metric of low doubling dimension. Large scale simulations, based on latency measurements from 6.25 million node-pairs, and an implementation deployed on PlanetLab both show that the framework is accurate and effective.

## 1. Introduction

A central problem in distributed systems is to find an efficient mapping of system functionality onto nodes based on network characteristics. In small systems, it is possible to perform extensive measurements and make decisions based on global information. For instance, in an online game with few servers, a client can simply measure its latency to all servers and bind to the closest one for minimal response time. However, collecting global information is infeasible for a significant set of recently emerging large-scale distributed applications, where global information is unwieldy and lack of centralized servers makes it difficult to find nodes that fit selection criteria. Yet many distributed applications, such as filesharing networks, content distribution networks, backup systems, anonymous communication networks, pub-sub systems, service discovery, and multi-player online games, could substantially benefit from selecting nodes based on their location in the network.

A general technique for finding nodes that optimize a given network metric is to perform a network embedding, that is, to map high-dimensional network measurements into a location in a smaller Euclidian space. For instance, recent work in network positioning maps a large vector of node-to-node latency measurements on the Internet into a single point in a d-dimensional space. The resulting embedded address facilitates location-aware node selection.

While this approach is quite general, it is neither accurate nor complete. The embedding process typically introduces significant errors. The selection of parameters, such as the constant d and the set of measurements taken to perform the embedding, is nontrivial and has a significant impact on the accuracy of the approach. Coordinates change over time due to changes in network latencies on the Internet, and introduce additional errors when performing latency estimates from coordinates computed at different times. Finally, finding a set of nodes that match desired criteria without centralized servers that retain O(N) state, an essential requirement in large-scale networks, requires additional mechanisms besides virtual coordinates. Peer-to-peer substrates that can naturally work with Euclidian coordinates, such as CAN and P-Trees, can reduce the state requirements per node; however, both systems introduce substantial complexity and bandwidth overhead in addition to the overhead of network embedding. And our simulation results show that even with a P2P substrate that always finds the best node based on virtual coordinates, the embedding error leads to a suboptimal choice.

This paper introduces a lightweight, scalable and accurate framework, called Meridian, for performing node selection based on a set of network positioning constraints. Meridian is based on a loosely-structured overlay network, uses direct measurements instead of a network embedding, and can solve spatial queries without an absolute coordinate space. It is similar in functionality to GNP combined with CAN in performing node selection based on network location.

Meridian is lightweight, scalable and accurate. Each Meridian node keeps track of a fixed number of peers and organizes them into concentric rings of exponentially increasing radii. A diverse node selection protocol is used in determining ring membership to maximize the marginal utility provided by each ring member. A query is matched against the relevant nodes in these rings, and optionally forwarded to a subset of the node's peers. Intuitively, the forwarding "zooms in" towards the solution space, handing off the query to a node that has more information to solve the problem due to the structure of the peer set. A scalable gossip protocol is used to notify other nodes of membership in the system. Meridian avoids incurring embedding errors by making no attempt to reconcile the latencies seen at participating nodes into a globally consistent coordinate space. Directly evaluating queries against relevant peers in each ring further reduces errors stemming from out of date coordinates.

In this paper, we focus on three commonly-encountered network positioning problems in distributed systems, and describe how the lightweight Meridian framework can be used to resolve them without computing virtual coordinates. The first, and most significant, problem is that of discovering the closest node to a targeted reference point. This is a basic operation in content distribution networks (CDNs), large-scale multiplayer games, and peer-to-peer overlays. Having the closest node serve the client or operate on the target can significantly reduce response time and aggregate network load. For instance, a geographically distributed peer-to-peer web crawler can reduce crawl time and minimize network load by delegating the crawl to the closest node to each target web server. Similarly, CDNs take network position into account when assigning clients to servers. And multiplayer games often perform a similar mapping from clients to nearby servers. In fact, the closest node discovery problem is so pervasive and so significant that we examine it in great detail. We also show that the Meridian framework can be used to find a node that offers minimal latencies to a given set of nodes. Intuitively, we want to select a node that is at the centerpoint of the region defined by the set members. This basic operation can be used, for instance, for location-aware leader election, where it would enable the chosen leader to minimize the average communication latency from the leader to set members. Such an operation can be used in tree construction for an application-level multicast system, where it can reduce transmission latencies by placing centrally-located nodes higher in the tree. Finally, we examine the problem of finding a set of nodes in a region whose boundaries are defined by latency constraints. For instance, given a set of latency constraints to well-known peering points, we show how Meridian can locate nodes in the region defined by the intersection of these constraints. This functionality is useful for ISPs and hosting services to cost effectively meet service-level agreements, for computational grids that can sell node clusters with specific inter-node latency requirements, and generally, for applications that require fine-grain selection of services based on latency to multiple targets.

We demonstrate through a theoretical analysis that our system provides robust performance, delivers high scalability and balances load evenly across the nodes. The analysis ensures that the performance of our system is not an artifact of our measurements.

We evaluate Meridian through simulation parameterized by a large-scale network measurement study, and through a deployment on PlanetLab. For our measurement study, we collected node-to-node round-trip latency measurements for 2500 nodes and 6.25 million node pairs on the Internet using the King measurement technique. We use 500 of these nodes as targets, and the remaining 2000 as the overlay nodes in our experiments.

Overall, this paper makes three contributions. First, it outlines a lightweight, scalable, and accurate system for keeping track of location-information for participating nodes. The system is simple, loosely-structured, and entails modest resources for maintenance. The paper shows how Meridian can efficiently find the closest node to a target, the latency minimizing node to a given set of nodes, and the set of nodes that lie in a region defined by latency constraints, frequently encountered building block operations in many location-sensitive distributed systems. Although less general than virtual coordinates, we show that Meridian incurs significantly less error. Second, the paper provides a theoretical analysis of our system that shows that Meridian provides robust performance, high scalability and good load balance. This analysis is general and applies to Internet latencies that cannot be accurately modeled with a Euclidean metric. Following a line of previous work on object location, we give guarantees for the family of growth-constrained metrics. Moreover, we support a much wider family of metrics of low doubling dimension which has recently become popular in the theoretical literature. Finally, the paper shows empirical results from both simulations using measurements from a large-scale network study and a PlanetLab deployment. The results confirm our theoretical analysis that Meridian is accurate, scalable, and load-balanced.
```
